chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: Yesterday I went down to the Piraeus with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, to offer my prayers to the goddess (Bendis, the Thracian Artemis); and I also wanted to see how they would celebrate the festival, since it was a new one. I was delighted with the procession put on by the locals, but the Thracians' procession was just as beautiful, if not more so. After we had finished our prayers and taken in the spectacle, we turned back toward the city. Just then, Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, happened to spot us from a distance as we were setting off home, and he told his servant to run ahead and ask us to wait for him. The servant caught hold of my cloak from behind and said, “Polemarchus wants you to wait.”
I turned around and asked him where his master was.
“There he is, coming along behind you,” the young man said, “if you'll just wait.”

“Of course we will,” said Glaucon. In a few minutes Polemarchus arrived, and with him came Adeimantus (Glaucon's brother), Niceratus the son of Nicias, and several others who had been at the procession.
Polemarchus said to me, “I can see, Socrates, that you and your friend are already on your way back to the city.”
“You're not wrong,” I said.
“But do you see,” he returned, “how many of us there are?”
“Of course.”
“And are you stronger than all of us put together? Because if not, you'll have to stay here.”
“Isn't there another option,” I said, “that we might persuade you to let us go?”
“But can you persuade us,” he said, “if we refuse to listen?”
“Certainly not,” Glaucon replied.
“Then we're not going to listen—you can count on that.”
Adeimantus added, “Hasn't anyone told you about the torch-race on horseback that's being held tonight in honour of the goddess?”
“On horseback!” I said. “That's something new. Will the riders carry torches and pass them to one another during the race?”

“Yes,” said Polemarchus, “and not only that—there'll be an all-night festival as well, which you really ought to see. Let's get up right after dinner and go watch; there'll be a gathering of young men, and we can have a good conversation. So stay, and don't be difficult.”
Glaucon said, “I suppose, since you insist, we'll have to.”
“Very well,” I replied.

So we went with Polemarchus to his house, where we found his brothers Lysias and Euthydemus, along with Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Charmantides of the deme of Paeania, and Cleitophon the son of Aristonymus. Cephalus, Polemarchus's father, was also there. I hadn't seen him for a long time, and I thought he had aged a great deal. He was sitting on a cushioned chair with a garland on his head, because he had just been offering sacrifices in the courtyard. There were other chairs arranged in a semicircle around him, and we sat down. He greeted me warmly and then said:

“Socrates, you don't come to see me as often as you ought. If I were still able to walk into town I wouldn't be asking you to come to me. But at my age I can barely get to the city anymore, and so you ought to come down to the Piraeus more often. Let me tell you something: the more the pleasures of the body fade, the greater my pleasure in good conversation. So don't refuse my request. Make our house your regular stop, and spend time with these young men. We're old friends, and you'll feel quite at home here.”

I replied, “There's nothing I like better, Cephalus, than talking with older men. I think of them as travellers who have already walked a road that I too may someday have to walk, and I like to ask them whether the way is smooth and easy or rough and hard. And here's a question I'd really like to ask you, since you've arrived at what the poets call the ‘threshold of old age’—is life harder at the end, or what is your report of it?”

“I'll tell you, Socrates, what my own experience is,” he said. “Men of my age tend to flock together—we're birds of a feather, as the old saying goes. At our gatherings, the usual complaint is: ‘I can't eat, I can't drink; the pleasures of youth and love are gone. Once there was a good time, but now it's over, and life is no longer life.’ Some complain about the slights they receive from their relatives and go on about all the ills old age has brought them. But to me, these people seem to blame what isn't really at fault. For if old age were the cause, I would feel the same way, and so would every other old man. But that hasn't been my own experience, nor that of others I've known. I remember the poet Sophocles being asked once, ‘How does love go with you now, Sophocles—are you still the man you were?’ And he answered, ‘Peace, man! I am only too glad to have escaped that, as from a mad and furious master.’ His words have often come back to me, and they seem as true now as when he said them. Old age has a great sense of calm and freedom. When the passions relax their hold, then, as Sophocles says, we are freed not from one mad master but from many. The truth, Socrates, is that these complaints, and the complaints about relatives, come down to the same cause—and the cause is not old age but a person's character and temperament. A person with a calm, happy nature will barely feel the pressure of age, but to someone of the opposite disposition, both youth and age are a burden.”

I listened with admiration and wanted to draw him out, so I said, “Yes, Cephalus, but I suspect that people in general aren't convinced when you talk this way. They think that old age sits lightly on you not because of your temperament but because you're rich—and wealth, everyone knows, is a great comforter.”

“You're right,” he replied. “They aren't convinced, and there's something in what they say—though not as much as they suppose. I could answer them the way Themistocles answered the man from Seriphos who was insulting him, saying that he was famous not for his own merits but because he was an Athenian. Themistocles said, ‘If you had been a Seriphian and I an Athenian, neither of us would have been famous.’ The same answer applies to those who aren't rich and find old age hard: a good man who is poor will not find old age easy, but a bad man who is rich can never find peace with himself either.”
“May I ask, Cephalus, whether you inherited most of your fortune or made it yourself?”

“Made it? Socrates, do you want to know how much I've made? In the art of making money, I fall midway between my grandfather and my father. My grandfather, whose name I bear, inherited about what I have now, and doubled and tripled it. My father Lysanias reduced the estate below its present value. For my part, I'll be satisfied if I leave these sons a little more than I received.”

“That's exactly why I asked the question,” I said. “I can see that you're indifferent about money, which is more typical of those who inherit fortunes than of those who make them. Self-made men have a double love of money: they love it as their own creation, the way poets love their poems or parents their children, in addition to the ordinary love of money for the uses it serves. This makes them very bad company—they can talk about nothing except the praises of wealth.”
“That's quite true,” he said.
“Yes, very true. But may I ask another question? What do you consider the greatest blessing that wealth has brought you?”

“One,” he said, “that I probably couldn't easily convince anyone else of. Let me tell you, Socrates: when a man comes to think himself near death, fears and anxieties start up in his mind that he never had before. The old tales about a world below and the punishments inflicted there for what was done up here, which he used to laugh at, now torment him with the thought that they might be true. Whether from the weakness of age, or because he is now closer to that other place, he sees these things more clearly. Suspicions and alarms crowd in upon him, and he begins to reflect on the wrongs he's done to others. If he finds that his transgressions add up to a great deal, he'll start up from his sleep like a frightened child, and he's filled with dark forebodings. But for a man who knows of no sin in himself, sweet hope, as Pindar charmingly says, is the kind nurse of his old age:”

“‘Hope,’ he says, ‘cherishes the soul of him who lives in justice and holiness, and is the nurse of his age and the companion of his journey—hope, which is mightiest to sway the restless soul of man.’”

“How admirable his words are! And here is the great blessing of wealth—not for every man, but for a good man: he has had no occasion to deceive or defraud others, whether intentionally or unintentionally. So when he goes down to the world below, he is not anxious about the offerings due to the gods or the debts he owes to men. Wealth contributes a great deal to this peace of mind. And so I say that, weighing one thing against another, of all the advantages wealth offers, this, to a man of sense, is the greatest.”

“Well said, Cephalus,” I replied. “But what about justice itself? Is it simply telling the truth and paying your debts—nothing more? And aren't there exceptions even to that? Suppose a friend, while he was in his right mind, left his weapons with me, and then asked for them back when he was out of his mind. Nobody would say I ought to return them, or that I'd be right to do so, any more than they'd say I ought always to tell the truth to someone in that state.”
“You're quite right,” he replied.
“So telling the truth and paying debts is not, after all, a correct definition of justice.”
“Quite right, Socrates—if Simonides is to be believed,” Polemarchus cut in.
“I'm afraid,” said Cephalus, “that I have to leave now, as I've got to look after the sacrifices. I'll hand over the argument to Polemarchus and the company.”
“Isn't Polemarchus your heir?” I said.
“Certainly,” he answered, and went off laughing to his sacrifices.
“Tell me then, heir of the argument,” I said, “what did Simonides say about justice that you think is right?”
“He said that paying back what one owes is just, and in saying so I think he's right.”

“I'd be reluctant to doubt the word of so wise and inspired a man, but his meaning—obvious to you, perhaps—escapes me. He clearly doesn't mean, as we were just saying, that I ought to return a deposit of weapons, or anything else, to someone who asks for it while out of his mind. And yet a deposit is certainly a debt.”
“True.”
So when the person who is asking me is not in his right mind, I ought by no means to return it to him?
“Certainly not.”
“When Simonides said that paying back a debt is justice, he didn't mean to include that case?”
“Certainly not; he thinks a friend should always do good to a friend, never evil.”
“So you think he means that returning a deposit of gold, if doing so would harm the receiver, is not what he means by ‘paying a debt,’ at least when the two parties are friends?”
“Yes.”
“And are enemies also to get what is owed them?”
“Absolutely,” he said. “They are to get what is owed them, and what an enemy owes an enemy is what is due and proper to him—that is, harm.”

“So Simonides, in the manner of poets, spoke darkly about the nature of justice. What he really meant was that justice consists in giving to each person what is proper to him, and this he called a ‘debt.’”
“That must have been his meaning.”
“By heaven!” I said. “And suppose we asked him: ‘What does medicine give, and to whom, as the ‘due or proper’ thing?’—what would he answer?”
“He would surely reply that medicine gives drugs, food, and drink to human bodies.”
“And what does cookery give, and to what?”
“Seasoning to food.”
“And what does justice give, and to whom?”
“If, Socrates, we are to follow the analogy of the earlier cases, then justice is the art of giving good to friends and evil to enemies.”
“So that's his meaning?”
“I think so.”
“Now, who is best at doing good to his friends and evil to his enemies in times of sickness?”
“A doctor.”
“And at sea, in the dangers of a voyage?”
“A pilot.”
“And in what situations, or with a view to what result, is the just man best able to harm his enemy and help his friend?”
“In making war against the one and in forming alliances with the other.”
“But when a man is well, my dear Polemarchus, there's no need for a doctor?”
“No.”
“And someone not on a voyage has no need for a pilot?”
“No.”
“So in peacetime, justice is of no use?”
“That's far from what I think.”
“You think justice is useful in peace as well as in war?”
“Yes.”
“Like farming for getting grain?”
“Yes.”
“Or shoemaking for getting shoes—that's what you mean?”
“Yes.”
“Then in what similar way is justice useful in peacetime?”
“In contracts, Socrates, justice is useful.”
“And by ‘contracts’ you mean partnerships?”
“Exactly.”
“But in a game of draughts, is the just man or the skilful player the more useful partner?”
“The skilful player.”
“And in laying bricks and stones, is the just man a better partner than the builder?”
“Quite the opposite.”
“Then in what kind of partnership is the just man a better partner than the harpist—since the harpist is certainly a better partner than the just man when it comes to playing the harp?”
“In a money partnership.”
“Yes, Polemarchus—but surely not in the use of money. You wouldn't want a just man to advise you about buying or selling a horse; someone who knows horses would be better for that, wouldn't he?”
“Certainly.”
“And when you want to buy a ship, the shipwright or the pilot would be better?”
“True.”
“Then in what joint use of silver or gold is the just man to be preferred?”
“When you want a deposit to be kept safe.”
“You mean when money isn't wanted for use, but just lies there?”
“Exactly.”
“So justice is useful when money is useless?”
“That's the inference.”
“And when you want to keep a pruning-hook safe, justice is useful both to the individual and to the state; but when you want to use it, then it's the vine-dresser's art?”
“Clearly.”
“And when you want to keep a shield or a lyre safe without using them, justice is useful; but when you want to use them, then the art of the soldier or musician takes over?”
“Certainly.”
“And so on for everything—justice is useful when things are useless, and useless when things are useful?”
“That's the inference.”
“Then justice isn't much good. But let's look at this further: isn't the man who is best at landing a blow in a boxing match, or any kind of fight, also best at warding off a blow?”
“Certainly.”
“And the person who is best at preventing or escaping from a disease is also best at producing one?”
“True.”
“And the best guard of a camp is the one best able to steal a march on the enemy?”
“Certainly.”
“So whoever is a good keeper of anything is also a good thief?”
“That seems to follow.”
“Then if the just man is good at keeping money, he's good at stealing it.”
“That's what the argument implies.”

“So the just man has turned out to be a thief! And this is a lesson you must have picked up from Homer. He, speaking of Autolycus, the maternal grandfather of Odysseus and one of his favourites, declares:”
“‘He was excellent above all men in theft and perjury.’”
“So you and Homer and Simonides all agree that justice is an art of theft—one to be practised ‘for the good of friends and the harm of enemies,’ as you were saying?”
“No, certainly not that,” he said, “though I don't know any longer what I did say; but I still stand by the latter words.”
“Well, here's another question: by ‘friends’ and ‘enemies,’ do we mean those who really are friends and enemies, or only those who seem to be?”
“Surely,” he said, “a man is likely to love those he thinks good and hate those he thinks evil.”
“Yes, but don't people often make mistakes about good and evil? Many who aren't good seem to be so, and the other way around?”
“That's true.”
“Then, for such people, the good will be enemies and the evil will be friends.” “True.”
“And in that case, they'll be right to do good to the evil and harm to the good?”
“Clearly.”
“But the good are just and would not do an injustice?”
“True.”
“So by your argument, it's just to injure those who do no wrong?”
“No, Socrates; that doctrine is immoral.”
“Then, I suppose, we should do good to the just and harm to the unjust?”
“I like that better.”

“But see the consequence: many people who don't understand human nature have friends who are in fact bad, and in that case they ought to do them harm; and they have good enemies whom they ought to benefit. If that's so, we'll be saying the very opposite of what we said Simonides meant.”
Very true, he said; and I think we had better correct an error into which we seem to have fallen in our use of the words ‘friend’ and ‘enemy.’
“What was the error, Polemarchus?” I asked.
“We assumed that a man is a friend if he seems to be good, or is thought good.”
“And how should we correct that?”

“We should rather say that a friend is one who both is and seems good, and that anyone who only seems good and is not really good only seems to be a friend but is not one. And the same applies to an enemy.”
“So you would say that the good are our friends and the bad our enemies?”
“Yes.”

“And instead of saying simply, as we did at first, that it's just to do good to our friends and harm to our enemies, we should now say: it's just to do good to our friends when they are good, and harm to our enemies when they are evil?”
“Yes, that appears to me to be the truth.”
“But should the just man injure anyone at all?”
“Undoubtedly he ought to injure those who are both wicked and his enemies.”
“When horses are injured, are they improved or made worse?”
“Made worse.”
“Made worse, that is, in the virtues proper to horses, not to dogs?”
“Yes, the virtues of horses.”
“And dogs are made worse in the virtues of dogs, not of horses?”
“Of course.”
“And won't men who are injured be made worse in what is the proper virtue of a man?”
“Certainly.”
“And that human virtue is justice?”
“To be sure.”
“Then men who are injured must necessarily become more unjust?”
“That's the result.”
“But can a musician, by his art, make men unmusical?”
“Certainly not.”
“Or a horseman, by his art, make men bad horsemen?”
“Impossible.”
“And can the just, by justice, make men unjust—or in general, can the good, by virtue, make men bad?”
“Certainly not.”
“Any more than heat can produce cold?”
“It cannot.”
“Or dryness produce moisture?”
“Clearly not.”
“Nor can the good harm anyone?”
“Impossible.”
“And the just is the good?”
“Certainly.”
“So to injure a friend, or anyone else, is not the act of a just man but of his opposite, the unjust?”
“I think what you say is quite true, Socrates.”

“So if a man says that justice consists in paying back debts, and that good is the debt the just man owes to his friends and evil the debt he owes to his enemies—he is not speaking wisely. For it is not true, since, as we have clearly shown, it is never just to injure another.”
“I agree,” said Polemarchus.
“Then you and I are ready to do battle with anyone who attributes such a saying to Simonides, or Bias, or Pittacus, or any other wise man or seer?”
“I am quite ready to fight at your side,” he said.
“Shall I tell you whom I believe the saying really belongs to?”
“Whom?”

“I think that Periander or Perdiccas, or Xerxes, or Ismenias the Theban, or some other rich and powerful man with a high opinion of his own power, was the first to say that justice is ‘doing good to your friends and harm to your enemies.’”
“Most true,” he said.
“Yes,” I said, “but if this definition of justice also breaks down, what other one can we offer?”

Several times during the discussion, Thrasymachus had tried to seize the argument, but each time the rest of the company had held him back; they wanted to hear the end. But when Polemarchus and I stopped talking and there was a pause, he could no longer keep quiet. Gathering himself up, he sprang at us like a wild beast looking to devour us. The whole company was panic-stricken at the sight of him.

He roared at the whole company: “What nonsense, Socrates, has got hold of you all? Why are you so foolishly giving in to one another? I tell you, if you really want to know what justice is, you shouldn't only ask but answer too. And you shouldn't try to win honour for yourself by simply refuting your opponent—you ought to have your own answer. Plenty of people can ask questions but can't answer them. Now I won't let you say that justice is duty, or advantage, or profit, or gain, or interest—this sort of nonsense won't do with me. I must have clarity and precision.”

I was panic-stricken by his words and couldn't look at him without trembling. In fact, I believe that if I hadn't fixed my eye on him, I would have been struck dumb. But when I saw his fury rising, I looked at him first and was therefore able to reply.

“Thrasymachus,” I said, with a quiver, “don't be so hard on us. If Polemarchus and I have made some small mistake in the argument, I assure you it wasn't intentional. If we were looking for a piece of gold, you wouldn't imagine that we were ‘giving in to each other’ and so losing our chance of finding it. Why then, when we're looking for justice, which is more precious than any amount of gold, do you say we're weakly yielding to each other and not doing our utmost to get at the truth? My good friend, we are most willing and anxious to do so, but the fact is we can't. And if so, you people who know everything ought to pity us, not be angry with us.”

“How like Socrates!” he replied, with a bitter laugh. “That's your ironical style. Didn't I foresee—haven't I already told you—that whatever he was asked he'd refuse to answer, and try irony or any other dodge to avoid answering?”

“You're a philosopher, Thrasymachus,” I replied, “and you know perfectly well that if you ask someone what numbers make up twelve, and forbid him to answer ‘twice six,’ or ‘three times four,’ or ‘six times two,’ or ‘four times three,’ because ‘this sort of nonsense won't do’—then obviously, if that's your way of putting the question, no one can answer you. But suppose he retorted, ‘Thrasymachus, what do you mean? If one of these forbidden numbers is the true answer, am I to give some other number that isn't the right one? Is that your point?’ How would you reply to him?”
“As if the two cases were at all alike!” he said.
“Why shouldn't they be?” I replied. “And even if they aren't, but only seem so to the person being asked, shouldn't he say what he thinks, whether you and I forbid him or not?”
“So you're going to give one of the forbidden answers?”
“I dare say I may, notwithstanding the danger, if on reflection I approve of any of them.”
“But what if I give you a different answer about justice, better than any of these?” he said. “What do you think you deserve to have done to you?”
“Done to me?—What the ignorant deserve: I must learn from the wise. That is what I deserve.”
“What—and no payment! A charming idea!”
“I'll pay when I have the money,” I replied.
“But you have it, Socrates,” said Glaucon; “and you, Thrasymachus, needn't worry about money—we'll all chip in for Socrates.”
“Yes,” he said, “and then Socrates will do what he always does: refuse to answer himself, but take someone else's answer and pull it to pieces.”

“Why, my good friend,” I said, “how can anyone answer who knows, and admits he knows, just nothing—and who, even if he has some faint ideas of his own, is told by a man of authority not to utter them? It's more natural that the speaker should be someone like yourself who claims to know and can tell what he knows. So will you kindly answer, for the company's sake and mine?”

Glaucon and the rest joined in my request, and Thrasymachus, as anyone could see, was in reality eager to speak. He thought he had an excellent answer and would distinguish himself. But at first he affected to insist that I should answer. Finally he consented to begin. “Behold,” he said, “the wisdom of Socrates! He refuses to teach, but goes around learning from others—and never even says ‘thank you.’”

“That I learn from others is quite true,” I replied, “but that I am ungrateful I totally deny. Money I have none, and so I pay in praise, which is all I have. How ready I am to praise anyone who seems to me to speak well, you'll very soon find out when you answer; for I expect you'll answer well.”
“Listen, then,” he said. “I declare that justice is nothing other than the interest of the stronger. Now why don't you praise me? But of course you won't.”

“Let me first understand you,” I replied. “Justice, you say, is the interest of the stronger. What, Thrasymachus, do you mean by this? Surely you don't mean that, because Polydamas the pancratiast is stronger than we are, and finds that eating beef is good for his physical strength, eating beef is therefore equally good for us who are weaker, and right and just for us?”
“That's disgusting of you, Socrates; you take my words in the sense most damaging to the argument.”
“Not at all, my good sir,” I said; “I'm trying to understand them, and I wish you would be a little clearer.”
Well, he said, have you never heard that forms of government differ from one another? There are tyrannies, and there are democracies, and there are aristocracies.
“Yes, I know.”
“And in each state, the government is the ruling power?”
“Certainly.”

“And the different forms of government make laws—democratic, aristocratic, tyrannical—each with a view to its own interest. And these laws, made by each government for its own interest, are the justice they hand down to their subjects, and anyone who breaks them they punish as a lawbreaker and an unjust person. This, then, is what I mean when I say that in every state the same principle of justice applies: it is the interest of the government. And since the government has the power, the only reasonable conclusion is that, everywhere, there is one principle of justice—the interest of the stronger.”

“Now I understand you,” I said. “Whether you are right or not, I'll try to find out. But let me point out that in defining justice, you yourself used the word ‘interest,’ which you forbade me to use. True, you added the words ‘of the stronger.’”
“A small addition, you must admit.”

“Great or small, never mind: we must first enquire whether what you are saying is true. We both agree that justice is some kind of interest, but you add ‘of the stronger’; about this addition I am not so sure, and so I must investigate further.”
“Proceed.”
“I will. And first tell me: do you grant that it is just for subjects to obey their rulers?”
“I do.”
“But are the rulers of states absolutely infallible, or are they sometimes liable to err?”
“To be sure,” he replied, “they are liable to err.”
“So in making their laws, they may sometimes make them rightly, and sometimes not?”
“True.”
“When they make them rightly, they make them agreeably to their own interest; when they go wrong, contrary to their interest. You admit that?”
“Yes.”
“And the laws they make must be obeyed by their subjects—and that's what you call justice?”
“No doubt.”
“So by your argument, justice is not only obedience to the interest of the stronger but also the reverse?”
“What are you saying?” he asked.

“I'm only repeating what you said, I believe. Let me reconsider: haven't we admitted that rulers may be mistaken about their own interest in what they command, and that to obey them is justice? Hasn't that been admitted?”
“Yes.”

“Then you must also have acknowledged that justice is not for the interest of the stronger, when rulers unintentionally command things that harm themselves. For if, as you say, justice is the obedience a subject renders to the commands of the stronger, then, O wisest of men, is there any escape from the conclusion that the weaker are commanded to do, not what is in the interest of the stronger, but what is to his harm?”
“Nothing could be clearer, Socrates,” said Polemarchus.
“Yes,” said Cleitophon, breaking in, “if you're allowed to be his witness.”

“But there's no need for any witness,” said Polemarchus, “because Thrasymachus himself admits that rulers may sometimes command what is not in their own interest, and that it is just for subjects to obey them.”
“Yes, Polemarchus—Thrasymachus did say that for subjects to do what their rulers command is just.”

“Yes, Cleitophon, but he also said that justice is the interest of the stronger. Having admitted both these propositions, he further acknowledged that the stronger may command the weaker who are his subjects to do what is not in his own interest. From which it follows that justice is just as much the injury as the interest of the stronger.”
“But,” said Cleitophon, “what he meant by ‘the interest of the stronger’ was what the stronger thought to be his interest—that's what the weaker had to do. That was what he called justice.”
“Those were not his words,” retorted Polemarchus.

“Never mind,” I replied. “If he now says that's what they were, let us accept his statement. Tell me, Thrasymachus: did you mean by justice what the stronger thought to be his interest, whether it really was so or not?”
“Certainly not,” he said. “Do you suppose I call the stronger the one who is mistaken, at the moment he is mistaken?”
“Yes,” I said; “my impression was that you did, when you admitted that the ruler was not infallible but might sometimes be mistaken.”

“You argue like a lawyer's informer, Socrates. Do you mean, for example, that someone who is mistaken about the sick counts as a physician in that he is mistaken? Or that someone who errs in arithmetic or grammar is an arithmetician or grammarian at the very moment of making the mistake, in respect of the mistake? True, we say that the physician, or arithmetician, or grammarian has made a mistake, but that is only a way of speaking; the fact is that neither the grammarian nor anyone else with skill ever makes a mistake insofar as he is what his name implies. None of them errs unless his skill fails him, and when his skill fails, he ceases to be a skilled craftsman. No craftsman, sage, or ruler errs at the time when he is what his name implies, though we commonly say that he does, and I adopted that common way of speaking. But to be perfectly precise—since you are such a lover of precision—we should say that the ruler, insofar as he is a ruler, is unerring; and being unerring, he always commands what is in his own interest. The subject is required to carry out his commands. So, as I said at first and now repeat, justice is the interest of the stronger.”
“So, Thrasymachus, do I really seem to you to argue like an informer?”
“Certainly,” he replied.
“And do you suppose I ask these questions with any design of damaging you in the argument?”
“No,” he replied, “‘suppose’ is not the word—I know it. But you won't succeed; you'll be found out, and by sheer force of argument you will never prevail.”

“I won't even try, my dear fellow. But to avoid any further misunderstandings, let me ask: in what sense are you using the word ‘ruler’ or ‘stronger,’ whose interest, as you said, it is just for the weaker to serve? Are you speaking of a ruler in the popular sense or the strict sense?”
“In the strictest possible sense,” he said. “Now cheat and play the informer if you can—I ask for no quarter. But you never will be able.”
“And do you imagine,” I said, “that I'm mad enough to try and cheat you, Thrasymachus? I might as well try to shave a lion.”
“Why, you just tried it a minute ago, and you failed.”

“Enough of these pleasantries,” I said. “Better I should ask you a question. Is the physician, taken in that strict sense you speak of, a healer of the sick or a maker of money? Remember, I'm now speaking of the true physician.”
“A healer of the sick,” he replied.
“And the pilot—the true pilot—is he a captain of sailors or just a sailor?”
“A captain of sailors.”

“The fact that he sails on the ship doesn't count; nor should he be called a sailor. The title ‘pilot,’ which distinguishes him, has nothing to do with sailing—it refers to his skill and his authority over the sailors.”
“Very true,” he said.
“Now,” I said, “every art has an interest?”
“Certainly.”
“Which the art has to consider and provide for?”
“Yes, that's what the art aims at.”
“And the interest of any art is its own perfection—this and nothing else?”
“What do you mean?”

“I mean what I can illustrate negatively by the example of the body. Suppose you were to ask me whether the body is self-sufficient or has needs; I would answer, ‘Certainly the body has needs; for the body can be ill and in need of healing, and so has interests that the art of medicine serves; this is the origin and purpose of medicine.’ Am I right?”
“Quite right,” he replied.

“But does the art of medicine, or any other art, have any fault or deficiency in itself—the way the eye may be deficient in sight, or the ear fail at hearing, and so need another art to provide for the interests of seeing and hearing? Has art, I ask, any similar liability to fault or defect? Does every art need another supplementary art to serve its interests, and that another, and another, without end? Or do the arts only need to look after their own interests? Or do they need neither themselves nor any other art to look after them—having no faults or defects, they have nothing to correct, either through their own art or through any other; they need only consider the interests of their subject-matter. For every art remains pure and faultless as long as it remains true—that is, as long as it is perfect and unimpaired. Take the words in your precise sense, and tell me whether I'm right.”
“Yes, clearly.”
“So medicine does not consider the interest of medicine, but the interest of the body?”
“True,” he said.

“And the art of horsemanship doesn't consider the interests of the art of horsemanship, but the interests of the horse; and the other arts don't care for themselves, because they have no needs; they care only for their subject-matter?”
“True,” he said.
“But surely, Thrasymachus, the arts are the superiors and rulers of their own subjects?”
To this he assented with a great deal of reluctance.
“So,” I said, “no science or art considers or enjoins the interest of the stronger or superior, but only the interest of the subject and weaker?”
He tried to contest this proposition as well, but finally gave in.

“Then,” I continued, “no physician, insofar as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient. The true physician is also a ruler, with the human body as his subject, and he is not a mere money-maker—that's been admitted?”
“Yes.”
“And the pilot likewise, in the strict sense of the word, is a ruler of sailors and not just a sailor?”
“That has been admitted.”
“And such a pilot and ruler will provide for and prescribe for the interest of the sailor under him, and not for his own or the ruler's?”
He reluctantly said yes.

“So, Thrasymachus,” I said, “no one in any kind of rule, insofar as he is a ruler, considers or enjoins what is in his own interest; he always aims at what is in the interest of his subject, or suitable to his art. That is what he looks to, and that alone he considers in everything he says and does.”

When we had reached this point in the argument and everyone saw that the definition of justice had been completely overturned, Thrasymachus, instead of replying to me, said, “Tell me, Socrates, have you got a nurse?”
“Why do you ask such a question?” I said. “You ought rather to be answering mine.”
“Because she lets you snivel, and never wipes your nose; she hasn't even taught you to tell the shepherd from the sheep.”
“What makes you say that?” I replied.

“Because you fancy that the shepherd or cowherd fattens and tends the sheep or oxen with a view to their own good and not to the good of himself or his master; and you further imagine that rulers of states, if they are true rulers, don't think of their subjects as sheep, and aren't studying their own advantage day and night. You are so totally off track in your ideas about the just and the unjust that you don't even realize that justice and the just are in reality another person's good—the interest of the ruler and stronger—and the loss of the subject and servant; and that injustice is the opposite: the unjust is master over the truly simple and just. He is the stronger, and his subjects do what is in his interest and serve his happiness, which is very far from being their own. Consider further, most foolish Socrates, that the just is always a loser compared to the unjust. First, in private contracts: wherever an unjust man is the partner of a just one, you'll find that when the partnership is dissolved, the unjust one always has more and the just less. Second, in dealings with the State: when there is an income-tax, the just man pays more and the unjust less on the same income; and when there's something to be received, the one gets nothing and the other gets much. Watch also what happens when they hold office: the just man neglects his own affairs, possibly suffers other losses, gets nothing out of the public (because he is just), and is even hated by his friends and acquaintances because he refuses to serve them in unlawful ways. But all this is reversed in the case of the unjust man. I'm speaking, as before, of injustice on a large scale, where the advantage of the unjust is most obvious. My meaning will be clearest if we turn to the highest form of injustice—tyranny—in which the criminal is the happiest of men, and the sufferers, and those who refuse to do injustice, are the most miserable. Tyranny takes away others' property by fraud and force, not bit by bit but wholesale, sweeping up both sacred and profane, private and public. For any one of these wrongs committed singly, a man would be punished and disgraced—such people are called temple-robbers, kidnappers, burglars, swindlers, and thieves. But when a man, in addition to taking the citizens' money, has enslaved them, instead of these reproachful names he is called happy and blessed—and not only by his fellow citizens but by everyone who hears he has achieved the consummation of injustice. Mankind censures injustice fearing that they may become its victims, not because they shrink from committing it. And thus, as I've shown, Socrates, injustice, on a sufficient scale, has more strength, freedom, and mastery than justice; and, as I said at first, justice is the interest of the stronger, whereas injustice is a man's own profit and interest.”

When Thrasymachus had said this, having, like a bath-man, deluged our ears with his torrent of words, he intended to go away. But the company wouldn't let him; they insisted that he stay and defend his position. I also added my own humble request that he not leave us. “Thrasymachus,” I said to him, “my excellent man, how suggestive your remarks are! Are you going to run off before you have properly taught or learned whether they are true? Is the attempt to determine the way of human life such a small matter in your eyes—to determine how life may be lived by each of us to the greatest advantage?”
“And do I differ from you,” he said, “on the importance of the enquiry?”

“You seem rather,” I replied, “to have no care or thought about us, Thrasymachus. Whether we live better or worse from not knowing what you claim to know is a matter of indifference to you. Come, friend, do not keep your knowledge to yourself; we are a large party, and any benefit you confer on us will be richly repaid. For my own part, I openly declare that I am not convinced, and that I do not believe injustice is more profitable than justice, even when uncontrolled and allowed free rein. Granted that there might be an unjust man able to commit injustice by fraud or force, still this does not convince me of the superior advantage of injustice; and there may be others in the same state as me. Perhaps we are wrong; and if so, you, in your wisdom, should convince us that we are mistaken in preferring justice to injustice.”
“And how am I to convince you,” he said, “if you're not already convinced by what I've just said? What more can I do for you? Would you have me put the proof bodily into your souls?”

“Heaven forbid!” I said. “I would only ask you to be consistent—or, if you change, change openly and without deception. For I must point out, Thrasymachus, if you recall what was said earlier, that although you began by defining the true physician in an exact sense, you were not so exact when speaking of the shepherd. You thought that the shepherd, as shepherd, tends his sheep not with a view to their own good but like a mere diner or banqueter—for the pleasures of the table—or like a trader taking them to market; not as a shepherd. Yet surely the art of the shepherd is concerned only with the good of his flock; he only needs to provide the best for them, since the perfection of the art is already ensured whenever all its requirements are met. And that was what I was saying about the ruler. I conceived that the art of the ruler, considered as ruler, whether in a state or in private life, could only have regard for the good of his flock or subjects; whereas you seem to think that the rulers in states—that is, the true rulers—like being in authority.”
“Think! No, I am sure of it.”

“Then why, in the case of lesser offices, do men never take them willingly without payment, unless they believe that they govern for the advantage not of themselves but of others? Let me ask you a question: aren't the various arts different because each has a separate function? And, my illustrious friend, do tell me what you think, so we can make a little progress.”
“Yes, that's the difference,” he replied.
“And each art provides us with a particular good, not just a general one—medicine gives us health, navigation gives us safety at sea, and so on?”
“Yes,” he said.

“And the art of earning wages has the special function of providing wages; but we don't confuse it with other arts, any more than we confuse the art of the pilot with the art of medicine just because the pilot's health may improve on a sea voyage. You wouldn't say, would you, that navigation is the art of medicine, at least if we're going to adopt your exact use of language?”
“Certainly not.”
“Or, because a man is in good health when he receives his wages, you wouldn't say that the art of wage-earning is medicine?”
“No.”
“Nor would you say that medicine is the art of receiving wages because a man takes fees while engaged in healing?”
“Certainly not.”
“And we've admitted that the good each art gives is specific to that art?”
“Yes.”
“Then if there is any good that all craftsmen share in common, it must be attributed to something of which they all make common use?”
“True,” he replied.
“And when a craftsman benefits by receiving wages, the advantage comes from an additional use of the art of wage-earning, not from the art he practises?”
He reluctantly assented.

“So wages are not derived by the several craftsmen from their respective arts. The truth is that while the art of medicine gives health, and the art of the builder builds a house, another art attends them—the art of wage-earning. The various arts may be doing their own work and benefiting what they preside over, but would the craftsman derive any benefit from his art unless he were paid as well?”
“I suppose not.”
“But does he therefore confer no benefit when he works for nothing?”
“Of course, he does confer a benefit.”

“So now, Thrasymachus, there is no longer any doubt that neither arts nor governments provide for their own interests; but, as we were saying, they rule and provide for the interests of their subjects, who are the weaker, not the stronger. They attend to their subjects' good, not to that of the superior. And that, my dear Thrasymachus, is the reason, as I was just saying, why no one is willing to govern: because no one wants to take on the task of correcting other people's evils without being paid. The true craftsman, in carrying out his work and giving orders to another, doesn't aim at his own interest but always at his subjects'; and so, for rulers to be willing to rule, they must be paid in one of three ways: money, honour, or a penalty for refusing.”
“What do you mean, Socrates?” said Glaucon. “I understand the first two forms of payment well enough, but what penalty are you talking about? How can a penalty be a payment?”

“You mean,” I said, “that you don't understand the nature of this payment, which is the great inducement for the best men to rule? Of course you know that ambition and avarice are thought to be, and indeed are, a disgrace?”
“Very true.”

“So,” I said, “money and honour have no attraction for them; good men do not wish to be seen openly demanding payment for governing and earning the name of hirelings, nor do they want to take it secretly out of the public funds and earn the name of thieves. And since they are not ambitious, they do not care about honour. So necessity must be laid upon them, and they must be induced to serve by fear of punishment. That, I take it, is why a forwardness to take office, instead of waiting to be compelled, has been considered dishonourable. The worst part of the punishment is that anyone who refuses to rule is liable to be ruled by someone worse than himself. Fear of this, I think, is what induces good men to take office—not because they want to, but because they can't help it; not with any idea that they'll get any benefit or enjoyment from it, but as a necessity, because they are not able to commit the task of ruling to anyone better than themselves, or even as good. For there is reason to think that if a city were composed entirely of good men, avoiding office would be as much of a contest as seeking it is now. Then we would have clear proof that the true ruler is not meant by nature to regard his own interest, but the interest of his subjects; and everyone who knew this would rather receive a benefit from another than have the trouble of conferring one himself. So I am far from agreeing with Thrasymachus that justice is the interest of the stronger. This point we don't need to pursue further now. But when Thrasymachus says that the life of the unjust is more advantageous than that of the just, his new statement seems to me far more serious. Which of us, Glaucon, has spoken the truth? And which kind of life do you prefer?”
“For my part,” he answered, “I deem the life of the just the more advantageous.”
“Did you hear all the advantages Thrasymachus attributed to the unjust just now?”
“Yes, I heard him,” he replied, “but he hasn't convinced me.”
“Then shall we try to find some way, if we can, of convincing him that he is saying what is not true?”
“By all means,” he replied.

“Now if he makes a set speech and we make another, listing all the advantages of being just, and then he replies and we respond, we'll have to count and measure the goods each side claims, and in the end we'll need judges to decide. But if we go on as we've been doing, by making admissions to one another, we'll combine the roles of judge and advocate in ourselves.”
“Very good,” he said.
“And which method would you prefer?” I asked.
“The one you're proposing.”
“Well, then, Thrasymachus,” I said, “suppose you begin at the beginning and answer me. You say that perfect injustice is more profitable than perfect justice?”
“Yes, that is what I say, and I have given you my reasons.”
“And what is your view of them? Would you call one of them virtue and the other vice?”
“Certainly.”
“I suppose you'd call justice virtue and injustice vice?”
“What a charming notion! Very likely, seeing that I affirm injustice to be profitable and justice not.”
“Then what would you say?”
“The opposite,” he replied.
“And you'd call justice vice?”
“No, I'd rather say sublime simplicity.”
“Then would you call injustice malignity?”
“No; rather, discretion.”
“And do the unjust seem to you to be wise and good?”

“Yes,” he said, “at least those of them who can be perfectly unjust and who have the power to subdue states and nations. Perhaps you imagine me to be talking about cutpurses. Even that profession, if undetected, has advantages—though they are not to be compared with those I was just describing.”
“I don't think I misunderstand you, Thrasymachus,” I replied, “but I can't help being amazed when you classify injustice with wisdom and virtue, and justice with their opposite.”
“Yes, that is how I classify them.”

“Now,” I said, “you are on more substantial and almost unanswerable ground; for if you had admitted, as others do, that the injustice you maintain to be profitable was vice and deformity, we could have answered you on accepted principles. But as it is, I see that you'll call injustice honourable and strong, and that you'll attribute to the unjust all the qualities we before attributed to the just, since you don't hesitate to rank injustice with wisdom and virtue.”
“You have guessed most correctly,” he replied.

“Then I certainly ought not to shrink from pursuing the argument, as long as I have reason to think that you, Thrasymachus, are speaking your real mind. For I do believe that you are now in earnest and not merely amusing yourself at our expense.”
“Whether I am in earnest or not, what is that to you? Your job is to refute the argument.”
“Very true,” I said; “that is what I have to do. But will you be so good as to answer one more question? Does the just man try to gain any advantage over another just man?”
“Far from it; if he did he wouldn't be the simple, amusing creature he is.”
“And would he try to go beyond just action?”
“He would not.”
“And how would he regard the attempt to gain an advantage over the unjust? Would he consider it just or unjust?”
“He would consider it just and would try to gain the advantage; but he wouldn't be able to.”

“Whether he would or wouldn't be able is not the point. My question is only whether the just man, while refusing to have more than another just man, would wish and claim to have more than the unjust?”
“Yes, he would.”
“And what about the unjust? Does he claim to have more than the just man and to do more than is just?”
“Of course,” he said, “for he claims to have more than everyone.”
“And the unjust man will strive and struggle to obtain more than the unjust man, or action, so that he may have more than all?”
“True.”
“We may put it like this, then,” I said: “the just man does not desire more than his like, but more than his unlike; whereas the unjust desires more than both his like and his unlike?”
“Nothing,” he said, “could be better than that statement.”
“And the unjust is good and wise, and the just is neither?”
“Good again,” he said.
“And is not the unjust like the wise and good, and the just unlike them?”
“Of course,” he said, “the one who is of a certain nature is like those of that nature; the one who is not, is not.”
“Each of them, then, is such as those he resembles?”
“Certainly,” he replied.
“Very well, Thrasymachus,” I said. “Now to the case of the arts: you'd admit that one man is a musician and another is not?”
“Yes.”
“And which is wise and which is foolish?”
“Clearly the musician is wise, and the non-musician is foolish.”
“And he is good insofar as he is wise, and bad insofar as he is foolish?”
“Yes.”
“And you'd say the same of the physician?”
“Yes.”
“And do you think, my excellent friend, that a musician, when tuning a lyre, would desire or claim to exceed another musician in tightening or loosening the strings?”
“I don't think so.”
“But he would claim to exceed the non-musician?”
“Of course.”
“And what would you say of the physician? In prescribing food and drink, would he wish to go beyond another physician, or beyond the practice of medicine?”
“He would not.”
“But he would wish to go beyond the non-physician?”
“Yes.”

“And about knowledge and ignorance in general—see whether you think that anyone who has knowledge would wish to say or do more than another man who has knowledge in the same case. Wouldn't he rather say or do the same as his like in the same case?”
“That, I suppose, can hardly be denied.”
“And what of the ignorant man? Wouldn't he desire to have more than either the knowing or the ignorant?”
“I dare say.”
“And the knowing is wise?”
“Yes.”
“And the wise is good?”
“True.”
“Then the wise and good will not desire to gain more than his like, but more than his unlike and opposite?”
“I suppose so.”
“Whereas the bad and ignorant will desire to gain more than both?”
“Yes.”
“But didn't we say, Thrasymachus, that the unjust goes beyond both his like and his unlike? Weren't those your words?”
“They were.”
“And you also said that the just will not go beyond his like, but his unlike?”
“Yes.”
“Then the just is like the wise and good, and the unjust is like the evil and ignorant?”
“That is the inference.”
“And each of them is such as those he resembles?”
“That was admitted.”
“Then the just has turned out to be wise and good, and the unjust evil and ignorant.”

Thrasymachus made all these admissions—not fluently, as I'm repeating them, but with great reluctance. It was a hot summer's day, and the sweat poured off him in torrents. And then I saw what I had never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. Since we had now agreed that justice was virtue and wisdom, and injustice vice and ignorance, I moved on to another point.
“Well, Thrasymachus,” I said, “that matter is settled. But weren't we also saying that injustice had strength? Do you remember?”

“Yes, I remember,” he said; “but don't suppose that I approve of what you're saying or have no answer. If I were to answer, you'd be sure to accuse me of making a speech. So either let me say my piece in full, or, if you prefer to ask questions, go ahead and I'll answer ‘Very good,’ as one does to old women telling stories, and nod ‘Yes’ and ‘No.’”
“Certainly not,” I said, “if it's contrary to your real opinion.”
“Yes,” he said, “I will—to please you, since you won't let me speak. What else do you want?”
“Nothing in the world,” I said; “and if you're so disposed, I'll ask and you shall answer.”
“Proceed.”

“Then I'll repeat the question I asked before, so our examination of the relative nature of justice and injustice may go on in order. A claim was made that injustice is stronger and more powerful than justice; but now that justice has been identified with wisdom and virtue, it is easily shown to be stronger than injustice, since injustice is ignorance. This no one can any longer question. But I want to look at the matter from a different angle, Thrasymachus. You would not deny that a state may be unjust and may be unjustly attempting to enslave other states, or may have already enslaved them and be holding many of them in subjection?”
“True,” he replied; “and I would add that the best and most perfectly unjust state is the one most likely to do so.”

“I know,” I said, “that that was your position. But what I want to consider next is whether this power, which the superior state possesses, can exist and be exercised without justice, or only with it.”
“If you're right in your view, and justice is wisdom, then only with justice; but if I am right, then without it.”
“I'm delighted, Thrasymachus, to see you not only nodding assent and dissent, but giving excellent answers.”
“That is out of courtesy to you,” he replied.

“You are very kind,” I said. “And would you have the goodness to tell me whether a state, or an army, or a band of robbers and thieves, or any other gang of wrongdoers, could act at all if they injured one another?”
“No indeed,” he said, “they could not.”
“But if they abstained from injuring one another, they could act together better?”
“Yes.”
“And this is because injustice creates divisions, hatred, and fighting, while justice produces harmony and friendship—isn't that so, Thrasymachus?”
“I agree,” he said, “because I do not wish to quarrel with you.”

“How good of you,” I said. “But I'd also like to know whether injustice, having this tendency to stir up hatred wherever it exists—among slaves or among free men—will not set them at variance with one another and with the just, and make them incapable of common action?”
“Certainly.”
“And even if injustice is found in only two, will they not quarrel and fight and become enemies to one another and to the just?”
“They will.”
“And suppose injustice is found in a single person: would your wisdom say that she loses her natural power or that she retains it?”
“Let us assume that she retains her power.”

“Isn't the power injustice exercises of such a nature that wherever she takes up residence—in a city, in an army, in a family, or in any other body—that body is first of all rendered incapable of united action by reason of sedition and distraction; and doesn't it become its own enemy, at variance with all that opposes it, and with the just? Isn't this the case?”
“Yes, certainly.”

“And isn't injustice equally fatal when it exists in a single person: in the first place, rendering him incapable of action because he is not at unity with himself, and in the second place, making him an enemy to himself and to the just? Isn't that true, Thrasymachus?”
“Yes.”
“And surely, my friend, the gods are just?”
“Granted that they are.”
“But if so, the unjust will be the gods' enemies, and the just their friends?”
“Feast away in triumph, and take your fill of the argument; I won't oppose you, for fear of displeasing the company.”

“Well then, proceed with your answers, and let me finish my meal. For we have already shown that the just are clearly wiser and better and abler than the unjust, and that the unjust are incapable of common action. What's more, to speak as we did of evil men acting at any time vigorously together is not strictly true; for if they had been perfectly evil, they would have fallen upon one another. Evidently there must have been some remnant of justice in them that allowed them to combine; if there had not been, they would have injured one another as well as their victims. They were only half-villains in their enterprises; had they been whole villains, utterly unjust, they would have been utterly incapable of action. That, I believe, is the truth of the matter, not what you said at first. But whether the just have a better and happier life than the unjust is a further question we proposed to consider. I think they do, and for the reasons I have given; but I'd still like to look into it further, for no small matter is at stake here—nothing less than the conduct of human life.”
“Proceed.”
“I will proceed by asking a question: wouldn't you say that a horse has some end?”
“I should.”
“And the end or function of a horse, or of anything, would be that which cannot be accomplished, or not as well accomplished, by anything else?”
“I don't understand,” he said.
“Let me explain. Can you see except with the eye?”
“Certainly not.”
“Or hear except with the ear?”
“No.”
“These, then, may truly be called the ends of these organs?”
“They may.”
“But you can cut off a vine-branch with a dagger or a chisel, and in many other ways?”
“Of course.”
“And yet not as well as with a pruning-hook made for the purpose?”
“True.”
“May we not say, then, that this is the end of a pruning-hook?”
“We may.”
“Then now I think you'll have no difficulty understanding my earlier question, whether the end of anything is what cannot be accomplished, or not as well accomplished, by anything else?”
“I understand your meaning,” he said, “and I assent.”
“And whatever has an end also has an excellence? Need I ask whether the eye has an end?”
“It has.”
“And does the eye have an excellence?”
“Yes.”
“And the ear has an end and an excellence too?”
“True.”
“And the same is true of all other things—they each have an end and a special excellence?”
“That is so.”
“Well, can the eyes fulfil their end if they lack their own proper excellence and have a defect instead?”
“How can they,” he said, “if they are blind and cannot see?”

“You mean, if they have lost their proper excellence, which is sight. But I haven't got to that point yet. I'd rather ask the question more generally, and only enquire whether the things that fulfil their ends do so by their own proper excellence, and fail of fulfilling them by their own defect?”
“Certainly,” he replied.
“I might say the same of the ears—when deprived of their proper excellence, they cannot fulfil their end?”
“True.”
“And the same observation applies to all other things?”
“I agree.”

“Now, does not the soul have an end that nothing else can fulfil? For example, to superintend and command and deliberate and the like. Are not these functions proper to the soul, and can they rightly be assigned to anything else?”
“To nothing else.”
“And is not life to be counted among the ends of the soul?”
“Assuredly,” he said.
“And has not the soul an excellence too?”
“Yes.”
“And can it fulfil its own ends when deprived of that excellence, or not?”
“It cannot.”
“So an evil soul must necessarily be an evil ruler and superintendent, and the good soul a good ruler?”
“Yes, necessarily.”
“And we have admitted that justice is the excellence of the soul, and injustice the defect of the soul?”
“That has been admitted.”
“Then the just soul and the just man will live well, and the unjust will live badly?”
“That is what your argument proves.”
“And he who lives well is blessed and happy, and he who lives badly the reverse?”
“Certainly.”
“Then the just is happy, and the unjust miserable?”
“So be it.”
“But happiness, not misery, is profitable.”
“Of course.”
“Then, my blessed Thrasymachus, injustice can never be more profitable than justice.”
“Let this, Socrates,” he said, “be your entertainment at the Bendidea.”

“For which I thank you,” I said, “now that you have grown gentle with me and left off scolding. Still, I have not been well entertained—though that was my own fault, not yours. Like an epicure who snatches a taste of every dish brought to the table, not giving himself time to enjoy the one before, so I have jumped from one subject to another without having discovered what I was looking for at first: the nature of justice. I abandoned that enquiry and turned to consider whether justice is virtue and wisdom, or evil and folly. Then, when a further question arose about the comparative advantages of justice and injustice, I could not help moving on to that too. And the result of the whole discussion is that I know nothing at all. For I do not know what justice is, and therefore I am not likely to know whether it is or is not a virtue, nor can I say whether the just man is happy or unhappy.”

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: With these words, I thought I had brought the discussion to an end; but the end, as it turned out, was only a beginning. Glaucon, who is always the most pugnacious of men, was dissatisfied with Thrasymachus's retreat; he wanted to fight the battle out. So he said to me: “Socrates, do you wish really to persuade us, or only to seem to have persuaded us, that being just is always better than being unjust?”
“I'd wish really to persuade you,” I replied, “if I could.”

“Then you certainly haven't succeeded. Let me ask you now: how would you classify goods? Aren't there some that we welcome for their own sake, quite apart from their consequences—for example, harmless pleasures and enjoyments that delight us at the time, though nothing else follows from them?”
“I agree there is such a class,” I replied.
“And isn't there also a second class of goods—such as knowledge, sight, health—that are desirable both in themselves and for their results?”
“Certainly,” I said.

“And wouldn't you recognize a third class too, such as gymnastic exercise, the care of the sick, and the physician's art; also the various ways of making money—these do us good but we regard them as disagreeable, and no one would choose them for their own sake, but only for some reward or result that comes from them?”
“Yes,” I said, “there's this third class also. But why do you ask?”
“Because I want to know in which of the three classes you would place justice.”
“In the highest class,” I replied, “among those goods that someone who means to be happy desires both for their own sake and for the sake of their results.”

“Then the many disagree; they think justice belongs in the troublesome class, among goods pursued for the sake of rewards and reputation but which are, in themselves, disagreeable and rather to be avoided.”

“I know,” I said, “that this is how they think, and that this is the thesis Thrasymachus was maintaining just now when he censured justice and praised injustice. But I am too slow to be convinced by him.”

“I wish,” he said, “that you would hear me out as well, and then I'll see whether you and I agree. For Thrasymachus seems to me, like a snake, to have been charmed by your voice sooner than he should have been; but to my mind the nature of justice and injustice has not yet been made clear. Setting aside their rewards and results, I want to know what they are in themselves, and how they inwardly work in the soul. So, if you please, I'll revive Thrasymachus's argument. First I will speak of the nature and origin of justice according to the common view. Second, I'll show that everyone who practises justice does so against their will, by necessity, not as a good. Third, I'll argue that there is reason in this view, because the life of the unjust is far better than the life of the just—if what they say is true, Socrates, for I myself am not of their opinion. But still I'm perplexed when I hear the voices of Thrasymachus and countless others din in my ears; on the other hand, I have never yet heard the superiority of justice over injustice maintained by anyone in a satisfactory way. I want to hear justice praised for its own sake; then I shall be satisfied, and you are the person from whom I think I'm most likely to hear it. So I'll praise the unjust life to the utmost of my power, and my manner of speaking will indicate the manner in which I want to hear you praise justice and censure injustice. Will you tell me whether you approve of my proposal?”
“Indeed I do; nor can I imagine any theme about which a man of sense would more often wish to converse.”
“I am delighted,” he replied, “to hear you say so, and I'll begin, as I proposed, by speaking of the nature and origin of justice.”

“They say that to do injustice is, by nature, a good; to suffer injustice, an evil; but the evil of suffering it is greater than the good of doing it. So when men have both done and suffered injustice, and have had experience of both, they find that they can't avoid the one and obtain the other, so they conclude that they had better agree among themselves to have neither. Hence arise laws and mutual covenants, and what is ordained by law they call ‘lawful’ and ‘just.’ This, they say, is the origin and nature of justice: it is a mean or compromise between the best—doing injustice and not being punished—and the worst—suffering injustice without the power to retaliate. Justice, being midway between the two, is tolerated not as a good but as the lesser evil, and honoured only because men are unable to do injustice. No real man, they say, would ever submit to such an agreement if he could resist; he would be mad to do so. Such is the received account, Socrates, of the nature and origin of justice.”

“Now, that those who practise justice do so involuntarily, because they lack the power to be unjust, will best appear if we imagine something like this. Suppose we gave both the just and the unjust man the power to do whatever he liked; let us then watch and see where his desire would lead him. We would find the just and the unjust man proceeding along the same road, following his own interest, which every nature takes to be its good, and is only diverted into the path of justice by the force of law. The clearest form of such liberty would be the power said to have been possessed by Gyges, the ancestor of Croesus the Lydian. According to the story, Gyges was a shepherd in the service of the king of Lydia. There was a great storm, and an earthquake opened a chasm in the earth where he was feeding his flock. Amazed at the sight, he descended into the opening, where, among other marvels, he saw a hollow bronze horse with doors in it. Stooping to look inside, he saw a corpse of stature more than human, wearing nothing but a gold ring. He took the ring from the dead man's finger and climbed back up. The shepherds met together, as was their custom, to send their monthly report about the flocks to the king; Gyges came to their gathering wearing the ring. While sitting among them, he happened to turn the setting of the ring inside his hand, and instantly he became invisible to the others; they began to speak of him as though he were no longer present. He was astonished at this, and touching the ring again he turned the setting outward and reappeared. He made several trials of the ring, always with the same result: when he turned the setting inward, he became invisible; when outward, he reappeared. Whereupon he arranged to be chosen as one of the messengers sent to the king's court; as soon as he arrived, he seduced the queen, conspired with her against the king and killed him, and took the kingdom. Now suppose there were two such magic rings, and the just man put on one and the unjust the other. No one, we may be sure, would be so strong-willed as to stand firm in justice. No one would keep his hands off what wasn't his own when he could safely take what he wanted from the market, or go into houses and sleep with anyone he pleased, or kill or free from prison whomever he wished—in every respect acting like a god among men. The actions of the just would be identical with the actions of the unjust; both would come, in the end, to the same point. And this, we may truly affirm, is great proof that a man is just not willingly, not because he believes that justice is any good to him individually, but from necessity—for wherever anyone thinks he can safely be unjust, there he is unjust. Every man believes in his heart that injustice is far more profitable to the individual than justice, and anyone who argues as I have been will say that they are right. If someone who had acquired this power of invisibility never did any wrong or touched what was another's, onlookers would think him a most pitiable fool, although they would praise him to each other's faces, keeping up appearances out of fear that they themselves might suffer injustice. So much for that.”

“Now, if we're to form a real judgment about the lives of the just and the unjust, we must isolate them; there's no other way. How is this isolation to be achieved? I answer: let the unjust man be entirely unjust, and the just man entirely just; nothing is to be taken from either, and both are to be perfectly furnished for the work of their respective lives. First, let the unjust man be like other masters of a craft—like the skilful pilot or physician, who knows instinctively his own powers and keeps within their limits, and who, if he fails at any point, is able to recover. So let the unjust man make his unjust attempts in the right way, and stay hidden if he means to be great in his injustice (the man who is found out is nothing); the highest pitch of injustice is to be thought just when you are not. So let us assume in the perfectly unjust man the most perfect injustice; there is to be no deduction, but we must allow him, while doing the most unjust acts, to have acquired the greatest reputation for justice. If he makes a false step, he must be able to recover; he must be able to speak effectively if any of his deeds come to light, and to force his way through where force is required, by his courage and strength, command of money and of friends. Beside him, let us place the just man, in his nobleness and simplicity, wishing, as Aeschylus says, to be and not merely to seem good. There must be no seeming; for if he seems just, he will be honoured and rewarded, and then we won't know whether he is just for the sake of justice or for the sake of honours and rewards. So let him be clothed in justice only, and have no other covering; and he must be imagined in a state of life the opposite of the other's. Let him be the best of men but be thought the worst; then he will be put to the proof, and we will see whether he can withstand the fear of infamy and its consequences. Let him continue this way until the hour of his death: being just and seeming unjust. When both have reached the uttermost extreme—the one of justice, the other of injustice—let judgment be given which of them is the happier.”
“Heavens, my dear Glaucon!” I said. “How energetically you polish them up for the decision—first one, then the other—as if they were two statues.”

“I do my best,” he said. “And now that we know what they are like, there's no difficulty in tracing out the sort of life that awaits each. This I'll now describe; and since you may find the description a little too coarse, I'll ask you, Socrates, to imagine that the words that follow are not mine. Let me put them in the mouths of the eulogists of injustice. They will tell you that the just man who is thought unjust will be scourged, racked, bound, have his eyes burnt out; and finally, after suffering every kind of evil, he will be impaled. Then he will realize that he ought only to seem just, not really to be so. The words of Aeschylus may more truly be spoken of the unjust than of the just. For the unjust man pursues a reality; he does not live for appearances. He wants to be really unjust, not merely to seem so—”
“‘His mind has a soil deep and fertile, Out of which spring his prudent counsels.’”

“In the first place, he is thought just, and so he rules in the city; he can marry whomever he wishes, give in marriage to whomever he wishes; he can trade and deal where he likes, always to his own advantage, because he has no scruples about injustice. In every contest, public or private, he gets the better of his opponents and gains at their expense, and so grows rich; out of his gains he can benefit his friends and harm his enemies. He can also offer sacrifices and dedicate offerings to the gods abundantly and magnificently, and honour the gods, or any man he wants to honour, in a far better style than the just man can. And so, Socrates, gods and men are said to unite in making the life of the unjust better than the life of the just.”
I was about to answer Glaucon when Adeimantus, his brother, broke in. “Socrates,” he said, “you don't imagine that there's nothing more to be said?”
“Why, what else is there?” I answered.
“The strongest point of all hasn't even been mentioned,” he replied.

“Well then,” I said, “as the proverb goes, ‘Let brother help brother’—if Glaucon has left anything out, do you assist him. And yet I must confess that what he has already said is quite enough to lay me in the dust and take from me the power of helping justice.”

“Nonsense,” he replied. “But let me add something more. There's another side to Glaucon's argument about the praise and censure of justice and injustice that is equally required to bring out what I believe to be the truth. Parents and tutors are always telling their sons and their wards to be just; but why? Not for the sake of justice itself, but for the sake of character and reputation; in the hope of obtaining, for the one with a reputation for justice, some of those offices, marriages, and other advantages that Glaucon has listed as accruing to the unjust from a reputation of justice. This sort of person makes even more of appearances than the others, for they throw in the good opinion of the gods as well, and tell of the shower of benefits that the heavens, as they say, rain down on the pious. This is in keeping with the noble testimony of Hesiod and Homer; the former says that the gods make the oaks of the just men—”
“‘To bear acorns at their summit, and bees in the middle; And the sheep are bowed down with the weight of their fleeces,’”
“and many other such blessings are provided for them. Homer has a very similar strain, for he says of one whose fame is—”

“‘As the fame of some blameless king who, like a god, Maintains justice; to whom the black earth brings forth Wheat and barley, whose trees are bowed with fruit, And his sheep never fail to bear, and the sea gives him fish.’”

“Still grander are the gifts of heaven that Musaeus and his son vouchsafe to the just; they take them down into the world below, where they have the saints reclining on couches at a feast, everlastingly drunk, crowned with garlands. Their idea seems to be that an immortality of drunkenness is the highest reward of virtue. Some extend their rewards even further: the posterity, they say, of the faithful and just shall survive to the third and fourth generation. This is the style in which they praise justice. But about the wicked there is a different strain: they bury them in a slough in Hades, and make them carry water in a sieve; and while they are still alive they bring them to infamy, and inflict upon them the punishments Glaucon described as the portion of the just who are thought to be unjust. Nothing else does their invention supply. Such is their manner of praising the one and censuring the other.”

“Once more, Socrates, I'll ask you to consider another way of speaking about justice and injustice, which is not confined to the poets but is also found in prose writers. The universal voice of mankind is always declaring that justice and virtue are honourable, but painful and toilsome, while the pleasures of vice and injustice are easily obtained, and censured only by law and opinion. They say also that honesty is, for the most part, less profitable than dishonesty; and they are quite ready to call wicked men happy, and to honour them in public and private, when they are rich or otherwise influential, while they despise and overlook those who are weak and poor, even though acknowledging them to be better than the others. But most extraordinary of all is their way of speaking about virtue and the gods: they say the gods apportion calamity and misery to many good men, and good and happiness to the wicked. Mendicant prophets go to rich men's doors and persuade them that they have, committed to them by the gods, the power to atone for a man's own or his ancestor's sins with sacrifices and charms, rejoicings and feasts; they promise to harm an enemy, whether just or unjust, at a small cost, with magic arts and incantations, binding heaven, as they say, to execute their will. And the poets are the authorities to whom they appeal, now smoothing the path of vice with the words of Hesiod—”
“‘Vice may be had in abundance without trouble; the way is smooth and her dwelling-place is near. But before virtue the gods have set toil,’”
“and a tedious, uphill road; then citing Homer as a witness that the gods may be influenced by men. For he too says:—”

“‘The gods, too, may be turned from their purpose; and men pray to them and avert their wrath by sacrifices and soothing entreaties, and by libations and the odour of fat, when they have sinned and transgressed.’”

“And they produce a host of books by Musaeus and Orpheus, who were (they say) children of the Moon and the Muses, according to which they perform their rituals; and they persuade not only individuals but whole cities that expiation and atonement for sin can be made by sacrifices and amusements that fill a spare hour, and are equally at the service of the living and the dead. These latter they call ‘mysteries,’ and they redeem us from the pains of hell; but if we neglect them, no one knows what awaits us.”
