He went on: “Now when the young hear all this being said about virtue and vice, and the way gods and men regard them, how are their minds likely to be affected, my dear Socrates—those of them, I mean, who are quick-witted and, like bees on the wing, alight on every flower, and from all they hear are prone to draw conclusions about what sort of person they should be and what path to walk if they want to make the best of life? The youth will probably say to himself, in the words of Pindar—”
“‘Can I by justice or by crooked ways of deceit ascend a loftier tower which may be a fortress to me all my days?’”

“For what men say is: if I am really just and am not also thought just, there's no profit; only pain and loss—that's plain. But if, though unjust, I acquire the reputation of justice, a heavenly life is promised to me. Since then, as philosophers prove, appearance tyrannizes over truth and is the lord of happiness, it is to appearance I must devote myself. I will paint around myself a picture and shadow of virtue to be the vestibule and outside of my house; behind it I will trail the subtle and crafty fox, as Archilochus, greatest of sages, recommends. But someone may object, ‘The concealment of wickedness is often difficult.’ To which I answer: nothing great is easy. Yet the argument shows that this is the path along which we should go, if we wish to be happy. With a view to concealment, we will establish secret brotherhoods and political clubs. And there are professors of rhetoric who teach the art of persuading courts and assemblies; so, partly by persuasion and partly by force, I shall make unlawful gains and escape punishment. Still, I hear a voice saying that the gods cannot be deceived, nor can they be compelled. But what if there are no gods? Or suppose they take no care about human affairs—why should we mind about concealment? Even if there are gods, and they do care about us, we know them only from tradition and the poets' genealogies; and these are the very persons who say that the gods can be influenced and turned by ‘sacrifices and soothing entreaties and by offerings.’ Let us be consistent, then, and believe both or neither. If the poets speak truly, we had better be unjust, and offer of the fruits of injustice; for if we are just, although we may escape heaven's vengeance, we shall lose the gains of injustice. But if we are unjust, we keep the gains, and by our sinning and praying, and praying and sinning, the gods will be appeased, and we shall not be punished. ‘But there is a world below in which either we or our posterity will suffer for our unjust deeds.’ ‘Yes, my friend’ (such will be the reflection), ‘but there are mysteries and atoning deities, and these have great power.’ That is what mighty cities declare; and the children of the gods, who were their poets and prophets, bear the same witness.”

“On what principle, then, shall we any longer choose justice rather than the worst injustice?—when, if we unite the latter with a deceitful regard for appearances, we shall fare to our heart's content with gods and men alike, in life and after death, as the most numerous and highest authorities tell us. Knowing all this, Socrates, how can any man of superior mind, body, rank, or wealth be willing to honour justice? Or even to refrain from laughing when he hears justice praised? And even if someone is able to disprove the truth of my words, and is satisfied that justice is best, still he is not angry with the unjust but very ready to forgive them, because he also knows that men are not just of their own free will—unless perhaps some divinity within him has inspired him with a hatred of injustice, or he has attained knowledge of the truth; but no other man. Only he blames injustice who, because of cowardice or age or some other weakness, lacks the power to be unjust himself. This is proved by the fact that when he does get the power, he immediately becomes unjust as far as he can.”

“The cause of all this, Socrates, was indicated at the start of the argument, when my brother and I told you how astonished we were to find that of all the professing panegyrists of justice—from the ancient heroes whose memory has been preserved to the men of our own time—not one has ever blamed injustice or praised justice except with a view to the glories, honours, and benefits that flow from them. No one has ever adequately described, either in verse or prose, the true and essential nature of either of them, as it abides in the soul, invisible to any human or divine eye; or shown that of all the things a man has within his soul, justice is the greatest good and injustice the greatest evil. Had this been the universal strain, and had you tried to persuade us of it from youth upwards, we would not now be watching each other to prevent wrongdoing; every man would be his own watchman, afraid that, if he did wrong, he would be harbouring within himself the greatest of evils. I dare say Thrasymachus and others would seriously hold the language I have merely been repeating, and words even stronger than these about justice and injustice—grossly, I believe, perverting their true nature. But I speak with this vehemence—I must frankly confess—because I want to hear from you the opposite side. I ask you to show not only the superiority of justice over injustice, but what effect each has on the possessor that makes the one a good and the other an evil to him. And please, as Glaucon requested, exclude reputations. Unless you take from each man his true reputation and add on the false, we shall say that you are not praising justice but only the appearance of it; we'll think you are only exhorting us to keep injustice dark, and that you really agree with Thrasymachus that justice is another's good and the interest of the stronger, and that injustice is a man's own profit and interest, though injurious to the weaker. Now, since you have admitted that justice is one of that highest class of goods, which are desired indeed for their results but to a far greater extent for their own sakes—like sight, hearing, knowledge, or health, or any other real and natural and not merely conventional good—I would ask you, in your praise of justice, to consider one point only: I mean the essential good and evil that justice and injustice work in the possessors of them. Let others praise justice and censure injustice, magnifying the rewards and honours of the one and the penalties of the other; that sort of argument, coming from them, I can tolerate; but from you, who have spent your whole life considering this question, unless I hear the contrary from your own lips, I expect something better. So I say: not only prove to us that justice is better than injustice, but show what each does to the soul of its possessor that makes the one a good and the other an evil, whether seen or unseen by gods and men.”

I had always admired the genius of Glaucon and Adeimantus, but on hearing these words I was more delighted still, and said: “Sons of an illustrious father, the admirer of Glaucon began his elegiac verses in honour of you, after you distinguished yourselves at the battle of Megara, not badly, when he wrote—”
“‘Sons of Ariston,’ he sang, ‘divine offspring of an illustrious hero.’”

“The epithet is very apt, for there is something truly divine in being able to argue, as you have done, for the superiority of injustice, and in remaining unconvinced by your own arguments. I do believe that you are not convinced—I infer this from your general character, for had I judged only by your speeches I would have mistrusted you. But now, the greater my confidence in you, the greater my difficulty in knowing what to say. I'm caught between two things: on the one hand, I feel I'm unequal to the task; and my inadequacy is brought home by the fact that you were not satisfied with the answer I gave to Thrasymachus, in which, I thought, I proved the superiority of justice over injustice. And yet I cannot refuse to help, while breath and speech remain to me; I fear it would be impious to be present while justice is slandered and not lift a hand in her defence. So I had better give what help I can.”

Glaucon and the rest earnestly begged me not to let the question drop, but to go on with the enquiry. They wanted to arrive at the truth, first about the nature of justice and injustice, and second about their relative advantages. I told them what I really thought: that the enquiry would be a serious one, requiring very good eyes. “Seeing, then,” I said, “that we are not great wits, I think we had better adopt a method I can illustrate as follows. Suppose a short-sighted person had been asked to read small letters from a distance, and it occurred to someone else that the same letters might be found elsewhere in a larger size and in a larger place—if they were identical, and he could read the larger ones first and then move on to the smaller ones—that would have been thought a great piece of luck.”
“Very true,” said Adeimantus. “But how does the illustration apply to our enquiry?”
“I'll tell you,” I replied. “Justice, which is the subject of our enquiry, is, as you know, sometimes spoken of as the virtue of an individual, and sometimes as the virtue of a State.”
“True,” he replied.
“And isn't a State larger than an individual?”
“It is.”

“Then in the larger thing, the quantity of justice is likely to be larger and more easily seen. I propose, therefore, that we enquire into the nature of justice and injustice, first as they appear in the State, and then in the individual, going from the greater to the lesser, and comparing them.”
“That,” he said, “is an excellent proposal.”
“And if we imagine the State in the process of being created, we shall see the justice and injustice of the State also being created.”
“I dare say.”
“When the State is completed, there is hope that the object of our search will be more easily found.”
“Yes, far more easily.”
“But should we attempt to construct one?” I said. “Doing so, I am inclined to think, will be a very serious task. Think it over.”
“I have thought it over,” said Adeimantus, “and am eager for you to proceed.”
“A State,” I said, “arises, in my view, out of the needs of mankind: no one is self-sufficient, but all of us have many wants. Can any other origin of a State be imagined?”
“There can be no other.”

“Then, since we have many needs, and many people are required to supply them, one takes a helper for one purpose, another for another; and when these partners and helpers are gathered together into one habitation, the body of inhabitants is called a State.”
“True,” he said.
“And they exchange with one another—one gives, another receives—under the idea that the exchange will be to their mutual good.”
“Very true.”
“Then,” I said, “let us begin and create, in thought, a State; and yet the true creator is necessity, who is the mother of our invention.”
“Of course,” he replied.
“Now the first and greatest of necessities is food, which is the condition of life and existence.”
“Certainly.”
“The second is a dwelling, and the third is clothing and the like.”
“True.”

“Let us see, then, how our city will be able to supply this great demand. We may suppose that one man is a farmer, another a builder, someone else a weaver—shall we add to them a shoemaker, or perhaps some other purveyor to our bodily needs?”
“Quite right.”
“The barest notion of a State must include four or five men.”
“Clearly.”

“And how will they proceed? Will each bring the result of his labour into a common stock—the farmer, for example, producing for four, and labouring four times as long and as much as he needs in providing food, which he supplies to the others as well as to himself? Or will he have nothing to do with the others, and not trouble himself to produce for them, but provide for himself alone, a fourth of the food in a fourth of the time, and in the remaining three-quarters of his time be employed making a house, or a coat, or a pair of shoes, having no partnership with others, but supplying himself with all his own needs?”
Adeimantus thought that he should aim at producing food only, and not try to produce everything.

“Probably,” I replied, “that would be the better way. And when I hear you say this, I am myself reminded that we are not all alike; there are differences of nature among us, and these fit us for different occupations.”
“Very true.”
“And will a work be better done when the workman has many occupations, or when he has only one?”
“When he has only one.”
“Further, there can be no doubt that a work is spoilt when it is not done at the right time?”
“No doubt.”
“For business is not disposed to wait for the one doing it to have leisure; the doer must follow up what he is doing, and make the business his first object.”
“He must.”

“And if so, we must infer that everything is produced more plentifully, more easily, and of better quality when one man does one thing that suits his nature, and does it at the right time, and leaves other things to others.”
“Undoubtedly.”

“Then more than four citizens will be required, for the farmer will not make his own plough or mattock or other farming tools, if they are to be any good. Neither will the builder make his own tools—and he too needs many. And similarly with the weaver and shoemaker.”
“True.”
“So carpenters and smiths and many other artisans will be partners in our little State, which is already beginning to grow?”
“True.”

“Yet even if we add cowherds, shepherds, and other herdsmen, so that our farmers may have oxen to plough with, and builders as well as farmers may have draught animals, and curriers and weavers can have fleeces and hides, still our State will not be very large.”
“That is true; yet it won't be a very small State either, if it contains all these.”
“Then, again, there's the location of the city—to find a place where nothing needs to be imported is well-nigh impossible.”
“Impossible.”
“So there must be another class of citizens who bring the required supplies from another city?”
“There must.”
“But if the trader goes empty-handed, having nothing the other city needs, he'll come back empty-handed.”
“That is certain.”
“Therefore, what they produce at home must be not only enough for themselves, but also enough in quantity and quality to accommodate those from whom they obtain their own supplies.”
“Very true.”
“So more farmers and more artisans will be required?”
“They will.”
“Not to mention the importers and exporters, called merchants?”
“Yes.”
“So we shall need merchants?”
“We shall.”
“And if the goods are to be carried over the sea, we'll also need skilled sailors, and in considerable numbers?”
“Yes, in considerable numbers.”
“Then again, within the city, how will they exchange their products? Securing such exchange was, as you'll remember, one of our main objects in forming a society and establishing a State.”
“Clearly they'll buy and sell.”
“Then they'll need a marketplace, and a money-token for purposes of exchange.”
“Certainly.”
“Suppose now that a farmer, or an artisan, brings something to market, and arrives at a time when no one is there to exchange with him: is he to abandon his calling and sit idle in the marketplace?”

“Not at all; he will find people there who, seeing the need, take on the role of salesmen. In well-ordered states these are typically the weakest in physical strength, and therefore of little use for any other purpose; their duty is to stay in the market, giving money in exchange for goods to those who want to sell and taking money from those who want to buy.”

“This need, then, creates a class of retail traders in our State. Isn't ‘retailer’ the term for those who sit in the marketplace buying and selling, while those who travel from city to city are called merchants?”
“Yes,” he said.

“And there's another class of servants who are hardly intellectually our equals, but have plenty of bodily strength for labour, which they accordingly sell—they are called, if I am not mistaken, hirelings, ‘hire’ being the name given to the price of their labour.”
“True.”
“Then hirelings will also make up part of our population?”
“Yes.”
“And now, Adeimantus, is our State matured and complete?”
“I think so.”
“Where, then, is justice, and where injustice, and in what part of the State did they arise?”
“Probably in the dealings of these citizens with one another. I can't imagine they would more likely be found anywhere else.”
“I dare say you're right,” I said. “We had better think the matter through and not shrink from the enquiry.”

“Let us consider, first of all, what their way of life will be now that we have established them. Won't they produce corn, wine, clothes, and shoes, and build houses? And when they're housed, in summer they'll mostly work stripped and barefoot, but in winter substantially clothed and shod. They will feed on barley-meal and wheat flour, baking and kneading it, making noble cakes and loaves; these they'll serve up on a mat of reeds or on clean leaves, reclining themselves on beds strewn with yew or myrtle. And they and their children will feast, drinking the wine they have made, wearing garlands on their heads, singing the praises of the gods, in happy conversation with one another. They'll take care that their families don't exceed their means, keeping an eye on poverty and war.”
“But,” said Glaucon, breaking in, “you haven't given them a relish for their meal.”

“True,” I replied, “I forgot; of course they must have a relish—salt, olives, cheese, and they'll boil roots and herbs as country people do. For a dessert we shall give them figs, peas, and beans; and they'll roast myrtle-berries and acorns at the fire, drinking in moderation. With such a diet they may be expected to live in peace and health to a good old age, and leave a similar life to their children after them.”
“Yes, Socrates,” he said, “and if you were providing for a city of pigs, how else would you feed the beasts?”
“But what would you have, Glaucon?” I replied.

“Why,” he said, “you should give them the ordinary conveniences of life. People who mean to be comfortable are accustomed to reclining on couches and dining off tables, and they should have sauces and sweets, the way we have them now.”

“Yes,” I said, “now I understand. The question you'd have me consider is not only how a State is created, but how a luxurious State is created; and perhaps there's no harm in this, for in such a State we shall be more likely to see how justice and injustice arise. In my opinion, the true and healthy constitution of the State is the one I have described. But if you want to see a State in a fever of luxury, I have no objection. For I suspect that many will not be satisfied with the simpler way of life. They will want to add sofas and tables and other furniture, as well as dainties, perfumes, incense, courtesans, and cakes—all of these, not of one sort only, but in every variety. We must go beyond the necessities of which I was first speaking, such as houses, clothes, and shoes; the arts of the painter and embroiderer will have to be set in motion, and gold, ivory, and all sorts of materials must be procured.”
“True,” he said.

“Then we must enlarge our borders, for the original healthy State is no longer adequate. The city will have to fill up and swell with a multitude of callings not required by any natural need—such as the whole tribe of hunters and actors, of whom one large class is concerned with forms and colours, another with the votaries of music—poets and their entourage of rhapsodists, players, dancers, contractors; also makers of various kinds of articles, including women's dresses. We'll also need more servants. Won't tutors also be wanted, and wet-nurses and dry-nurses, tirewomen and barbers, as well as confectioners and cooks? And swineherds too, who were not needed, and therefore had no place, in the earlier version of our State, but are needed now. They mustn't be forgotten. And there will be animals of many other kinds, if people eat them.”
“Certainly.”
“And living this way, we'll have much greater need of physicians than before?”
“Much greater.”
“And the country that was enough to support the original inhabitants will now be too small, and no longer sufficient?”
“Quite true.”

“Then we'll want a slice of our neighbours' land for pasture and tillage, and they'll want a slice of ours—if, like ourselves, they exceed the limits of necessity and give themselves up to the unlimited accumulation of wealth?”
“That, Socrates, will be inevitable.”
“So we shall go to war, Glaucon. Shall we not?”
“Most certainly,” he replied.

“Then, without deciding yet whether war does good or harm, we may at least say that we have now discovered war to derive from causes that are also the causes of almost all the evils in States, private as well as public.”
“Undoubtedly.”

“And our State must once more enlarge; and this time the enlargement will be nothing short of a whole army, to go out and fight the invaders for all we have, as well as for the things and persons we were describing above.”
“Why?” he said. “Aren't they capable of defending themselves?”
“No,” I said, “not if we were right in the principle all of us acknowledged when we were framing the State—the principle, as you'll remember, that one man cannot practise many arts well.”
“Very true,” he said.
“But isn't war an art?”
“Certainly.”
“And an art requiring as much attention as shoemaking?”
“Quite true.”

“And the shoemaker was not allowed by us to be a farmer, or a weaver, or a builder—in order that we might have our shoes well made; but to him and to every other worker was assigned one task, the one he was by nature fitted for, and he was to continue at it all his life long and at nothing else. He was not to let opportunities slip, and in that way he would become a good workman. Now nothing could be more important than that the work of a soldier should be well done. But is war an art so easily learned that a man can be a warrior and also a farmer, a shoemaker, or some other artisan—although no one in the world would be a good dice or draughts player who merely took up the game as a recreation and had not devoted himself to it, and it alone, from his earliest years? No tools will make a man a skilled workman or master of defence, nor will they be of any use to someone who has not learned how to handle them and has never given them any attention. How, then, can a man who takes up a shield or other implement of war become a good fighter in a day, whether in heavy armour or any other kind of troops?”
“Yes,” he said; “the tools that would teach men their own use would be beyond price.”
“And the higher the duties of the guardian,” I said, “the more time, skill, art, and application he'll need?”
“No doubt,” he replied.
“Won't he also require a natural aptitude for his calling?”
“Certainly.”
“So it will be our task to select, if we can, natures fitted for guarding the city?”
“It will.”
“And the selection will be no easy matter,” I said; “but we must be brave and do our best.”
“We must.”
“Isn't the noble youth very like a well-bred dog in respect of guarding and watching?”
“What do you mean?”
“I mean that both ought to be quick to see, and swift to overtake the enemy when they do; and strong too, if, when they have caught him, they have to fight with him.”
“All these qualities,” he replied, “will certainly be required by them.”
“Well, and your guardian must be brave, if he's to fight well?”
“Certainly.”

“And is he likely to be brave who has no spirit—whether horse or dog or any other animal? Have you never noticed how invincible and unconquerable spirit is, and how, when it is present, it makes the soul of any creature absolutely fearless and indomitable?”
“I have.”
“So we now have a clear notion of the bodily qualities required in a guardian.”
“True.”
“And the mental qualities too—his soul must be full of spirit?”
“Yes.”
“But aren't such spirited natures apt to be savage with one another, and with everyone else?”
“A difficulty by no means easy to overcome,” he replied.
“Whereas,” I said, “they ought to be dangerous to their enemies and gentle to their friends; otherwise they'll destroy themselves without waiting for their enemies to destroy them.”
“True,” he said.
“What's to be done, then?” I said. “How shall we find a gentle nature that also has a great spirit, since the one is the contradiction of the other?”
“True.”
“He won't be a good guardian if he lacks either of these two qualities; and yet the combination of them seems impossible; and so we must infer that a good guardian is impossible.”
“I'm afraid what you say is true,” he replied.
Feeling perplexed, I began to think back over what had been said. “My friend,” I said, “no wonder we're in a perplexity, for we have lost sight of the image we had before us.”
“What do you mean?” he said.
“I mean to say that there do exist natures gifted with those opposite qualities.”
“And where do you find them?”

“Many animals provide examples,” I replied. “Our friend the dog is a very good one; you know that well-bred dogs are perfectly gentle to their familiars and acquaintances, and the reverse to strangers.”
“Yes, I know.”
Then there is nothing impossible or contrary to nature in our finding a guardian who has a similar combination of opposite qualities?
“Certainly not.”
“Wouldn't the one fit to be a guardian, besides the spirited nature, also need the qualities of a philosopher?”
“I don't quite understand your meaning.”
“The trait I'm speaking of,” I replied, “may also be seen in the dog, and it is a remarkable trait in the animal.”
“What trait?”

“Well, a dog, whenever he sees a stranger, is angry; when he sees someone he knows, he welcomes him—even though the stranger has never done him any harm, and the acquaintance has never done him any good. Did that never strike you as curious?”
“The matter never struck me before; but I quite recognise the truth of your remark.”
“And surely this instinct of the dog is very charming—your dog is a true philosopher.”
“Why?”

“Why, because he distinguishes the face of a friend and of an enemy only by the test of knowing or not knowing. And must not an animal be a lover of learning who determines what he likes and dislikes by the test of knowledge and ignorance?”
“Most assuredly.”
“And isn't the love of learning the love of wisdom, which is philosophy?”
“They are the same,” he replied.
“And may we not say, confidently, of man as well, that he who is likely to be gentle to his friends and acquaintances must by nature be a lover of wisdom and knowledge?”
“That we may safely affirm.”
“Then a really good and noble guardian of the State will need to unite in himself philosophy, spirit, swiftness, and strength?”
“Undoubtedly.”

“So we have found the desired natures; and now that we have found them, how are they to be reared and educated? Isn't this an enquiry that may throw light on the greater enquiry, which is our final end—how do justice and injustice grow up in States? We don't want to omit anything relevant or draw the argument out inconveniently long.”
Adeimantus thought the enquiry would be of great service to us.
“Then,” I said, “my dear friend, the task must not be given up, even if somewhat long.”
“Certainly not.”
“Come then, let us pass a leisure hour in story-telling, and our story shall be the education of our heroes.”
“By all means.”
“And what shall their education be? Can we find a better one than the traditional sort?—and this has two divisions: gymnastic for the body, and music for the soul.”
“True.”
“Shall we begin education with music, and go on to gymnastic afterwards?”
“By all means.”
“And when you speak of music, do you include literature or not?”
“I do.”
“And literature may be either true or false?”
“Yes.”
“And the young should be trained in both kinds—and we begin with the false?”
“I don't understand your meaning,” he said.

“You know,” I said, “that we begin by telling children stories which, though not wholly without truth, are in the main fictitious; and these stories are told to them before they are of an age to learn gymnastics.”
“Very true.”
“That was my meaning when I said we must teach music before gymnastics.”
“Quite right,” he said.

“You know also that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is most readily taken.”
“Quite true.”

“And shall we carelessly allow children to hear any casual tales that may be made up by casual persons, and to receive into their minds ideas that are, for the most part, the very opposite of those we want them to have when they are grown?”
“We cannot.”

“So the first thing will be to establish a censorship of the writers of fiction, letting the censors accept any tale that is good and reject the bad; and we'll ask mothers and nurses to tell their children only the authorised ones. Let them form the mind with such tales, even more fondly than they shape the body with their hands. But most of those tales now in use must be discarded.”
“What tales do you mean?” he said.
“You may find a model of the smaller in the larger,” I said; “for they must be of the same type, and there is the same spirit in both.”
“Very likely,” he replied; “but I don't yet know what you mean by the greater.”
“Those,” I said, “narrated by Homer and Hesiod and the rest of the poets, who have ever been the great story-tellers of mankind.”
“But which stories do you mean,” he said, “and what fault do you find with them?”
“A most serious fault,” I said: “the fault of telling a lie—and, what's more, a bad lie.”
“But when is this fault committed?”
“Whenever an erroneous representation is made of the nature of gods and heroes—as when a painter paints a portrait that doesn't bear the shadow of a likeness to the original.”
“Yes,” he said, “that sort of thing is certainly blameworthy. But what stories do you mean?”

“First of all,” I said, “there's that greatest of all lies in the highest of quarters, which the poet told about Uranus, and a bad lie too—I mean what Hesiod says Uranus did, and how Cronus retaliated. The doings of Cronus, and the sufferings his son inflicted on him in turn, even if they were true, ought certainly not to be lightly told to young and thoughtless people; if possible, they should be buried in silence. If there is an absolute necessity for mentioning them, a chosen few might hear them as part of a mystery—and they should sacrifice, not the common Eleusinian pig, but some huge and unobtainable victim; and then the number of hearers would be very few indeed.”
“Why yes,” he said, “those stories are extremely objectionable.”

“Yes, Adeimantus; they are stories not to be repeated in our State. A young man should not be told that in committing the worst of crimes he is doing nothing outrageous; or that, if he chastises his father for wrongdoing, he is only following the example of the first and greatest among the gods.”
“I entirely agree,” he said. “In my opinion these stories are quite unfit to be repeated.”

“Nor, if we mean our future guardians to regard the habit of quarrelling among themselves as the basest of things, should any word be said to them about the wars in heaven, or about the plots and battles of the gods against one another—for they are not true. No, we shall never mention the battles of the giants, or let them be embroidered on garments; and we shall be silent about the innumerable other quarrels of gods and heroes with their friends and relatives. If they would only believe us, we would tell them that quarrelling is unholy, and that until now there has been no quarrel between citizens; this is what old men and old women should begin by telling children, and when they grow up, the poets should also be told to compose in a similar spirit. But the story of Hephaestus binding Hera his mother, or how Zeus on another occasion sent Hephaestus flying for taking her part when she was being beaten, and all the battles of the gods in Homer—these tales must not be admitted into our State, whether supposed to have an allegorical meaning or not. For a young person cannot judge what is allegorical and what is literal; anything he takes into his mind at that age is likely to become indelible and unalterable. So it is most important that the tales the young first hear should be models of virtuous thought.”
“There you are right,” he replied. “But if someone asks where such models are to be found and what tales we are speaking of, how shall we answer him?”

I said to him: “You and I, Adeimantus, at this moment, are not poets, but founders of a State. The founders of a State ought to know the general forms in which poets should cast their tales, and the limits that must be observed; but making the tales themselves is not their business.”
“Very true,” he said; “but what are these forms of theology you mean?”
“Something like this,” I replied: “God is always to be represented as he truly is, in whatever sort of poetry—epic, lyric, or tragic—the representation may be made.”
“Right.”
“And isn't he truly good, and must he not be represented as such?”
“Certainly.”
“And no good thing is harmful?”
“No, indeed.”
“And what is not harmful, harms not?”
“Certainly not.”
“And what harms not, does no evil?”
“No.”
“And can what does no evil be a cause of evil?”
“Impossible.”
“And the good is advantageous?”
“Yes.”
“And therefore the cause of well-being?”
“Yes.”
“So it follows that the good is not the cause of all things, but only of the good?”
“Assuredly.”

“Then God, if he is good, is not the author of all things, as the many assert, but the cause of a few only, and not of most of what befalls men. For few are the goods of human life, and many are the evils; the good is to be attributed to God alone, but for the evils, the causes must be sought elsewhere, and not in him.”
“That appears to me most true,” he said.
“Then we must not listen to Homer, or to any other poet who is guilty of the folly of saying that two casks”
“‘Lie at the threshold of Zeus, full of lots, one of good, the other of evil lots,’”
“and that he to whom Zeus gives a mixture of the two”
“‘Sometimes meets with evil fortune, at other times with good;’”
“but that he to whom is given the cup of unmixed ill,”
“‘Him wild hunger drives o'er the beauteous earth.’”
“And again—”
“‘Zeus, who is the dispenser of good and evil to us.’”

“And if anyone claims that the violation of oaths and treaties (which was really the work of Pandarus) was brought about by Athena and Zeus, or that the strife and contention of the gods was instigated by Themis and Zeus, he shall not have our approval. Nor will we allow our young men to hear the words of Aeschylus, that”
“‘God plants guilt among men when he desires utterly to destroy a house.’”

“And if a poet writes of the sufferings of Niobe—the subject of the tragedy in which these iambic verses occur—or of the house of Pelops, or of the Trojan War, or on any similar theme, either we must not allow him to say that these are the works of God, or if they are, he must devise some explanation of them like the one we are seeking: he must say that God did what was just and right, and that the sufferers were the better for being punished. But that those who are punished are miserable, and that God is the author of their misery—the poet is not to be permitted to say. Though he may say that the wicked are miserable because they need to be punished, and are benefited by receiving punishment from God; but that God, being good, is the author of evil to anyone—this is to be strenuously denied, and not said or sung or heard in verse or prose, by anyone, young or old, in any well-ordered commonwealth. Such a fiction is suicidal, ruinous, impious.”
“I agree with you,” he replied, “and am ready to give my assent to the law.”
“Let this, then, be one of our rules and principles about the gods, to which our poets and reciters will be expected to conform: that God is not the author of all things, but only of the good.”
“That will do,” he said.

“And what do you think of a second principle? Shall I ask you whether God is a magician, of such a nature as to appear insidiously now in one shape and now in another—sometimes changing himself and passing into many forms, sometimes deceiving us with the semblance of such transformations; or whether he is one and the same, immutably fixed in his own proper image?”
“I cannot answer you,” he said, “without more thought.”
“Well,” I said; “but if we suppose a change in anything, the change must be caused either by the thing itself or by some other thing?”
“Most certainly.”

“And things that are at their best are least liable to be altered or disturbed: for example, when healthiest and strongest, the human body is least liable to be affected by meats and drinks, and the plant that is in the fullest vigour suffers least from wind or the heat of the sun or any similar causes.”
“Of course.”
“And won't the bravest and wisest soul be least confused or deranged by any external influence?”
“True.”
“And the same principle, I suppose, applies to all composite things—furniture, houses, garments: when good and well made, they are least altered by time and circumstances.”
“Very true.”
“So everything that is good, whether made by art or by nature, or both, is least liable to suffer change from without?”
“True.”
“But surely God and the things of God are in every way perfect?”
“Of course they are.”
“Then he can hardly be compelled by external influence to take many shapes?”
“He cannot.”
“But may he not change and transform himself?”
“Clearly,” he said, “that must be the case, if he is changed at all.”
“And will he then change himself for the better and fairer, or for the worse and more unsightly?”
“If he changes at all, he can only change for the worse, for we can't suppose him to be deficient in either virtue or beauty.”
“Very true, Adeimantus. But then, would anyone, god or man, desire to make himself worse?”
“Impossible.”
“Then it is impossible that God should ever be willing to change; being, as is supposed, the fairest and best that is conceivable, every God remains absolutely and forever in his own form.”
“That necessarily follows,” he said, “in my judgment.”
“Then, my dear friend,” I said, “let none of the poets tell us that”
“‘The gods, taking the disguise of strangers from other lands, walk up and down cities in all sorts of forms;’”
“and let no one slander Proteus and Thetis, and let no one, either in tragedy or any other kind of poetry, introduce Hera disguised in the likeness of a priestess asking alms”
“‘For the life-giving daughters of Inachus the river of Argos;’”

“—let us have no more lies of that sort. Nor must we have mothers, under the influence of the poets, scaring their children with a bad version of these myths—telling them how certain gods, as they say, ‘go about by night in the likeness of strangers in various forms.’ Let them beware of making cowards of their children, and at the same time uttering blasphemy against the gods.”
“Heaven forbid,” he said.
“But although the gods are themselves unchangeable, still, by witchcraft and deception, they may make us think they appear in various forms?”
“Perhaps,” he replied.
“Well, can you imagine that God will be willing to lie, whether in word or deed, or to put forth a phantom of himself?”
“I can't say,” he replied.
“Don't you know,” I said, “that the true lie, if such an expression may be allowed, is hated of gods and men?”
“What do you mean?” he said.

“I mean that no one is willingly deceived in what is the truest and highest part of himself, or about the truest and highest matters: there, above all, he is most afraid of having a lie in possession of him.”
“Still,” he said, “I don't understand you.”

“The reason is,” I replied, “that you attribute some profound meaning to my words; but I am only saying that deception, or being deceived or uninformed about the highest realities in the highest part of themselves—that is, in the soul—and to hold the lie there, is what mankind least like; that, I say, is what they utterly detest.”
“There is nothing more hateful to them.”

“And, as I was just now remarking, this ignorance in the soul of the deceived may be called the true lie; for the lie in words is only a kind of imitation and shadowy image of a prior affection of the soul, not pure unadulterated falsehood. Am I not right?”
“Perfectly right.”
“The true lie, then, is hated not only by gods but also by men?”
“Yes.”

“Whereas the lie in words is in certain cases useful and not hateful; in dealing with enemies, for example; or again, when those we call our friends, in a fit of madness or delusion, are going to do some harm, then it is useful, and is a kind of medicine or preventive. Also in the tales of mythology, of which we were just now speaking, because we do not know the truth about ancient times, we make falsehood as much like truth as we can, and so turn it to account.”
“Very true,” he said.
“But can any of these reasons apply to God? Can we suppose that he is ignorant of antiquity and therefore has recourse to invention?”
“That would be ridiculous,” he said.
“So the lying poet has no place in our idea of God?”
“I should say not.”
“Or perhaps he may tell a lie because he is afraid of enemies?”
“That is inconceivable.”
“But he may have friends who are senseless or mad?”
“But no mad or senseless person can be a friend of God.”
“So no motive can be imagined why God should lie?”
“None whatever.”
“Then the superhuman and divine is absolutely incapable of falsehood?”
“Yes.”
“So God is perfectly simple and true, both in word and deed; he changes not, he deceives not, either by sign or word, by dream or waking vision.”
“Your thoughts,” he said, “are the reflection of my own.”

“You agree with me, then,” I said, “that this is the second type or form in which we should write and speak about divine things: the gods are not magicians who transform themselves, nor do they deceive mankind in any way.”
“I grant that.”
“Then, although we admire Homer, we do not admire the lying dream that Zeus sends to Agamemnon; nor will we praise the verses of Aeschylus in which Thetis says that Apollo at her wedding”

“‘Was celebrating in song her fair progeny whose days were to be long, and to know no sickness. And when he had spoken of my lot as in all things blessed of heaven he raised a note of triumph and cheered my soul. And I thought that the word of Phoebus, being divine and full of prophecy, would not fail. And now he himself who uttered the strain, he who was present at the banquet, and who said this—he it is who has slain my son.’”

“These are the kinds of sentiments about the gods that will rouse our anger; and whoever utters them shall be refused a chorus. Nor shall we allow teachers to use them in instructing the young—meaning, as we do, that our guardians, as far as men can be, should be true worshippers of the gods and like them.”
“I entirely agree,” he said, “in these principles, and promise to make them my laws.”

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: So those are our principles of theology, I said. Certain stories should be told to our students from childhood, and others should not, if we want them to honor the gods, respect their parents, and value friendship with each other.
Yes, and I think our principles are right, he said.
But if they're going to be courageous, don't they need to learn other lessons too — lessons that will take away the fear of death? Can anyone be brave if he's terrified of dying?
Certainly not, he said.
And can a person be fearless of death, or choose death in battle over defeat and slavery, if he believes the underworld is real and terrible?
Impossible.

Then we need to control this category of stories too, and ask the poets not simply to demonize the world below but actually to praise it — making clear that their grim descriptions are false and harmful to our future warriors.
That will be our duty, he said.
Then, I said, we'll need to cut out many offensive passages, starting with lines like:
'I would rather be a serf on the land of a poor, landless man than rule over all the dead who have perished.'
We must also remove the verse about how Pluto feared
'That the grim, squalid halls the gods despise might be exposed to mortals and immortals alike.'
And again:
'Oh heavens! So in the house of Hades there really is a soul and a ghostly form, but with no mind at all!'
And about Tiresias:
'To him alone, even after death, Persephone granted reason — he alone has wisdom; the other souls are flitting shadows.'
And again:
'The soul, leaving the body, went down to Hades, mourning its fate, leaving behind its strength and youth.'
And again:
'The soul, shrieking, passed like smoke beneath the earth.'
And:
'As bats in the depths of a mysterious cave, when one drops from the cluster on the rock, fly shrieking and clinging to each other — so these souls moved together, shrieking as they went.'

We must ask Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we cut out these and similar passages. Not because they're bad poetry or unpleasing to hear — actually, the more poetically charming they are, the less suitable they are for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free and who should fear slavery more than death.
Undoubtedly.

We'll also need to get rid of all those terrible, frightening names for the underworld — Cocytus, Styx, ghosts beneath the earth, bloodless shades, and every similar word that makes listeners shudder to their very core. I'm not saying these horrifying stories don't have some use, but there's a real danger that our guardians' nerves will be made too fragile and sensitive by them.
There is a real danger, he said.
Then they have to go.
True.
A different, nobler strain must be composed for us to hear.
Clearly.
And shall we also get rid of the weeping and wailing of famous heroes?
Those will go with the rest.
But should they? Think about it: our principle is that a good person won't consider death terrible for any other good person who is his friend.
Yes, that's our principle.
So he won't grieve for his dead companion as if something terrible had happened?
He won't.
And we also maintain that such a person is self-sufficient when it comes to his own happiness, and therefore least dependent on others.
True, he said.
So for him, the loss of a son or brother, or the loss of his fortune, is the least devastating of all.
Certainly.
And therefore, when misfortune of this kind befalls him, he will be the least likely to lament, and he will bear it with the greatest calm of any man.
Yes, he'll feel such a loss far less than others would.

Then we'll be right to remove the lamentations of famous men, and hand them over to women — and not even respectable women — or to men of inferior character. That way, those we're educating to be defenders of the country will be ashamed to do anything similar.
That's absolutely right.

So we'll once more ask Homer and the other poets not to show Achilles, the son of a goddess, first lying on his side, then on his back, then on his face, then leaping up and pacing in a frenzy along the barren shore, then scooping up ashes in both hands and pouring them over his head, weeping and wailing in all the various ways Homer describes. Nor should they show Priam, a man related to the gods, begging and groveling,
'Rolling in the dirt, calling out loudly to each man by name.'
And we'll insist even more strongly that they never show the gods themselves lamenting, saying things like:
'Ah, my suffering! Ah, that I bore the bravest of men, only to grieve!'
And if they must bring in the gods, they should at least not dare to so completely misrepresent the greatest of gods as to have him say:
'Oh heavens! With my own eyes I watch a dear friend chased around the city walls, and my heart aches.'
Or again:
'Woe is me, that fate decrees my beloved Sarpedon, dearest of mortals to me, must fall at the hands of Patroclus, son of Menoetius.'

Because, my dear Adeimantus, if our young people take these unworthy portrayals of the gods seriously instead of laughing at them as they should, they'll hardly think it beneath their own dignity — being merely human — to behave the same way. They won't feel any shame or self-control, and will break into weeping and wailing at the slightest provocation.
That's very true, he said.
Yes, I replied; but surely that is exactly what ought not to happen, as the argument has just proved to us. We must abide by that proof until a better argument disproves it.
It shouldn't happen.
Our guardians also shouldn't be prone to excessive laughter. When someone indulges in a fit of laughter beyond all measure, it almost always triggers an equally violent reaction.
I believe so.
Then people of worth, even mortals, must not be portrayed as overcome by laughter. And this applies even more to portrayals of the gods.
Much more so, as you say, he said.
So we shall not allow an expression like Homer's to be used about the gods, when he describes how—
'Uncontrollable laughter broke out among the blessed gods when they saw Hephaestus bustling about the hall.'
By your reasoning, we can't allow that.
If you want to attribute that reasoning to me, fine. But we certainly can't allow it.

Next, truth must be highly valued. If, as we were saying, lying is useless to the gods and useful to humans only as a kind of medicine, then its use should be restricted to doctors. Private citizens have no business with it.
Clearly not, he said.

Then if anyone at all is to have the privilege of lying, it should be the rulers of the State; and they may be permitted to lie, whether in dealing with enemies or with their own citizens, for the public good. But nobody else should meddle with anything of the kind. And although the rulers have this privilege, for a private man to lie to them in return is an even more heinous offense than for a patient to lie to his doctor about his bodily illnesses, or for a student at the gymnasium to lie to his trainer, or for a sailor to lie to the captain about what is happening with the ship and the rest of the crew, or about how things are going with himself or his fellow sailors.
Very true, he said.
So if the ruler catches anyone else in the state lying —
'Any craftsman, whether priest, doctor, or carpenter' —
he'll punish him for introducing a practice that's just as destructive to a state as it is to a ship.
Absolutely, he said, if our idea of the state is ever carried out.
Next, our young people must be self-disciplined?
Certainly.
And isn't self-discipline mainly about obedience to leaders and self-control over physical pleasures?
True.
Then we'll approve of passages like Diomedes' words in Homer:
'Friend, sit still and do as I say.'
And the lines that follow:
'The Greeks marched with fierce determination... in silent reverence for their commanders.'
And other sentiments of the same kind.
We will.
What about this line —
'You wine-soaked fool with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer!' —
and the insults that follow? Would you say that these or similar impertinent remarks from private citizens to their rulers, whether in verse or prose, are appropriate?
They are not.
They may very possibly afford some amusement, but they do not contribute to self-discipline. And so they are likely to do harm to our young men — you would agree with me there?
Yes.
And then, having the wisest man in the world declare that nothing is more glorious than
'When the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the wine-bearer carries wine from the bowl and pours it into the cups' —
is that fitting or conducive to self-discipline for a young person to hear? Or the line —
'The saddest fate of all is to die of hunger'?

What would you say about the story of Zeus, who, while all other gods and mortals were asleep and he alone was awake, lay making plans — but forgot them all in an instant because of his lust? He was so overwhelmed at the sight of Hera that he wouldn't even go inside, but wanted to lie with her right there on the ground, declaring he had never desired her so much, not even when they first came together
'Without their parents' knowledge.'
Or the tale of how Hephaestus, because of similar behavior, bound Ares and Aphrodite in chains?
I strongly agree, he said, that they should not hear that sort of thing.
On the other hand, any deeds of endurance performed or described by famous men — these our students should see and hear. For example:
'He struck his chest and rebuked his own heart: Bear up, my heart! You have endured far worse than this.'
Certainly, he said.
Next, we must not let our guardians be lovers of gifts or lovers of money.
Certainly not.
Nor should we sing to them about
'Gifts that sway the gods, gifts that sway mighty kings.'

Nor is Phoenix, the tutor of Achilles, to be approved or considered to have given his pupil good counsel when he told him that he should accept the gifts of the Greeks and help them, but that without a gift he should not lay his anger aside. Nor will we believe or admit that Achilles himself was such a lover of money that he took Agamemnon's gifts; or that, having received payment, he returned the dead body of Hector, but refused to do so without being paid.
No, he said, those are not sentiments we can approve.

Out of love for Homer, I hesitate to say it, but attributing these feelings to Achilles — or believing they're accurately attributed to him — borders on impiety. Nor can I accept his insolence toward Apollo, where he says:
'You have wronged me, most hateful of gods. I would take revenge on you if only I had the power.'

Or his defiance of the river-god, on whose divinity he was ready to lay hands. Or his offering of his own hair to the dead Patroclus — hair previously dedicated to the river Spercheius. Or that he dragged Hector's body around Patroclus's tomb and slaughtered captives at the funeral pyre. I cannot believe he did any of this, any more than I can let our citizens believe it. This was supposedly the student of the wise Chiron, son of a goddess and of Peleus — the gentlest of men, third in descent from Zeus. It's absurd to think he was so disturbed as to be torn between two incompatible passions: pettiness mixed with greed, combined with contempt for both gods and men.
You're absolutely right, he said.

And let us equally refuse to believe, or allow to be repeated, the tale of Theseus son of Poseidon, or of Peirithous son of Zeus, going out to perpetrate a horrid rape; or of any other hero or son of a god daring to do such impious and dreadful things as are falsely ascribed to them in our day. Let us further compel the poets to declare either that these acts were not done by them, or that they were not the sons of gods — both things they shall not be permitted to affirm in the same breath. We will not have them trying to persuade our youth that the gods are the authors of evil, and that heroes are no better than ordinary men — sentiments which, as we were saying, are neither pious nor true, for we have already proved that evil cannot come from the gods.
Absolutely not.

Furthermore, such stories will have a terrible effect on those who hear them. Everyone will start excusing their own vices once they're convinced that similar wickedness is constantly being committed by —
'The relatives of the gods, kin of Zeus himself, whose ancestral altar stands high on Mount Ida in the air,'
and who still have
'The blood of gods flowing in their veins.'
Therefore let's put an end to such tales, before they breed moral laxity among the young.
By all means, he said.

But now that we are determining which classes of subjects are or are not to be spoken of, let us see whether any have been omitted. The manner in which gods and demigods and heroes and the world below should be treated has already been laid down.
Very true.
That leaves the question of how to portray human beings. That's obviously the remaining topic.
Clearly.
But we can't answer that question yet, my friend.
Why not?

Because, if I'm not mistaken, we'll have to say that poets and storytellers commit the gravest error when they tell us that wicked people are often happy and good people miserable, and that injustice is profitable when undetected while justice is a personal loss and someone else's gain. We'll forbid them from saying these things and command them to say the opposite.
Of course we will, he said.
But if you agree I'm right about this, then I can claim you've already accepted the principle we've been arguing for all along.
I accept your point.
We can't settle what should and shouldn't be said about human beings until we've discovered what justice is and how it naturally benefits whoever possesses it, whether or not he appears just.
Very true, he said.
That's enough about the content of stories. Let's now talk about style. Once we've covered both content and style, we'll have dealt with the topic completely.
I don't understand what you mean, said Adeimantus.

Then I must make you understand; and perhaps I may be clearer if I put the matter this way. You are aware, I suppose, that all mythology and poetry is a narration of events — either past, present, or yet to come?
Certainly, he said.
And narration can be straightforward storytelling, dramatic imitation, or a combination of both?
I still don't quite understand, he said.

I fear I must be a ridiculous teacher when I have so much trouble making myself understood. Like a bad speaker, then, I will not take the whole subject at once, but break off a piece in illustration of my meaning. You know the first lines of the Iliad, in which the poet tells how Chryses prayed Agamemnon to release his daughter, and how Agamemnon flew into a passion with him; whereupon Chryses, failing in his object, invoked the anger of the god against the Achaeans. Now as far as these lines,
'And he prayed to all the Greeks, but especially to the two sons of Atreus, the leaders of the people' —

the poet is speaking in his own voice. He never pretends to be anyone else. But in what follows, he takes on the character of Chryses and does everything he can to make us think the speaker isn't Homer but the old priest himself. And he uses this double approach throughout his account of events at Troy, in Ithaca, and throughout the Odyssey.
Yes.
And it remains narrative both in the speeches he puts into characters' mouths and in the connecting passages between them?
Exactly.
But when the poet speaks in the person of another, may we not say that he assimilates his style to that of the person who, as he tells you, is about to speak?
Certainly.
And this adaptation — through voice and gesture — to imitate the person whose character he's assuming, that's what we mean by dramatic imitation?
Of course.
So in those parts, the poet's narrative works through imitation?
Exactly.

But if the poet never hides behind characters and always appears as himself, then there's no imitation — it's pure narration. To make sure you understand and don't say 'I don't get it' again, let me show how the change works. If Homer had written, 'The priest came with a ransom for his daughter, begging the Greeks and especially the kings,' and then continued in his own voice instead of speaking as Chryses, it would have been narration rather than imitation. It would have gone something like this (I'm no poet, so I'll skip the meter): 'The priest came and prayed that the gods would grant the Greeks victory at Troy and a safe return home. He asked them to release his daughter and accept his ransom, out of respect for the god. The other Greeks agreed. But Agamemnon was furious and told him to leave and never come back, or the god's staff and garlands wouldn't protect him. His daughter would not be released, he said — she would grow old with him in Argos. He warned the old man to go and not provoke him if he wanted to get home safely. The old man left in fear and silence. Once he was away from the camp, he called on Apollo by his many names, reminding him of every temple he had built and every sacrifice he had made, and praying that the god would repay his devotion by punishing the Greeks with his arrows.' That's how it would read as pure narration.
I understand, he said.
Or you could imagine the opposite: the connecting passages removed, leaving only the dialogue.
I understand that too — you mean like in tragedy.

You have understood my meaning perfectly. And if I am not mistaken, what you failed to grasp before is now clear to you: that poetry and mythology are, in some cases, wholly imitative — tragedy and comedy are examples; there is also the opposite style, in which the poet is the only speaker — the dithyramb is the best example of this; and the combination of both is found in epic, and in several other styles of poetry. Do I take you with me?
Yes, now I see what you meant.
And remember what I said at the start: that we were done with content and could move on to style?
Yes, I remember.

What I meant was this: we need to decide about imitation. Should our poets be allowed to use it in their narratives? If so, in whole or in part? And if in part, which parts? Or should imitation be forbidden entirely?
You're really asking, I suspect, whether we should allow tragedy and comedy in our state?
Yes, I said; but there may be more than this at stake. I really do not know as yet, but wherever the argument may blow us, there we go.
Let's follow it then, he said.

Then, Adeimantus, let me ask you: ought our guardians to be imitators? Or has not this question been decided by the rule already laid down — that one man can do only one thing well, and not many; and that if he attempts many, he will altogether fail of gaining much reputation in any?
Certainly.
And the same is equally true of imitation: no one man can imitate many things as well as he can imitate a single one.
True.

Then the same person won't be able to live a serious life and also be a skilled imitator of many different characters. Even closely related forms of imitation can't be mastered by the same person — for instance, tragic and comic playwrights. Didn't you just call those forms of imitation?
Yes, and you're right that the same people can't do both successfully.
Any more than the same people can be both reciters and actors?
True.
And even comic and tragic actors are different people, though both are just imitators.
They are.
Human nature, Adeimantus, seems to be cut into even finer specializations. It's no better at imitating many things well than it is at doing many things well in real life.
Very true, he said.

So if we stick with our original principle that guardians must dedicate themselves entirely to maintaining the state's freedom — making that their sole profession and doing nothing else — then they shouldn't practice or imitate anything outside their role. If they do imitate, they should imitate from youth onward only characters suited to their calling: the courageous, self-disciplined, reverent, free-spirited, and the like. They should not study or practice imitating anything base or shameful, in case they end up becoming what they imitate. Haven't you noticed how imitations, when they start in youth and continue into later life, eventually become habits and a second nature, affecting body, voice, and mind?
Yes, certainly, he said.

Then we won't allow those we claim to care about — those who should grow into good men — to imitate a woman, whether young or old, quarreling with her husband, defying the gods in arrogant self-satisfaction, or suffering from grief, sorrow, or tears. And certainly not a woman who's sick, in love, or in labor.
Exactly right, he said.
Nor must they play the parts of slaves, male or female, performing the work of slaves?
They must not.

Nor bad people — whether cowards or others — who do the opposite of what we've prescribed: people who mock, ridicule, or insult each other drunk or sober, or who offend against themselves and others in word or deed, as such people do. Nor should they be trained to imitate the speech or actions of the mad or wicked. Madness, like vice, should be understood but not practiced or imitated.
Very true, he said.
Should they imitate metalworkers, or other craftsmen, or rowers, or the officers who direct them?
How could they, he said, when they're not even allowed to pay attention to such occupations?
Nor may they imitate the neighing of horses, the bellowing of bulls, the murmur of rivers and the roll of the ocean, thunder, and all that sort of thing?
No, he said. If we've forbidden imitating madness, they can't imitate the sounds of madness either.

You mean, I said, if I understand you rightly, that there is one sort of narrative style which may be employed by a truly good man when he has something to say, and that another sort will be used by a man of an opposite character and education.
What are these two styles? he asked.

Suppose, I answered, that a just and good man, in the course of a narration, comes upon some saying or action of another good man. I should imagine that he will gladly personate him, and will not be ashamed of this sort of imitation: he will be most ready to play the part of the good man when he is acting firmly and wisely; less so when he is overtaken by illness, or love, or drink, or has met with any other disaster. But when he comes to a character unworthy of him, he will not make a study of that; he will disdain such a person, and will assume his likeness, if at all, only for a moment, and only when the character is performing some good action. At other times he will be ashamed to play a part which he has never practised, nor will he like to shape and fashion himself after baser models. He feels that the exercise of such an art, unless done in jest, is beneath him, and his mind revolts at it.
That's what I'd expect, he said.

Then he will adopt a mode of narration like the one we have illustrated out of Homer — that is, his style will be both imitative and narrative; but there will be very little of the former, and a great deal of the latter. Do you agree?
Certainly. That's the model such a speaker must naturally follow.

But there's another type who will narrate anything at all, and the worse his character, the more shameless he'll be about it. Nothing will be beneath him. He'll eagerly imitate everything — not as a joke, but in complete earnest and before a large audience. As I was saying, he'll try to reproduce thunder, wind, hail, creaking wheels and pulleys, the sounds of flutes, pipes, trumpets, and every kind of instrument. He'll bark like a dog, bleat like a sheep, or crow like a rooster. His entire art will consist of imitating voices and gestures, with very little actual narration.
Yes, that will be his style, he said.
So those are the two kinds of style?
Yes.

And you would agree with me in saying that one of these two styles is simple and has only slight changes; and if the harmony and rhythm are also chosen for their simplicity, the result is that the speaker, if he speaks correctly, is always pretty much the same in style, and will keep within the limits of a single harmony (for the changes are not great), and in the same way will make use of nearly the same rhythm?
That's exactly right, he said.
Whereas the other style requires every kind of harmony and every kind of rhythm, since the style itself involves every kind of variation.
That's perfectly true, he said.
And do not these two styles, or the mixture of the two, comprehend all poetry and every form of expression in words? No one can say anything except in one or the other, or in both together.
They cover everything, he said.
So which should our state allow? All three styles? Or only one of the two pure forms? Or the mixed one?
If I had my way, I'd only admit the pure imitator of virtue.

Yes, Adeimantus, but the mixed style is also very charming. And the purely imitative style — the opposite of what you've chosen — is the most popular with children, their caretakers, and the general public.
I don't deny it.
But I suppose you would argue that such a style is unsuitable to our State, in which human nature is not twofold or manifold, for one man plays one part only?
Yes, completely unsuitable.

And that's why, in our state alone, a shoemaker is just a shoemaker and not also a ship's captain; a farmer is just a farmer and not also a judge; a soldier is just a soldier and not also a trader — and so on throughout?
True, he said.

So if one of these versatile imitators comes along — so clever he can imitate anything — and offers to perform for us, we'll honor him like a sacred and wonderful being. But we'll also tell him that our state has no place for people like him. We'll anoint his head with perfume, crown him with a wreath of wool, and then send him off to another city. Because we intend to use, for the health of our souls, the rougher, stricter kind of poet or storyteller — one who imitates only the virtuous style and follows the models we established when we first began planning the education of our soldiers.
That's certainly what we'll do, if it's in our power, he said.
Then now, my friend, I said, that part of music or literary education which relates to the story or myth may be considered finished; for we have discussed both the matter and the manner.
I think so too, he said.
Next comes melody and song.
Obviously.
By now, everyone can already see what we should say about them, if we're going to be consistent with ourselves.
I'm afraid, said Glaucon, laughing, that 'everyone' doesn't quite include me. I can't say right now what the rules should be, though I can probably guess.
At the very least, you know that a song has three elements: words, melody, and rhythm? That much I can assume?
Yes, he said, you can assume that much.
And as for the words, there won't be any difference between words that are set to music and words that aren't? Both must follow the same rules we've already established?
Yes.
And the melody and rhythm must follow the words?
Certainly.
We said, when discussing content, that we have no need for songs of lamentation and sorrow?
True.
And which musical modes express sorrow? You're the musical one — you tell me.
The harmonies you mean are the mixed or tenor Lydian, and the full-toned or bass Lydian, and others like them.
These, then, I said, must be banished; even to women who have a character to maintain they are of no use, and much less to men.
Certainly.
Next, drunkenness, laziness, and self-indulgence are completely inappropriate for our guardians.
Completely.
And which modes are soft and associated with drinking?
The Ionian and the Lydian, he said. They're called 'relaxed' modes.
Do those have any military use?
Quite the reverse, he replied; and if so, the Dorian and the Phrygian are the only ones you have left.

I answered: Of the harmonies I know nothing, but I want to have one warlike harmony, to sound the note or accent that a brave man utters in the hour of danger and stern resolve, or when his cause is failing and he is going to wounds or death, or is overtaken by some other evil, and at every such crisis meets the blows of fortune with firm step and a determination to endure; and another to be used by him in times of peace and freedom of action, when there is no pressure of necessity, and he is seeking to persuade God by prayer, or man by instruction and admonition, or, on the other hand, when he is expressing his willingness to yield to persuasion or entreaty or admonition, and which represents him when by prudent conduct he has attained his end, not carried away by his success, but acting moderately and wisely under the circumstances, and acquiescing in the event. These two harmonies I ask you to leave — the strain of necessity and the strain of freedom, the strain of the unfortunate and the strain of the fortunate, the strain of courage and the strain of temperance; these, I say, leave.
And those, he said, are exactly the Dorian and Phrygian modes I was just talking about.
Then, I said, if these and these only are to be used in our songs and melodies, we shall not want a multiplicity of notes or a panharmonic scale?
I suppose not.
Then we shall not maintain the makers of lyres with three corners and complex scales, or the makers of any other many-stringed, curiously harmonised instruments?
Certainly not.

And what about flute-makers and flute-players? Will you let them into our state, given that the flute is the most varied of all instruments? Even those elaborate multi-mode compositions are really just imitations of the flute.
Obviously not.
That leaves the lyre and the harp for use in the city, and a simple pipe for the shepherds in the countryside.
That's the logical conclusion.
We're really just preferring Apollo and his instruments over Marsyas and his, I said. Nothing unusual about that.
Not at all, he said.
And so, by the dog of Egypt, without even realizing it we've been purging the state that we earlier called luxurious.
And wisely so, he said.

Then let us now finish the purgation, I said. Next in order after harmonies, rhythms will naturally follow, and they should be subject to the same rules; for we ought not to seek out complex systems of metre, or metres of every kind, but rather to discover which rhythms are the expressions of a courageous and harmonious life. And when we have found them, we shall adapt the foot and the melody to words having a like spirit — not the words to the foot and the melody. To say what these rhythms are will be your duty; you must teach me them, as you have already taught me the harmonies.

But indeed, he replied, I cannot tell you. I only know that there are some three principles of rhythm out of which metrical systems are framed, just as in sounds there are four notes out of which all the harmonies are composed — that is an observation I have made. But of what sort of lives they are severally the imitations, I am unable to say.

Then, I said, we must take Damon into our counsels, and he will tell us which rhythms express meanness, insolence, fury, or other unworthiness, and which are to be reserved for the expression of opposite feelings. I vaguely remember him mentioning a complex Cretic rhythm, and a dactylic or heroic rhythm, and arranging them in some manner I do not quite understand, making the rhythms equal in the rise and fall of the foot, long and short syllables alternating. Unless I am mistaken, he also spoke of an iambic and a trochaic rhythm, and assigned to them short and long quantities. In some cases he appeared to praise or censure the movement of the foot quite as much as the rhythm, or perhaps a combination of the two — for I am not certain what he meant. These matters, however, as I was saying, had better be referred to Damon himself, for the analysis would be a difficult one. (Socrates expresses himself carelessly, in accordance with his assumed ignorance of the subject. In the first part he seems to speak of paeonic rhythms in the ratio 3/2; in the second of dactylic and anapaestic rhythms in the ratio 1/1; and in the last clause of iambic and trochaic rhythms in the ratio 1/2 or 2/1.)
It certainly would.
But one thing we can see clearly: grace and the absence of grace are the result of good and bad rhythm.
Absolutely.

And good and bad rhythm naturally follow good and bad style. The same is true of harmony and discord — they follow the character of the words, since our principle is that rhythm and harmony are governed by the words, not the reverse.
Exactly, he said. They should follow the words.
And won't the character of the words and the style depend on the character of the soul?
Yes.
And everything else follows from the style?
Yes.

Then beauty of style, harmony, grace, and good rhythm all depend on simplicity — I mean the true simplicity of a rightly and nobly ordered mind and character, not the 'simplicity' that's just a polite word for foolishness?
Very true, he said.
And if our young people are to fulfill their purpose in life, must they not pursue these qualities of grace and harmony constantly?
They must.

And every creative art is full of these qualities — painting, weaving, embroidery, architecture, every kind of craftsmanship. Nature too, in both animals and plants, shows grace or its absence. Ugliness, discord, and clumsy movement are closely related to bad language and bad character, just as grace and harmony are twin sisters of goodness and virtue, bearing their likeness.
Absolutely true, he said.

So should our supervision extend only to poets, requiring them to express the image of goodness in their work or face expulsion? Or should the same control apply to all other artists too, forbidding them from depicting vice, excess, meanness, and indecency in sculpture, building, or any other creative art? Anyone who can't follow this rule must be prevented from practicing in our state. We don't want our guardians growing up surrounded by images of moral ugliness, like cattle in a poisonous pasture, grazing day by day on harmful influences until they've unknowingly accumulated a festering corruption in their own souls. Instead, our artists should be those gifted at discerning the true nature of beauty and grace. Then our young people will live in a land of health, surrounded by beautiful sights and sounds, receiving goodness from every direction. Beauty, streaming from fine works of art, will flow into their eyes and ears like a health-giving breeze from a pure region, and from their earliest years will gently draw their souls into harmony and sympathy with the beauty of reason.
There could be no finer education than that, he said.

That's why musical education is the most powerful instrument of all, Glaucon. Rhythm and harmony penetrate deep into the soul, grip it powerfully, and bring it grace — making the soul of the well-educated person graceful, and the soul of the poorly educated person graceless. The person who has received this true inner education will perceive faults and flaws in art and nature with the sharpest eye. With genuine taste, he'll praise and welcome the good, absorb it into his soul, and become noble and good himself. At the same time, he'll rightly criticize and reject the bad — even in his youth, before he can fully understand why. And when reason eventually arrives, he'll greet it as a familiar friend, recognized from the education that prepared him.
Yes, he said, I quite agree with you in thinking that our youth should be trained in music, and for the reasons you mention.

Think of it like learning to read, I said. We were satisfied when we knew the letters of the alphabet — just a few letters in all their various sizes and combinations. We didn't dismiss them as unimportant whether they appeared in a large or small space, but we were eager to recognize them everywhere. We didn't consider ourselves literate until we could spot them wherever they appeared.
True.
And we can recognize the reflections of letters in water or mirrors only when we already know the letters themselves. The same skill gives us knowledge of both.
Exactly.

In the same way, neither we nor our guardians can be truly cultivated until we recognize the essential forms of self-discipline, courage, generosity, and magnanimity — along with their opposites — in all their combinations, wherever they appear. We must be able to detect them and their reflections in both great and small matters, believing they all fall within a single field of study.
Absolutely.
And when a beautiful soul is found in harmony with a beautiful form, and the two are cast in the same mold — wouldn't that be the most beautiful sight for anyone with eyes to see?
The most beautiful indeed.
And the most beautiful is also the most lovable?
We can assume so.
