And the person with a harmonious spirit will be most drawn to the most beautiful. But he won't love someone whose soul is disharmonious?
True, he said — not if the disharmony is in the soul. But if it's just a physical imperfection, he'll be patient with it and love the person all the same.
I see, I said, that you speak from experience, and I agree. But let me ask: does excessive pleasure have any connection with self-discipline?
How could it? he said. Pleasure robs a person of their faculties just as much as pain does.
Or any connection with virtue in general?
None at all.
Any connection with indulgence and excess?
The strongest possible connection.
And is there any greater or more intense pleasure than sexual love?
None — and none more irrational.
But true love is a love of beauty and order — temperate and harmonious?
Exactly, he said.
Then nothing excessive or irrational should come near true love?
Certainly not.
Then mad or intemperate pleasure must never be allowed to come near the lover and his beloved; neither of them can have any part in it if their love is of the right sort?
Absolutely not, Socrates.

Then I suppose that, in the city we are founding, you would make a law to the effect that a friend should use no other familiarity with his love than a father would use with his son, and then only for a noble purpose, and he must first have the other's consent. This rule is to limit him in all his dealings with the beloved, and he is never to be seen going further; or, if he exceeds, he is to be deemed guilty of coarseness and bad taste.
I completely agree, he said.
So that concludes our discussion of the arts, which ends, fittingly, with the love of beauty. For what else should the arts ultimately lead to, if not the love of beauty?
I agree, he said.
After the arts comes physical training, which our young people must undertake next.
Certainly.

Gymnastic, as well as music, should begin in the early years, and the training in it should be careful and should continue through life. Now my belief is — and I should like to have your opinion to confirm my own — not that a good body, by any bodily excellence, improves the soul, but on the contrary, that a good soul, by her own excellence, improves the body as far as this may be possible. What do you say?
Yes, I agree.
Then once we've properly educated the mind, we can hand over the details of physical care to it. To avoid going on too long, we'll just sketch the general principles.
Very good.
That they must abstain from intoxication has already been remarked by us; for of all persons, a guardian should be the last to get drunk and not know where in the world he is.
Yes, he said. It would be absurd for a guardian to need another guardian to look after him.
But next, what shall we say of their food? For these men are in training for the greatest contest of all — are they not?
Yes, he said.
Would the habits of ordinary athletes suit them?
Why not?

I am afraid, I said, that a bodily habit such as theirs is a sleepy sort of thing, and rather perilous to health. Do you not observe that these athletes sleep away their lives, and are liable to most dangerous illnesses if they depart, even in the slightest degree, from their customary regimen?
Yes, I've noticed that.

Then, I said, a finer sort of training will be required for our warrior-athletes, who are to be like wakeful dogs, and to see and hear with the utmost keenness. Amid the many changes of water and of food, of summer heat and winter cold, which they will have to endure on campaign, they must not be liable to break down in health.
That's my view too.
The truly excellent physical training is the twin sister of the simple music we were just describing.
How so?
There's a kind of physical training that, like our music, is simple and good — especially military training.
What do you mean?

We can learn from Homer. He feeds his heroes on campaign with soldiers' rations. They don't eat fish, even though they're camping by the sea, and they're only allowed roasted meat, not boiled — it's the most practical food for soldiers, since they only need a fire and don't have to carry pots and pans around.
True.

And I can hardly be mistaken in saying that sweet sauces are nowhere mentioned in Homer. In proscribing them, however, he is not alone; all professional athletes are well aware that a man who is to be in good condition should take nothing of the kind.
Yes, he said. They know it and they're right to avoid it.
So you wouldn't approve of lavish Syracusan dinners or the refinements of Sicilian cooking?
I think not.
Nor, if a man is to be in good condition, would you allow him to have a Corinthian girl as his fair friend?
Certainly not.
Or the famous Athenian pastries?
Certainly not.
We could compare all that elaborate eating and living to those complex, multi-mode musical compositions with every kind of rhythm.
Exactly.
In music, complexity bred indiscipline. In diet, it breeds disease. But simplicity in music produces self-discipline in the soul, and simplicity in physical training produces health in the body.
Absolutely true, he said.

But when intemperance and diseases multiply in a State, halls of justice and of medicine are always being opened; and the arts of the doctor and the lawyer give themselves airs, finding how keen is the interest which not only the slaves but the freemen of a city take about them.
Of course.

And yet what greater proof can there be of a bad and disgraceful state of education than this: that not only artisans and the meaner sort of people need the skill of first-rate physicians and judges, but also those who would profess to have had a liberal education? Is it not disgraceful, and a great sign of want of good breeding, that a man should have to go abroad for his law and physic because he has none of his own at home, and must therefore surrender himself into the hands of other men, whom he makes lords and judges over him?
Absolutely disgraceful, he said.

Would you say 'most,' I replied, when you consider that there is a further stage of the evil — in which a man is not only a lifelong litigant, passing all his days in the courts, either as plaintiff or defendant, but is actually led by his bad taste to pride himself on his litigiousness? He imagines himself a master in dishonesty, able to take every crooked turn, to wriggle into and out of every hole, bending like a withy and getting out of the way of justice — and all for what? In order to gain small points not worth mentioning, not knowing that to order his life so as to be able to do without a napping judge is a far higher and nobler thing. Is not that still more disgraceful?
Yes, he said, that's even more disgraceful.

Well, I said, and to require the help of medicine not when a wound has to be cured, or on occasion of an epidemic, but just because, through indolence and a habit of life such as we have been describing, men fill themselves with waters and winds as if their bodies were a marsh, compelling the ingenious sons of Asclepius to find more names for diseases such as flatulence and catarrh — is not this, too, a disgrace?
Yes, he said. Those are certainly strange, newfangled names for diseases.

The kind that didn't exist in Asclepius's day, I said. I base this on the fact that when the hero Eurypylus was wounded at Troy, Homer describes him drinking a concoction of strong wine mixed with barley meal and grated cheese — definitely not what a doctor would recommend. Yet the sons of Asclepius who were there didn't criticize the woman who served it or scold Patroclus for the treatment.
That's certainly an unusual drink for someone in his condition, he said.

Not so extraordinary, I replied, if you bear in mind that in former days, as is commonly said, before the time of Herodicus, the guild of Asclepius did not practise our present system of medicine, which may be said to educate diseases. But Herodicus, being a trainer, and himself of a sickly constitution, discovered, by a combination of training and doctoring, a way of torturing first and chiefly himself, and secondly the rest of the world.
How so? he said.

By inventing a drawn-out death, I said. He had a fatal illness that he endlessly managed, and since recovery was impossible, he spent his entire life as a chronic invalid. He couldn't do anything except tend to himself, and he was in constant anxiety whenever he deviated even slightly from his routine. So by the power of medical science, he dragged himself to old age while dying the whole time.
What a wonderful reward for his skill!

Yes — exactly the reward you'd expect for someone who didn't understand that Asclepius chose not to teach his descendants this kind of medicine. The reason wasn't ignorance. It was because Asclepius knew that in a well-organized society, everyone has a job to do and no one has the leisure to spend their life being ill. We see this clearly with working people, but absurdly, we don't apply the same logic to the wealthy.
How do you mean? he said.

I mean this: when a carpenter is ill, he asks the physician for a rough and ready cure — an emetic, or a purge, or a cautery, or the knife; these are his remedies. And if someone prescribes him a course of dietetics, and tells him that he must swathe and swaddle his head, and all that sort of thing, he replies at once that he has no time to be ill, and that he sees no good in a life spent nursing his disease to the neglect of his customary employment. So, bidding goodbye to this sort of physician, he resumes his ordinary habits, and either gets well and lives and does his business, or, if his constitution fails, he dies and has no more trouble.
Yes, he said; and a man in his condition of life ought to use the art of medicine thus far only.
Has he not an occupation, I said? And what profit would there be in his life if he were deprived of his occupation?
Exactly, he said.
But with the rich man it is otherwise. Of him we do not say that he has any specially appointed work that he must perform if he would live.
People generally assume he has nothing to do.
Haven't you heard Phocylides' saying that once a man has enough to live on, he should practice virtue?
I think he should start even sooner than that, he said.

Let us not have a dispute with him about this, I said; but rather ask ourselves: is the practice of virtue obligatory on the rich man, or can he live without it? And if it is obligatory on him, then let us raise a further question: does this dieting of disorders, which is an impediment to the application of the mind in carpentering and the mechanical arts, not equally stand in the way of the sentiment of Phocylides?
Of that, he replied, there can be no doubt. Such excessive care of the body, when carried beyond the rules of gymnastic, is most hostile to the practice of virtue.

Yes indeed, I replied, and equally incompatible with the management of a house, an army, or an office of state. And, what is most important of all, irreconcilable with any kind of study, thought, or self-reflection. There is a constant suspicion that headache and giddiness are to be ascribed to philosophy, and hence any practice or test of virtue in the higher sense is absolutely stopped; for a man is always fancying that he is being made ill, and is in constant anxiety about the state of his body.
That's very likely.

So we can assume that Asclepius intended his art only for people who were naturally healthy and lived well but happened to contract a specific illness. He cured them with purges and surgery and told them to carry on as usual, keeping the state's interests in mind. But bodies that were thoroughly diseased, he wouldn't have tried to cure with drawn-out treatments. He didn't want to prolong worthless lives or have sickly parents producing even sicklier children. If a person couldn't live a normal life, there was no point in treating him, since such a cure would benefit neither the patient nor the state.
You're making Asclepius sound like a statesman, he said.

That's clearly what he was. And his character is further shown by his sons. They were heroes at Troy who practiced the kind of medicine I'm describing. Remember how they treated Menelaus when Pandarus wounded him? They
'Sucked the blood from the wound and applied soothing remedies,'

but they never prescribed what the patient should eat or drink afterwards — in the case of Menelaus, any more than in the case of Eurypylus. The remedies, as they conceived, were enough to heal any man who before he was wounded had been healthy and regular in his habits; and even though he did happen to drink a posset of Pramnian wine, he might recover all the same. But they would have nothing to do with unhealthy and intemperate subjects, whose lives were of no use either to themselves or to others; the art of medicine was not designed for their good, and though they were as rich as Midas, the sons of Asclepius would have declined to attend them.
Very shrewd people, those sons of Asclepius.

Naturally, I said. Yet the tragedians and Pindar go against our principles. They acknowledge that Asclepius was Apollo's son but claim he was bribed to heal a rich man at the point of death, and for that he was struck by lightning. But according to our established principle, we won't accept both claims together. If he was a god's son, he wasn't greedy. If he was greedy, he wasn't a god's son.

All of that is excellent, Socrates. But let me ask you something: shouldn't a state have good doctors? And aren't the best doctors those who have treated the greatest number of different conditions, both healthy and sick? Similarly, aren't the best judges those who have experience with all kinds of moral character?
Yes, I said, I want good doctors and good judges too. But do you know what I mean by 'good'?
Tell me.
I will, but let me point out that your question combines two things that aren't really the same.
How so? he said.

Why, I said, you join physicians and judges. Now the most skilful physicians are those who, from their youth upwards, have combined with the knowledge of their art the greatest experience of disease; they had better not be robust in health, and should have had all manner of diseases in their own persons. For the body, as I conceive it, is not the instrument with which they cure the body — if that were so, we could never allow them to be or to have been sickly; but they cure the body with the mind, and the mind which has become and is sick can cure nothing.
Very true, he said.

But with the judge it is otherwise; since he governs mind by mind, he ought not therefore to have been trained among vicious minds, and to have associated with them from youth upwards, and to have gone through the whole calendar of crime, only in order that he may quickly infer the crimes of others as he might their bodily diseases from his own self-consciousness. The honourable mind which is to form a healthy judgment should have had no experience or contamination of evil habits when young. And this is the reason why, in youth, good men often appear to be simple, and are easily imposed upon by the dishonest, because they have no examples of what evil is in their own souls.
Yes, he said, they're much too easily taken in.

That's why, I said, a judge should not be young. He should have learned to recognize evil not through his own experience but through long observation of evil in others. Knowledge, not personal vice, should be his guide.
Yes, that would be the ideal judge.

Yes, I replied, and he will be a good man — which is my answer to your question — for he is good who has a good soul. But the cunning and suspicious nature of which we spoke — he who has committed many crimes, and fancies himself a master in wickedness — when among his fellows is wonderful in the precautions he takes, because he judges of them by himself; but when he gets into the company of men of virtue, who have the experience of age, he appears to be a fool again, owing to his unseasonable suspicions. He cannot recognise an honest man, because he has no pattern of honesty in himself. At the same time, since the bad are more numerous than the good, and he meets with them more often, he thinks himself, and is thought by others, to be rather wise than foolish.
Very true, he said.

Then the good and wise judge we're looking for isn't this kind of person, but the other. Vice can never understand virtue, but a virtuous nature, educated over time, will come to understand both virtue and vice. The virtuous person, not the vicious one, becomes truly wise — in my opinion.
And in mine, he said.

This is the kind of medicine and the kind of law you'll establish in your state. They'll serve better natures, providing health to both soul and body. But those whose bodies are incurably diseased will be allowed to die, and those whose souls are incurably corrupt will be put to death.
That's clearly best for both the patients and the state.
And our young people, educated in the simple music that inspires self-discipline, will be reluctant to go to court.
Clearly.
And the person trained in this music who also practices simple physical training will have no need for medicine except in extreme cases.
I'm sure of it.

The very exercises and toils he undergoes are intended to stimulate the spirited element of his nature, not to increase his strength; he will not, like common athletes, use exercise and regimen to develop his muscles.
Exactly right, he said.
And the arts and physical training are not actually designed, as people commonly think, one for training the soul and the other for training the body.
Then what are they really for? he asked.
I believe, I said, that both are primarily aimed at improving the soul.
How can that be? he said.
Haven't you noticed, I said, the effect on the mind of exclusive devotion to physical training versus exclusive devotion to the arts?
What effects do you mean? he said.
Exclusive physical training produces hardness and brutality. Exclusive devotion to the arts produces softness and weakness.
Yes, he said, I am quite aware that the mere athlete becomes too much of a savage, and that the mere musician is melted and softened beyond what is good for him.
Yet surely, I said, this ferocity only comes from spirit, which, if rightly educated, would give courage, but if too much intensified, is liable to become hard and brutal.
I think so too.
And the gentleness comes from the philosophical side of our nature. When properly educated, it produces moderation. But when over-indulged, it becomes excessive softness.
True.
And we said our guardians should have both qualities?
Yes.
And the two should be in harmony?
Absolutely.
And the harmonious soul is both self-disciplined and courageous?
Yes.
And the disharmonious soul is cowardly and crude?
Very true.

And when a man allows music to play upon him, and to pour into his soul through the funnel of his ears those sweet and soft and melancholy airs we were just now speaking of, and his whole life is passed in warbling and the delights of song — in the first stage of the process the passion or spirit within him is tempered like iron, and made useful instead of brittle and useless. But, if he carries on the softening and soothing process, in the next stage he begins to melt and waste, until he has wasted away his spirit and cut out the sinews of his soul; and he becomes a feeble warrior.
Very true.

If his spirit was naturally weak to begin with, this happens quickly. But if he has a strong spirit, music gradually weakens it until he becomes hypersensitive. At the slightest provocation, he flares up and is just as quickly extinguished. Instead of being spirited, he becomes irritable, volatile, and impossible to deal with.
Exactly.

And in physical training: if someone trains intensely and eats heavily while completely neglecting the arts and philosophy, at first his excellent physical condition fills him with pride and energy, and he feels twice the man he was.
Certainly.

But what happens next? If he does nothing else — never engages with learning, inquiry, thought, or any cultivation of the mind — whatever intelligence he has grows weak, dull, and blind. His mind never wakes up or receives nourishment, and his senses are never cleansed of their fog.
True, he said.

He ends up hating learning and civilized life. He never uses persuasion, only force. He lives like a wild beast — all violence and aggression — in ignorance and crudeness, with no sense of grace or proportion.
That's exactly right, he said.

Since there are two elements of human nature — the spirited and the philosophical — it seems as if some god gave humanity two arts to correspond to them (and only indirectly to the body and soul): the arts and physical training. The purpose is to tune these two elements, like the strings of an instrument, tightening or relaxing each until they're in proper harmony.
That seems to be the intention.

And the person who blends the arts and physical training in the finest proportions, tempering them most skillfully in the soul, can rightly be called the true musician and harmonist — far more than someone who merely tunes instrument strings.
You're quite right, Socrates.
Our state will always need someone like this as its director, if the government is to last.
Absolutely necessary.

Such, then, are our principles of nurture and education. Where would be the use of going into further details about the dances of our citizens, or about their hunting and coursing, their gymnastic and equestrian contests? For these all follow the general principle, and having found that, we shall have no difficulty in discovering them.
I imagine they won't be, he said.
Very good, I said. Then what is the next question? Must we not ask who are to be rulers and who are to be subjects?
Certainly.
Obviously the older should rule the younger.
Obviously.
And the best among the older should rule.
That too is clear.
And aren't the best farmers those most devoted to farming?
Yes.
And since we want the best guardians for our city, shouldn't they be those with the most guardian-like character?
Yes.
And to this end they ought to be wise and efficient, and to have a special care of the State?
True.
And a person is most likely to care about what he loves?
Of course.
And he will be most likely to love that which he regards as having the same interests as himself, and that of which the good or evil fortune is supposed by him at any time most to affect his own?
Very true, he said.

Then there must be a selection. Let us note, among the guardians, those who in their whole life show the greatest eagerness to do what is for the good of their country, and the greatest repugnance to doing anything against her interests.
Those are the right people.
And they must be tested at every stage of life to see whether they hold firm to this conviction and never, through force or trickery, forget or abandon their sense of duty to the state.
Abandon it how? he asked.

Let me explain, I said. A conviction can leave someone's mind either willingly or unwillingly. Willingly, when someone lets go of a false belief and learns the truth. Unwillingly, when someone is robbed of a true belief.
I understand the willing kind, he said, but I still need to learn about the unwilling.

Don't you see, I said, that people are unwillingly deprived of good things and willingly deprived of bad ones? Losing the truth is a bad thing, and having the truth is good. And to understand things as they are is to have the truth?
Yes, he said. I agree that people are deprived of truth against their will.
And isn't this involuntary loss caused by theft, force, or enchantment?
I still don't follow, he said.

I must be speaking like a playwright — too obscurely. By 'theft,' I just mean that some people are gradually argued out of their beliefs without realizing it, and others simply forget over time. Do you see what I mean now?
Yes.
By 'force,' I mean people who are compelled to change their minds by pain or suffering.
I understand, he said. You're right.
And by 'enchantment,' I mean people who change their beliefs either through the seduction of pleasure or the pressure of fear.
Yes, he said. Everything that deceives is a kind of enchantment.

So, as I was saying, we need to find out which guardians are the best at holding firm to their conviction that the state's interest should guide their lives. We must test them from youth onward, putting them in situations where they're most likely to forget or be tricked out of this belief. Those who remember and resist deception make the cut; those who fail are rejected. Right?
Yes.
And there should also be toils and pains and conflicts prescribed for them, in which they will be made to give further proof of the same qualities.
Very right, he said.

And then, I said, we must try them with enchantments — that is the third sort of test — and see how they will behave. Just as those who take colts amid noise and tumult do so to see if they are of a timid nature, so we must take our youth amid terrors of some kind, and again pass them into pleasures, and prove them more thoroughly than gold is proved in the furnace, that we may discover whether they are armed against all enchantments and of a noble bearing always — good guardians of themselves and of the music they have learned, retaining under all circumstances a rhythmical and harmonious nature, such as will be most serviceable to the individual and to the State. And whoever, at every age — as boy, as youth, and in mature life — has come out of the trial victorious and pure, he shall be appointed a ruler and guardian of the State; he shall be honoured in life and in death, and shall receive burial and other memorials of honour, the greatest we have to give. But he who fails, we must reject. I am inclined to think that this is the sort of way in which our rulers and guardians should be chosen and appointed. I speak generally, and not with any pretension to exactness.
Speaking generally, I agree, he said.

And perhaps the word 'guardian' in its fullest sense should apply only to this higher class, who protect us from foreign enemies and keep peace among our own citizens — preventing the ones from wanting to harm us and the others from having the power to. The younger people we previously called guardians would be more properly termed 'auxiliaries' — supporters who carry out the rulers' decisions.
I agree, he said.
Now, how might we devise one of those useful falsehoods we talked about earlier — a single noble lie that might persuade even the rulers themselves, or at least the rest of the citizens?
What kind of lie? he said.

Nothing new, I said — just an old Phoenician tale about something that's supposedly happened in many places before, or so the poets say and have made the world believe. It hasn't happened in our time, and I'm not sure it could be made believable today.
You seem very hesitant to say it!
You'll understand my hesitation when you hear it, I said.
Just say it, he said. Don't be afraid.

All right, here goes — though I honestly don't know how to say this with a straight face, or what words to use for such an audacious fiction. I plan to introduce it gradually, first to the rulers, then to the soldiers, and finally to the general public. They'll be told that their youth and education were a kind of dream. In reality, they were being formed and nourished in the womb of the earth, along with their weapons and equipment. When they were fully made, the earth — their mother — sent them up to the surface. So they must think of their country as their mother and nurse, defend her against attack, and regard their fellow citizens as brothers born from the same earth.
I can see why you were embarrassed to tell that lie, he said.

True, I replied; but there is more to come — I have only told you half. 'Citizens,' we shall say to them in our tale, 'you are brothers, yet God has framed you differently. Some of you have the power of command, and in the composition of these he has mingled gold, wherefore they have the greatest honour; others he has made of silver, to be auxiliaries; others again, who are to be farmers and craftsmen, he has composed of bronze and iron. And the species will generally be preserved in the children. But as all are of the same original stock, a golden parent will sometimes have a silver son, or a silver parent a golden son. And God proclaims as a first principle to the rulers, and above all else, that there is nothing which they should so anxiously guard, or of which they should be such good guardians, as the purity of the race. They should observe what elements are mingled in their offspring; for if the son of a golden or silver parent has an admixture of bronze and iron, then nature orders a transposition of ranks, and the eye of the ruler must not be pitiful towards the child because he has to descend in the scale and become a farmer or artisan — just as there may be sons of artisans who, having an admixture of gold or silver in them, are raised to honour and become guardians or auxiliaries. For an oracle says that when a man of bronze or iron guards the State, it will be destroyed.' Such is the tale; is there any possibility of making our citizens believe in it?
Not in the present generation, he replied; there is no way of accomplishing this. But their sons may be made to believe the tale, and their sons' sons, and posterity after them.

I see the difficulty, I said. But even so, fostering this belief would make people care more about the city and about each other. But enough about the fiction — let it spread on the wings of rumor. Meanwhile, let's arm our earth-born heroes and lead them out under their rulers' command. Let them survey the land and choose the best spot for a camp — a position from which they can suppress any internal rebellion and also defend against external enemies who might descend like wolves on the fold. Once they've set up camp, let them offer sacrifices to the proper gods and prepare their quarters.
Just so, he said.
And their dwellings must be such as will shield them against the cold of winter and the heat of summer.
You mean houses, I assume, he said.
Yes, but soldiers' houses — not shopkeepers' houses.
What's the difference? he said.

I'll try to explain, I said. It would be monstrous and shameful for a shepherd to keep watchdogs that, from lack of discipline or hunger or bad habits, turned on the sheep and attacked them — acting like wolves instead of dogs.
Truly monstrous, he said.
So every precaution must be taken to prevent our auxiliaries, who are stronger than the citizens, from turning into savage tyrants instead of friendly allies.
Yes, great care is needed.
And wouldn't a genuinely good education be the best safeguard?
But they're already well-educated, he said.

I'm not so sure about that, Glaucon. But I am certain that they need to be, and that true education — whatever it turns out to be — will do the most to civilize them in their treatment of each other and of those they protect.
Very true, he said.

And beyond their education, their living conditions and possessions should be arranged so as not to undermine their virtue as guardians or tempt them to prey on the other citizens. Any reasonable person would agree with this.
They would.

Then let's consider how they should live to achieve our aims. First, none of them should own any private property beyond what's strictly necessary. They shouldn't have private houses or storerooms that anyone can't enter. Their provisions should be only what trained warriors of courage and discipline need — nothing more. They should agree to receive a fixed salary from the citizens, enough for the year's expenses and no more, and they should eat together in common messes, like soldiers in camp. As for gold and silver, we'll tell them they already carry a divine metal within their souls and have no need of the human kind. They must not contaminate the sacred with the profane, because that common metal has been the source of countless crimes. Their own gold is pure. They alone among all citizens may never touch, handle, or be under the same roof with gold and silver, nor wear it, nor drink from vessels made of it. This will be their salvation, and they will save the state. But the moment they acquire private homes, land, or money of their own, they'll become property managers and farmers instead of guardians — enemies and tyrants instead of allies of the other citizens. They'll spend their lives in hatred and plots, in far greater terror of internal enemies than external ones. And the hour of ruin for both themselves and the entire state will be at hand. For all these reasons, shouldn't we say that this is how our state should be organized, and these should be the rules for our guardians regarding their houses and everything else?
Yes, said Glaucon.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: At this point Adeimantus broke in with a question: How would you respond, Socrates, if someone said you're making these guardians miserable — and that it's their own fault? The city essentially belongs to them, but they get nothing out of it. Other people acquire land, build fine houses, furnish them beautifully, make their own sacrifices to the gods, and entertain guests. They have gold and silver and everything that supposedly makes people happy. But our guardians are no better than hired soldiers stationed in the city who do nothing but stand guard.

Yes, I said; and you may add that they are only fed, and not paid in addition to their food like other men; so they cannot, even if they wanted to, go on a journey of pleasure — they have no money to spend on a mistress or any other luxurious fancy which, as the world goes, is thought to be happiness. Many other accusations of the same kind could be added.
Right, said he. Let's take all of that as part of the charge.
You want to know how we'd answer? I said.
Yes.

If we proceed along the old path, I said, I believe we shall find the answer. And our answer will be that, even as they are, our guardians may very likely be the happiest of men; but that our aim in founding the State was not the disproportionate happiness of any one class, but the greatest happiness of the whole. We thought that in a State ordered with a view to the good of the whole, we should be most likely to find justice, and in the ill-ordered State, injustice; and, having found them, we could then decide which of the two is the happier. At present, I take it, we are fashioning the happy State not piecemeal, or with a view to making a few citizens happy, but as a whole; and by and by we will proceed to view the opposite kind of State. Suppose we were painting a statue, and someone came up and said, ‘Why don't you put the most beautiful colours on the most beautiful parts of the body? The eyes ought to be purple, but you have made them black.' To him we might fairly answer, ‘Sir, you surely wouldn't have us beautify the eyes to such a degree that they are no longer eyes. Consider rather whether, by giving this and every feature its due proportion, we make the whole beautiful.' And so I say to you: do not compel us to assign to the guardians a sort of happiness which will make them anything but guardians. We too could clothe our husbandmen in royal apparel, and set crowns of gold on their heads, and bid them till the ground as much as they like and no more. Our potters, too, could be allowed to recline on couches and feast by the fireside, passing round the winecup, while their wheel is conveniently at hand, and working at pottery only as much as they please. In this way we might make every class happy — and then, as you imagine, the whole State would be happy. But do not put this idea into our heads; for, if we listen to you, the husbandman will no longer be a husbandman, the potter will cease to be a potter, and no one will have the character of any distinct class in the State. Now this is not of much consequence where the corruption of society, and pretension to be what you are not, is confined to cobblers; but when the guardians of the laws and of the government are only seeming and not real guardians, then see how they turn the State upside down; and on the other hand, they alone have the power of giving order and happiness to the State. We mean our guardians to be true saviours, not destroyers, of the State, whereas our opponent is thinking of peasants at a festival, enjoying a life of revelry, not of citizens doing their duty to the State. But if so, we are speaking of different things, and he is speaking of something which is not a State. Therefore we must consider whether, in appointing our guardians, we should look to their greatest happiness individually, or whether this principle of happiness rather resides in the State as a whole. If the latter is the truth, then the guardians and auxiliaries, and all others equally with them, must be compelled or induced to do their own work in the best way. And thus the whole State will grow up in a noble order, and the several classes will receive the proportion of happiness which nature assigns to them.
I think you're absolutely right.
I wonder if you'll agree with another observation of mine.
What is it?
There seem to be two things that corrupt the crafts.
What are they?
Wealth and poverty.
How do they work?
Think about it: when a potter gets rich, will he still put the same effort into his work?
Certainly not.
He'll get lazier and more careless?
Very true.
And the result is that he becomes a worse potter?
Yes, much worse.
On the other hand, if he's too poor to afford proper tools and materials, his work will suffer just as much, and he won't be able to train his apprentices properly either.
Certainly not.
So whether it's wealth or poverty, both workers and their work suffer?
That's clear.
Here, then, is a discovery of new evils, I said, against which the guardians will have to watch, or they will creep into the city unobserved.
What evils?
Wealth, I said, and poverty: the one is the parent of luxury and indolence, and the other of meanness and viciousness, and both of discontent.

That is very true, he replied; but still I should like to know, Socrates, how our city will be able to go to war, especially against an enemy who is rich and powerful, if deprived of the sinews of war.
There would certainly be a difficulty, I replied, in going to war with one such enemy; but where there are two of them, there is no difficulty at all.
How do you mean? he said.
First, I said, if we have to fight, our side will be trained warriors fighting against an army of rich men.
True, he said.
And do you not suppose, Adeimantus, that a single boxer, perfect in his art, would easily be a match for two stout and well-to-do gentlemen who were not boxers?
Maybe not if they both attacked at once.

What, now, I said, if he were able to run away, and then turn and strike at the one who first came up? And supposing he were to do this several times under the heat of a scorching sun, might he not, being an expert, overturn more than one stout personage?
Certainly, he said. That wouldn't be surprising at all.
And rich men probably have an even bigger advantage in boxing skill compared to their military skill.
Probably.
So we can assume our warriors could handle opponents two or three times their number?
I agree — I think you're right.

And suppose that before the battle, we sent an embassy to one of the two enemy cities, telling the truth: 'We have no gold or silver and aren't allowed to have any. But you do. So join us in the war and take the other city's wealth.' Who, hearing this, would choose to fight against lean, tough dogs rather than join the dogs against fat, tender sheep?
That is not likely; and yet there might be a danger to the poor State if the wealth of many States were to be gathered into one.
How naive of you to call any of those places a 'state'!
Why?

You should use the plural. None of them is really one city — each is many cities, as they say in the game. Every city, however small, is really divided into two: the city of the rich and the city of the poor. These are at war with each other, and within each there are many smaller factions. If you treat them all as a single state, you're completely off the mark. But if you treat them as many and offer the wealth, power, or people of one faction to the others, you'll always have many allies and few enemies. Our state, as long as its wise order is maintained, will be the greatest of all — not in reputation or appearance, but in actual power, even if it has only a thousand defenders. You'll hardly find another state equal to it, among Greeks or non-Greeks, though many will seem as great or many times greater.
That's very true, he said.
And what, I said, will be the best limit for our rulers to fix when they are considering the size of the State and the amount of territory they are to include, and beyond which they will not go?
What limit would you suggest?
The state should grow only as far as it can while remaining unified. That's the proper limit.
Good answer, he said.
Here then, I said, is another order which will have to be conveyed to our guardians: let our city be reckoned neither large nor small, but one and self-sufficing.
That's not too demanding, he said.

And the other, I said, of which we were speaking before, is lighter still — I mean the duty of degrading the offspring of the guardians when inferior, and of elevating into the rank of guardians the offspring of the lower classes when naturally superior. The intention was that, in the case of the citizens generally, each individual should be put to the use for which nature intended him — one man to one work — and then every man would do his own business, and be one and not many; and so the whole city would be one and not many.
Yes, that's not difficult, he said.

The regulations which we are prescribing, my good Adeimantus, are not, as might be supposed, a number of great principles, but trifles all, if care is taken of, as the saying goes, the one great thing — a thing, however, which I would rather call not great, but sufficient for our purpose.
What is it? he asked.

Education, I said, and nurture. If our citizens are well educated and grow into sensible men, they will easily see their way through all these matters, as well as others I omit — such as marriage, the possession of women, and the procreation of children, which will all follow the general principle that friends have all things in common, as the proverb says.
That will be the best approach.

And once a state gets off to a good start, it gains momentum like a wheel. Good education produces good character, and good character taking root in good education improves even further — and this improvement carries forward through generations, just as in animal breeding.
Very likely, he said.

So to sum up: this is the point our rulers must focus on above all else — that the arts and physical training be preserved in their original form, with no innovations allowed. When someone quotes the line about people always wanting
'The newest song the singers have to sing,'

they will be afraid that the poet may be praising, not new songs, but a new kind of song; and this ought not to be praised, nor should it be conceived to be the poet's meaning, for any musical innovation is full of danger to the whole State, and ought to be prohibited. So Damon tells me, and I quite believe him: he says that when the modes of music change, the fundamental laws of the State always change with them.
You can add my vote to Damon's and yours, said Adeimantus.
Then our guardians must build their fortress on the foundation of the arts?
Yes, he said. The lawlessness you describe sneaks in too easily.
Right — it comes in disguised as harmless amusement.

Yes, and it seems harmless enough at first. But gradually this spirit of license finds a home and seeps into people's habits and customs. From there, with growing force, it invades business contracts. From contracts, it moves into laws and the constitution itself, with complete recklessness, until finally, Socrates, it overturns all rights, public and private.
Is that really how it happens? I said.
That's what I believe, he said.
Then, as I was saying, our young people must be trained strictly from the start. If their amusements become lawless and they become lawless themselves, they can never grow into virtuous citizens.
Very true, he said.

But when children make a good start in play and develop habits of order through the arts, this orderliness — so different from the disorder of the others — will follow them through everything and become a force for growth. And if the state's standards ever slip, this habit will restore them.
Very true, he said.
Young people raised this way will discover for themselves the minor rules that their predecessors entirely neglected.
What kind of rules?

I mean such things as these: when the young are to be silent before their elders; how they are to show respect to them by standing and making them sit; what honour is due to parents; what garments or shoes are to be worn; the mode of dressing the hair; deportment and manners in general. Would you agree with me?
Yes.
But I don't think there's much point in legislating about such things. Written laws on these matters are unlikely to be either effective or lasting.
Impossible.
It seems, Adeimantus, that the direction education takes in childhood determines a person's entire future life. Like attracts like.
Of course.
Until it reaches some grand result, which may be good or may be the opposite.
That can't be denied.
And for that reason, I won't try to legislate further about these things.
Naturally enough.

Well, and about the business of the agora, and the ordinary dealings between man and man, or again about agreements with artisans; about insult and injury, or the commencement of actions and the appointment of juries — what would you say? There may also arise questions about any impositions and exactions of market and harbour dues which may be required, and in general about the regulations of markets, police, harbours, and the like. But, oh heavens, shall we condescend to legislate on any of these particulars?
I don't think so, he said. Good people won't need laws imposed on them for these things. They'll figure out whatever regulations are needed soon enough on their own.
Yes, my friend — as long as God preserves the laws we've already given them.
Without divine help, said Adeimantus, they'll spend forever endlessly making and amending their laws and their lives, always hoping to achieve perfection.
Like those chronic invalids, I said, who have no self-control and refuse to change their bad habits?
Exactly.

Yes, I said; and what a delightful life they lead! They are always doctoring themselves, increasing and complicating their disorders, and always fancying that they will be cured by any nostrum which anybody advises them to try.
That's very common with that sort of patient, he said.

And the charming thing is that they consider anyone who tells them the truth their worst enemy — namely, that unless they stop overeating, overdrinking, womanizing, and being lazy, no drug or surgery or spell or charm will help them.
Charming indeed! he said. I see nothing charming about getting angry at someone who tells you what you need to hear.
You're not a fan of these people, I take it.
Not at all.

Nor would you praise the behaviour of States which act like the men I was just describing. For are there not ill-ordered States in which the citizens are forbidden under pain of death to alter the constitution; and yet he who most sweetly courts those who live under this regime, and indulges them and fawns upon them and is skilful in anticipating and gratifying their humours, is held to be a great and good statesman — do not these States resemble the persons I was describing?
They do, he said — these states are just as bad as those individuals, and I'm far from praising them.
But don't you admire the nerve and skill of these eager servants of political corruption?
Yes, he said, I do; but not all of them, for there are some whom the applause of the multitude has deluded into the belief that they are really statesmen, and these are not much to be admired.
What do you mean? Have some sympathy for them. When a man can't measure and a crowd of equally incapable people declare he's four cubits tall, can he help believing them?
I suppose not.

Well, then, do not be angry with them; for are they not as good as a play, trying their hand at paltry reforms such as I was describing? They are always fancying that by legislation they will make an end of frauds in contracts and the other rascalities I was mentioning, not knowing that they are in reality cutting off the heads of a hydra.
Yes, that's exactly what they're doing.

I conceive, I said, that the true legislator will not trouble himself with this class of enactments — whether concerning laws or the constitution — either in an ill-ordered or in a well-ordered State; for in the former they are quite useless, and in the latter there will be no difficulty in devising them; and many of them will naturally flow out of our previous regulations.
Then what work of legislation remains for us? he asked.
Nothing for us, I said. But for Apollo, the god of Delphi, the greatest, noblest, and most important matters remain.
What are those?

The founding of temples and sacrifices, and the whole service of gods, demigods, and heroes. Also the arrangements for the dead, and the rites required to honor those in the world below. We don't know about these things ourselves, and as founders of a city, we'd be foolish to trust any authority other than our ancestral god. He sits at the center, at the navel of the earth, and interprets religion for all of humanity.
You're right — that's what we'll do.

So then, son of Ariston: where in all of this is justice? Now that our city has been built, light a candle and search. Get your brother, Polemarchus, and the rest of our friends to help. Let's find where justice and injustice are, how they differ, and which one a person who wants to be happy should choose — whether or not gods and humans are watching.
That's absurd, said Glaucon. You promised to do the searching yourself, saying it would be impious not to come to justice's defense.
I do not deny that I said so, and, as you remind me, I will be as good as my word; but you must join in the search.
We will, he said.
Here's how I think we can find it: I'll start from the assumption that our state, if properly organized, is perfect.
That's a safe assumption.
And being perfect, it must be wise, brave, self-disciplined, and just.
Clearly.
And whichever of these qualities we identify, the remaining ones will be whatever we haven't yet found.
Right.

If there were four things, and we were searching for one of them, wherever it might be, the one sought for might be known to us from the first, and there would be no further trouble; or we might know the other three first, and then the fourth would clearly be the one left.
Very true, he said.
The same method should work for the virtues, since there are also four.
Obviously.
The first virtue I see in our state is wisdom, and there's something peculiar about it.
What's that?
Our state is said to be wise because it has good judgment?
Very true.
And good judgment is clearly a kind of knowledge. People don't make good decisions through ignorance but through knowledge.
Obviously.
But there are many kinds of knowledge in a state.
Of course.
There is the knowledge of the carpenter; but is that the sort of knowledge which gives a city the title of wise and good in counsel?
Certainly not. That would only give the city a reputation for good woodwork.
Then a city is not to be called wise because it possesses a knowledge which counsels for the best about wooden implements?
Certainly not.
Nor by reason of a knowledge which advises about brazen pots, I said, nor as possessing any other similar knowledge?
None of those.
Nor yet by reason of a knowledge which cultivates the earth; that would give the city the name of agricultural?
Yes.

So here's the key question: is there any knowledge in our newly founded state, held by any group of citizens, that deals not with some particular aspect of the state, but with the state as a whole — considering how it can best manage its internal affairs and its relations with other states?
There certainly is.
What is this knowledge, and who has it?
It is the knowledge of the guardians, he replied, and is found among those whom we were just now describing as perfect guardians.
And what does the city derive from possessing this knowledge?
The reputation of being sound in judgment and truly wise.
And will our city have more of these true guardians, or more blacksmiths?
Far more blacksmiths, he said.
Will not the guardians be the smallest of all the classes who receive a name from the profession of some kind of knowledge?
By far the smallest.

So it's through its smallest part — the ruling and guiding element — and the knowledge residing in that part, that the whole state, constituted according to nature, will be wise. And this class, which nature ordains should be the smallest, possesses the only knowledge worthy of the name wisdom.
Absolutely true.
So we've discovered one of our four virtues and where it lives in the state — more or less satisfactorily, I'd say.
Very satisfactorily, in my humble opinion.
Again, I said, there is no difficulty in seeing the nature of courage, and in what part of the State that quality resides which gives the State the name of courageous.
How do you mean?
When we call a state courageous or cowardly, we're obviously thinking of the part that goes to war on the state's behalf.
Obviously, he said.
The rest of the citizens may be courageous or may be cowardly, but their courage or cowardice will not, as I conceive, have the effect of making the city either the one or the other.
Certainly not.

A city is courageous because of that portion of itself which preserves, under all circumstances, the correct belief about what should and should not be feared — the belief our lawgiver instilled through education. That's what I'm calling courage.
I should like to hear what you are saying once more, for I don't think I perfectly understand you.
Courage is a kind of preservation.
Preservation of what?

Of the opinion respecting things to be feared — what they are and of what nature — which the law implants through education. And I mean by the words ‘under all circumstances' to imply that, in pleasure or in pain, or under the influence of desire or fear, a man preserves and does not lose this opinion. Shall I give you an illustration?
Please.

You know, I said, that dyers, when they want to dye wool for making the true sea-purple, begin by selecting their white colour first; this they prepare and dress with much care and pains, so that the white ground may take the purple hue in full perfection. The dyeing then proceeds; and whatever is dyed in this manner becomes a fast colour, and no washing either with lyes or without them can take away its bloom. But when the ground has not been duly prepared, you will have noticed how poor is the look, whether of purple or of any other colour.
Yes, he said, I know those dyes look washed-out and pathetic.

That's exactly what we were doing when we selected our soldiers and educated them in the arts and physical training. We were contriving influences that would prepare them to absorb the dye of our laws perfectly, so their beliefs about what's dangerous and what's not would be permanently fixed by their upbringing — immune to those powerful solvents: pleasure (the most potent of all), sorrow, fear, and desire. This universal preserving power — the ability to maintain the correct, law-given belief about real and false dangers through everything — that's what I call courage. Unless you disagree.

I don't disagree at all, he said. I assume you mean to distinguish this from the mindless bravery of an untrained person or an animal — that kind of 'courage' isn't what the law prescribes and should have a different name.
Absolutely.
Then I accept your account of courage?

Yes, I said — accept it as the courage of a citizen, and you won't be far wrong. We can examine it more precisely later, but for now we're looking for justice, not courage, and this is sufficient for our purposes.
You're right, he said.
Two virtues remain to be found in the state: self-discipline first, then justice, which is the goal of our whole search.
Exactly.
Can we find justice without dealing with self-discipline?

I do not know how that can be accomplished, he said; nor do I desire that justice should be brought to light and temperance lost sight of. Therefore I wish that you would do me the favour of considering temperance first.
Of course — I wouldn't refuse that request.
Then let's examine it, he said.
All right, I said. As far as I can see, self-discipline is more like a kind of harmony or agreement than the previous virtues.
How so? he asked.

Self-discipline, I said, is the ordering and control of certain pleasures and desires. That's oddly captured in the expression 'being master of yourself,' and you can find traces of the same idea throughout our language.
Certainly, he said.
But isn't 'master of himself' a strange expression? The master would also be the slave, and the slave the master — both refer to the same person.
Of course.

What the expression really means, I think, is that within the human soul there's a better element and a worse one. When the better element controls the worse, we say the person is 'master of himself' — and this is praise. But when the better element, which is also smaller, is overwhelmed by the greater mass of the worse — through bad education or bad company — the person is called a 'slave to himself' and unprincipled.
That makes sense.

And now, I said, look at our newly-created State, and there you will find one of these two conditions realized; for the State, as you will acknowledge, may be justly called master of itself, if the words ‘temperance' and ‘self-mastery' truly express the rule of the better part over the worse.
Yes, he said. I see that what you say is true.

Let me further note that the manifold and complex pleasures, desires, and pains are generally found in children and women and servants, and in the so-called freemen who are of the lowest and more numerous class.
Certainly, he said.
Whereas the simple, moderate desires that follow reason and are guided by good judgment are found in only a few — the best born and best educated.
Very true.
Both groups exist in our state, and the base desires of the many are controlled by the virtuous desires and wisdom of the few.
I see that, he said.
Then if there be any city which may be described as master of its own pleasures and desires, and master of itself, ours may claim such a designation?
Certainly, he said.
And it can also be called self-disciplined, for the same reasons?
Yes.
And if there be any State in which rulers and subjects will be agreed as to the question of who are to rule, that again will be our State?
Without a doubt.
And with this agreement, in which class does self-discipline reside — in the rulers or the subjects?
In both, I'd say, he replied.
Do you see that we weren't far off when we guessed that self-discipline is a kind of harmony?
Why?

Why, because temperance is unlike courage and wisdom, each of which resides in a part only — the one making the State wise, the other valiant; not so temperance, which extends to the whole, and runs through all the notes of the scale, and produces a harmony of the weaker and the stronger and the middle class, whether you suppose them to be stronger or weaker in wisdom, or power, or numbers, or wealth, or anything else. Most truly, then, may we deem temperance to be the agreement of the naturally superior and inferior, as to the right to rule of either, both in states and in individuals.
I completely agree.
Good. So three of the four virtues have been found in our state. The remaining one — the one that completes the state's excellence — must be justice. If only we knew what it was.
Obviously.

The time then has arrived, Glaucon, when, like huntsmen, we should surround the cover and look sharp so that justice does not steal away and pass out of sight and escape us; for beyond a doubt she is somewhere in this country. Watch, therefore, and strive to catch a sight of her, and if you see her first, let me know.
Would that I could! But you should regard me rather as a follower who has just eyes enough to see what you show him — that is about as much as I am good for.
Then join me in a prayer and follow.
Lead the way.
The path is unclear, I said, and the forest is dark and confusing. But we must press on.
Let's go.
Wait — I think I see something! I'm picking up a trail. I don't think our quarry will escape.
Good news! he said.
We've really been quite foolish.
Why?

Why, my good sir, at the beginning of our enquiry, ages ago, there was justice tumbling out at our feet, and we never saw her; nothing could be more ridiculous. Like people who go about looking for what they have in their hands — that was the way with us — we looked not at what we were seeking, but at what was far off in the distance; and therefore, I suppose, we missed her.
What do you mean?
I mean to say that in reality, for a long time past, we have been talking of justice, and have failed to recognise her.
You're taking a long time to get to the point.

Well then, tell me, I said, whether I am right or not: you remember the original principle which we were always laying down at the foundation of the State — that one man should practise one thing only, the thing to which his nature was best adapted; now justice is this principle, or a part of it.
Yes, we said that repeatedly.
And we also said that justice means doing your own work and not meddling in other people's business. We said it many times, and others have said the same.
Yes, we did.
So doing your own work, in a certain sense, is justice. Can you tell me how I arrive at this conclusion?
I can't, but I'd like to hear.

Because I think that this is the only virtue which remains in the State when the other virtues of temperance, courage, and wisdom are abstracted; and that this is the ultimate cause and condition of the existence of all of them, and while remaining in them is also their preservative. And we were saying that if the three were discovered by us, justice would be the fourth, or remaining one.
That necessarily follows.

But here's the test: if we had to decide which of these four contributes most to the state's excellence — the agreement between rulers and subjects, the soldiers' preservation of correct beliefs about dangers, the wisdom and vigilance of the rulers, or this other quality I'm describing, found in everyone from children to rulers — the quality of each person doing their own work and not meddling in others' — it would be hard to say which matters most.
It certainly would be difficult, he said.
So the power of each person doing their own work seems to compete with the other political virtues: wisdom, self-discipline, and courage.
Yes, he said.
And the virtue that competes with them is justice?
Exactly.
Let us look at the question from another point of view. Are not the rulers in a State those to whom you would entrust the office of determining suits at law?
Certainly.
And are suits decided on any other ground but that a man may neither take what is another's, nor be deprived of what is his own?
Yes, that's the principle.
And that's a just principle?
Yes.
Then on this view also, justice will be admitted to be the having and doing what is a man's own, and what belongs to him?
Very true.

Think, now, and say whether you agree with me or not. Suppose a carpenter to be doing the business of a cobbler, or a cobbler of a carpenter; and suppose them to exchange their implements or their duties, or the same person to be doing the work of both — or whatever the change — do you think that any great harm would result to the State?
Not much.

But when the cobbler, or any other man whom nature designed to be a trader, having his heart lifted up by wealth, or strength, or the number of his followers, or any like advantage, attempts to force his way into the class of warriors, or a warrior into that of legislators and guardians for which he is unfitted, and either takes the implements or the duties of the other; or when one man is trader, legislator, and warrior all in one — then I think you will agree with me in saying that this interchange and this meddling of one with another is the ruin of the State.
Absolutely.
So when three distinct classes meddle in each other's business, or one class tries to become another, that's the greatest harm to the state and would be rightly called the worst kind of wrongdoing?
Precisely.
And the greatest wrongdoing against one's own city is what you'd call injustice?
Certainly.
That, then, is injustice. Conversely, when traders, auxiliaries, and guardians each mind their own business — that's justice, and that's what will make the city just.
I agree completely.

We will not, I said, be over-positive as yet; but if, on trial, this conception of justice be verified in the individual as well as in the State, there will be no longer any room for doubt; if it be not verified, we must have a fresh enquiry. First let us complete the old investigation which we began, as you remember, under the impression that if we could previously examine justice on the larger scale, there would be less difficulty in discerning her in the individual. That larger example appeared to be the State, and accordingly we constructed as good a one as we could, knowing well that in the good State justice would be found. Let the discovery which we made be now applied to the individual: if they agree, we shall be satisfied; or, if there be a difference in the individual, we will come back to the State and have another trial of the theory. The friction of the two, when rubbed together, may possibly strike a light in which justice will shine forth, and the vision which is then revealed we will fix in our souls.
Good method. Let's do it.
I proceeded to ask: when two things, a greater and a lesser, are called by the same name, are they alike or unlike in so far as they are called the same?
Alike, he said.
So the just person, considered purely in terms of justice, will be like the just state?
He will.

And a State was thought by us to be just when the three classes in the State severally did their own business; and also thought to be temperate and valiant and wise by reason of certain other affections and qualities of these same classes?
True, he said.

And so of the individual; we may assume that he has the same three principles in his own soul which are found in the State, and he may be rightly described in the same terms, because he is affected in the same manner?
Necessarily, he said.
Here we are again, my friend, stumbling onto an easy question: does the soul have these three elements or not?
Easy? Hardly, Socrates! The proverb is right: the good is hard.

So it seems. And honestly, I don't think our current method is rigorous enough to answer this precisely. The truly accurate method would be much longer. But we can reach a conclusion that's at least as good as what we've established so far.
That would satisfy me under the circumstances, he said.
And me too, I said.
Then don't give up, he said.

Must we not acknowledge, I said, that in each of us there are the same principles and habits which exist in the State? And that from the individual they pass into the State — how else could they come there? Take the quality of passion or spirit: it would be ridiculous to imagine that this quality, when found in States, is not derived from the individuals who are supposed to possess it — for example, the Thracians, Scythians, and in general the northern nations. The same may be said of the love of knowledge, which is the special characteristic of our part of the world, or of the love of money, which may with equal truth be attributed to the Phoenicians and Egyptians.
Exactly, he said.
That's not hard to see.
Not at all.

But the harder question is this: do we do everything with our whole soul, or are there three distinct parts — one that reasons, one that gets angry, and one that desires? Do we learn with one part, feel spirited with another, and experience appetite with a third? Or does the whole soul engage in each activity? That's the real difficulty.
Yes, he said, that is the difficulty.
Let's try to determine whether these are the same or different.
How? he asked.

The same thing obviously cannot do or undergo opposite things at the same time, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object. So whenever we find this happening in something, we'll know we're dealing with more than one thing.
Good.
For example, can the same thing be at rest and in motion at the same time, in the same respect?
Impossible.

Still, I said, let us have a more precise statement of terms, lest we should hereafter fall out by the way. Imagine the case of a man who is standing and also moving his hands and his head, and suppose a person to say that one and the same person is in motion and at rest at the same moment. To such a mode of speech we should object, and should rather say that one part of him is in motion while another is at rest.
Very true.

And suppose the objector to refine still further, and to draw the nice distinction that not only parts of tops, but whole tops, when they spin round with their pegs fixed on the spot, are at rest and in motion at the same time (and he may say the same of anything which revolves in the same spot) — his objection would not be admitted by us, because in such cases things are not at rest and in motion in the same parts of themselves; we should rather say that they have both an axis and a circumference, and that the axis stands still, for there is no deviation from the perpendicular; and that the circumference goes round. But if, while revolving, the axis inclines either to the right or left, forwards or backwards, then in no point of view can they be said to be at rest.
That's the correct description, he said.
So no such objection will confuse us or make us believe the same thing can simultaneously do or undergo opposites in the same part, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object.
It certainly won't confuse me, he said.

Yet, I said, that we may not be compelled to examine all such objections, and prove at length that they are untrue, let us assume their absurdity, and go forward on the understanding that hereafter, if this assumption turns out to be untrue, all the consequences which follow shall be withdrawn.
Yes, that's the best approach.

Well, I said, would you not allow that assent and dissent, desire and aversion, attraction and repulsion, are all of them opposites, whether they are regarded as active or passive — for that makes no difference in the fact of their opposition?
Yes, they're opposites.

Well, I said, and hunger and thirst, and the desires in general, and again willing and wishing — all these you would refer to the classes already mentioned. You would say — would you not? — that the soul of him who desires is seeking after the object of his desire; or that he is drawing to himself the thing which he wishes to possess; or again, when a person wants anything to be given him, his mind, longing for the realization of his desire, intimates his wish to have it by a nod of assent, as if he had been asked a question?
Very true.
And what would you say of unwillingness and dislike, and the absence of desire; should not these be referred to the opposite class of repulsion and rejection?
Certainly.
Admitting this to be true of desire generally, let us suppose a particular class of desires, and out of these we will select hunger and thirst, as they are termed, which are the most obvious of them.
All right, he said.
The object of one is food, and of the other, drink?
Yes.

And here comes the point: is not thirst the desire which the soul has of drink, and of drink only — not of drink qualified by anything else; for example, warm or cold, or much or little, or, in a word, drink of any particular sort? But if the thirst be accompanied by heat, then the desire is of cold drink; or, if accompanied by cold, then of warm drink; or, if the thirst be excessive, then the drink which is desired will be excessive; or, if not great, the quantity of drink will also be small. But thirst pure and simple will desire drink pure and simple, which is the natural satisfaction of thirst, as food is of hunger?
Yes, he said. Each simple desire is for its simple object, and a qualified desire is for a qualified object.

But we need to guard against a potential confusion. Someone might object that nobody desires just 'drink' — they desire good drink. And nobody desires just 'food' — they desire good food. Since good is the universal object of desire, thirst must really be thirst for good drink, and likewise for every other desire.
That objection might seem to have some force, he said.
But I'd maintain that among relative terms, some are qualified and their correlatives are qualified too, while others are simple and have simple correlatives.
I don't understand what you mean.
Well, you know that 'greater' is relative to 'less'?
Of course.
And 'much greater' is relative to 'much less'?
Yes.
And the sometime greater to the sometime less, and the greater that is to be to the less that is to be?
Certainly, he said.

And so of more and less, and of other correlative terms, such as the double and the half, or again, the heavier and the lighter, the swifter and the slower; and of hot and cold, and of any other relatives — is not this true of all of them?
Yes.

And does not the same principle hold in the sciences? The object of science is knowledge (assuming that to be the true definition), but the object of a particular science is a particular kind of knowledge. I mean, for example, that the science of house-building is a kind of knowledge which is defined and distinguished from other kinds, and is therefore termed architecture.
Certainly.
Because it has a specific quality that no other kind has?
Yes.
And it has that quality because it has a specific kind of object. The same is true of all other arts and sciences?
Yes.

Now, then, if I have made myself clear, you will understand my original meaning in what I said about relatives. My meaning was that if one term of a relation is taken alone, the other is taken alone; if one term is qualified, the other is also qualified. I do not mean to say that relatives may not be disparate, or that the science of health is healthy, or of disease necessarily diseased, or that the sciences of good and evil are therefore good and evil; but only that, when the term ‘science' is no longer used absolutely, but has a qualified object which in this case is the nature of health and disease, it becomes defined, and is hence called not merely science, but the science of medicine.
I fully understand, and I agree.
Now, wouldn't you say thirst is one of those relative terms with a clear correlative —
Yes — thirst is relative to drink.

And a specific kind of thirst is relative to a specific kind of drink. But thirst in itself is for neither much nor little, neither good nor bad, nor any particular kind of drink — just drink in itself?
Absolutely.
So the thirsty soul, insofar as it's thirsty, wants nothing but drink. That's what it yearns for and tries to get.
Clearly.

And if you suppose something which pulls a thirsty soul away from drink, that must be different from the thirsty principle which draws him like a beast to drink; for, as we were saying, the same thing cannot at the same time, with the same part of itself, act in contrary ways about the same thing.
Impossible.
No more than you can say that the hands of the archer push and pull the bow at the same time; what you say is that one hand pushes and the other pulls.
Exactly, he said.
Now, can someone be thirsty and yet not want to drink?
Yes, he said, that happens all the time.
Then what do we say? Isn't there something in the soul urging the person to drink, and something else holding them back — something different from and stronger than the urge to drink?
I'd say so.
And the restraining element comes from reason, while the driving and attracting element comes from bodily states and conditions?
Clearly.

Then we can reasonably assume these are two distinct elements: the part we reason with, which we'll call the rational element, and the part that craves, hungers, thirsts, and feels the pull of all desires, which we'll call the irrational or appetitive element — the companion of various pleasures and satisfactions.
Yes, it's reasonable to regard them as different, he said.
Good — so we've established two elements in the soul. But what about spirit, or passion? Is it a third element, or is it the same as one of the other two?
I'd be inclined to say it's a kind of desire.

Well, let me tell you a story I once heard and believe. Leontius, son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus along the outside of the north wall when he noticed some corpses lying at the place of execution. He felt a desire to look at them but also felt disgust and tried to turn away. For a while he struggled and covered his eyes. But finally the desire overpowered him, and he forced his eyes open and ran toward the bodies, saying: 'There — look, you wretches! Take your fill of this lovely sight!'
I've heard that story too, he said.
The moral of the tale is that anger at times goes to war with desire, as though they were two distinct things.
Yes, that's the meaning, he said.

And are there not many other cases in which we observe that, when a man's desires violently prevail over his reason, he reviles himself, and is angry at the violence within him; and that in this struggle — which is like the struggle of factions in a State — his spirit is on the side of his reason? But for the passionate or spirited element to take part with the desires when reason decides that she should not be opposed is a sort of thing which I believe you never observed occurring in yourself, nor, as I should imagine, in any one else?
Certainly not.

And consider this: when a person believes he's wronged someone, the nobler he is, the less he can bring himself to resent whatever suffering the wronged person inflicts on him — hunger, cold, or any other hardship. He considers such punishment just, and his spirit refuses to be stirred up against it.
True, he said.

But when a person believes he's the one being wronged, then he boils and rages, siding with what he believes is just. No matter how much hunger, cold, or other suffering he endures, he perseveres and fights on until he either wins or dies — or until reason, like a shepherd calling back his dog, tells his spirit to stand down.
That's a perfect analogy, he said. And in our state, we said the auxiliaries would be like dogs obeying the rulers, who are their shepherds.
I perceive, I said, that you quite understand me; there is, however, a further point which I wish you to consider.
What's that?

You remember that passion, or spirit, appeared at first sight to be a kind of desire, but now we should say quite the contrary; for in the conflict of the soul, spirit is arrayed on the side of the rational principle.
Absolutely.
