But is spirit different from reason too, or just a form of reason? If it's the latter, the soul has only two elements — rational and appetitive — rather than three. Or, just as the state had three classes (traders, auxiliaries, and rulers), might there be a third element in the soul — spirit — that naturally supports reason when it hasn't been corrupted by bad upbringing?
Yes, there must be a third, he said.
Yes, I replied, if passion — which has already been shown to be different from desire — turns out also to be different from reason.
And that's easy to prove. You can see it even in young children: they're full of spirit almost from birth, but some never seem to develop reason at all, and most develop it rather late.

Excellent, I said; and you may see passion equally in brute animals, which is a further proof of the truth of what you are saying. And we may once more appeal to the words of Homer, which have already been quoted by us,
'He struck his chest and rebuked his heart.'
In this verse, Homer clearly treats the part that reasons about better and worse as different from the unreasoning anger that it rebukes.
Very true, he said.
And so, after much tossing, we have reached land, and are fairly agreed that the same principles which exist in the State exist also in the individual, and that they are three in number.
Exactly.
Doesn't it follow that the individual is wise in the same way and by the same quality that makes the state wise?
Certainly.
And the same quality that makes the state brave makes the individual brave, and the same relationship between the individual and every other virtue holds true?
Absolutely.
And the individual will be acknowledged by us to be just in the same way in which the State is just?
That follows necessarily.
We can't have forgotten that the state's justice consisted in each of the three classes doing its own work?
I don't think we've forgotten.
We must recollect that the individual in whom the several qualities of his nature do their own work will be just, and will do his own work?
Yes, we must remember that too.
Shouldn't the rational element rule, since it's wise and responsible for the whole soul? And shouldn't the spirited element be its ally and subject?
Certainly.

And as we said, the combined influence of the arts and physical training will bring them into harmony — strengthening reason with noble ideas and education, while moderating and civilizing the wildness of spirit through rhythm and harmony?
Exactly, he said.

And these two, thus nurtured and educated, and having learned truly to know their own functions, will rule over the concupiscent — which in each of us is the largest part of the soul, and by nature most insatiable of gain. Over this they will keep guard, lest, waxing great and strong with the fulness of bodily pleasures (as they are termed), the concupiscent soul, no longer confined to her own sphere, should attempt to enslave and rule those who are not her natural-born subjects, and so overturn the whole life of man.
Very true, he said.

Together, these two will be the best defenders of the whole soul and body against external threats — one providing counsel, the other fighting under the leader's direction and bravely carrying out his commands.
True.
We call a person brave when their spirited element preserves, through pleasure and pain, reason's commands about what should and shouldn't be feared?
Right, he said.

And him we call wise who has in him that little part which rules and which proclaims these commands — that part being supposed to have a knowledge of what is for the interest of each of the three parts and of the whole?
Certainly.

And a person is self-disciplined when all three elements are in friendly harmony — when the ruling principle of reason and the two subordinate principles of spirit and appetite all agree that reason should rule, without rebellion?
Certainly, he said. That's the true account of self-discipline in both the state and the individual.
And surely, I said, we have explained again and again how and by virtue of what quality a man will be just.
Yes, we certainly have.
And is justice dimmer in the individual, and is her form different, or is she the same which we found her to be in the State?
There's no difference, in my opinion.
Because, if any doubt is still lingering in our minds, a few commonplace instances will satisfy us of the truth of what I am saying.
What kind of examples?

If the case were put to us, must we not admit that the just State, or the man who is trained in the principles of such a State, will be less likely than the unjust to make away with a deposit of gold or silver? Would any one deny this?
No one, he said.
Will the just man or citizen ever be guilty of sacrilege or theft, or treachery either to his friends or to his country?
Never.
Would he ever break his oaths or agreements?
Impossible.
No one will be less likely than the just man to commit adultery, or to dishonour his father and mother, or to fail in his religious duties?
No one.
And the reason is that each part of his soul is doing its own work, whether ruling or being ruled?
Exactly.
Are you satisfied that this quality — what makes both states and people like this — is justice? Or do you hope to discover something else?
No, I'm satisfied.
Then our dream has come true! Remember the suspicion we had at the very start, that some divine power must have guided us to a basic form of justice?
Yes, certainly.

And the division of labour which required the carpenter and the shoemaker and the rest of the citizens to be doing each his own business, and not another's, was a shadow of justice, and for that reason it was of use?
Clearly.

But in reality, justice was such as we were describing, being concerned however not with the outward man, but with the inward, which is the true self and concernment of man. For the just man does not permit the several elements within him to interfere with one another, or any of them to do the work of others; he sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself. When he has bound together the three principles within him — which may be compared to the higher, lower, and middle notes of the scale, and the intermediate intervals — when he has bound all these together, and is no longer many, but has become one entirely temperate and perfectly adjusted nature, then he proceeds to act, if he has to act, whether in a matter of property, or in the treatment of the body, or in some affair of politics or private business; always thinking and calling that which preserves and cooperates with this harmonious condition just and good action, and the knowledge which presides over it, wisdom; and that which at any time impairs this condition, he will call unjust action, and the opinion which presides over it, ignorance.
Socrates, you've spoken the exact truth.
Very good; and if we were to affirm that we had discovered the just man and the just State, and the nature of justice in each of them, we should not be telling a falsehood?
Certainly not.
Can we say so, then?
Let's say so.
Now we need to consider injustice.
Clearly.

Injustice must be a conflict among the three elements — meddling, interference, and rebellion of one part against the whole. It's the attempt by a subordinate part to seize unlawful authority, like a subject revolting against a rightful ruler. This confusion and disorder is injustice, and also intemperance, cowardice, ignorance — every form of vice.
Exactly.
And if the nature of justice and injustice is known, then the meaning of acting unjustly and being unjust, or again of acting justly, will also be perfectly clear?
What do you mean? he said.
Why, I said, they are like disease and health — being in the soul just what disease and health are in the body.
How? he said.
What's healthy causes health; what's unhealthy causes disease.
Yes.
And just actions produce justice; unjust actions produce injustice?
Certainly.

And the creation of health is the institution of a natural order and government of one by another in the parts of the body; and the creation of disease is the production of a state of things at variance with this natural order?
True.

And is not the creation of justice the institution of a natural order and government of one by another in the parts of the soul? And the creation of injustice the production of a state of things at variance with the natural order?
Exactly, he said.
Then virtue is the health and beauty and well-being of the soul, and vice the disease and weakness and deformity of the same?
True.
And good practices lead to virtue, bad practices to vice?
Certainly.

But we still haven't answered our original question about the comparative benefit of justice versus injustice. Which is more profitable: to be just and act justly, whether or not gods and men are watching? Or to be unjust and act unjustly, as long as you escape punishment and reform?

Socrates, the question has become absurd at this point. We know that when the body's constitution breaks down, life is unbearable even with every luxury and all the power in the world. And shall we be told that life is still worth living when the soul's vital principle is corrupted and destroyed — as long as the person can do whatever they want, except acquire justice and virtue, or escape injustice and vice? Given what we've shown these to be?
Yes, I said, the question is, as you say, ridiculous. Still, as we are near the spot at which we may see the truth in the clearest manner with our own eyes, let us not faint by the way.
Absolutely not, he said.
Come up here then, I said, and look down at the many forms of vice — at least the ones worth examining.
Lead the way, he said.

I said: The argument seems to have reached a height from which, as from some tower of speculation, a man may look down and see that virtue is one, but that the forms of vice are innumerable — there being four special ones which are deserving of note.
What do you mean? he said.
I mean, I replied, that there appear to be as many forms of the soul as there are distinct forms of the State.
How many?
Five types of government and five corresponding types of soul, I said.
What are they?
The first, I said, is the form we've been describing. It can be called either monarchy or aristocracy, depending on whether one exceptional person rules or several.
True, he said.

But I regard the two names as describing one form only; for whether the government is in the hands of one or of many, if the governors have been trained in the manner which we have supposed, the fundamental laws of the State will be maintained.
That's true, he said.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: So that's the good and true state, and the good and true person follows the same pattern. If this form is right, every other is wrong. And the corruption takes four forms, affecting both the organization of the state and the character of the individual soul.
What are they? he said.

I was proceeding to tell the order in which the four evil forms appeared to me to succeed one another, when Polemarchus, who was sitting a little way off, just beyond Adeimantus, began to whisper to him. Stretching forth his hand, he took hold of the upper part of his coat by the shoulder and drew him towards him, leaning forward so as to be quite close, and saying something in his ear, of which I only caught the words, ‘Shall we let him off, or what shall we do?'
Certainly not, said Adeimantus, raising his voice.
Who won't you let off? I asked.
You, he said.
Why me in particular?

Because we think you're being lazy and trying to cheat us out of a whole major section of the argument. You think you can slip past us with that casual remark that 'in the matter of women and children, friends share everything in common' — as if that were self-evident!
And wasn't I right, Adeimantus?

Yes, he said; but what is right in this particular case, like everything else, requires to be explained; for community may be of many kinds. Please, therefore, say what sort of community you mean. We have been long expecting that you would tell us something about the family life of your citizens — how they will bring children into the world, and rear them when they have arrived, and, in general, what the nature of this community of women and children is. For we are of opinion that the right or wrong management of such matters will have a great and paramount influence on the State for good or evil. And now, since the question is still undetermined, and you are taking in hand another State, we have resolved, as you heard, not to let you go until you give an account of all this.
Count me in on that resolution, said Glaucon.
And you can consider us all equally agreed, said Thrasymachus.

I said, You know not what you are doing in thus assailing me. What an argument are you raising about the State! Just as I thought I had finished, and was only too glad that I had laid this question to sleep, and was reflecting how fortunate I was in your acceptance of what I then said, you ask me to begin again at the very foundation, ignorant of what a hornet's nest of words you are stirring up. Now I foresaw this gathering trouble, and avoided it.
What do you think we came here for? said Thrasymachus. To prospect for gold, or to hear ideas?
Ideas, yes — but ideas should have a limit.

Socrates, said Glaucon, a whole lifetime is the only limit that wise people set on listening to discussions like these. Don't worry about us — just take heart and answer the question your own way. What kind of community of women and children will there be among our guardians? How will the period from birth to education be managed — since that seems to need the most care? Tell us how you'd handle it.

Yes, my friend, but the answer is far from easy. Many more doubts arise here than about anything we've discussed before. People will question whether what I'm describing is even possible, and even if possible, whether it's actually desirable. So I'm reluctant to tackle the subject — I'm afraid my ideas will turn out to be nothing more than wishful thinking.
Don't be afraid, he said. Your audience won't be hard on you. They're not skeptical or hostile.
I take it you're trying to encourage me with those words, my friend.
Yes, he said.

Then let me tell you that you are doing just the reverse; the encouragement which you offer would have been all very well had I myself believed that I knew what I was talking about. To declare the truth about matters of high interest which a man honours and loves among wise men who love him need occasion no fear or faltering in his mind; but to carry on an argument when you are yourself only a hesitating enquirer, which is my condition, is a dangerous and slippery thing. And the danger is not that I shall be laughed at (of which the fear would be childish), but that I shall miss the truth where I have most need to be sure of my footing, and drag my friends after me in my fall. And I pray Nemesis not to visit upon me the words I am going to utter. For I do indeed believe that to be an involuntary homicide is a less crime than to be a deceiver about beauty, or goodness, or justice in the matter of laws. And that is a risk which I would rather run among enemies than among friends, and therefore you do well to encourage me.
Glaucon laughed and said: Well then, Socrates, if your argument does us any harm, we'll acquit you in advance of intellectual homicide and clear you of deception. Speak with confidence.
Fair enough, I said. The law says that once acquitted, a person is free from guilt. And what holds in law may hold in argument.
Then why hesitate?

Well, I replied, I suppose that I must retrace my steps and say what I perhaps ought to have said before in the proper place. The part of the men has been played out, and now, properly enough, comes the turn of the women. Of them I will proceed to speak, and the more readily since I am invited by you.

For people born and educated like our citizens, I think the only way to settle the question of women and children is to follow the path we started on, when we said the men were to be guardians and watchdogs of the community.
True.
Let us further suppose the birth and education of our women to be subject to similar or nearly similar regulations; then we shall see whether the result accords with our design.
What do you mean?

What I mean may be put into the form of a question, I said: are dogs divided into hes and shes, or do they both share equally in hunting and in keeping watch and in the other duties of dogs? Or do we entrust to the males the entire and exclusive care of the flocks, while we leave the females at home, under the idea that the bearing and suckling of their puppies is labour enough for them?
No, he said — they share alike. The only difference is that males are stronger and females weaker.
But can you use different animals for the same purpose unless they're bred and raised the same way?
You can't.
So if women are to have the same duties as men, they must have the same education?
Yes.
The education we assigned to men was the arts and physical training.
Yes.
Then women must also learn the arts, physical training, and the art of war, and must practice them alongside men?
That seems to follow.
I expect, I said, that many of our proposals will seem ridiculous if they're actually carried out.
No doubt.

And the most ridiculous sight of all will be women exercising naked in the training grounds alongside men, especially the older women. They certainly won't be a pretty picture — any more than those enthusiastic old men who keep coming to the gym despite their wrinkles and sagging bodies.
Yes indeed, he said. That would look pretty ridiculous by today's standards.

But since we've committed to speaking our minds, we mustn't be afraid of the jokes that wits will aim at this kind of innovation — all the comedy about women learning the arts and physical training, and especially about them wearing armor and riding horses!
Very true.

Still, having begun, we must push forward through the rough terrain. Let's ask these comedians to be serious for once. Not long ago, Greeks considered it shameful and ridiculous for men to be seen naked — as many non-Greek peoples still do today. When the Cretans and then the Spartans first introduced public nudity, the wits of the time no doubt mocked it just as much.
No doubt.

But when experience showed that to let all things be uncovered was far better than to cover them up, and the ludicrous effect to the outward eye vanished before the better principle which reason asserted, then the man was perceived to be a fool who directs the shafts of his ridicule at any other sight but that of folly and vice, or seriously inclines to weigh the beautiful by any other standard but that of the good.
Very true.

So first, whether we're joking or serious, let's settle the fundamental question: is it in women's nature to share in all the activities of men, or in none, or in some but not others? And specifically, is warfare one of those activities they can share in? This will give us the best starting point and lead to the fairest conclusion.
That's the best approach.
Shall we take the other side first and begin by arguing against ourselves? In this way the adversary's position will not be undefended.
Why not? he said.

Then let us put a speech into the mouths of our opponents. They will say: ‘Socrates and Glaucon, no adversary need convict you, for you yourselves, at the first foundation of the State, admitted the principle that everybody was to do the one work suited to his own nature.' And certainly, if I am not mistaken, such an admission was made by us. ‘And do not the natures of men and women differ very much indeed?' And we shall reply: Of course they do. Then we shall be asked, ‘Whether the tasks assigned to men and to women should not be different, and such as are agreeable to their different natures?' Certainly they should. ‘But if so, have you not fallen into a serious inconsistency in saying that men and women, whose natures are so entirely different, ought to perform the same actions?' What defence will you make for us, my good sir, against any one who offers these objections?
That is not an easy question to answer when asked suddenly; and I shall, and I do, beg of you to draw out the case on our side.

These are the objections, Glaucon, and there are many others of a like kind, which I foresaw long ago; they made me afraid and reluctant to take in hand any law about the possession and nurture of women and children.
I can see why, he said. This problem is anything but easy.
Why yes, I said, but the fact is that when a man is out of his depth, whether he has fallen into a little swimming bath or into mid-ocean, he has to swim all the same.
Very true.
So we'd better swim and try to reach shore. Maybe a dolphin will save us, like the one that saved Arion.
I suppose so, he said.

Well then, let us see if any way of escape can be found. We acknowledged — did we not? — that different natures ought to have different pursuits, and that men's and women's natures are different. And now what are we saying? — that different natures ought to have the same pursuits. This is the inconsistency which is charged upon us.
Precisely.
The art of verbal contradiction is truly powerful, Glaucon!
Why do you say that?

Because I think that many a man falls into the practice against his will. When he thinks that he is reasoning, he is really disputing, just because he cannot define and divide, and so know that of which he is speaking; and he will pursue a merely verbal opposition in the spirit of contention and not of fair discussion.
Yes, he replied, such is very often the case; but what has that to do with us and our argument?
A great deal. We're in danger of falling into exactly this kind of verbal dispute.
How so?

We've been bravely insisting on the verbal truth that different natures should have different occupations. But we never stopped to ask what we actually meant by 'sameness' or 'difference' of nature, or what kinds of difference are relevant to assigning different occupations.
No, he said, we never considered that.

I said: Suppose, by way of illustration, we were to ask the question whether there is not an opposition in nature between bald men and hairy men; and if this is admitted by us, then, if bald men are cobblers, we should forbid the hairy men to be cobblers, and conversely?
That would be absurd, he said.

Absurd — and for a good reason. When we founded the state, we never meant that every difference in nature should determine different occupations. We only meant differences relevant to the occupation in question. A doctor and someone with a doctor's mind have the same nature in the relevant sense.
True.
While a doctor and a carpenter have different natures?
Certainly.

So if men and women turn out to differ in their aptitude for a specific art or occupation, then we should assign that occupation to one sex or the other. But if the only difference is that women bear children and men beget them, that doesn't prove women are different from men in any way relevant to education. We should continue to maintain that our guardians and their wives should share the same occupations.
Very true, he said.
Next, we shall ask our opponent how, in reference to any of the pursuits or arts of civic life, the nature of a woman differs from that of a man?
That's fair.
And perhaps he, like yourself, will reply that to give a sufficient answer on the instant is not easy; but after a little reflection there is no difficulty.
Perhaps.

Suppose then that we invite him to accompany us in the argument, and then we may hope to show him that there is nothing peculiar in the constitution of women which would affect them in the administration of the State.
By all means.

Let us say to him: Come now, and we will ask you a question — when you spoke of a nature gifted or not gifted in any respect, did you mean to say that one man will acquire a thing easily, another with difficulty; that a little learning will lead the one to discover a great deal, whereas the other, after much study and application, no sooner learns than he forgets; or again, did you mean that the one has a body which is a good servant to his mind, while the body of the other is a hindrance to him? Would not these be the sort of differences which distinguish the man gifted by nature from the one who is ungifted?
No one would deny that.

And can you mention any pursuit of mankind in which the male sex has not all these gifts and qualities in a higher degree than the female? Need I waste time in speaking of the art of weaving, and the management of pancakes and preserves, in which womankind does really appear to be great, and in which for her to be beaten by a man is of all things the most absurd?
You are quite right, he replied, in maintaining the general inferiority of the female sex: although many women are in many things superior to many men, yet on the whole what you say is true.

And if so, my friend, I said, there is no special faculty of administration in a state which a woman has because she is a woman, or which a man has by virtue of his sex, but the gifts of nature are alike diffused in both; all the pursuits of men are the pursuits of women also, but in all of them a woman is inferior to a man.
Very true.
Then shall we impose all our rules on men and none on women?
That would be absurd.
One woman has a gift of healing, another not; one is a musician, and another has no music in her nature?
Very true.
And one woman has an aptitude for athletics and military service, while another is unwarlike and hates exercise?
Certainly.
And one woman is philosophical, another is hostile to philosophy. One is spirited, another lacks spirit?
That's true too.
So one woman will have the guardian temperament and another won't. Wasn't it qualities like these that determined which men we selected as guardians?
Yes.
Men and women alike possess the qualities that make a guardian. They differ only in degree of strength.
Obviously.
So women with these qualities should be selected as companions and colleagues of men with the same qualities, since they're alike in capacity and character?
Very true.
And shouldn't the same natures have the same occupations?
They should.
Then, as we were saying before, there is nothing unnatural in assigning music and gymnastic to the wives of the guardians — to that point we come round again.
Certainly not.
The law we established was in harmony with nature and therefore not impossible or utopian. The current practice, which contradicts it, is what actually violates nature.
That seems to be true.
We needed to establish two things: first, that our proposals are possible; second, that they're beneficial.
Yes.
And the possibility has been established?
Yes.
Now we need to show the great benefit?
Exactly.
You'd agree that the same education that makes a man a good guardian will also make a woman a good guardian, since their fundamental nature is the same?
Yes.
Let me ask you something.
What?
Would you say all people are equally excellent, or that some are better than others?
Some are better.
And in the commonwealth which we were founding, do you conceive the guardians who have been brought up on our model system to be more perfect men, or the cobblers whose education has been cobbling?
What a ridiculous question!
You've answered it, I said. So may we also say that our guardians are the best citizens?
By far.
And their wives will be the best women?
Yes, by far.
And can there be anything better for the interests of the State than that the men and women of a State should be as good as possible?
Nothing.
And that's what education in the arts and physical training, as we've described it, will accomplish?
Certainly.
So our proposal is not only possible but maximally beneficial to the state?
True.

Then let the guardians' wives strip for exercise — their virtue will be their clothing — and share in warfare and the defense of the state. We'll assign lighter tasks to women, since they're the physically weaker sex, but otherwise their duties will be the same as men's. And anyone who laughs at the sight of women exercising for the noblest reasons is plucking
'An unripe fruit of wisdom,'
and he himself is ignorant of what he is laughing at, or what he is about; for that is, and ever will be, the best of sayings: that the useful is the noble and the hurtful is the base.
Very true.

Here, then, is one difficulty in our law about women, which we may say that we have now escaped; the wave has not swallowed us up alive for enacting that the guardians of either sex should have all their pursuits in common; to the utility and also to the possibility of this arrangement, the consistency of the argument with itself bears witness.
A mighty wave indeed, and you've made it through, he said.
You won't think it was so mighty when you see the next one, I said.
Let me see it.

The next law, which follows from everything before it, is this: the guardians' wives shall be held in common, and their children shall be raised in common. No parent shall know their own child, nor any child their parent.
That's a much bigger wave, he said. The possibility and the usefulness of such a law are both much more questionable.
I don't think the usefulness can be seriously disputed, I said. Having wives and children in common would bring enormous benefits. The real question is whether it's possible.
I think serious doubts can be raised about both, he said.

You imply that the two questions must be combined, I replied. Now I meant that you should admit the utility; and in this way, as I thought, I should escape from one of them, and then there would remain only the possibility.
Your escape attempt has been detected. You'll have to defend both.

Well, I said, I submit to my fate. Yet grant me a little favour: let me feast my mind with the dream as day-dreamers are in the habit of feasting themselves when they are walking alone. For before they have discovered any means of effecting their wishes — that is a matter which never troubles them — they would rather not tire themselves by thinking about possibilities; but assuming that what they desire is already granted to them, they proceed with their plan, and delight in detailing what they mean to do when their wish has come true — that is a way which they have of not doing much good to a capacity which was never good for much. Now I myself am beginning to lose heart, and I should like, with your permission, to pass over the question of possibility at present. Assuming, therefore, the possibility of the proposal, I shall now proceed to enquire how the rulers will carry out these arrangements, and I shall demonstrate that our plan, if executed, will be of the greatest benefit to the State and to the guardians. First of all, then, if you have no objection, I will endeavour with your help to consider the advantages of the measure; and hereafter the question of possibility.
I have no objection. Proceed.

First, I think that if our rulers and their auxiliaries are to be worthy of the name which they bear, there must be willingness to obey in the one and the power of command in the other. The guardians must themselves obey the laws, and they must also imitate the spirit of them in any details which are entrusted to their care.
That's right, he said.

You, I said, who are their legislator, having selected the men, will now select the women and give them to them. They must be, as far as possible, of like natures with them; and they must live in common houses and meet at common meals. None of them will have anything specially his or her own; they will be together, and will be brought up together, and will associate at gymnastic exercises. And so they will be drawn by a necessity of their natures to have intercourse with each other — necessity is not too strong a word, I think?
Not mathematical necessity, he said, but the other kind — the necessity of attraction, which lovers understand. That kind of necessity is far more persuasive for most people.
True, I said. But this, Glaucon, like everything else, must proceed in an orderly way. In a city of the blessed, unregulated sexual relations would be unholy, and the rulers will forbid them.
Yes, and rightly so, he said.
Then clearly, the next step is to make marriages as beneficial as possible. And marriages will be deemed sacred?
Exactly.

And how can marriages be made most beneficial? — that is a question which I put to you, because I see in your house dogs for hunting, and of the nobler sort of birds not a few. Now, I beseech you, tell me, have you ever attended to their pairing and breeding?
In what way?
Well, even though they're all good stock, aren't some better than others?
True.
And do you breed from all of them indiscriminately, or do you select only the best?
Only the best.
And do you breed from the very youngest or the very oldest, or only those in their prime?
Only those in their prime.
And if you didn't breed carefully, your dogs and birds would deteriorate badly?
Certainly.
The same goes for horses and other animals?
Undoubtedly.
Good heavens, my friend! I said. What extraordinary skill our rulers will need if the same principle applies to humans!
It certainly does apply. But why does it require extraordinary skill?

Because, I said, our rulers will often have to practise upon the body corporate with medicines. Now you know that when patients do not require medicines, but have only to be put under a regimen, the inferior sort of practitioner is deemed to be good enough; but when medicine has to be given, then the doctor should be more of a man.
That's true, but what are you getting at?
I mean that our rulers will need to employ a good deal of deception and manipulation for the benefit of their subjects. We said earlier that such tools, used as medicines, could be beneficial.
And we were right.
And this 'medicine' will be especially necessary in regulating marriages and births.
How so?

We've already established that the best should mate with the best as often as possible, and the worst with the worst as seldom as possible. The offspring of the first pairing should be raised, while the offspring of the second should not, if we want to keep the flock in top condition. All of this must be kept secret from everyone except the rulers, or our guardian 'herd' will break into rebellion.
Very true.

Had we not better appoint certain festivals at which we will bring together the brides and bridegrooms, and sacrifices will be offered and suitable hymeneal songs composed by our poets? The number of weddings is a matter which must be left to the discretion of the rulers, whose aim will be to preserve the average of population. There are many other things which they will have to consider, such as the effects of wars and diseases and any similar agencies, in order, as far as this is possible, to prevent the State from becoming either too large or too small.
Certainly, he said.
We shall have to invent some ingenious kind of lots which the less worthy may draw on each occasion of our bringing them together, and then they will accuse their own ill-luck and not the rulers.
Of course, he said.

And our bravest and best young men, in addition to other honors and rewards, should have more opportunities to be with women. Their courage gives them the right, and such fathers should produce as many children as possible.
True.
And the proper officers, whether male or female or both — for offices are to be held by women as well as by men —
Yes —

The proper officers will take the offspring of the good parents to the pen or fold, and there they will deposit them with certain nurses who dwell in a separate quarter; but the offspring of the inferior, or of the better when they chance to be deformed, will be put away in some mysterious, unknown place, as they should be.
Yes, he said. That must be done if the guardian breed is to remain pure.

They will provide for their nurture, and will bring the mothers to the fold when they are full of milk, taking the greatest possible care that no mother recognises her own child; and other wet-nurses may be engaged if more are required. Care will also be taken that the process of suckling shall not be protracted too long; and the mothers will have no getting up at night or other trouble, but will hand over all this sort of thing to the nurses and attendants.
You're giving the guardians' wives an easy time when it comes to childbearing, he said.
As they should, I said. But let's continue with our plan. We said the parents should be in the prime of life?
Very true.
And what is the prime of life? May it not be defined as a period of about twenty years in a woman's life, and thirty in a man's?
Which years exactly?

A woman, I said, at twenty years of age may begin to bear children to the State, and continue to bear them until forty; a man may begin at twenty-five, when he has passed the point at which the pulse of life beats quickest, and continue to beget children until he is fifty-five.
Certainly, he said, both in men and women those years are the prime of physical as well as of intellectual vigour.

Anyone outside these age ranges who participates in public breeding will be declared guilty of an unholy and impious act. Any child resulting from such a union — if one slips into existence — will have been conceived not under the auspices of the sacred ceremonies and prayers that priests, priestesses, and the whole city will offer at each wedding festival, asking that each new generation improve upon the last, but under the shadow of darkness and undisciplined desire.
Very true, he said.

And the same law will apply to any one of those within the prescribed age who forms a connection with any woman in the prime of life without the sanction of the rulers; for we shall say that he is raising up a bastard to the State, uncertified and unconsecrated.
Very true, he said.

Once men and women pass the age of childbearing, we'll set them free to be with whomever they wish — except that a man may not be with his daughter or granddaughter, or his mother or grandmother, and women may not be with their sons or fathers, or their grandsons or grandfathers. We'll grant this freedom along with strict instructions to prevent any pregnancies from coming to term. And if a child is somehow born despite these precautions, the parents must understand that such an offspring cannot be maintained.
That also, he said, is a reasonable proposition. But how will they know who are fathers and daughters, and so on?

They will never know. The way will be this: dating from the day of the hymeneal, the bridegroom who was then married will call all the male children who are born in the seventh and tenth month afterwards his sons, and the female children his daughters; and they will call him father, and he will call their children his grandchildren, and they will call the elder generation grandfathers and grandmothers. All who were begotten at the time when their fathers and mothers came together will be called their brothers and sisters, and these, as I was saying, will be forbidden to intermarry. This, however, is not to be understood as an absolute prohibition of the marriage of brothers and sisters; if the lot favours them, and they receive the sanction of the Pythian oracle, the law will allow them.
Exactly right, he said.

So that's the plan, Glaucon, for how our guardians will share wives and children. Now we need to confirm that this arrangement is consistent with the rest of our political system and is in fact the best arrangement. Shall we?
Yes, certainly.

Shall we try to find a common basis by asking of ourselves what ought to be the chief aim of the legislator in making laws and in the organization of a State — what is the greatest good, and what is the greatest evil — and then consider whether our previous description has the stamp of the good or of the evil?
By all means.
Can there be any greater evil than discord and division where there should be unity? Or any greater good than the bond of unity?
There cannot.
And there is unity where there is community of pleasures and pains — where all the citizens are glad or grieved on the same occasions of joy and sorrow?
No doubt.

Yes; and where there is no common but only private feeling, a State is disorganized — when you have one half of the world triumphing and the other plunged in grief at the same events happening to the city or the citizens?
Certainly.
And these divisions typically originate in disputes about 'mine' and 'not mine,' 'his' and 'not his'?
Exactly.
And isn't the best-ordered state the one where the most people apply the words 'mine' and 'not mine' to the same things?
Absolutely.

Or that again which most nearly approaches to the condition of the individual — as in the body, when but a finger of one of us is hurt, the whole frame, drawn towards the soul as a centre and forming one kingdom under the ruling power therein, feels the hurt and sympathizes all together with the part affected, and we say that the man has a pain in his finger; and the same expression is used about any other part of the body, which has a sensation of pain at suffering, or of pleasure at the alleviation of suffering.
Very true, he said. And I agree that in the best-ordered state, this common feeling comes closest to being realized.
So when any citizen experiences good or ill fortune, the whole state will treat it as their own, and will rejoice or grieve together?
That's how it must be in a well-ordered state, he said.
It will now be time, I said, for us to return to our State and see whether this or some other form is most in accordance with these fundamental principles.
Very good.
Like every other state, ours has rulers and subjects?
True.
And all will call each other 'citizens'?
Of course.
But what else do people in other states call their rulers, besides 'citizens'?
Usually 'masters.' In democracies, they just call them 'rulers.'
And in our state, what do the people call the rulers besides 'citizens'?
Saviors and helpers, he said.
And what do the rulers call the people?
Their providers and supporters.
And what do rulers in other states call the people?
Slaves.
And what do rulers call each other in other states?
Fellow-rulers.
And in ours?
Fellow-guardians.
Did you ever know an example in any other State of a ruler who would speak of one of his colleagues as his friend and of another as not being his friend?
Yes, very often.
And the friend he regards and describes as one in whom he has an interest, and the other as a stranger in whom he has no interest?
Exactly.
But would any of our guardians think of another guardian as a stranger?

Certainly he would not; for every one whom they meet will be regarded by them either as a brother or sister, or father or mother, or son or daughter, or as the child or parent of those who are thus connected with him.

Capital, I said; but let me ask you once more: shall they be a family in name only, or shall they in all their actions be true to the name? For example, in the use of the word ‘father,' would the care of a father be implied and the filial reverence and duty and obedience to him which the law commands? And is the violator of these duties to be regarded as an impious and unrighteous person who is not likely to receive much good either at the hands of God or of man? Are these to be, or not to be, the strains which the children will hear repeated in their ears by all the citizens about those who are intimated to them to be their parents and the rest of their kinsfolk?
These, he said, and none other; for what can be more ridiculous than for them to utter the names of family ties with the lips only, and not to act in the spirit of them?

Then in our city, more than any other, when anything happens to a citizen, everyone will say together: 'What happens to you, happens to me.' As I described before, when one citizen does well or poorly, the whole city will share that experience.
Very true.
And agreeably to this mode of thinking and speaking, were we not saying that they will have their pleasures and pains in common?
Yes, and rightly so.
And they'll have a shared interest in what they each call 'my own' — and this shared interest will produce shared feelings of pleasure and pain?
Yes, far more than in other states.
And the reason for this, beyond the general constitution of the state, is the community of women and children among the guardians?
That will be the chief reason.

And this unity of feeling we admitted to be the greatest good, as was implied in our own comparison of a well-ordered State to the relation of the body and the members, when affected by pleasure or pain?
We did, and rightly.
Then the community of wives and children among the guardians is clearly the source of the state's greatest good?
Certainly.

And this agrees with the other principle which we were affirming — that the guardians were not to have houses or lands or any other property; their pay was to be their food, which they were to receive from the other citizens, and they were to have no private expenses; for we intended them to preserve their true character of guardians.
Right, he said.

Both the sharing of property and the sharing of families will make them more truly guardians. They won't tear the city apart by arguing over 'mine' and 'not mine' — each person dragging acquisitions into their private house, where they have a private wife and children and private pleasures and pains. Instead, all will be affected by the same pleasures and pains because they agree about what is near and dear to them, and they'll all work toward a common goal.
Certainly, he said.

And since they have nothing they can call their own except their own persons, there will be no lawsuits or complaints among them. All those quarrels that arise from money, children, or family relations will simply disappear.
Of course they will.

Neither will trials for assault or insult ever be likely to occur among them. For that equals should defend themselves against equals we shall maintain to be honourable and right; we shall make the protection of the person a matter of necessity.
Good, he said.
Yes, and there's another benefit to this law: if someone has a grievance against another, he'll settle it on the spot rather than letting it escalate into something dangerous.
Certainly.
Older people will be charged with supervising and disciplining younger ones.
Obviously.

Nor can there be a doubt that the younger will not strike or do any other violence to an elder, unless the magistrates command him; nor will he slight him in any way. For there are two guardians, shame and fear, mighty to prevent him: shame, which makes men refrain from laying hands on those who are to them in the relation of parents; fear, that the injured one will be succoured by the others who are his brothers, sons, and fathers.
True, he said.
So in every way, these laws will keep the citizens at peace with each other?
Yes, very much so.
And since the guardians won't quarrel among themselves, there's no danger of the rest of the city dividing against them or against each other.
None whatever.

I hardly like even to mention the little meannesses of which they will be rid, for they are beneath notice: such, for example, as the flattery of the rich by the poor, and all the pains and pangs which men experience in bringing up a family, and in finding money to buy necessaries for their household, borrowing and then repudiating, getting how they can, and giving the money into the hands of women and slaves to keep — the many evils of so many kinds which people suffer in this way are mean enough and obvious enough, and not worth speaking of.
Yes, he said. You don't need eyes to see those.
And from all these evils they will be delivered, and their life will be blessed as the life of Olympic victors and yet more blessed.
How so?

The Olympic victor, I said, is deemed happy in receiving a part only of the blessedness which is secured to our citizens, who have won a more glorious victory and have a more complete maintenance at the public cost. For the victory which they have won is the salvation of the whole State; and the crown with which they and their children are crowned is the fulness of all that life needs; they receive rewards from the hands of their country while living, and after death have an honourable burial.
Yes, glorious rewards indeed, he said.

Do you remember, I said, how earlier someone — I won't name names — criticized us for making our guardians unhappy, since they had nothing while they could have had everything? We replied that if the occasion arose, we might revisit the question, but for now we were focused on making them true guardians and shaping the state for the happiness of the whole, not of any one class.
Yes, I remember.
And now that the guardians' life turns out to be far nobler and better than even Olympic victors' — can it really be compared to the life of shoemakers or any other workers?
Certainly not.

But I should repeat what I said before: if any guardian tries to achieve happiness in a way that stops him from being a guardian, if he's not content with this safe and harmonious life — which is, in my judgment, the best of all lives — but is seduced by some foolish, youthful notion of happiness into seizing the whole state for himself, then he'll learn how wise Hesiod was when he said: 'the half is more than the whole.'
If he were to consult me, I should say to him: stay where you are, when you have the offer of such a life.

Then you agree, I said, that men and women should share a common way of life, as we've described — common education, common children. They'll guard the citizens together, whether staying in the city or going to war. They'll keep watch together and hunt together like dogs. In all things and in every way possible, women will share with men. In doing this, they'll be doing what's best and won't be violating but preserving the natural relationship between the sexes.
I agree, he said.
We still need to determine, I said, whether this kind of community is actually possible among humans, as it is among animals, and if so, how.
You've anticipated the very question I was about to ask.
There's no difficulty in seeing how they'll wage war, I said.
How?

Why, of course they will go on expeditions together; and will take with them any of their children who are strong enough, that, after the manner of the artisan's child, they may look on at the work which they will have to do when they are grown up. And besides looking on, they will have to help and be of use in war, and to wait upon their fathers and mothers. Did you never observe in the arts how the potters' boys look on and help, long before they touch the wheel?
Yes, I have.
And shall potters be more careful in educating their children and in giving them the opportunity of seeing and practising their duties than our guardians will be?
That would be ridiculous, he said.
There's also the effect on the parents. Having their children present will be the greatest incentive to bravery, as it is for all animals.
True, Socrates. But there's a serious risk: if they lose the battle — which happens often in war — the children will be lost along with the parents, and the state will never recover.
True, I said. But would you never allow them to face any risk?
I'm not saying that.
Well, but if they are ever to run a risk, should they not do so on some occasion when, if they escape disaster, they will be the better for it?
Obviously.
Whether the future soldiers do or do not see war in the days of their youth is a very important matter, for the sake of which some risk may fairly be incurred.
Yes, very important.
This, then, must be our first step — to make our children spectators of war; but we must also contrive that they shall be secured against danger. Then all will be well.
True.
Their parents may be supposed not to be blind to the risks of war, but to know, as far as human foresight can, what expeditions are safe and what dangerous?
We can assume so.
They'll take the children on the safe ones and be cautious about the dangerous ones?
True.
And they'll put the children under the command of experienced veterans who'll serve as their guides and teachers?
Very appropriate.
Still, the dangers of war can't always be predicted. There's always an element of chance.
True.
Then against such chances the children must be at once furnished with wings, in order that in the hour of need they may fly away and escape.
What do you mean? he said.

I mean that we must mount them on horses in their earliest youth, and when they have learnt to ride, take them on horseback to see war. The horses must not be spirited and warlike, but the most tractable and yet the swiftest that can be had. In this way they will get an excellent view of what is hereafter to be their own business; and if there is danger they have only to follow their elder leaders and escape.
I think you're right, he said.

Now, what about the treatment of enemies? What should the rules be for our soldiers among themselves and toward their opponents? First, any soldier who deserts his post or throws away his weapons or commits any other act of cowardice should be demoted to the rank of a craftsman or farmer. What do you think?
Absolutely.
And anyone who lets himself be taken prisoner might as well be handed over to the enemy as a gift. They can do whatever they want with him.
Certainly.

But the hero who has distinguished himself, what shall be done to him? In the first place, he shall receive honour in the army from his youthful comrades; every one of them in succession shall crown him. What do you say?
Agreed.
And they'll shake his hand?
Agreed to that too.
But my next proposal you might not accept.
What is it?
That he should be kissed by them.

I'd go even further, he said. While the campaign lasts, no one he wants to kiss should be allowed to refuse. That way, if anyone has a lover in the army, man or woman, they'll be all the more eager to win the prize of valor.

Capital, I said. That the brave man is to have more wives than others has been already determined, and he is to have first choices in such matters more than others, in order that he may have as many children as possible?
Agreed.

Again, there is another manner in which, according to Homer, brave youths should be honoured; for he tells how Ajax, after he had distinguished himself in battle, was rewarded with long chines, which seems to be a compliment appropriate to a hero in the flower of his age, being not only a tribute of honour but also a very strengthening thing.
Very true, he said.

Then in this, I said, Homer shall be our teacher; and we too, at sacrifices and on like occasions, will honour the brave according to the measure of their valour, whether men or women, with hymns and those other distinctions which we were mentioning; also with
'Seats of honor, and meats, and overflowing cups.'
And by honoring them this way, we'll also be training them.
Excellent, he said.
Yes, I said; and when a man dies gloriously in war, shall we not say, in the first place, that he is of the golden race?
Certainly.
And we have Hesiod's authority for saying that when such people die,
'They become holy spirits on earth, guardians of good, protectors against evil, watchers over mortal humanity'?
Yes, we accept his authority.
We'll consult the oracle about how to bury these divine and heroic figures, and what special honors to give them, and then follow its instructions?
By all means.

And for all time, we'll revere their graves and worship at their tombs as heroes. The same honors will extend to anyone judged exceptionally good, whether they die in battle, of old age, or any other way.
Very right, he said.
Now, how should our soldiers treat their enemies?
In what respect?

First of all, in regard to slavery: do you think it right that Hellenes should enslave Hellenic States, or allow others to enslave them, if they can help it? Should not their custom be to spare them, considering the danger which there is that the whole race may one day fall under the yoke of the barbarians?
Sparing them is infinitely better.
Then no Hellene should be owned by them as a slave; that is a rule which they will observe and advise the other Hellenes to observe.
Certainly, he said. That way Greeks will be united against the barbarians and keep their hands off each other.

And what about the slain? Should the victors strip their bodies of anything besides armor? Doesn't the habit of looting the dead give cowards an excuse to avoid the actual fighting? Many armies have been lost because soldiers were busy plundering instead of fighting.
Very true.

And is there not illiberality and avarice in robbing a corpse, and also a degree of meanness and womanishness in making an enemy of the dead body when the real enemy has flown away and left only his fighting gear behind him? Is not this rather like a dog who cannot get at his assailant, quarrelling with the stones which strike him instead?
Very like a dog, he said.
Then we must forbid stripping corpses and preventing their burial?
Yes, we absolutely must.

And we won't display captured weapons in temples, especially Greek weapons — not if we want to maintain good relations with other Greeks. In fact, we should be concerned that dedicating spoils taken from fellow Greeks might be sacrilege, unless the god himself commands it.
Very true.
And what about devastating Greek territory or burning houses?
I'd like to hear your opinion, he said.
Both should be forbidden, in my view. We should take only the year's harvest and nothing more. Shall I explain why?
Please.

Why, you see, there is a difference in the names ‘discord' and ‘war,' and I imagine there is also a difference in their natures. The one is expressive of what is internal and domestic, the other of what is external and foreign; and the first of the two is termed discord, and only the second, war.
That's a very proper distinction, he said.
And isn't it equally proper to say that the Greek race is united by blood and friendship, and that barbarians are alien and foreign to them?
Very good, he said.

And therefore, when Hellenes fight with barbarians and barbarians with Hellenes, they will be described by us as being at war when they fight, and by nature enemies; and this kind of antagonism should be called war. But when Hellenes fight with one another, we shall say that Hellas is then in a state of disorder and discord, they being by nature friends; and such enmity is to be called discord.
I agree.

Consider then, I said, when that which we have acknowledged to be discord occurs, and a city is divided, if both parties destroy the lands and burn the houses of one another — how wicked the strife appears! No true lover of his country would bring himself to tear in pieces his own nurse and mother. There might be reason in the conqueror depriving the conquered of their harvest, but still they would have the idea of peace in their hearts, and would not mean to go on fighting for ever.
Yes, he said, that's a much better attitude.
And the city we're founding will be a Greek city?
It should be, he said.
Then its citizens will be good and civilized?
Very much so.
And as Greeks, they'll love their fellow Greeks and think of Greece as their own land, sharing in common religious life?
Most certainly.
And any difference which arises among them will be regarded by them as discord only — a quarrel among friends, which is not to be called a war?
Certainly not a war.
And they'll quarrel as people who expect to reconcile eventually?
Certainly.
They'll correct each other as friends, not enslave or destroy — acting as correctors, not enemies.
Exactly.

Being Greeks themselves, they won't devastate Greek land, burn houses, or treat an entire city's population — men, women, and children — as their enemies. They know that the guilt of war belongs only to a few, while the many are their friends. For all these reasons, they won't waste the land or destroy homes. Their hostility will last only until the innocent majority forces the guilty few to make amends.
I agree, he said, that our citizens should treat Greek enemies this way — and treat barbarians the way Greeks currently treat each other.
Then let's add this law for our guardians: they shall neither devastate Greek land nor burn Greek houses.
Agreed. And we can agree that these rules, like all our previous ones, are very good.

But still I must say, Socrates, that if you are allowed to go on in this way you will entirely forget the other question which at the commencement of this discussion you thrust aside: is such an order of things possible, and how, if at all? For I am quite ready to acknowledge that the plan which you propose, if only feasible, would do all sorts of good to the State. I will add, what you have omitted, that your citizens will be the bravest of warriors, and will never leave their ranks, for they will all know one another, and each will call the other father, brother, son; and if you suppose the women to join their armies, whether in the same rank or in the rear, either as a terror to the enemy or as auxiliaries in case of need, I know that they will then be absolutely invincible. And there are many domestic advantages which might also be mentioned, and which I fully acknowledge. But, as I admit all these advantages and as many more as you please, if only this State of yours were to come into existence, we need say no more about them. Assuming then the existence of the State, let us now turn to the question of possibility and ways and means — the rest may be left.

If I loiter for a moment, you instantly make a raid upon me, I said, and have no mercy. I have hardly escaped the first and second waves, and you seem not to be aware that you are now bringing upon me the third, which is the greatest and heaviest. When you have seen and heard the third wave, I think you will be more considerate, and will acknowledge that some fear and hesitation was natural respecting a proposal so extraordinary as that which I have now to state and investigate.
The more appeals of this sort which you make, he said, the more determined are we that you shall tell us how such a State is possible: speak out and at once.
Let me start by reminding you that we arrived here while searching for justice and injustice.
True, he said. But what of it?

I just want to ask: if we find what justice is, will we demand that the just person be a perfect embodiment of it? Or will we be satisfied with an approximation — with them coming closer to justice than anyone else?
The approximation will be enough.

We were enquiring into the nature of absolute justice and into the character of the perfectly just, and into injustice and the perfectly unjust, that we might have an ideal. We were to look at these in order that we might judge of our own happiness and unhappiness according to the standard which they exhibited and the degree in which we resembled them, but not with any view of showing that they could exist in fact.
True, he said.
Would a painter be any less skilled because, after creating an ideal portrait of a perfectly beautiful person, he couldn't prove such a person actually exists?
He'd be no less skilled.
Well, weren't we creating an ideal of a perfect state?
Of course.
And is our theory any worse because we can't prove such a city could actually be built exactly as described?
Not at all, he said.
That's the truth. But if you want me to try to show how and under what conditions the possibility is greatest, you'll need to grant me the same assumptions as before.
What assumptions?

I want to know whether ideals are ever fully realized in language? Does not the word express more than the fact, and must not the actual, whatever a man may think, always, in the nature of things, fall short of the truth? What do you say?
I do.

Then you must not insist on my proving that the actual State will in every respect coincide with the ideal. If we are only able to discover how a city may be governed nearly as we proposed, you will admit that we have discovered the possibility which you demand, and will be contented. I am sure that I should be contented — will not you?
Me too.

Let me next endeavour to show what is that fault in States which is the cause of their present maladministration, and what is the least change which will enable a State to pass into the truer form; and let the change, if possible, be of one thing only, or, if not, of two; at any rate, let the changes be as few and slight as possible.
Certainly, he said.
I think, I said, that there might be a reform of the State if only one change were made, which is not a slight or easy thing, though still a possible one.
What is it?

Now then, I said, I go to meet that which I liken to the greatest of the waves; yet shall the word be spoken, even though the wave break and drown me in laughter and dishonour; and do you mark my words.
Go on.

Unless philosophers become kings, or those who are now called kings and rulers come to be genuinely and thoroughly inspired by philosophy — unless political power and philosophical wisdom are united in the same persons, while those who currently pursue one without the other are compelled to step aside — there will be no end to the troubles of states, nor of the human race itself. Only then will this state we've been describing have any chance of coming to life and seeing the light of day. This is what I've been afraid to say, because I knew how utterly paradoxical it would sound. It's hard for people to accept that no other arrangement can bring happiness, whether in public or private life.

Socrates, what do you mean? I would have you consider that the word which you have uttered is one at which numerous persons, and very respectable persons too, in a figure pulling off their coats all in a moment, and seizing any weapon that comes to hand, will run at you might and main, before you know where you are, intending to do heaven knows what; and if you don't prepare an answer, and put yourself in motion, you will be ‘pared by their fine wits,' and no mistake.
And you got me into this, I said.

True, and I was right to. But I'll do everything I can to get you out — I'll give you my goodwill, my encouragement, and perhaps I can answer your questions better than someone else. With this kind of support, do your best to show the skeptics you're right.

I ought to try, I said, since you offer me such invaluable assistance. And I think that, if there is to be a chance of our escaping, we must explain to them whom we mean when we say that philosophers are to rule in the State; then we shall be able to defend ourselves. There will be discovered to be some natures who ought to study philosophy and to be leaders in the State; and others who are not born to be philosophers, and are meant to be followers rather than leaders.
Time for a definition, he said.
Follow me, I said, and I hope that I may in some way or other be able to give you a satisfactory explanation.
Go on.
I dare say that you remember, and therefore I need not remind you, that a lover, if he is worthy of the name, ought to show his love, not to some one part of that which he loves, but to the whole.
Actually, I don't quite follow. Please remind me.

Another person, I said, might fairly reply as you do; but a man of pleasure like yourself ought to know that all who are in the flower of youth do somehow or other raise a pang or emotion in a lover's breast, and are thought by him to be worthy of his affectionate regards. Is not this a way which you have with the fair: one has a snub nose, and you praise his charming face; the hook-nose of another has, you say, a royal look; while he who is neither snub nor hooked has the grace of regularity; the dark visage is manly, the fair are children of the gods; and as to the sweet ‘honey pale,' as they are called, what is the very name but the invention of a lover who talks in diminutives, and is not averse to paleness if appearing on the cheek of youth? In a word, there is no excuse which you will not make, and nothing which you will not say, in order not to lose a single flower that blooms in the spring-time of youth.
If you want to make me an authority on love for the sake of the argument, I'll accept.
And what do you say of lovers of wine? Do you not see them doing the same? They are glad of any pretext of drinking any wine.
Very true.

And the same is true of ambitious men; if they cannot command an army, they are willing to command a file; and if they cannot be honoured by really great and important persons, they are glad to be honoured by lesser and meaner people — but honour of some kind they must have.
Exactly.
Then answer me this: when someone desires something, do they desire the whole class or only part of it?
The whole.
Then the philosopher — the lover of wisdom — desires not just part of wisdom, but all of it?
Yes, all of it.

And he who dislikes learning, especially in youth, when he has no power of judging what is good and what is not, such a one we maintain not to be a philosopher or a lover of knowledge, just as he who refuses his food is not hungry, and may be said to have a bad appetite and not a good one?
Very true, he said.
But someone who has a taste for every kind of knowledge, who's curious to learn and is never satisfied — that person can rightly be called a philosopher, don't you think?

Glaucon said: If curiosity makes a philosopher, you will find many a strange being will have a title to the name. All the lovers of sights have a delight in learning, and must therefore be included. Musical amateurs, too, are a folk strangely out of place among philosophers, for they are the last persons in the world who would come to anything like a philosophical discussion, if they could help, while they run about at the Dionysiac festivals as if they had let out their ears to hear every chorus; whether the performance is in town or country — that makes no difference — they are there. Now are we to maintain that all these, and any who have similar tastes, as well as the professors of quite minor arts, are philosophers?
Certainly not, I said. They're only imitations of philosophers.
Then who are the true philosophers? he asked.
Those who love the vision of truth, I said.
That sounds right, he said, but what do you mean exactly?
To another, I replied, I might have a difficulty in explaining; but I am sure that you will admit a proposition which I am about to make.
Grant you what?
That since beauty is the opposite of ugliness, they are two distinct things?
Of course.
And since they're two, each is one?
True.

The same applies to just and unjust, good and evil, and every other form: each is one in itself. But through their various combinations with actions, objects, and each other, each appears in many different guises and seems to be many.
Very true.
This is the distinction I draw between the sight-lovers and art-lovers on one hand, and those who alone deserve the name 'philosopher' on the other.
How do you distinguish them? he said.

The lovers of sounds and sights, I replied, are, as I conceive, fond of fine tones and colours and forms and all the artificial products that are made out of them, but their mind is incapable of seeing or loving absolute beauty.
True, he said.
And very few can attain the vision of beauty itself.
Very true.

Now consider someone who has a sense for beautiful things but no sense of beauty itself — someone who, even if guided toward that knowledge, can't follow. Is that person awake or dreaming? Think about it: isn't the dreamer, whether asleep or awake, the person who mistakes the copy for the real thing?
I'd certainly say such a person is dreaming.

But take the case of the other, who recognises the existence of absolute beauty and is able to distinguish the idea from the objects which participate in the idea, neither putting the objects in the place of the idea nor the idea in the place of the objects — is he a dreamer, or is he awake?
Fully awake.
And can we say that the mind of the one who knows has knowledge, while the mind of the one who merely believes has opinion?
Certainly.
But suppose that the latter should quarrel with us and dispute our statement, can we administer any soothing cordial or advice to him, without revealing to him that there is sad disorder in his wits?
We should certainly try, he said.

Then let's think of how to address them. We'll start by reassuring them that we welcome whatever knowledge they have, and we're glad they have it. But we'd like to ask a question: does the person who knows, know something or nothing? (You'll answer for him.)
I answer that he knows something.
Something that exists, or something that doesn't?
Something that exists. How could something nonexistent be known?
So we can be confident, from every angle we've examined, that what fully exists can be fully known, and what doesn't exist at all can't be known at all?
Absolutely certain.
Good. But if there be anything which is of such a nature as to be and not to be, that will have a place intermediate between pure being and the absolute negation of being?
Yes, between them.

And, as knowledge corresponded to being and ignorance of necessity to not-being, for that intermediate between being and not-being there has to be discovered a corresponding intermediate between ignorance and knowledge, if there be such?
Certainly.
Do we acknowledge that opinion exists?
Of course.
Is opinion the same faculty as knowledge, or a different one?
A different one.
So opinion and knowledge deal with different subjects, corresponding to their difference as faculties?
Yes.
Knowledge is related to what exists and aims to know what exists. But before going further, let me make a distinction.
What distinction?
Let me place faculties in their own category. They are powers in us — and in everything else — by which we do what we do. Sight and hearing, for instance, are faculties. Is my meaning clear?
Yes, I understand perfectly.

Here's how I think about them: I can't see faculties, so I can't distinguish them by color, shape, or any visible feature. I identify a faculty only by its domain and its result. If two faculties have the same domain and produce the same result, I call them the same. If they differ in either domain or result, I call them different. Would you agree with that approach?
Yes.
And will you be so very good as to answer one more question? Would you say that knowledge is a faculty, or in what class would you place it?
Knowledge is certainly a faculty — the mightiest of all.
And is opinion also a faculty?
Of course. Opinion is the power by which we form opinions.
But didn't you agree just now that knowledge and opinion are not the same?
How could any thinking person identify what's infallible with what makes mistakes?
Excellent — that proves we clearly recognize them as distinct.
Yes.
So if knowledge and opinion are distinct faculties, they must have distinct domains?
That's certain.
The domain of knowledge is what exists — knowledge aims to know the nature of what is?
Yes.
And the function of opinion is to opine?
Yes.
Does opinion deal with the same subject as knowledge? Can the same thing be both known and merely opined?

Nay, he replied, that has been already disproven; if difference in faculty implies difference in the sphere or subject-matter, and if, as we were saying, opinion and knowledge are distinct faculties, then the sphere of knowledge and of opinion cannot be the same.
So if the domain of knowledge is what exists, the domain of opinion must be something else?
Yes, something else.

Is nonexistence the domain of opinion? Or rather — how can you have an opinion about something that doesn't exist at all? When you form an opinion, isn't it always about something? Can you have an opinion about nothing?
Impossible.
Someone who has an opinion has an opinion about some one thing?
Yes.
But nonexistence isn't 'some one thing' — it's properly nothing?
True.
We assigned ignorance to nonexistence, and knowledge to existence?
True, he said.
So opinion is concerned neither with existence nor with nonexistence?
Neither.
And therefore opinion is neither knowledge nor ignorance?
It seems not.
But is opinion to be sought without and beyond either of them, in a greater clearness than knowledge, or in a greater darkness than ignorance?
Neither.
So opinion strikes you as darker than knowledge but lighter than ignorance?
Yes, and by a significant margin.
And it falls between them?
Yes.
Then opinion is intermediate?
No question.

But were we not saying before, that if anything appeared to be of a sort which is and is not at the same time, that sort of thing would appear also to lie in the interval between pure being and absolute not-being; and that the corresponding faculty is neither knowledge nor ignorance, but will be found in the interval between them?
True.
And something has now been found in that interval, which we call opinion?
Yes.

Then we still need to find the object that partakes of both existence and nonexistence, that can't properly be called either one — the thing that, once discovered, we can rightfully call the subject of opinion. We'll assign the extremes to the extreme faculties and the middle to the middle faculty.
True.

With this established, I'd like to ask the person who denies the existence of any absolute, unchanging form of beauty — the one who believes only in the many beautiful things, the lover of sights who can't stand being told that beauty is one, or that justice is one, or that anything has a single nature. Let me ask him: among all these many beautiful things, is there one that won't also appear ugly? Among all the just things, one that won't also seem unjust? Among all the holy things, one that won't also seem unholy?
No, he said. Everything beautiful will in some respect be found ugly, and the same goes for the rest.
And can't the many things that are 'doubles' also be 'halves' — doubles of one thing and halves of another?
Quite true.
And things called great, small, heavy, or light — can't they equally well be described by the opposite term?
True. Each will always have a claim to both descriptions.
Can any one of these many things be said to definitively be what it's called, rather than not be it?

He replied: They are like the punning riddles which are asked at feasts, or the children's puzzle about the eunuch aiming at the bat, with what he hit him, as they say in the puzzle, and upon what the bat was sitting. The individual objects of which I am speaking are also a riddle, and have a double sense: nor can you fix them in your mind, either as being or not-being, or both, or neither.

Then where should we place them? I asked. Can they have a better home than somewhere between pure existence and pure nonexistence? They're clearly not darker than nonexistence or more real than full existence.
That's exactly right, he said.
So it seems we've discovered that the many conventional ideas most people have about beauty and everything else are tossing about in a region halfway between pure existence and pure nonexistence.
We have.

Yes; and we had before agreed that anything of this kind which we might find was to be described as matter of opinion, and not as matter of knowledge; being the intermediate flux which is caught and detained by the intermediate faculty.
Exactly.
