Then those who perceive many beautiful things but can't see beauty itself, and can't follow anyone who points the way to it — those who perceive many just things but not justice itself, and so on — such people have opinion but not knowledge?
That's certain.
But those who see the absolute, eternal, and unchangeable — they have knowledge, not mere opinion?
That can't be denied either.

The first group loves and embraces the objects of opinion; the second, the objects of knowledge. The first group, remember, are the ones who enjoyed beautiful sounds and sights but couldn't tolerate the existence of absolute beauty.
Yes, I remember.
Then would we be wrong to call them 'lovers of opinion' rather than 'lovers of wisdom'? And will they be very angry at us for saying so?
I'd tell them not to be angry. No one should be angry at the truth.
But those who love the truth in each thing are to be called lovers of wisdom — philosophers — not lovers of opinion.
Absolutely.

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: So there you have it, Glaucon. After a long and exhausting argument, the true philosophers and the false ones have finally come into view.
I don't think the road could have been any shorter, he said.

I suppose not, I said. And yet I think we'd have gotten a clearer picture of both if we could have stuck to just this one question, without all the other issues still waiting for us — issues anyone must face who wants to understand how the life of the just really differs from the life of the unjust.
So what's the next question? he asked.

Surely, I said, the one which follows next in order. Inasmuch as philosophers alone are able to grasp the eternal and unchangeable, and those who wander in the region of the many and variable are not philosophers, I must ask you which of the two classes should be the rulers of our State?
How should we decide that?
Whichever group is better at guarding the laws and institutions of the State — let them be the guardians.
Very good.
And surely, I said, there's no question that the person who's meant to guard something should have eyes rather than be blind?
No question at all.

Now consider those who lack real knowledge of each thing as it truly is, who have no clear model in their souls, and who can't look — like a painter looks at his subject — toward what is absolutely true, referring back to it constantly as their standard when they establish laws about beauty, goodness, and justice, or guard and preserve the laws that already exist. Aren't such people essentially blind?
They really are in that condition, he replied.
Then should we make them our guardians, when there are others who match them in experience and fall short in no virtue, and who also know the truth of each thing?
There can be no reason, he said, for rejecting those who have this greatest of all great qualities; they must always have the first place unless they fail in some other respect.
So let's work out, I said, how these same people can have both this knowledge and those other excellences.
By all means.

In the first place, as we began by observing, the nature of the philosopher has to be ascertained. We must come to an understanding about him, and when we have done so, then, if I am not mistaken, we shall also acknowledge that such a union of qualities is possible, and that those in whom they are united, and those only, should be rulers in the State.
What do you mean?
Let's take it as given that philosophical minds always love the kind of knowledge that reveals eternal reality — reality that doesn't shift with generation and decay.
Agreed.
And further, I said, let's agree that they love all of reality, every part of it, and won't willingly give up any portion — just as we said about the lover and the ambitious man.
True.
And if they are to be what we were describing, is there not another quality which they should also possess?
What quality?
Truthfulness. They'll never willingly let falsehood into their minds. They hate it, and they love the truth.
Yes, that's certainly true of them.

‘May be,' my friend, I replied, is not the word; say rather ‘must be affirmed.' For he whose nature is amorous of anything cannot help loving all that belongs or is akin to the object of his affections.
Right, he said.
And is there anything more closely related to wisdom than truth?
How could there be?
Can the same person love both wisdom and falsehood?
Never.
So the true lover of learning must, from his earliest years, pursue truth in every form?
Absolutely.
But we also know from experience that when someone's desires run strongly in one direction, they run more weakly in others — like a stream diverted into another channel.
True.

So the person whose desires are channeled toward knowledge in every form will be absorbed in the pleasures of the soul and will barely feel bodily pleasure — if he's a genuine philosopher and not a pretender.
That's absolutely certain.
A person like that will naturally be moderate and free from greed. The motives that drive other people to chase and spend money simply don't exist in his character.
Very true.
There's another mark of the philosophical nature we should consider.
What's that?
There must be no hidden corner of small-mindedness. Nothing is more opposed to a soul that constantly reaches for the wholeness of things, both divine and human, than pettiness.
Absolutely true, he replied.
And someone who possesses greatness of mind and contemplates all of time and all of existence — can such a person think human life is anything very important?
He can't.
So he won't consider death something to be feared?
No indeed.
Then a cowardly and small-natured person has no place in true philosophy?
Certainly not.
And someone who is well-balanced, neither greedy nor petty, neither boastful nor cowardly — can that person ever be unjust or harsh in his dealings?
Impossible.
So when you're trying to spot the philosophical nature in someone young, you'll look for whether he's just and gentle, or rude and antisocial. Those are the telltale signs.
True.
There's another point to note.
What's that?
Whether he takes pleasure in learning. No one will love something that causes him pain and in which he makes little progress despite great effort.
Certainly not.
And if he's forgetful and retains nothing of what he learns — won't he be like an empty vessel?
Of course.
Working hard for nothing, he'll end up hating himself and his fruitless activity.
A soul that can't retain knowledge doesn't belong among genuine philosophical natures. We have to insist that the philosopher has a good memory.
Certainly.
And an unharmonious, graceless nature can only tend toward disproportion?
Undoubtedly.
Do you think truth is more akin to proportion or to disproportion?
To proportion.
Then, besides the other qualities, we should look for a naturally well-proportioned and graceful mind, one that moves instinctively toward the true nature of everything.
Certainly.
So don't all these qualities we've been listing go together? Aren't they all necessary for a soul that is to have a full and complete grasp of reality?
They're absolutely necessary, he replied.
And isn't this a pursuit beyond criticism — one that only a person with a good memory, a quick mind, nobility, grace, and a kinship with truth, justice, courage, and temperance can follow?
Not even the god of jealousy could find fault with such a pursuit, he said.
And to people like this, I said — once perfected by years and education — and to them alone, you would entrust the State.

Here Adeimantus interposed and said: To these statements, Socrates, no one can offer a reply; but when you talk in this way, a strange feeling passes over the minds of your hearers. They fancy that they are led astray a little at each step in the argument, owing to their own want of skill in asking and answering questions; these littles accumulate, and at the end of the discussion they are found to have sustained a mighty overthrow, and all their former notions appear to be turned upside down. And as unskilful players of draughts are at last shut up by their more skilful adversaries and have no piece to move, so they too find themselves shut up at last; for they have nothing to say in this new game in which words are the counters; and yet all the time they are in the right. The observation is suggested to me by what is now occurring. For any one of us might say that, although in words he is not able to meet you at each step of the argument, he sees as a fact that the votaries of philosophy, when they carry on the study, not only in youth as a part of education, but as the pursuit of their maturer years, most of them become strange monsters, not to say utter rogues, and that those who may be considered the best of them are made useless to the world by the very study which you extol.
And do you think those who say that are wrong?
I can't say, he replied; but I'd like to know what you think.
My answer is that they're quite right.
Then how can you justify saying that cities won't be free of evil until philosophers rule them, when we've just agreed that philosophers are useless to cities?
That's a question, I said, that can only be answered with a parable.
Right, Socrates — and parables are something you're clearly not at all used to, he said with a smile.

I perceive, I said, that you are vastly amused at having plunged me into such a hopeless discussion; but now hear the parable, and then you will be still more amused at the meagreness of my imagination. For the manner in which the best men are treated in their own States is so grievous that no single thing on earth is comparable to it; and therefore, if I am to plead their cause, I must have recourse to fiction, and put together a figure made up of many things, like the fabulous unions of goats and stags which are found in pictures. Imagine then a fleet or a ship in which there is a captain who is taller and stronger than any of the crew, but he is a little deaf and has a similar infirmity in sight, and his knowledge of navigation is not much better. The sailors are quarrelling with one another about the steering — every one is of opinion that he has a right to steer, though he has never learned the art of navigation and cannot tell who taught him or when he learned, and will further assert that it cannot be taught, and they are ready to cut in pieces any one who says the contrary. They throng about the captain, begging and praying him to commit the helm to them; and if at any time they do not prevail, but others are preferred to them, they kill the others or throw them overboard, and having first chained up the noble captain's senses with drink or some narcotic drug, they mutiny and take possession of the ship and make free with the stores; thus, eating and drinking, they proceed on their voyage in such manner as might be expected of them. Him who is their partisan and cleverly aids them in their plot for getting the ship out of the captain's hands into their own, whether by force or persuasion, they compliment with the name of sailor, pilot, able seaman, and abuse the other sort of man, whom they call a good-for-nothing. But that the true pilot must pay attention to the year and seasons and sky and stars and winds, and whatever else belongs to his art, if he intends to be really qualified for the command of a ship, and that he must and will be the steerer, whether other people like it or not — the possibility of this union of authority with the steerer's art has never seriously entered into their thoughts or been made part of their calling. Now in vessels which are in a state of mutiny, and by sailors who are mutineers, how will the true pilot be regarded? Will he not be called by them a prater, a star-gazer, a good-for-nothing?
Of course, said Adeimantus.
I don't think you need me to spell out the parable, I said. You can see that it describes the true philosopher's relationship to the State.
Certainly.
So take this parable to whoever is surprised that philosophers get no respect in their cities. Explain it to him and try to convince him that it would be far more surprising if they did get respect.
I will.

Tell him this: he's right that the best philosophers are useless to the world. But tell him to blame their uselessness on the people who refuse to use them, not on the philosophers themselves. It's not natural for the pilot to beg the sailors to accept his command. That's not how it works. And the clever saying that 'the wise go knocking at rich men's doors' — the author of that was lying. The truth is this: when you're sick, you go to the doctor, whether you're rich or poor. And when you need to be governed, you go to the person who can govern. It makes no sense for the ruler to beg his subjects to be ruled. You'd be right to compare our present rulers to the mutinous sailors, and the true philosophers to the pilots they dismiss as useless stargazers.
Exactly, he said.

For these reasons, and among people like these, philosophy — the noblest of all pursuits — is unlikely to be valued by those on the other side. But the worst damage to philosophy isn't done by its opponents. It's done by its own supposed followers — the very people your accuser was talking about when he said that most of them are total rogues and the best are useless. And I agreed with him.
Yes.
And we've now explained why the good ones are useless?
True.
Then shall we proceed to show that the corruption of the majority is also unavoidable, and that this is not to be laid to the charge of philosophy any more than the other?
By all means.

Let's work through this step by step. Remember, we started by describing the nature of the philosopher. He follows truth as his leader in everything. If he falls short of that, he's a fraud and has no genuine connection to philosophy.
Yes, that was what we said.
Isn't this one quality alone sharply at odds with what people currently think about philosophers?
It certainly is, he said.

And haven't we a right to defend the philosopher by saying this: the true lover of knowledge always strives toward being — that's his nature? He won't rest in the world of shifting appearances. He'll press on — his desire won't fade and his edge won't be dulled — until he grasps the true nature of each thing with the part of his soul that's fit to grasp it. And when he approaches true reality, mingles with it, and generates understanding and truth, then at last he knows, truly lives, and is nourished. Then, and only then, does his labor end.
Nothing could be more accurate, he said.
And will the love of falsehood be any part of his nature? Won't he utterly hate it?
He will.
And when truth leads the way, we can't suspect any evil in the company that follows?
Impossible.
Justice and a sound mind will be in that company, with temperance right alongside?
True, he replied.

And there's really no need for me to parade the philosopher's virtues again. You'll remember we said courage, greatness of mind, quick comprehension, and memory were his natural gifts. And you objected that while no one could deny these claims in the abstract, when you look at actual philosophers, most of them are clearly useless and the majority are thoroughly bad. We were investigating the reasons for this accusation, and that's brought us back to examining what corrupts the philosophical nature and why so many are ruined.
Exactly.

And we have next to consider the corruptions of the philosophic nature, why so many are spoiled and so few escape spoiling — I am speaking of those who were said to be useless but not wicked — and, when we have done with them, we will speak of the imitators of philosophy, what manner of men are they who aspire after a profession which is above them and of which they are unworthy, and then, by their manifold inconsistencies, bring upon philosophy, and upon all philosophers, that universal reprobation of which we speak.
What corruptions are you talking about? he said.
I will see if I can explain them to you. Every one will admit that a nature having in perfection all the qualities which we required in a philosopher, is a rare plant which is seldom seen among men.
Rare indeed.
And think how many powerful forces conspire to destroy these rare natures!
What forces?

First — and this is the strangest part — their own virtues. Their courage, their temperance, every one of the qualities we praised: these very things corrupt and pull away from philosophy the soul that possesses them.
That is strange, he replied.
Then there are all the ordinary advantages people value — beauty, wealth, physical strength, powerful family connections. You know the kind of thing. These also corrupt and distract.
I understand the general idea, but I'd like you to be more precise.
Grasp the truth as a whole, I said, and in the right way; you will then have no difficulty in apprehending the preceding remarks, and they will no longer appear strange to you.
How should I do that? he asked.

Think of it this way, I said. We know that any seed or young growth — plant or animal — when it doesn't get the right nourishment, climate, or soil, suffers more the stronger it is. Bad conditions are a worse enemy to what's excellent than to what's mediocre.
Very true.
So it makes sense that the finest natures, placed in hostile conditions, take more damage than inferior ones. The greater the nature, the greater the contrast with its surroundings.
Certainly.

So, Adeimantus, isn't it the case that the most gifted minds, when badly educated, become the worst criminals? Don't great evils and pure wickedness spring from powerful natures that have been ruined, rather than from weak ones? A weak nature is never responsible for anything very great — whether good or evil.
I think you're right there.

The same goes for our philosopher. He's like a plant that must grow into every virtue if properly nurtured, but that becomes the most poisonous of weeds if sown in alien soil — unless some divine power preserves him. Now, do you really believe what people commonly say — that young people are corrupted by individual Sophists who teach them privately? Does that actually matter much? Aren't the people who say these things the greatest Sophists of all? Don't they themselves educate young and old, men and women, and shape everyone to their liking?
When does this happen? he said.

When they meet together, and the world sits down at an assembly, or in a court of law, or a theatre, or a camp, or in any other popular resort, and there is a great uproar, and they praise some things which are being said or done, and blame other things, equally exaggerating both, shouting and clapping their hands, and the echo of the rocks and the place in which they are assembled redoubles the sound of the praise or blame — at such a time will not a young man's heart, as they say, leap within him? Will any private training enable him to stand firm against the overwhelming flood of popular opinion? Or will he be carried away by the stream? Will he not have the notions of good and evil which the public in general have — he will do as they do, and as they are, such will he be?
Inevitably, Socrates. He'd have no choice.
And yet, I said, there's an even greater pressure we haven't mentioned.
What's that?
The not-so-gentle force of property seizure, imprisonment, or death — which these great educators, the public, apply when their words aren't enough to persuade.
They certainly do — and they mean it.
Now what opinion of any other Sophist, or of any private person, can be expected to overcome in such an unequal contest?
None, he replied.

None at all, I said. Even to try is sheer folly. There has never been — there is not now — there never will be a character shaped by any teaching that runs counter to the education imposed by the public. I'm speaking of human virtue only, my friend. Divine virtue, as the saying goes, is a different matter. You can be sure that if anything is saved and turns out well under our present corrupt governments, it is saved by the power of God.
I quite agree, he replied.
Then let me ask you to agree on one more point.
What are you going to say?

Why, that all those mercenary individuals, whom the many call Sophists and whom they deem to be their adversaries, do, in fact, teach nothing but the opinion of the many, that is to say, the opinions of their assemblies; and this is their wisdom. I might compare them to a man who should study the tempers and desires of a mighty strong beast who is fed by him — he would learn how to approach and handle him, also at what times and from what causes he is dangerous or the reverse, and what is the meaning of his several cries, and by what sounds, when another utters them, he is soothed or infuriated. And you may suppose further, that when, by continually attending upon him, he has become perfect in all this, he calls his knowledge wisdom, and makes of it a system or art, which he proceeds to teach, although he has no real notion of what he means by the principles or passions of which he is speaking, but calls this honourable and that dishonourable, or good or evil, or just or unjust, all in accordance with the tastes and tempers of the great brute. Good he pronounces to be that in which the beast delights and evil to be that which he dislikes; and he can give no other account of them except that the just and noble are the necessary, having never himself seen, and having no power of explaining to others, the nature of either, or the difference between them, which is immense. By heaven, would not such a one be a rare educator?
Remarkable indeed.

And in what way does he who thinks that wisdom is the discernment of the tempers and tastes of the motley multitude, whether in painting or music, or, finally, in politics, differ from him whom I have been describing? For when a man consorts with the many, and exhibits to them his poem or other work of art or the service which he has done the State, making them his judges when he is not obliged, the so-called necessity of Diomede will oblige him to produce whatever they praise. And yet the reasons they give in confirmation of their own notions about the honourable and good are utterly ludicrous. Did you ever hear any of them which were not?
No, and I don't expect to.

So you see the truth of what I've been saying? Now consider this: can the masses ever be brought to believe in the existence of absolute beauty as opposed to the many beautiful things, or in the absolute form of anything as opposed to its many instances?
Certainly not.
Then the masses can never be philosophers?
Impossible.
And so philosophers must inevitably face the masses' disapproval?
They must.
And the disapproval of individuals who associate with the mob and try to please them?
That's obvious.

Given all this, do you see any way for the philosophical nature to be preserved and to stay true to its calling? Remember what we said: he was supposed to have quickness, memory, courage, and greatness of mind.
Yes.
Will not such a one from his early childhood be in all things first among all, especially if his bodily endowments are like his mental ones?
Certainly, he said.
And his friends and fellow citizens will want to use him for their own purposes as he gets older?
No question.
Falling at his feet, they will make requests to him and do him honour and flatter him, because they want to get into their hands now, the power which he will one day possess.
That often happens, he said.

And what will a man such as he is be likely to do under such circumstances, especially if he be a citizen of a great city, rich and noble, and a tall, proper youth? Will he not be full of boundless aspirations, and fancy himself able to manage the affairs of Hellenes and of barbarians, and having got such notions into his head will he not dilate and elevate himself in the fulness of vain pomp and senseless pride?
He certainly will.

And if, while he's in this state of mind, someone approaches him gently and tells him the truth — that he's actually foolish and needs to acquire real understanding, which can only be gotten through hard work — do you think he'll be eager to listen, given all these influences working against it?
Not at all.

And even if someone, through natural goodness or sound judgment, does have his eyes opened a little and is humbled and drawn toward philosophy — how will his friends react when they see themselves losing the advantage they expected from his company? Won't they do and say anything to prevent him from yielding to his better nature? They'll work against his teacher too — through private schemes and public prosecutions if necessary.
No doubt about it.
Then how can someone in these circumstances ever become a philosopher?
It's impossible.

So were we not right in saying that the very qualities which make a person philosophical can, if he's poorly educated, pull him away from philosophy? And that wealth, status, and the rest of life's supposed advantages do the same?
We were quite right.

Thus, my excellent friend, is brought about all that ruin and failure which I have been describing of the natures best adapted to the best of all pursuits. They are natures which we maintain to be rare at any time; this being the class out of which come the men who are the authors of the greatest evil to States and individuals; and also of the greatest good when the tide carries them in that direction; but a small man never was the doer of any great thing either to individuals or to States.
That is absolutely true, he said.

And so philosophy is left abandoned, her marriage incomplete. Her true partners have deserted her and gone off to live false, unworthy lives. Meanwhile, others who don't deserve her — seeing she has no family to protect her — move in, abuse her, and heap on her the very reproaches you mentioned: that her followers are either worthless or, in most cases, thoroughly bad.
That's certainly what people say.

And what else would you expect? I said. Think of all the petty characters who see this territory open — a field rich with impressive titles and grand appearances — and leap into philosophy from their trades, like prisoners escaping into a sanctuary. They're probably the cleverest at their own miserable crafts. But even in its degraded state, philosophy retains a dignity that the other arts lack. And that dignity attracts many whose natures are flawed and whose souls are warped by their occupations, just as their bodies are warped by their trades. Isn't this inevitable?
Yes.

They're exactly like a bald little tinker who's just gotten out of prison and come into money. He takes a bath, puts on a new suit, and dresses himself up as a bridegroom — about to marry his master's daughter, who's been left poor and alone.
A perfect parallel.
What kind of offspring will come from such a marriage? Won't they be base and illegitimate?
Absolutely.

And when people who are unworthy of education attach themselves to philosophy — which is above their station — what kind of ideas and opinions will they produce? Won't they be mere sophisms that may sound impressive but contain nothing genuine, nothing truly worthy of wisdom?
No doubt, he said.

So, Adeimantus, only a very small remnant of worthy followers of philosophy will survive. Perhaps someone of noble character detained in exile and kept free from corrupting influences remains devoted to her. Or a great soul born in a small city whose politics he rightly despises and ignores. A gifted few may come from other professions that they justly look down on. And perhaps some are held back by Theages' bridle — everything in Theages' life was pushing him toward politics, but his poor health kept him from it. My own case — the inner sign that guides me — is barely worth mentioning; it's been given to almost no one else. Those who belong to this small group have tasted how sweet and blessed philosophy truly is. They've also seen clearly enough the madness of the masses. They know that no one in politics is honest, and that there's no ally with whom they could fight for justice and survive. Such a person is like someone who's fallen in among wild animals: he won't join in their savagery, but he can't fight them all alone. He'd be killed before he could do the world any good. So he holds his peace and goes his own way — like someone who steps under the shelter of a wall during a storm of dust and driving rain. Watching the rest of humanity drenched in wickedness, he's content if he can somehow keep himself clean from injustice and impiety, and depart this life at peace, with good will and bright hope.
Well, he said, that's no small achievement before he goes.
No small achievement — but not the greatest either, unless he finds a State that suits him. In the right State, he would grow even greater and become the savior of his country as well as of himself.
I think we've now explained well enough why philosophy has such a bad reputation. The charges against her are unjust — have I covered that sufficiently, or would you like to add anything?
Nothing more on that subject, he replied; but I should like to know which of the governments now existing is in your opinion the one adapted to her.

Not one of them, I said. And that's exactly my complaint against them — none of our existing states is worthy of the philosophical nature. That's why it gets twisted and corrupted. It's like an exotic seed planted in foreign soil: it loses its character and is overpowered by its surroundings. But if philosophy ever finds a state as perfect as she herself is, then it will be clear that she is truly divine, and that everything else — human natures and institutions alike — is merely mortal. And now I know you're going to ask: what is that state?
Actually, no, he said — you're wrong about that. I was going to ask whether it's the state we've been founding in this conversation, or some other one.

Ours, in most respects, I replied. But you may remember that we said there would always need to be some living authority in the State who holds the same understanding of the constitution that guided you, as legislator, when you were laying down the laws.
That was said, he replied.
Yes, but not satisfactorily. You frightened us with your objections, which made clear that the discussion would be long and difficult. And what still remains to discuss is anything but easy.
What remains?
The question of how the study of philosophy can be organized so that it doesn't destroy the State. All great undertakings carry risk. As they say, what's good is hard.
Still, he said, let's clear this up. That will make the inquiry complete.

If anything stops me, I said, it won't be lack of desire but lack of ability. You can see how eager I am. And notice how boldly and even recklessly I'm about to declare that the State should pursue philosophy in a completely different way than it does now.
What way?

As things stand now, I said, students of philosophy are far too young. They pick it up barely past childhood, dabbling in it during whatever time they can spare from money-making and housekeeping. Even the ones who are considered the most philosophically inclined give up when they hit the real difficulty — I mean dialectic. Later in life, if someone invites them, they might attend the occasional lecture, and they make a big deal out of that — but they don't treat philosophy as their real business. And by old age, most of them are snuffed out more thoroughly than the sun of Heraclitus — because unlike his sun, they never rekindle.
What should they do instead?

The exact opposite. In childhood and youth, their studies and their philosophy should be suited to their age. During their growing years, the main focus should be on developing their bodies, so they have strong bodies to serve them later when philosophy demands their full attention. As they mature and their minds begin to ripen, increase the exercise of the soul. And when their physical strength fades and they're past the age for civic and military duties — then let them roam freely in the pastures of philosophy, devoting themselves to nothing else, if they're meant to live happily here and crown this life with equal happiness in the next.

How truly in earnest you are, Socrates! he said; I am sure of that; and yet most of your hearers, if I am not mistaken, are likely to be still more earnest in their opposition to you, and will never be convinced; Thrasymachus least of all.

Don't stir up trouble between Thrasymachus and me, I said. We've only just become friends — not that we were ever really enemies. I'll keep trying until I either convert him and everyone else, or at least do them some good for the day when they live again in another existence and encounter arguments like these.
You're talking about a time rather far off.

Rather, I replied, of a time which is as nothing in comparison with eternity. Nevertheless, I do not wonder that the many refuse to believe; for they have never seen that of which we are now speaking realized. They have seen only a conventional imitation of philosophy, consisting of words artificially brought together, not, like these of ours, having a natural unity. But a human being who in word and work is perfectly moulded, as far as he can be, into the proportion and likeness of virtue — such a man ruling in a city which bears the same image, they have never yet seen, neither one nor many of them. Do you think that they ever did?
Never.

No, my friend, and they have seldom, if ever, heard free and noble sentiments; such as men utter when they are earnestly and by every means in their power seeking after truth for the sake of knowledge, while they look coldly on the subtleties of controversy, of which the end is opinion and strife, whether they meet with them in the courts of law or in society.
They're strangers to such talk, he said.

And this was what we foresaw, and this was the reason why truth forced us to admit, not without fear and hesitation, that neither cities nor States nor individuals will ever attain perfection until the small class of philosophers whom we termed useless but not corrupt are providentially compelled, whether they will or not, to take care of the State, and until a like necessity be laid on the State to obey them; or until kings, or if not kings, the sons of kings or princes, are divinely inspired with a true love of true philosophy. That either or both of these alternatives are impossible, I see no reason to affirm: if they were so, we might indeed be justly ridiculed as dreamers and visionaries. Am I not right?
Quite right.

If then, in the countless ages of the past, or at the present hour in some foreign clime which is far away and beyond our ken, the perfected philosopher is or has been or hereafter shall be compelled by a superior power to have the charge of the State, we are ready to assert to the death that this our constitution has been, and is — yea, and will be whenever the Muse of Philosophy is queen. There is no impossibility in all this; that there is a difficulty, we acknowledge ourselves.
That's my view as well, he said.
But you'd say the majority disagrees?
I'd imagine so, he replied.

O my friend, I said, do not attack the multitude: they will change their minds if, not in an aggressive spirit, but gently and with the view of soothing them and removing their dislike of over-education, you show them your philosophers as they really are, and describe, as you were just now doing, their character and profession; and then mankind will see that he of whom you are speaking is not such as they supposed. If they view him in this new light, they will surely change their notion of him, and answer in another strain. Who can be at enmity with one who loves them? Who that is himself gentle and free from envy will be jealous of one in whom there is no jealousy? Nay, let me answer for you, that in a few this harsh temper may be found, but not in the majority of mankind.
I quite agree, he said.

And don't you think, as I do, that the hostility most people feel toward philosophy comes from the pretenders — people who barge in uninvited, constantly complaining and attacking each other, turning philosophy into a contest between personalities instead of a search for truth? Nothing could be less worthy of philosophy.
Nothing could be less worthy.

For the person whose mind is fixed on true reality, Adeimantus, has no time to look down at the petty affairs of men, or to fill himself with envy and hostility by fighting against them. His gaze is always directed upward, toward things that are fixed, unchanging, and orderly — things that neither harm nor are harmed by one another but exist in perfect rational harmony. He imitates these things and makes himself as much like them as he can. Don't you think a person becomes like whatever he spends his time admiring?
That's inevitable.
So the philosopher, holding communion with what is divine and orderly, becomes orderly and divine himself — as far as human nature allows. Though he'll still face plenty of slander, of course.
Of course.

And if he's called upon to shape not only himself but human nature in general — in states and in individuals — molding it according to the pattern he sees in that higher realm, will he be a clumsy craftsman of justice, temperance, and every civic virtue?
Anything but clumsy.

And if people realize that what we're saying about him is true, will they be angry at philosophy? Will they refuse to believe us when we say that no state can be happy unless its constitution is designed by artists who work from the divine pattern?
They won't be angry if they understand, he said. But how would these artists go about their work?

They will begin by taking the State and the manners of men, from which, as from a tablet, they will rub out the picture, and leave a clean surface. This is no easy task. But whether easy or not, herein will lie the difference between them and every other legislator: they will have nothing to do either with individual or State, and will inscribe no laws, until they have either found, or themselves made, a clean surface.
They'd be quite right, he said.
Having done that, they'd start sketching the outline of a constitution.
No doubt.

And as they fill in the picture, I imagine they'd constantly look back and forth — first at absolute justice, beauty, and temperance, then at the human version they're creating. They'd mix and blend the various elements of life into the image of a true human being, guided by that quality which Homer calls, when it appears among men, the form and likeness of God.
Very true, he said.
They'd erase one feature and paint in another, over and over, until they'd made human character as close as possible to the divine pattern.
Indeed, he said, they couldn't produce a finer picture than that.

So are we starting to win over those opponents you described — the ones who were charging at us with full force? Are they getting any calmer now that we've shown them what kind of artist designs constitutions — the very person they were so furious about when we put the State in his hands?
Much calmer, if they have any sense.
Where can they still find grounds for objection? Will they deny that the philosopher is a lover of truth and reality?
That would be unreasonable.
Or that his nature, as we've described it, is akin to the highest good?
They can't deny that either.
But again, will they tell us that such a nature, placed under favourable circumstances, will not be perfectly good and wise if any ever was? Or will they prefer those whom we have rejected?
Surely not.
Then will they still be angry at our saying that until philosophers rule, neither states nor individuals will have any rest from evil, and our ideal state will never be realized?
I think they'll be less angry.
Shall we say they're not just less angry but actually quite gentle — that they've been won over and, if only out of embarrassment, can't refuse to agree?
By all means, he said.
Then let us suppose that the reconciliation has been effected. Will any one deny the other point, that there may be sons of kings or princes who are by nature philosophers?
No one could deny that, he said.

And when they have come into being, will any one say that they must of necessity be destroyed? That they can hardly be saved is not denied even by us; but that in the whole course of ages no single one of them can escape — who will venture to affirm this?
Who could say that!
But one is enough, I said. Let one man like this gain a city that's willing to obey him, and he could bring the ideal state into being — the one the world finds so incredible.
Yes, one is enough.
If the ruler established the laws and institutions we've described, and the citizens were willing to obey — that's at least possible?
Certainly.
And that other people might approve of what we approve — that's no miracle or impossibility?
I think not.
And we've already shown at length that all this, if possible, is certainly for the best.
We have.
And now we say not only that our laws, if they could be enacted, would be for the best, but also that the enactment of them, though difficult, is not impossible.
Very good.

Well then — painfully and with great effort we've finished that topic. What remains is to discuss how and through what studies the saviors of our constitution will be produced, and at what ages they should take up each study.
Certainly.

I was too clever earlier when I skipped over the thorny questions about women, procreation, and the appointment of rulers — I knew these would provoke jealousy and be hard to work out. But that cleverness didn't help much: I had to deal with them anyway. The women and children are now settled, but the question of rulers needs to be examined from scratch. We said, you'll recall, that they must love their country, must be tested by pleasures and pains, and must never, in hardship or danger or any crisis, lose their patriotism. Whoever failed the test was rejected; whoever came through pure, like gold in the refiner's fire, was to be made ruler and given honors in life and after death. That was the gist of it, but the argument averted its eyes and hurried past, afraid to stir up the difficulty we now face.
I remember perfectly, he said.
Yes, my friend, and at the time I shrank from saying what I'm about to say. But now let me say it boldly: the perfect guardian must be a philosopher.
Yes, let that be affirmed, he said.
And don't expect there to be many of them. The qualities we said were essential rarely come together in one person. They're usually found in fragments.
What do you mean? he said.

Think about it, I replied. Quick intelligence, memory, shrewdness, cleverness, and similar qualities don't often coexist with high spirits and greatness of mind. People who have these intellectual gifts tend not to live steady, orderly lives — they're pulled this way and that by their impulses, and all their stability drains away.
Very true, he said.

On the other hand, the steady, dependable types — the ones who are like rocks in battle, immovable in the face of fear — tend to be equally immovable when it comes to learning. They're sluggish, always yawning, always drowsy whenever anything intellectual is required of them.
Quite true.
And yet we were saying that both qualities were necessary in those to whom the higher education is to be imparted, and who are to share in any office or command.
We certainly did, he said.
And this combination is rare?
Very rare.

Then the aspirant must not only be tested in those labours and dangers and pleasures which we mentioned before, but there is another kind of probation which we did not mention — he must be exercised also in many kinds of knowledge, to see whether the soul will be able to endure the highest of all, or will faint under them, as in any other studies and exercises.
That's the right way to test them, he said. But what do you mean by the highest knowledge?
You remember, I said, that we divided the soul into three parts and identified the natures of justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom?
If I'd forgotten that, he said, I wouldn't deserve to hear the rest.
And do you remember the qualification we added before discussing those virtues?
What qualification?

We said that to see them in their true perfection, we'd need to take a longer road. By that route, they would become fully clear. But we could also sketch them roughly at the level of our earlier discussion. You all said that would be good enough, and so we continued — but the result, it seemed to me, was far from precise. Whether you were satisfied is for you to say.
I thought — and the others agreed — that you gave us a reasonable account of them.

But my friend, I said, any account that falls short of the whole truth is not a reasonable measure. Nothing incomplete is the measure of anything, though people are too ready to settle for less and think they don't need to search further.
That's a common tendency in people who are lazy.
Yes, I said. And it's the very worst tendency in a guardian of the State and its laws.
True.

Then the guardian, I said, must take the longer road and work just as hard at learning as at physical training. Otherwise he'll never reach the highest knowledge — the one that most truly belongs to him, as we were just saying.
Wait, he said — is there something even higher than justice and the other virtues?

Yes, I said, there is. And of the virtues too we must behold not the outline merely, as at present — nothing short of the most finished picture should satisfy us. When little things are elaborated with an infinity of pains in order that they may appear in their full beauty and utmost clearness, how ridiculous that we should not think the highest truths worthy of attaining the highest accuracy!
Absolutely, he said. But do you think we'll let you off without asking what this highest knowledge is?

Nay, I said, ask if you will; but I am certain that you have heard the answer many times, and now you either do not understand me, or, as I rather think, you are disposed to be troublesome. For you have often been told that the idea of good is the highest knowledge, and that all other things become useful and advantageous only by their use of this. You can hardly be ignorant that of this I was about to speak, concerning which, as you have often heard me say, we know so little; and without which, any other knowledge or possession of any kind will profit us nothing. Do you think that the possession of all other things is of any value if we do not possess the good? Or the knowledge of all other things if we have no knowledge of beauty and goodness?
Of course not.
You also know that most people say pleasure is the good, while the more refined say it's knowledge?
Yes.
And you know that those who say knowledge can't explain what knowledge they mean, and end up having to say 'knowledge of the good'?
How absurd!

Yes, I said, that they should begin by reproaching us with our ignorance of the good, and then presume our knowledge of it — for the good they define to be knowledge of the good, just as if we understood them when they use the term ‘good' — this is of course ridiculous.
Exactly right, he said.
And those who define the good as pleasure are in the same muddle — they're forced to admit that there are bad pleasures as well as good ones.
Certainly.
Which means they're admitting that the same things are both good and bad?
True.
So clearly this question is full of difficulties.
Full of them.

And here's another thing we can see: when it comes to justice and beauty, many people are content with appearances — they'll do, have, or seem to have what appears just or beautiful, even if it isn't real. But with the good? No one is satisfied with what merely appears good. Everyone wants the real thing. When it comes to the good, appearances are scorned by everyone.
Very true, he said.

This, then — this thing that every soul pursues, making it the goal of all its actions, sensing that it exists but unable to grasp its nature, unable to achieve the same certainty about it as about other things, and therefore missing whatever value those other things might have — should the best men in our State, to whom everything is entrusted, remain in the dark about something this important?
Certainly not, he said.

I don't think anyone who doesn't understand how beauty and justice are connected to the good will make a very good guardian of them. And I suspect that without knowledge of the good, no one can truly know anything else.
That's a shrewd suspicion, he said.
And if our guardian has this knowledge, our State will be in perfect order?
Of course, he replied; but I wish that you would tell me whether you conceive this supreme principle of the good to be knowledge or pleasure, or different from either?
There it is, I said. I knew all along that a demanding fellow like you wouldn't be satisfied with what other people think about these things.
Well, Socrates, he said, it doesn't seem right that someone who's spent his entire life studying philosophy should only be able to repeat other people's opinions without ever stating his own.
But does anyone have the right to speak with authority about what he doesn't know?
Not, he said, with the assurance of positive certainty; he has no right to do that: but he may say what he thinks, as a matter of opinion.

Haven't you noticed, I said, that opinions without knowledge are poor, ugly things? The best of them are blind. People who hold a true opinion without understanding are no better than blind travelers who happen to be on the right road.
Very true.
So you'd rather see what's blind and crooked and base, when others can show you brightness and beauty?

Still, I must implore you, Socrates, said Glaucon, not to turn away just as you are reaching the goal; if you will only give such an explanation of the good as you have already given of justice and temperance and the other virtues, we shall be satisfied.

So will I, my friend — more than satisfied. But I'm afraid I'll fail and make a fool of myself with my clumsy efforts. No, let's not try to define the good itself right now — that's too ambitious for the present moment. But I can tell you about the child of the good, the thing most like it. Would you like to hear about that? If not, we'll drop it.
By all means, he said, tell us about the child, and you shall remain in our debt for the account of the parent.

I do indeed wish, I replied, that I could pay, and you receive, the account of the parent, and not, as now, of the offspring only. Take, however, this latter by way of interest, and at the same time have a care that I do not render a false account, although I have no intention of deceiving you.
We'll watch carefully. Go ahead.
Yes, I said, but I must first come to an understanding with you, and remind you of what I have mentioned in the course of this discussion, and at many other times.
What?
The familiar distinction: there are many beautiful things and many good things, and so on for every category — and we apply the word 'many' to all of them.
True, he said.
And then there is absolute beauty and absolute good — a single Form for each of those things we call 'many.' Each group of many things can be brought under one idea, which is the essence of each.
Very true.
The many things are seen but not known; the Forms are known but not seen.
Exactly.
And what is the organ by which we see visible things?
Sight, he said.
And we hear with hearing, I said, and perceive other things with the other senses?
True.
But have you ever noticed that sight is by far the most elaborate and expensive piece of engineering among the senses?
No, I hadn't thought about that, he said.
Then think about this: does hearing need anything beyond the ear and the sound — any third element — for hearing to take place?
Nothing at all.
No, indeed, I replied; and the same is true of most, if not all, the other senses — you would not say that any of them requires such an addition?
Certainly.
But have you noticed that sight and visibility do require something extra?
What do you mean?

Sight resides in the eyes, and the person who has eyes wants to see. Color is present in the things to be seen. But unless there's a third element, specifically suited for this purpose, the eyes will see nothing and the colors will remain invisible.
What element are you talking about?
The one you call light, I replied.
True, he said.
So the bond between sight and visibility is a noble one — far nobler than the bonds connecting the other senses to their objects. And light itself is no ordinary thing.
Far from ordinary, he said.
And among the gods of heaven, which one is the lord of this element? Whose light is it that enables the eye to see and the visible to appear?
The sun, obviously — as you and everyone else would say.
Now, may I describe the relationship between sight and the sun in this way?
How?
Neither sight nor the eye that contains it is the sun.
No.
Yet of all the sense organs, the eye is the most sun-like?
By far.
And the power that the eye possesses is a kind of gift dispensed by the sun?
Exactly.
So the sun is not sight itself, but the cause of sight — recognized by sight?
True, he said.

This, then, is what I call the child of the good. The good produced the sun in its own likeness. What the good is in the realm of thought — in relation to mind and the objects of thought — the sun is in the visible world — in relation to sight and the objects of sight.
Can you spell that out a bit more? he said.
You know, I said, that when you look at things in the dark — lit only by moonlight or starlight — your eyes see dimly and seem almost blind, as if they had no clear vision at all.
Very true.
But when they are directed towards objects on which the sun shines, they see clearly and there is sight in them?
Certainly.

Well, the soul works the same way. When it's directed toward what is illuminated by truth and reality, it perceives, understands, and seems full of intelligence. But when it turns toward the dim realm of becoming and perishing, it gropes around with mere opinions, shifting from one view to another, and seems to have no intelligence at all.
Just so.

Now, this thing that gives truth to the objects of knowledge and the power of knowing to the knower — I want you to call that the Form of the Good. It's the cause of knowledge and truth, insofar as truth is known. Beautiful as both knowledge and truth are, you'll be right to think of the Good itself as something even more beautiful. Just as light and sight can be called sun-like but are not the sun, so knowledge and truth can be called good-like but are not the Good. The Good holds an even higher place of honor.
What incredible beauty, he said — if it's the source of knowledge and truth and yet surpasses them in beauty! Surely you don't mean that the good is pleasure?
Don't even suggest it, I replied. But consider the image from another angle.
Which angle?
The sun, you'd agree, not only makes things visible but also gives them generation, nourishment, and growth — though the sun itself is not generation?
Certainly.
In the same way, the good not only makes things knowable but gives them their very being and essence — yet the good itself is not essence. It surpasses essence in dignity and power.
By the light of heaven! said Glaucon, with mock solemnity. What an extraordinary idea!
Blame yourself, I said. You're the one who forced me to share my thoughts.
And pray continue to utter them; at any rate let us hear if there is anything more to be said about the similitude of the sun.
Oh, there's a great deal left, I said.
Then don't leave anything out, however small.
I'll try not to, I said. But I suspect quite a lot will have to be left out.
I hope not, he said.

Now picture this, I said. There are two ruling powers: one presides over the intellectual realm, the other over the visible realm. (I won't say 'heaven,' in case you think I'm playing word games.) Do you have this distinction — visible and intelligible — clearly in mind?
I do.

Now take a line which has been cut into two unequal parts, and divide each of them again in the same proportion, and suppose the two main divisions to answer, one to the visible and the other to the intelligible, and then compare the subdivisions in respect of their clearness and want of clearness, and you will find that the first section in the sphere of the visible consists of images. And by images I mean, in the first place, shadows, and in the second place, reflections in water and in solid, smooth and polished bodies and the like. Do you understand?
Yes, I follow.
The second subdivision of the visible includes the actual things of which those images are copies — the animals we see, the plants, and everything made by human hands.
Very good.
Would you say that these two subdivisions differ in their degree of truth — that copies stand to originals as the realm of opinion stands to the realm of knowledge?
Absolutely.
Now consider how the intelligible realm should be divided.
How?

Like this: in the lower subdivision, the soul uses the objects from the visible realm as images. It can only proceed by hypothesis, moving downward to a conclusion rather than upward to a first principle. In the higher subdivision, the soul moves beyond hypotheses, ascending to a first principle that is not hypothetical, proceeding through Forms alone — by means of Forms, through Forms, and ending in Forms.
I don't quite follow, he said.

Then I will try again; you will understand me better when I have made some preliminary remarks. You are aware that students of geometry, arithmetic, and the kindred sciences assume the odd and the even and the figures and three kinds of angles and the like in their several branches of science; these are their hypotheses, which they and everybody are supposed to know, and therefore they do not deign to give any account of them either to themselves or others; but they begin with them, and go on until they arrive at last, and in a consistent manner, at their conclusion?
Yes, I know that, he said.

And do you not know also that although they make use of the visible forms and reason about them, they are thinking not of these, but of the ideals which they resemble; not of the figures which they draw, but of the absolute square and the absolute diameter, and so on — the forms which they draw or make, and which have shadows and reflections in water of their own, are converted by them into images, but they are really seeking to behold the things themselves, which can only be seen with the eye of the mind?
That's true.

This is the kind of thing I called intelligible — but in pursuing it, the soul is forced to rely on hypotheses. It can't rise above the realm of hypothesis, so it uses physical objects (which themselves have copies further down the scale) as images. Relative to those lower copies, these objects are treated as clear and valuable, but the inquiry itself remains tethered to its assumptions.
I see, he said. You're talking about geometry and its sister disciplines.

And when I talk about the higher division of the intelligible, I mean the kind of knowledge that reason itself achieves through the power of dialectic. Here, hypotheses aren't treated as starting points but as genuine hypotheses — stepping stones and launching points into a realm that lies beyond hypothesis, where reason grasps the first principle of everything. Having seized that principle, reason then follows out everything that depends on it, descending step by step back down — but using nothing from the sensible world along the way. The entire journey proceeds through Forms, by means of Forms, and ends in Forms.

I think I understand you, he replied, though not perfectly — what you're describing sounds enormously ambitious. But let me say what I take you to mean. The knowledge that dialectic deals with — the knowledge of being and reality — is clearer than what the mathematical sciences achieve. Those sciences start from hypotheses and are grasped by understanding rather than by the senses. But because they don't ascend to a first principle, they fall short of true reason, even though their objects become knowable through reason when a first principle is supplied. I take it you'd call the mathematical way of thinking 'understanding' rather than 'reason' — placing it between mere opinion and full rational knowledge.

You have quite conceived my meaning, I said; and now, corresponding to these four divisions, let there be four faculties in the soul — reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, faith (or conviction) to the third, and perception of shadows to the last — and let there be a scale of them, and let us suppose that the several faculties have clearness in the same degree that their objects have truth.
I understand, he replied. I agree and accept your arrangement.

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: Now, I said, let me show you an image of how far human nature is enlightened or unenlightened. Picture people living in an underground cave with a long entrance open to the daylight. They've been there since childhood, with their legs and necks chained so they can't move, forced to look only straight ahead — the chains prevent them from turning their heads. Behind and above them, a fire blazes in the distance. Between the fire and the prisoners there's a raised walkway, and along it runs a low wall — like the screen that puppet-masters put up in front of themselves, over which they show their puppets.
I see.

Now imagine people walking along behind this wall, carrying all sorts of objects — statues, figures of animals made of wood and stone and other materials — that stick up above the wall. Some of these people are talking, others are silent.
That's a strange image, and strange prisoners, he said.
They're just like us, I replied. Tell me — can they see anything of themselves or each other except the shadows cast by the fire on the wall of the cave facing them?
How could they, he said, if they've been forced to keep their heads still their whole lives?
And they'd only see shadows of the objects being carried behind them?
Yes, he said.
And if they could talk to each other, wouldn't they assume that the shadows they saw were real things — that the names they gave the shadows referred to actual objects passing before them?
Very true.
And if the cave had an echo from the far wall, whenever one of the people behind them spoke, wouldn't the prisoners think the sound came from the passing shadow?
No question, he replied.
To these prisoners, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but shadows.
That's certain.

And now look again, and see what will naturally follow if the prisoners are released and disabused of their error. At first, when any of them is liberated and compelled suddenly to stand up and turn his neck round and walk and look towards the light, he will suffer sharp pains; the glare will distress him, and he will be unable to see the realities of which in his former state he had seen the shadows. And then conceive some one saying to him that what he saw before was an illusion, but that now, when he is approaching nearer to being and his eye is turned towards more real existence, he has a clearer vision — what will be his reply? And you may further imagine that his instructor is pointing to the objects as they pass and requiring him to name them — will he not be perplexed? Will he not fancy that the shadows which he formerly saw are truer than the objects which are now shown to him?
Much more real.

And if he were forced to look directly at the light of the fire, wouldn't the pain in his eyes make him turn away and retreat to the things he could see clearly — which he'd still believe were more real than what was being shown to him?
True, he said.

And if he were dragged by force up the steep, rough passage and held in the sunlight — wouldn't he be in pain and furious about it? When he faced the light, his eyes would be so dazzled that he couldn't see any of the things now called real.
Not right away, he said.

He will require to grow accustomed to the sight of the upper world. And first he will see the shadows best, next the reflections of men and other objects in the water, and then the objects themselves; then he will gaze upon the light of the moon and the stars and the spangled heaven; and he will see the sky and the stars by night better than the sun or the light of the sun by day?
Certainly.
And last of all, he'd be able to look at the sun itself — not just its reflection in water, but the actual sun in its proper place — and contemplate it as it really is.
Certainly.

Then he'd work out that the sun is responsible for the seasons and the years, that it governs everything in the visible world, and that it is, in a way, the cause of everything he and his fellow prisoners used to see.
Clearly, he said — that's where his reasoning would lead him.
And when he remembered his old home in the cave, and the so-called wisdom of the place, and his fellow prisoners — don't you think he'd count himself lucky and feel sorry for them?
Very much so.

And if they used to award honors among themselves to whoever was quickest to spot the passing shadows, or who could best remember which shadows came first, which followed, and which appeared together, and could therefore best predict what would come next — do you think he'd want those honors? Would he envy the ones who held power and prestige down there? Wouldn't he rather say, with Homer —
'Better to be a poor man's servant above ground'
— and endure anything rather than go back to thinking and living as they do?
Yes, he said, I think that he would rather suffer anything than entertain these false notions and live in this miserable manner.
Imagine once more, I said, such a one coming suddenly out of the sun to be replaced in his old situation; would he not be certain to have his eyes full of darkness?
To be sure, he said.

And if there were a contest, and he had to compete in measuring the shadows with the prisoners who had never moved out of the den, while his sight was still weak, and before his eyes had become steady (and the time which would be needed to acquire this new habit of sight might be very considerable), would he not be ridiculous? Men would say of him that up he went and down he came without his eyes; and that it was better not even to think of ascending; and if any one tried to loose another and lead him up to the light, let them only catch the offender, and they would put him to death.
No question, he said.

Now, my dear Glaucon, you can apply this whole allegory to what we've been discussing. The cave is the visible world, the fire is the sun, and the journey upward into the sunlight represents the soul's ascent into the intelligible world. That, at least, is my belief — whether it's true, only God knows. But my view is this: in the world of knowledge, the Form of the Good is the last thing to be seen, and it takes real effort to see it. But once seen, the conclusion is inescapable — it is the cause of everything right and beautiful; in the visible world it produces light and the lord of light, and in the intelligible world it is the source of truth and reason. Anyone who wants to act wisely, in public or private life, must keep his eye fixed on it.
I agree, he said, as far as I can follow you.

Then you won't be surprised, I said, that those who reach this vision are reluctant to go back to human affairs. Their souls are always straining toward the higher world where they long to dwell. And that's perfectly natural, if our allegory holds.
Yes, perfectly natural.

And is it surprising if someone who has passed from divine contemplation back into the human world stumbles and makes a fool of himself — if, while still blinking and before his eyes have adjusted to the darkness, he's forced to argue in courtrooms or other public places about shadows and images of justice, and to compete with people who have never seen the real thing?
Not surprising at all, he replied.

Anyone with sense will remember that confusion of the eyes comes in two forms and from two causes — moving from light into darkness, and moving from darkness into light. The same is true of the mind's eye. When you see someone whose vision is confused and weak, don't be too quick to laugh. First ask whether that soul has come from a brighter life and can't yet see because it's not used to the dark, or whether it has come from ignorance into the light and is dazzled by the brightness. You'd consider the first person fortunate and pity the second. And if you wanted to laugh at someone, there'd be more reason to laugh at the soul coming up from below into the light than at the one coming down from the light into the cave.
That's a very fair distinction, he said.
If that's right, I said, then certain educators are wrong when they claim they can put knowledge into a soul that didn't have it before — as if they could put sight into blind eyes.
They certainly do claim that, he replied.

But our argument shows that the power and capacity for learning already exists in the soul. Just as the eye can't turn from darkness to light without turning the whole body, so the organ of knowledge can only be turned from the world of becoming to the world of being by turning the whole soul — until it can bear to look at the brightest and best of being: that is, the Good.
Very true.

Then there must be an art of turning the soul as effectively and quickly as possible — not an art of implanting sight, since sight already exists but is pointing the wrong way. It needs to be redirected toward the truth.
Yes, he said, such an art seems likely to exist.

Now, the other so-called virtues of the soul seem to be somewhat like physical qualities — they can be developed through habit and practice even when they're not innate. But the virtue of wisdom is different. It contains something more divine, which never loses its power. Depending on which way it's turned, it becomes either useful or harmful. Haven't you noticed how sharp the vision of a clever criminal can be — how keenly his wretched little soul sees the path to its goals? His eyesight isn't defective; it's just been conscripted into the service of evil. The sharper his vision, the more damage he does.
Very true, he said.

But what if there had been a circumcision of such natures in the days of their youth, and they had been severed from those sensual pleasures — such as eating and drinking — which, like leaden weights, were attached to them at their birth, and which drag them down and turn the vision of their souls upon the things that are below? If, I say, they had been released from these impediments and turned in the opposite direction, the very same faculty in them would have seen the truth as keenly as they see what their eyes are turned to now.
Very likely.

Yes, I said; and there is another thing which is likely, or rather a necessary inference from what has preceded, that neither the uneducated and uninformed of the truth, nor yet those who never make an end of their education, will be able ministers of State: not the former, because they have no single aim of duty which is the rule of all their actions, private as well as public; nor the latter, because they will not act at all except upon compulsion, fancying that they are already dwelling apart in the islands of the blest.
Very true, he replied.

So our task as founders of the State, I said, is to compel the best minds to reach the highest knowledge — the knowledge of the Good — by continuing their ascent. But once they've ascended and seen enough, we must not let them do what they do now.
What do you mean?
I mean we can't let them stay in the upper world. They must go back down into the cave and share in the prisoners' labors and honors, whatever those may be worth.
But isn't that unjust? he said. Should we give them a worse life when they could have a better one?

You've forgotten again, my friend, I said. The legislator's goal isn't to make any one class in the State exceptionally happy, but to spread happiness across the whole State. He uses persuasion and necessity to bind the citizens together, making each class share its benefits with the others. He creates such citizens not to let them go their own way, but to use them as instruments for binding the whole State together.
True, he said — I had forgotten.

Consider, Glaucon, that there's no injustice in what we're asking of our philosophers. We'll explain it to them this way: In other states, philosophers grow up on their own, without the government's help. Having educated themselves, they owe nothing to a system that did nothing for them, and it's fair enough that they refuse to participate. But you — we brought you into the world to be rulers of the hive, kings of yourselves and of the other citizens. We've educated you far better and more completely than philosophers elsewhere, and you're better equipped to participate in both worlds. So each of you, when your turn comes, must go down to where the others live and get used to seeing in the dark. Once you've adjusted, you'll see ten thousand times better than the cave-dwellers. You'll know what each shadow is and what it represents, because you've seen the beautiful, the just, and the good in their true form. And so our State will be governed in waking reality, not in a dream — unlike other states where rulers fight over shadows and tear each other apart in the struggle for power, as if power were some great prize. The truth is that the best-governed state is always the one where the rulers are least eager to govern, and the worst-governed is the one where they're most eager.
Quite true, he replied.
And when our pupils hear this, will they refuse to take their turn at governing — when they're allowed to spend most of their time together in the light?
Impossible, he answered. They're just men, and the demands we place on them are just. Each one will take office as a duty — a stern necessity — not in the spirit of our current rulers.

Exactly, my friend, I said. And that's the key: you must provide your future rulers with a life better than that of a ruler, and only then will you have a well-ordered State. Only a state that can offer this will be governed by the truly rich — rich not in gold and silver, but in the virtue and wisdom that make for genuine happiness. If people go into public service poor and hungry for personal advantage, hoping to snatch some good from their position, good government is impossible. They'll fight over office, and the resulting civil wars will destroy both the rulers and the State.
Absolutely true, he replied.
Is there any life that looks down on political ambition other than the life of true philosophy? Do you know of any?
None that I know of, he said.
And the people who govern should not be lovers of power — otherwise there will be rival lovers who fight over it.
No question.

Then who should we compel to serve as guardians? It should be the people who are wisest about governing and who have the best track record of administering the State — but who also have other honors and a life better than politics.
Those are the ones, he replied, and I would choose them.
Now, shall we consider how such guardians will be produced — how they'll be brought from darkness into light, as some are said to have ascended from the underworld to the gods?
By all means, he replied.

The process, I said, is not the turning over of an oyster-shell (in allusion to a game in which two parties fled or pursued according as an oyster-shell which was thrown into the air fell with the dark or light side uppermost), but the turning round of a soul passing from a day which is little better than night to the true day of being, that is, the ascent from below, which we affirm to be true philosophy?
Quite so.
Then we need to ask: what kind of knowledge has the power to accomplish this turn?
Certainly.
What sort of knowledge is there which would draw the soul from becoming to being? And another consideration has just occurred to me: you will remember that our young men are to be warrior athletes?
Yes, we said that.
Then this knowledge must have an additional quality.
What quality?
It must be useful in war.
Yes, if possible.
Our earlier educational scheme had two parts, didn't it?
Just so.
Gymnastics dealt with the growth and decay of the body — so it belongs to the world of becoming and perishing?
True.
So that's not the knowledge we're looking for?
No.
What about music — which also played a role in our earlier program?

Music, as you'll recall, he said, was the counterpart of gymnastics. It trained the guardians through habit — harmony made them harmonious, rhythm made them rhythmical — but it gave them no real knowledge. Its words, whether fictional or factual, had elements of rhythm and harmony, but there was nothing in music that aimed at the kind of good we're now seeking.

You remember perfectly, I said. There really was nothing of that sort in music. But then, my dear Glaucon, what branch of knowledge has this power? All the practical arts we dismissed as beneath our guardians.
That's right. But if we exclude music, gymnastics, and the practical arts — what's left?

Well, I said, if there's nothing special left, we'll have to find something universal — something every art, science, and discipline uses in common, and that everyone has to learn as part of a basic education.
What would that be?
Something quite humble, I said — the ability to distinguish one, two, and three. In a word: number and calculation. Every art and science depends on them, doesn't it?
Yes.
The humble matter of distinguishing one, two, and three — in a word, number and calculation. Don't all arts and sciences necessarily make use of them?
Yes.
Including the art of war?
Obviously.

Then Palamedes, whenever he appears in tragedy, proves Agamemnon ridiculously unfit to be a general. Did you never remark how he declares that he had invented number, and had numbered the ships and set in array the ranks of the army at Troy; which implies that they had never been numbered before, and that Agamemnon must be supposed literally to have been incapable of counting his own feet — how could he if he was ignorant of number? And if that is true, what sort of general must he have been?
A very strange one, if that's true, he said.
So we'd agree that a warrior needs to know arithmetic?
Certainly he should, if he is to have the smallest understanding of military tactics, or indeed, I should rather say, if he is to be a man at all.
I wonder if you see this study the way I do.
What's your view?
It seems to me to be exactly the kind of study we're looking for — one that naturally draws the mind toward reflection and toward being. But it's never been properly used for that purpose.
Can you explain? he said.

I'll try, I said. Follow along with me and say yes or no as I try to distinguish which kinds of knowledge have this power of attracting the soul — so we can determine whether arithmetic is one of them, as I suspect.
Go ahead, he said.

I mean to say that objects of sense are of two kinds: some of them do not invite thought because the sense is an adequate judge of them; while in the case of other objects, sense is so untrustworthy that further enquiry is imperatively demanded.
You're obviously talking about optical illusions, he said — how things look different at a distance or in paintings with light and shadow.
No, I said, that's not what I mean at all.
Then what do you mean?

The perceptions that don't invite thought are the ones where the senses don't simultaneously present opposite impressions.
