The ones that do invite thought present contradictory information — near or far, the sensation of one quality arrives tangled up with its opposite. An example will make this clearer: here are three fingers — the little finger, the second finger, and the middle finger.
Very good.
Assume they're seen up close. Here's the important point.
What is it?

Each of them looks equally like a finger, whether you see it in the middle or at the edge, whether it's white or dark, thick or thin — it doesn't matter. In all these cases, most people's minds aren't compelled to ask 'What is a finger?' because sight never suggests that a finger is anything other than a finger.
True.
So there's nothing here that invites or arouses thought.
Nothing, he said.

But is this equally true of the greatness and smallness of the fingers? Can sight adequately perceive them? And is no difference made by the circumstance that one of the fingers is in the middle and another at the extremity? And in like manner, does the touch adequately perceive the qualities of thickness or thinness, of softness or hardness? And so of the other senses: do they give perfect intimations of such matters? Is not their mode of operation on this wise — the sense which is concerned with the quality of hardness is necessarily concerned also with the quality of softness, and only intimates to the soul that the same thing is felt to be both hard and soft?
You're quite right, he said.

And the soul must be puzzled by this: if the sense of touch tells it that the same thing is both hard and soft, what does that mean? And what about light and heavy — if what's light is also heavy, and what's heavy is also light?
Yes, he said, these messages are puzzling and demand investigation.
So naturally, I said, the soul calls on calculation and intelligence for help — to figure out whether it's dealing with one thing or two.
True.
And if they turn out to be two, each of them is one and distinct?
Certainly.
And if each is one and both together are two, the soul will think of them as divided — because if they were undivided, it could only think of them as one.
True.
Now, sight did perceive big and small, but only in a confused way — jumbled together rather than distinguished.
Yes.
But thought, wanting to bring clarity to the confusion, was forced to separate big and small and see them as distinct.
Very true.
And isn't this the starting point of asking: what is big? And what is small?
Exactly.
And this is how the distinction between the visible and the intelligible first arose.
Absolutely right.

This was what I meant when I spoke of impressions which invited the intellect, or the reverse — those which are simultaneous with opposite impressions invite thought; those which are not simultaneous do not.
I understand now, he said, and I agree.
So which class do unity and number belong to?
I'm not sure, he replied.

Think a little and you will see that what has preceded will supply the answer. For if simple unity could be adequately perceived by the sight or by any other sense, then, as we were saying in the case of the finger, there would be nothing to attract towards being. But when there is some contradiction always present, and one is the reverse of one and involves the conception of plurality, then thought begins to be aroused within us, and the soul, perplexed and wanting to arrive at a decision, asks: ‘What is absolute unity?' This is the way in which the study of the one has a power of drawing and converting the mind to the contemplation of true being.
And this happens especially with the number one, he said. We see the same thing as both one and infinitely many.
Yes, I said. And what's true of one must be true of all numbers.
Certainly.
And all arithmetic and calculation deal with number?
Yes.
And they clearly lead the mind toward truth?
In a truly remarkable way.

Then this is knowledge of the kind for which we are seeking, having a double use, military and philosophical; for the man of war must learn the art of number or he will not know how to array his troops, and the philosopher also, because he has to rise out of the sea of change and lay hold of true being, and therefore he must be an arithmetician.
That's right.
And our guardian is both soldier and philosopher?
Certainly.

Then this is a kind of knowledge which legislation may fitly prescribe; and we must endeavour to persuade those who are to be the principal men of our State to go and learn arithmetic, not as amateurs; they must carry on the study until they see the nature of numbers with the mind only. Nor again, like merchants or retail-traders, with a view to buying or selling, but for the sake of their military use, and of the soul herself; and because this will be the easiest way for her to pass from becoming to truth and being.
Excellent, he said.

And now that we've discussed arithmetic, I said, notice how elegant this science really is, and how many ways it serves our purpose — when pursued in the spirit of a philosopher rather than a shopkeeper.
How do you mean?

I mean, as I was saying, that arithmetic has a very great and elevating effect, compelling the soul to reason about abstract number, and rebelling against the introduction of visible or tangible objects into the argument. You know how steadily the masters of the art repel and ridicule any one who attempts to divide absolute unity when he is calculating, and if you divide, they multiply (meaning either (1) that they integrate the number because they deny the possibility of fractions; or (2) that division is regarded by them as a process of multiplication, for the fractions of one continue to be units), taking care that one shall continue one and not become lost in fractions.
Very true.

Now, suppose a person were to say to them: O my friends, what are these wonderful numbers about which you are reasoning, in which, as you say, there is a unity such as you demand, and each unit is equal, invariable, indivisible — what would they answer?
They would answer, as I should conceive, that they were speaking of those numbers which can only be realized in thought.
So you see that this branch of knowledge genuinely deserves to be called necessary — since it clearly requires the mind to use pure intelligence in pursuit of pure truth.
Yes, that's one of its defining features.

And have you noticed that people who are naturally good at calculation tend to be quick at every other subject too? Even naturally slow people become much sharper after arithmetic training, even if they gain no other benefit from it.
Very true, he said.
And I don't think you'll find many subjects harder to study, or indeed as hard.
You won't.
So for all these reasons, arithmetic should be part of the training for the best natures — and it must not be abandoned.
I agree.
Good. That's our first subject. Now, shall we look at the related science to see if it also serves our purpose?
You mean geometry?
Exactly.

Clearly, he said, we are concerned with that part of geometry which relates to war; for in pitching a camp, or taking up a position, or closing or extending the lines of an army, or any other military manoeuvre, whether in actual battle or on a march, it will make all the difference whether a general is or is not a geometrician.

True, I said, but for that purpose only a little geometry or arithmetic is needed. The real question is whether the more advanced parts of geometry help make it easier to perceive the Form of the Good. And as I've been saying, anything that forces the soul to turn toward the place where the fullest reality resides — that's what we need.
True, he said.
So if geometry leads us to contemplate being, it serves our purpose. If it only deals with becoming, it doesn't.
That's our position.
Yet anybody who has the least acquaintance with geometry will not deny that such a conception of the science is in flat contradiction to the ordinary language of geometricians.
How so?

They have in view practice only, and are always speaking, in a narrow and ridiculous manner, of squaring and extending and applying and the like — they confuse the necessities of geometry with those of daily life; whereas knowledge is the real object of the whole science.
Absolutely, he said.
Then we need to add this further point?
What's that?
That the knowledge geometry seeks is knowledge of what is eternal — not of anything that comes into being and passes away.
That can easily be granted — it's true.
Then geometry, my noble friend, will draw the soul toward truth and create the philosophical spirit — lifting upward what is now wrongly allowed to sink downward.
Nothing is more likely to do so.
Then we must firmly require that the citizens of your ideal city study geometry. And the science has side benefits too — not trivial ones.
What kind? he said.

The military advantages you mentioned, I said. And beyond that, in every field of knowledge, experience shows that someone who has studied geometry is immeasurably quicker to learn than someone who hasn't.
The difference is enormous, he said.
So shall we make this our second required subject for the young?
Let's do that, he replied.
And shall we make astronomy the third?
I'm strongly in favor, he said. Observing seasons, months, and years is as essential to a general as it is to a farmer or sailor.

I am amused, I said, at your fear of the world, which makes you guard against the appearance of insisting upon useless studies; and I quite admit the difficulty of believing that in every man there is an eye of the soul which, when by other pursuits lost and dimmed, is by these purified and re-illumined, and is more precious far than ten thousand bodily eyes, for by it alone is truth seen. Now there are two classes of persons: one class of those who will agree with you and will take your words as a revelation; another class to whom they will be utterly unmeaning, and who will naturally deem them to be idle tales, for they see no sort of profit which is to be obtained from them. And therefore you had better decide at once with which of the two you are proposing to argue. You will very likely say with neither, and that your chief aim in carrying on the argument is your own improvement; at the same time you do not grudge to others any benefit which they may receive.
I think I'd prefer to argue mainly for my own benefit.
Then let's step back, I said. We got the order of the sciences wrong.
What was the mistake? he said.

After plane geometry, I said, we proceeded at once to solids in revolution, instead of taking solids in themselves; whereas after the second dimension the third, which is concerned with cubes and dimensions of depth, ought to have followed.
You're right, Socrates. But so little seems to be known about solid geometry.

Why, yes, I said, and for two reasons: in the first place, no government patronises them; this leads to a want of energy in the pursuit of them, and they are difficult; in the second place, students cannot learn them unless they have a director. But then a director can hardly be found, and even if he could, as matters now stand, the students, who are very conceited, would not attend to him. That, however, would be otherwise if the whole State became the director of these studies and gave honour to them; then disciples would want to come, and there would be continuous and earnest search, and discoveries would be made. For even now, disregarded as they are by the world, and maimed of their fair proportions, and although none of their votaries can tell the use of them, still these studies force their way by their natural charm, and very likely, if they had the help of the State, they would some day emerge into light.
Yes, he said, there is a remarkable charm in them. But I don't quite follow the new order. You started with plane geometry?
Yes, I said.
Then you placed astronomy next, and now you're stepping back?
Yes — in my rush to get through everything, I skipped over solid geometry (whose pathetic neglect made me jump ahead) and went straight to astronomy, which is really the study of solids in motion.
True, he said.
So let's assume solid geometry would flourish if the State supported it, and move on to astronomy as our fourth subject.

Fair enough, he replied. And now, Socrates, since you criticized my crude praise of astronomy earlier, let me praise it on your terms instead. Surely everyone can see that astronomy forces the soul to look upward and leads us from this world to a higher one.
Everyone except me, I said. I don't see it that way at all.
Then what would you say?
I'd say that the people who try to dress astronomy up as philosophy are actually making us look downward, not upward.
What do you mean? he asked.

You seem to have a pretty generous definition of 'looking upward,' I said. If someone throws his head back and stares at patterns on the ceiling, you'd probably count that as intellectual contemplation rather than just using his eyes. Maybe you're right and I'm the fool. But here's what I think: the only knowledge that makes the soul look truly upward is knowledge of what IS — knowledge of the invisible. Whether someone gazes at the sky or squints at the ground, if he's trying to learn some fact about the sensible world, I deny that he can learn — because nothing sensible is the subject of genuine knowledge. His soul is looking downward, not up, even if he floats on his back in the ocean to do his studying.
That's a fair rebuke, he said. I deserve it. But how should astronomy be studied, then, to serve the kind of knowledge we're talking about?

Like this, I said: the visible sky is beautiful — the most beautiful and perfect of visible things. But precisely because it's visible, it must be regarded as far inferior to the true motions of absolute speed and absolute slowness, moving in relation to each other and carrying what they contain, in true number and true form. These can be grasped by reason and intelligence, but not by sight.
True, he replied.

The spangled heavens should be used as a pattern and with a view to that higher knowledge; their beauty is like the beauty of figures or pictures excellently wrought by the hand of Daedalus, or some other great artist, which we may chance to behold. Any geometrician who saw them would appreciate the exquisiteness of their workmanship, but he would never dream of thinking that in them he could find the true equal or the true double, or the truth of any other proportion.
No, he replied. That would be absurd.

And the true astronomer will feel the same way when he looks at the movements of the stars. He'll think the heavens have been fashioned by their creator as beautifully as possible. But he'll never suppose that the exact ratios of night to day, or day to month, or month to year, or the precise relationships of the stars to each other — things that are material and visible — can also be perfectly eternal and free from all deviation. That would be absurd. And it would be equally absurd to spend enormous effort trying to determine their exact values.
I quite agree — though I'd never thought of it that way before.

So in astronomy, as in geometry, I said, we should work with problems and leave the visible heavens alone if we want to approach the subject properly and make the soul's natural gift of reason truly useful.
That, he said, would demand infinitely more work than current astronomers do.
Yes, I said. And there are many other areas where we'll need to take a similarly ambitious approach if our education is to be worth anything. But can you think of another suitable subject?
Not off the top of my head, he said.
Motion, I said, has many forms, and not one only; two of them are obvious enough even to wits no better than ours; and there are others, as I imagine, which may be left to wiser persons.
What are the two?
There's a second form that corresponds to the one we've been discussing.
What would that be?

The second, I said, would seem relatively to the ears to be what the first is to the eyes; for I conceive that as the eyes are designed to look up at the stars, so are the ears to hear harmonious motions; and these are sister sciences — as the Pythagoreans say, and we, Glaucon, agree with them?
We do, he replied.

But since this is a complex field, I said, we'd better learn from the Pythagoreans — they can tell us about it and whether there are any further applications. Through it all, though, we must keep our own higher purpose in view.
What purpose?

That our students must reach a certain perfection in all their knowledge — and not fall short of it, as I was saying they currently do in astronomy. In the science of harmony, the same thing happens. The teachers of harmony compare the sounds and intervals they hear, and their labor is just as futile as the astronomers'.

Exactly! he said. And it's comical to hear them talk about their 'condensed intervals' and all that. They stick their ears right up to the strings like people trying to overhear their neighbor through a wall — one group insisting they can detect an intermediate note, claiming to have found the smallest measurable interval, while the other group insists the two notes have merged into one. Both groups set their ears above their understanding.

You mean, I said, those people who torment and rack the strings on their pegs. I could extend the metaphor and talk about the blows of the plectrum, and accuse the strings of being either too reluctant or too eager to sound — but that would be tedious. What I really mean is that these aren't the people I have in mind. I'm talking about the Pythagoreans, whom we just proposed to consult about harmony. They make the same mistake as the astronomers: they investigate the numerical relationships in the harmonies they hear, but they never rise to the level of real problems — asking why some numbers are harmonious and others aren't.
That, he said, would require more than human knowledge.
I'd call it useful knowledge, I replied — if it's pursued for the sake of the beautiful and the good. Pursued for any other reason, it's useless.
Very true, he said.

Now, when all these studies reach the point where they connect and relate to one another, and their mutual relationships become clear — then, I think, and not until then, does pursuing them have real value for our purposes. Otherwise there's no profit in them.
I suspect you're right, he said. But you're describing an enormous undertaking, Socrates.
What — the prelude? I said. Don't you realize that all of this is merely the prelude to the real subject we need to learn? You surely wouldn't mistake a skilled mathematician for a dialectician.
Certainly not, he said. I've hardly ever met a mathematician who could actually reason.
But do you imagine that men who are unable to give and take a reason will have the knowledge which we require of them?
They cannot.

And so, Glaucon, we've finally arrived at the real thing — the song that dialectic sings. It belongs to the intellect alone, but the faculty of sight provides an analogy. Remember how sight, in our allegory, progressed from looking at shadows to looking at real animals and stars and finally at the sun itself? So too with dialectic: when someone sets out to discover the absolute through reason alone, without any help from the senses, and perseveres through pure intelligence until grasping the absolute Good — he arrives at the summit of the intellectual world, just as the man in our allegory arrived at the summit of the visible.
Exactly, he said.
And this progression is what you'd call dialectic?
True.

But the release of the prisoners from chains, and their translation from the shadows to the images and to the light, and the ascent from the underground den to the sun, while in his presence they are vainly trying to look on animals and plants and the light of the sun, but are able to perceive even with their weak eyes the images in the water (which are divine), and are the shadows of true existence (not shadows of images cast by a light of fire, which compared with the sun is only an image) — this power of elevating the highest principle in the soul to the contemplation of that which is best in existence, with which we may compare the raising of that faculty which is the very light of the body to the sight of that which is brightest in the material and visible world — this power is given, as I was saying, by all that study and pursuit of the arts which has been described.

I agree with what you're saying, he replied. It may be hard to accept, but from another point of view it's even harder to deny. Still, this isn't something we can settle in passing — we'll have to come back to it. So for now, whether our conclusion is right or wrong, let's assume all this and move from the prelude to the main theme. Tell us: what is dialectic? What are its divisions? And what are the paths that lead there — since those paths will also lead to our final destination.

Dear Glaucon, I said, you wouldn't be able to follow me the rest of the way, though I'd try my best. What you'd see would not be a mere image of truth, but the truth itself — or at least something very close to it. Whether what I'd show you would be actual reality, I can't say for certain. But I am confident it would be something like it.
No doubt, he replied.
But I must also remind you that the power of dialectic alone can reveal this truth — and only to someone who has already mastered the studies we've been discussing.
You can be just as confident of that, he said.

And assuredly no one will argue that there is any other method of comprehending by any regular process all true existence, or of ascertaining what each thing is in its own nature; for the arts in general are concerned with the desires or opinions of men, or are cultivated with a view to production and construction, or for the preservation of such productions and constructions. And as to the mathematical sciences which, as we were saying, have some apprehension of true being — geometry and the like — they only dream about being, but never can they behold the waking reality so long as they leave the hypotheses which they use unexamined, and are unable to give an account of them. For when a man knows not his own first principle, and when the conclusion and intermediate steps are also constructed out of he knows not what, how can he imagine that such a fabric of convention can ever become science?
It can't, he said.

Then dialectic — and dialectic alone — goes straight to the first principle, doing away with hypotheses to establish itself on solid ground. The eye of the soul, literally buried in a swamp of ignorance, is gently lifted by dialectic. She uses the sciences we've been discussing as helpers in this work of conversion. We call them sciences by convention, but they really deserve a different name — something implying more clarity than opinion but less than knowledge. Earlier we called this 'understanding.' But why argue about terminology when we have such important realities to consider?
Why indeed, he said. Any name that captures the thought clearly enough will do.

So we're satisfied with our earlier scheme: four divisions — two for intellect, two for opinion. The first is knowledge proper, the second understanding, the third belief, the fourth conjecture. The first pair deals with being, the second with becoming. And the proportions hold:
As being is to becoming, so is pure intellect to opinion. As intellect is to opinion, so is knowledge to belief, and understanding to conjecture.
But let's put off the further subdivision of the objects of opinion and intellect — that inquiry would be many times longer than everything we've discussed so far.
I agree, as far as I can follow, he said.

And do you also agree, I said, in describing the dialectician as one who attains a conception of the essence of each thing? And he who does not possess and is therefore unable to impart this conception, in whatever degree he fails, may in that degree also be said to fail in intelligence? Will you admit so much?
Yes, he said. How could I deny it?

And the same applies to the Good. Unless someone can rationally define the Form of the Good, separating it from everything else; unless he can survive every objection like a soldier in battle, refuting them not by appealing to opinion but to truth, never stumbling at any point in the argument — unless he can do all this, you'd say he knows neither the Good nor any other good. He grasps only a shadow, guided by opinion rather than knowledge — dreaming his way through this life until he arrives at the next world and falls asleep forever.
I'd certainly say all of that.

And surely you would not have the children of your ideal State, whom you are nurturing and educating — if the ideal ever becomes a reality — you would not allow the future rulers to be like posts (literally ‘lines,' probably the starting-point of a race-course), having no reason in them, and yet to be set in authority over the highest matters?
Certainly not.
Then you'll establish a law requiring them to receive the kind of education that equips them to ask and answer questions with the greatest possible skill?
Yes, he said. You and I will make that law together.
So dialectic stands as the capstone of all the sciences — nothing higher can be placed above it. The nature of knowledge goes no further.
I agree, he said.
But to whom we are to assign these studies, and in what way they are to be assigned, are questions which remain to be considered.
Clearly.
You remember how the rulers were chosen earlier?
Of course, he said.

The same types of character should be chosen again — the most reliable, the bravest, and ideally the most physically impressive. But beyond noble and spirited temperaments, they must have natural gifts that suit this particular education.
What gifts?

Mental sharpness and a quick capacity for learning. The mind flags more easily from the strain of study than the body does from gymnastics — the work belongs entirely to the mind and doesn't share the burden with the body.
Very true, he replied.

Further, he of whom we are in search should have a good memory, and be an unwearied, solid man who is a lover of labour in any line; or he will never be able to endure the great amount of bodily exercise and to go through all the intellectual discipline and study which we require of him.
He certainly needs natural gifts, he said.

The problem right now is that philosophy's students have no real calling for it, and that's why she's fallen into disrepute. As I said before, only her true children — not imposters — should take her hand.
What do you mean?

In the first place, her votary should not have a lame or halting industry — I mean, that he should not be half industrious and half idle: as, for example, when a man is a lover of gymnastic and hunting, and all other bodily exercises, but a hater rather than a lover of the labour of learning or listening or enquiring. Or the occupation to which he devotes himself may be of an opposite kind, and he may have the other sort of lameness.
Very true, he said.

And as to truth, I said, is not a soul equally to be deemed halt and lame which hates voluntary falsehood and is extremely indignant at herself and others when they tell lies, but is patient of involuntary falsehood, and does not mind wallowing like a swinish beast in the mire of ignorance, and has no shame at being detected?
Absolutely.

And when it comes to temperance, courage, greatness of mind, and every other virtue — we must be just as careful to distinguish the genuine article from the counterfeit. Where there's no such discernment, states and individuals unwittingly make rulers or friends of people who are lame in some dimension of virtue.
That's very true, he said.

We must be careful about all of this, I said. If the people we introduce to this demanding system of education are sound in body and mind, justice itself won't fault us, and we'll be saviors of the State. But if we admit people of the wrong sort, the opposite will happen — we'll pour an even greater flood of ridicule on philosophy than she already endures.
That would be shameful.
It certainly would, I said. Though I'm afraid I may be making myself a bit ridiculous right now too.
How so?

I forgot, I said, that we weren't being entirely serious, and I got too passionate. While I was speaking, I looked at philosophy and saw how shamefully she's being treated, and I felt a surge of indignation against those responsible — I got more heated than I should have.
Not at all — I was listening and didn't find you excessive.

Well, I who was speaking certainly felt it. But let me remind you: although we chose old men last time, we shouldn't do so now. Solon was wrong when he said a person can learn many things as he grows old. An old man can learn no better than he can run. Youth is the time for extraordinary effort.
Of course.

And, therefore, calculation and geometry and all the other elements of instruction, which are a preparation for dialectic, should be presented to the mind in childhood; not, however, under any notion of forcing our system of education.
Why not?
Because a free person should never learn anything under conditions of slavery. Physical exercise done under compulsion doesn't harm the body, but knowledge forced into the mind takes no hold.
Very true.
So, my friend, I said, don't use force in educating children. Let it be a kind of play. That way you'll also be better able to discover each child's natural bent.
That makes good sense, he said.
Do you remember that we also said the children should be taken to watch battles on horseback, and brought close up — like young hounds — to get a taste of danger?
Yes, I remember.
Well, the same principle applies to their studies. Whoever excels across all these trials — labors, lessons, dangers — should be selected for a special group.
At what age?

At the age when the necessary gymnastics are over: the period, whether of two or three years, which passes in this sort of training is useless for any other purpose; for sleep and exercise are unpropitious to learning; and the trial of who is first in gymnastic exercises is one of the most important tests to which our youth are subjected.
Of course, he replied.

After that, at twenty, the best will be promoted and given higher status. The studies they encountered in scattered form during childhood will now be brought together, so they can see how the sciences relate to each other and to the nature of being.
Yes, he said — that's the only kind of learning that really lasts.
And the ability to see these connections is the best test of dialectical talent. The person with a comprehensive mind is the born dialectician.
I agree, he said.

So you'll need to keep these criteria in mind. Those who show the most of this comprehensive ability, who are most steadfast in their studies and in military and civic duties — when they reach thirty, you'll select them from the best and raise them to still higher honor. Then you must test them through dialectic to find which of them can give up the use of the senses and travel, in the company of truth, toward being itself. And here, my friend, great caution is needed.
Why great caution?
Haven't you noticed, I said, what an evil dialectic has introduced?
What evil?
It fills its students with lawlessness.
It certainly does, he said.
Do you think that's surprising? Is there anything unnatural about it? Will you make some allowance for them?
Allowance for what?

Think of it this way, I said. Imagine a boy raised in great wealth by a large family, surrounded by flatterers. When he grows up, he discovers that the people he called his parents aren't his real parents — but he can't find out who his real parents are. Can you guess how he'd behave toward his flatterers and his supposed parents, first when he doesn't know the truth, and then after he discovers it? Or shall I guess?
Go ahead.

Then I should say that, while he is ignorant of the truth, he will be likely to honour his father and his mother and his supposed relations more than the flatterers; he will be less inclined to neglect them when in need, or to do or say anything against them; and he will be less willing to disobey them in any important matter.
Naturally.

But when he has made the discovery, I should imagine that he would diminish his honour and regard for them, and would become more devoted to the flatterers; their influence over him would greatly increase; he would now live after their ways, and openly associate with them, and, unless he were of an unusually good disposition, he would trouble himself no more about his supposed parents or other relations.
That's all very plausible. But how does it apply to philosophy students?
Like this: there are certain principles about justice and honor that we've been taught since childhood. We grew up obeying and respecting them, like parental authority.
True.
And there are opposing habits and pleasures that flatter and attract the soul but have no influence on people with any sense of right — who continue to obey and honor their inherited principles.
True.

Now, when the questioning spirit arrives and asks 'What is honor? What is justice?' — and argument after argument tears down the answers the young person learned from his teachers, until he's driven to believe that nothing is truly honorable or just — or the opposite — and the same for everything he once valued most — what do you think happens? Will he still honor and obey those principles?
Impossible.
And when he no longer considers them honorable or natural, and he can't discover what's truly right — what life will he pursue, if not the one that flatters his desires?
Nothing else.
So from a law-keeper he becomes a law-breaker?
Inevitably.
And all of this is perfectly natural for students of philosophy as I've described them — and, as I said, very much deserving of our sympathy.
Yes, he said — and pitiable too.
Therefore, that your feelings may not be moved to pity about our citizens who are now thirty years of age, every care must be taken in introducing them to dialectic.
Certainly.

There's a real danger that they'll taste the thrill of argument too early. You know how it is with young people: once they discover the power of refutation, they use it as a game — constantly contradicting and tearing down anyone they can, like puppies who love to pull and rip at whatever comes near them.
They certainly love nothing more, he said.

And when they have made many conquests and received defeats at the hands of many, they violently and speedily get into a way of not believing anything which they believed before; and hence, not only they, but philosophy and all that relates to it, is apt to have a bad name with the rest of the world.
All too true, he said.

But an older person won't indulge in this kind of madness. He'll imitate the person who genuinely seeks truth through dialogue, not the one who argues just for the fun of contradicting. His greater maturity will bring more honor to the pursuit, not less.
Very true, he said.
And weren't we guarding against exactly this when we said that the students admitted to dialectic must be orderly and steady by nature — not, as things are now, any random person who shows up?
Exactly right.
Now suppose the study of dialectic replaces gymnastics and is pursued intensely and exclusively for twice the number of years spent on physical training. Would that be enough?
Would you say six years or four? he asked.

Make it five, I replied. After that, they must be sent back down into the cave and made to hold whatever military or civic offices are appropriate for young people. This will give them practical experience, and we'll be able to test whether they stand firm when pulled in every direction by temptation, or whether they give way.
And how long should this stage last?

Fifteen years, I answered. And when they reach fifty, those who have survived and distinguished themselves in every action and every branch of knowledge must finally reach the summit. They must raise the eye of their soul to the universal light that illuminates all things and behold the absolute Good. For that is the pattern by which they must order the State and the lives of individuals, as well as the remainder of their own lives. They'll spend most of their time in philosophy, but when their turn comes, they'll take on the work of governing — not as some heroic feat, but simply as a duty. When they've raised up a new generation like themselves to be the next guardians, they'll depart to the Islands of the Blessed. The city will honor them with public memorials and sacrifices — as demigods, if the oracle approves, or at the very least as blessed and godlike.
What a sculptor you are, Socrates! You've carved these rulers to perfection.
Yes, I said, Glaucon, and of our governesses too; for you must not suppose that what I have been saying applies to men only and not to women, as far as their natures can go.
You're right, he said, since we've given them equal share in everything, just like the men.

Well then, I said — would you agree that what we've said about the State and its government isn't just a dream? It's difficult, certainly, but not impossible — and possible only in the way we've described: when true philosopher-kings arise in a state, one or more of them, who despise the honors of this present world as petty and worthless, who value justice above all things and regard it as the greatest necessity, whose service to justice shapes every institution — when such rulers set their own city in order?
How will they do it?

They will begin by sending out into the country all the inhabitants of the city who are more than ten years old, and will take possession of their children, who will be unaffected by the habits of their parents; these they will train in their own habits and laws — I mean in the laws which we have given them: and in this way the State and constitution of which we were speaking will soonest and most easily attain happiness, and the nation which has such a constitution will gain most.
Yes, I think that's right, Socrates. You've described very well how such a state could come into being, if it ever does.
So we've said enough about the perfect State and the kind of person who embodies it. It's clear enough what he would look like.
Clear enough, he replied. And I agree that there's nothing more to be said on this point.

chapters.title: Book VIII
paragraphs: And so, Glaucon, we have arrived at the conclusion that in the perfect State wives and children are to be in common; and that all education and the pursuits of war and peace are also to be common, and the best philosophers and the bravest warriors are to be their kings?
That has been agreed, replied Glaucon.

Yes, I said. And we further agreed that the rulers, once appointed, will take their soldiers and house them in the kind of dwellings we described — common to all, with nothing private or individual. And about their property — you remember what we decided?

Yes, I remember. No one was to have any ordinary possessions. They were to be warrior athletes and guardians, receiving only their maintenance from the other citizens instead of an annual salary. Their job was to look after themselves and the whole State.
Right, I said. Now that we've finished that part of our task, let's find where we got sidetracked so we can get back on the main path.

There is no difficulty in returning; you implied, then as now, that you had finished the description of the State: you said that such a State was good, and that the man was good who answered to it, although, as now appears, you had more excellent things to relate both of State and man. And you said further that if this was the true form, then the others were false; and of the false forms, you said, as I remember, that there were four principal ones, and that their defects, and the defects of the individuals corresponding to them, were worth examining. When we had seen all the individuals, and finally agreed as to who was the best and who was the worst of them, we were to consider whether the best was not also the happiest, and the worst the most miserable. I asked you what were the four forms of government of which you spoke, and then Polemarchus and Adeimantus put in their word; and you began again, and have found your way to the point at which we have now arrived.
Your memory is excellent, I said.
Then like a wrestler, he replied, get back into the same position. Let me ask the same question, and give me the answer you were about to give then.
If I can, I will, I said.
I'd particularly like to hear about those four constitutions you mentioned.

That's an easy question, I said. The four governments I meant, insofar as they have distinct names, are: first, the Cretan and Spartan type, which is widely admired. Second comes oligarchy — not so highly regarded, and full of evils. Third is democracy, which naturally follows oligarchy though it's very different. And last comes tyranny, great and infamous, which differs from all the rest and is the fourth and worst disorder a state can suffer. I can't think of any other constitution with a truly distinct character. There are hereditary monarchies and purchased governments and various intermediate forms, but these are hard to classify and can be found equally among Greeks and non-Greeks.
Yes, he replied, we certainly hear of many curious forms of government like that.

Do you realize, I said, that governments are as varied as the characters of the people in them? There must be as many types of the one as there are of the other. States aren't made of wood and stone — they're made of the human natures they contain, and those natures tip the scales and drag everything else along with them.
Yes, he said. States are as the men are — they grow out of human characters.
Then if there are five types of constitution, there must be five types of individual character?
Certainly.
The man who corresponds to aristocracy — the one we rightly call just and good — we've already described.
We have.

Then let us now proceed to describe the inferior sort of natures, being the contentious and ambitious, who answer to the Spartan polity; also the oligarchical, democratical, and tyrannical. Let us place the most just by the side of the most unjust, and when we see them we shall be able to compare the relative happiness or unhappiness of him who leads a life of pure justice or pure injustice. The enquiry will then be completed. And we shall know whether we ought to pursue injustice, as Thrasymachus advises, or in accordance with the conclusions of the argument to prefer justice.
Absolutely, he replied. We must do as you say.

Shall we follow our old plan, which we adopted with a view to clearness, of taking the State first and then proceeding to the individual, and begin with the government of honour? I know of no name for such a government other than timocracy, or perhaps timarchy. We will compare with this the like character in the individual; and, after that, consider oligarchy and the oligarchical man; and then again we will turn our attention to democracy and the democratical man; and lastly, we will go and view the city of tyranny, and once more take a look into the tyrant's soul, and try to arrive at a satisfactory decision.
That's an excellent approach.

First, then, I said, let's ask how timocracy — the government of honor — arises from aristocracy — the government of the best. One thing is clear: all political revolutions originate in divisions within the ruling class. A government that's united, however small, can't be overthrown.
Very true, he said.

In what way, then, will our city be moved, and in what manner will the two classes of auxiliaries and rulers disagree among themselves or with one another? Shall we, after the manner of Homer, pray the Muses to tell us ‘how discord first arose'? Shall we imagine them in solemn mockery, to play and jest with us as if we were children, and to address us in a lofty tragic vein, making believe to be in earnest?
How would they address us?

After this manner: A city which is thus constituted can hardly be shaken; but, seeing that everything which has a beginning has also an end, even a constitution such as yours will not last for ever, but will in time be dissolved. And this is the dissolution: In plants that grow in the earth, as well as in animals that move on the earth’s surface, fertility and sterility of soul and body occur when the circumferences of the circles of each are completed, which in short-lived existences pass over a short space, and in long-lived ones over a long space. But to the knowledge of human fecundity and sterility all the wisdom and education of your rulers will not attain; the laws which regulate them will not be discovered by an intelligence alloyed with sense, but will escape them, and they will bring children into the world when they ought not. Now that which is of divine birth has a period which is contained in a perfect number (that is, a cyclical number, such as 6, which is equal to the sum of its divisors 1, 2, 3, so that when the circle or time represented by 6 is completed, the lesser times or rotations represented by 1, 2, and 3 are also completed); but the period of human birth is comprehended in a number in which first increments by involution and evolution (or squared and cubed), obtaining three intervals and four terms of like and unlike, waxing and waning numbers, make all the terms commensurable and agreeable to one another. (Probably the numbers 3, 4, 5, 6, of which the first three are the sides of the Pythagorean triangle. The terms will then be 3 cubed, 4 cubed, 5 cubed, which together equal 6 cubed, or 216.) The base of these (three), with a third added (four), when combined with five (twenty) and raised to the third power, furnishes two harmonies: the first a square which is a hundred times as great (400 = 4 x 100; or, the first a square of 100 x 100 = 10,000; the whole number being 17,500, a square of 100 and an oblong of 100 by 75); and the other a figure having one side equal to the former, but oblong, consisting of a hundred numbers squared upon rational diameters of a square (omitting fractions) the side of which is five (7 x 7 = 49 x 100 = 4,900), each of them being less by one (than the perfect square which includes the fractions, that is, 50), or less by two perfect squares of irrational diameters (of a square the side of which is five, that is, 50 + 50 = 100); and a hundred cubes of three (27 x 100 = 2,700 + 4,900 + 400 = 8,000). Now this number represents a geometrical figure which has control over the good and evil of births. For when your guardians are ignorant of the law of births, and unite bride and bridegroom out of season, the children will not be goodly or fortunate. And though only the best of them will be appointed by their predecessors, still they will be unworthy to hold their fathers’ places, and when they come into power as guardians, they will soon be found to fail in taking care of us, the Muses, first by undervaluing music; which neglect will soon extend to gymnastic; and hence the young men of your State will be less cultivated. In the succeeding generation, rulers will be appointed who have lost the guardian power of testing the metal of your different races, which, like Hesiod’s, are of gold and silver and brass and iron. And so iron will be mingled with silver, and brass with gold, and hence there will arise dissimilarity and inequality and irregularity, which always and in all places are causes of hatred and war. This the Muses affirm to be the stock from which discord has sprung, wherever arising; and this is their answer to us.
Yes, and we can assume they speak truly.
Of course they speak truly, I said. How could the Muses lie?
And what do the Muses say happens next?

When discord arose, the two races pulled in different directions. The iron and bronze types turned to acquiring money, land, houses, gold, and silver. But the gold and silver types, having no desire for wealth because true riches were in their nature, inclined toward virtue and the old order. They struggled, and finally compromised: they divided land and houses into private property, enslaved the people they'd formerly protected as free citizens, and made them subjects and servants. Then they devoted themselves to war and to guarding against these new subjects.
I think you've captured the origin of the change correctly.
And the new government that emerges — it'll be a form midway between oligarchy and aristocracy?
Exactly.

That's how the change happens. Now, after the change, how will they proceed? Since this new State sits between oligarchy and the ideal State, it'll partly follow one and partly the other, with some distinctive features of its own.
True, he said.

In honoring rulers, in keeping the warrior class away from farming and trade, in common meals, in attention to gymnastics and military training — in all these respects, this State will resemble the former one.
True.

But it'll be afraid to let philosophers into power, since the available philosophers are no longer simple and sincere but of mixed character. It will turn instead to spirited, less complicated people who are naturally suited for war rather than peace. It will value military strategy and cunning, and wage wars endlessly. In these respects, the State will be distinctive.
Yes.

Yes, I said; and men of this stamp will be covetous of money, like those who live in oligarchies; they will have a fierce secret longing after gold and silver, which they will hoard in dark places, having magazines and treasuries of their own for the deposit and concealment of them; also castles which are just nests for their eggs, and in which they will spend large sums on their wives, or on any others whom they please.
That's exactly right, he said.

And they're stingy because they have no legitimate way to acquire the money they crave. So they spend other people's money on their pleasures, enjoying them in secret, running from the law like children from their father. They've been educated by force rather than persuasion, because they neglected the true Muse — the companion of reason and philosophy — and honored gymnastics over music.
No question, he said. The government you're describing is a mixture of good and evil.

Why, there is a mixture, I said; but one thing, and one thing only, is predominantly seen — the spirit of contention and ambition; and these are due to the prevalence of the passionate or spirited element.
Without a doubt, he said.

Such is the origin and such the character of this State, which has been described in outline only; the more perfect execution was not required, for a sketch is enough to show the type of the most perfectly just and most perfectly unjust; and to go through all the States and all the characters of men, omitting none of them, would be an interminable labour.
Very true, he replied.
Now, what kind of man corresponds to this government? How did he come into being, and what is he like?
I think, said Adeimantus, that in the spirit of contention which characterises him, he is not unlike our friend Glaucon.
Perhaps, I said, he may be like him in that one point; but there are other respects in which he is very different.
In what ways?

He should be more assertive and less refined, though still a friend of culture. He's a good listener but no speaker. He tends to be harsh with servants — unlike the truly educated man, who is too dignified for that — but courteous to free citizens and remarkably obedient to authority. He loves power and honor, claiming the right to rule not on the basis of eloquence or any such quality, but because he's a soldier and has proven himself in arms. He's also devoted to athletics and hunting.
Yes, that's the character that matches timocracy.

Such a person will scorn wealth when he's young. But as he ages, he'll be drawn to money more and more, because there's an avaricious streak in him. He's not single-mindedly devoted to virtue, having lost his best guardian.
Who was that? said Adeimantus.
Philosophy, I said — tempered with music, the only thing that can take up residence in a person's soul and preserve his virtue throughout life.
Good, he said.
Such, I said, is the timocratic youth, and he resembles the timocratic State.
Exactly.

His origin goes like this: he's often the young son of a brave father who lives in a poorly governed city. The father refuses its honors and offices, avoids the courts, and doesn't exert himself in public — he's willing to give up his rights just to avoid trouble.
And how does the son turn out?

The son's character starts to develop when he hears his mother complaining that her husband holds no position in the government, which means she gets no standing among other women. She sees him indifferent to money, refusing to fight in the courts or the assembly, taking whatever happens to him calmly. She notices that his thoughts are always turned inward and that he treats her with considerable neglect. So she tells the son that his father is only half a man, far too passive — adding all the other complaints about her own mistreatment that women love to rehearse.
Yes, said Adeimantus. Women certainly give us plenty of those complaints, and the complaints are just like them.

And you know, I said, that the old servants also, who are supposed to be attached to the family, from time to time talk privately in the same strain to the son; and if they see any one who owes money to his father, or is wronging him in any way, and he fails to prosecute them, they tell the youth that when he grows up he must retaliate upon people of this sort, and be more of a man than his father. He has only to walk abroad and he hears and sees the same sort of thing: those who do their own business in the city are called simpletons, and held in no esteem, while the busybodies are honoured and applauded. The result is that the young man, hearing and seeing all these things — hearing, too, the words of his father, and having a nearer view of his way of life, and making comparisons of him and others — is drawn opposite ways: while his father is watering and nourishing the rational principle in his soul, the others are encouraging the passionate and appetitive; and he, being not originally of a bad nature, but having kept bad company, is at last brought by their joint influence to a middle point, and gives up the kingdom which is within him to the middle principle of contentiousness and passion, and becomes arrogant and ambitious.
You've described his origin perfectly.
So now we have the second form of government and the second type of character?
We have.
Next, let's look at another man who, as Aeschylus puts it,
'Is set against another state' —
or rather, following our plan, let's start with the state.
By all means.
I believe oligarchy comes next.
And what exactly do you mean by oligarchy?
A government resting on a valuation of property, in which the rich have power and the poor man is deprived of it.
I understand, he replied.
Should I start by describing how the transition from timocracy to oligarchy happens?
Yes.
Well, I said, you don't need special insight to see how one turns into the other.
How?
The hoarding of gold by private individuals is what ruins timocracy. They invent illegal ways to spend it — what do they or their wives care about the law?
True enough.
And then one person, seeing another getting rich, tries to keep up, and soon the whole citizen body is consumed with the love of money.
Likely enough.

And so they grow richer and richer. The more they think about making fortunes, the less they think about virtue. When riches and virtue are put on opposite sides of a scale, one always rises as the other falls.
True.
And as wealth and wealthy people gain honor in the State, virtue and virtuous people lose it.
Clearly.
And whatever is honored gets cultivated, while whatever is dishonored gets neglected.
Obviously.
So eventually, instead of being lovers of rivalry and glory, they become lovers of trade and money. They honor and look up to the rich man and make him ruler, while the poor man is despised.
That's what happens.

They next proceed to make a law which fixes a sum of money as the qualification of citizenship; the sum is higher in one place and lower in another, as the oligarchy is more or less exclusive; and they allow no one whose property falls below the amount fixed to have any share in the government. These changes in the constitution they effect by force of arms, if intimidation has not already done their work.
Very true.
And that, broadly speaking, is how oligarchy is established.
Yes, he said. But what are the features of this form of government, and what are the defects we mentioned?

First of all, I said, think about the nature of that property qualification. Imagine if pilots were chosen based on their wealth, and a poor man were refused permission to steer even if he were the better pilot.
You mean they'd shipwreck?
Yes. And doesn't the same principle apply to governing anything?
I'd imagine so.
Including a city? Or would you exclude that?
No, he said. A city is the strongest case of all, since ruling a city is the greatest and most difficult task there is.
So this is the first major defect of oligarchy?
Clearly.
And here's another defect just as bad.
What's that?
The inevitable split: such a state isn't one state but two — one of the poor and one of the rich — living side by side and constantly conspiring against each other.
That's certainly just as bad.

Here's another shameful feature: they can't wage war properly. Either they arm the masses, in which case they're more afraid of their own people than the enemy, or they don't call them up for battle — in which case they're oligarchs indeed, few in fighting as they are few in ruling. And their love of money makes them unwilling to pay taxes.
How shameful!
And as we said before, under this kind of constitution the same people have too many occupations — they're farmers, tradesmen, and soldiers all at once. Does that seem right?
Not at all.
There's another evil that may be the greatest of all, and it first appears in this type of state.
What evil?

A man can sell everything he owns, and another can buy it all up. After the sale, the seller can still live in the city even though he's no longer really part of it — he's not a merchant, not a craftsman, not a cavalry soldier, not an infantry soldier. He's just a poor, helpless nobody.
Yes, that's an evil that first appears in this kind of state.
And there's certainly no prevention of it in oligarchies. They have both extremes — enormous wealth and total poverty.
True.

But think about this: when this man was wealthy and spending money, was he actually any use to the State as a citizen? Or was he only pretending to belong to the ruling class, when in reality he was neither ruler nor subject — just a spendthrift?
As you say — he only seemed to be a ruler. He was just a spendthrift.
May we not say that this is the drone in the house who is like the drone in the honeycomb, and that the one is the plague of the city as the other is of the hive?
Exactly, Socrates.

Now, God has made all the flying drones without stings, Adeimantus. But among the walking drones, some are stingless and others have terrible stings. The stingless ones end up as paupers in their old age. The stinging ones become what we call the criminal class.
Very true, he said.
So wherever you see paupers in a state, you can be sure that somewhere nearby there are thieves, pickpockets, temple robbers, and criminals of every kind hiding.
Clearly.
And in oligarchical states — do you find paupers?
Yes, he said. Nearly everyone who isn't a ruler is a pauper.
And may we be so bold as to affirm that there are also many criminals to be found in them, rogues who have stings, and whom the authorities are careful to restrain by force?
We certainly can.
And the existence of such people is caused by lack of education, poor upbringing, and the bad constitution of the State?
True.
Well then, that's the form and those are the evils of oligarchy. There are probably many others too.
Very likely.

Then oligarchy, or the form of government in which the rulers are elected for their wealth, may now be dismissed. Let us next proceed to consider the nature and origin of the individual who answers to this State.
By all means.
Does the timocratic man change into the oligarchical man in something like this way?
How?

A time arrives when the representative of timocracy has a son: at first he begins by emulating his father and walking in his footsteps, but presently he sees him of a sudden foundering against the State as upon a sunken reef, and he and all that he has is lost; he may have been a general or some other high officer who is brought to trial under a prejudice raised by informers, and either put to death, or exiled, or deprived of the privileges of a citizen, and all his property taken from him.
Nothing more likely.

The son has witnessed all of this. He's a ruined man. His fear drives ambition and spirit headlong from the throne in his soul. Humbled by poverty, he turns to money-making. Through mean, penny-pinching savings and hard work, he puts together a fortune. Don't you think he'll then seat the appetitive, money-loving element on the vacant throne of his soul and let it reign like a great king, complete with crown and scepter and sword?
Very much so, he replied.

And when he has made reason and spirit sit down on the ground obediently on either side of their sovereign, and taught them to know their place, he compels the one to think only of how lesser sums may be turned into larger ones, and will not allow the other to worship and admire anything but riches and rich men, or to be ambitious of anything so much as the acquisition of wealth and the means of acquiring it.
There is no transformation, he said, so swift or sure as the conversion of an ambitious youth into a greedy one.
And this greedy man — he's the oligarchical youth?
Yes, he said. At any rate, the individual he emerged from resembles the state that produced oligarchy.
Let's consider whether there's any real likeness between them.
Very good.
First, they both place the highest value on wealth?
Certainly.
They're also both penny-pinching and hardworking. The individual satisfies only his necessary desires and keeps his spending to those. He suppresses his other desires as wasteful.
True.

He's a shabby fellow who saves a little from everything and builds up his private hoard. Isn't this the kind of man ordinary people actually admire? Isn't he the very image of the state he represents?
It seems so to me. At any rate, money is highly valued by both him and the State.
You see, of course, that he's not a cultivated man, I said.
I think not, he said. If he were, he'd never have made a blind god the director of his life's chorus, or given that god the seat of honor.

Good point! I said. But consider: don't we also have to admit that, because of this lack of culture, he harbors drone-like desires — the desires of a pauper and a criminal — which he forcibly suppresses through the discipline of his general way of life?
True.
Do you know where to look to see his criminal side?
Where?
Watch him when he gets the chance to act dishonestly — like when he's the guardian of an orphan.
Indeed.

Then it'll be perfectly clear that in his everyday dealings — the ones that give him his reputation for honesty — he keeps his bad impulses in check through a kind of enforced virtue. He doesn't persuade them that wrong is wrong, or tame them with reason. He restrains them by necessity and fear, because he's terrified of losing his property.
Absolutely.
Yes, indeed, my dear friend, but you will find that the natural desires of the drone commonly exist in him all the same whenever he has to spend what is not his own.
Yes, and they'll be strong too.
So this man is at war with himself — he's two men, not one. But generally his better desires will prevail over his worse ones.
True.
For these reasons, he'll be more respectable than most people. But the true virtue of a harmonious, unified soul will be far from him.
I'd expect so.

And of course, this miser will be a poor competitor in any public contest — whether for prizes of victory or other worthy honors. He won't spend money on glory. He's terrified of rousing his expensive appetites and inviting them into the fight. He battles with only a fraction of his resources, oligarch-style, and usually loses the prize while keeping his money.
Very true.
Can we still doubt that the miser and money-maker is the counterpart of the oligarchical State?
No doubt at all.
Next comes democracy. We still need to examine how it arises and what it's like, so we can then look at the democratic individual and bring him before the court.
That's our method, he said.
Well, I said, how does the transition from oligarchy to democracy happen? Isn't it like this: the supreme good that oligarchy pursues is wealth — and its appetite for wealth is insatiable?
What happens then?

The rulers, knowing that their power rests on their wealth, refuse to pass laws restraining the extravagance of young spendthrifts — because they profit from their ruin. They lend them money at interest and buy up their estates, making themselves richer and more powerful.
Obviously.
It should be clear that the love of wealth and the spirit of moderation can't coexist in the same state to any significant degree. One or the other will be abandoned.
That's pretty clear.
And in oligarchies, through widespread recklessness and extravagance, people of good family are often reduced to poverty?
Yes, often.

And still they remain in the city; there they are, ready to sting and fully armed, and some of them owe money, some have forfeited their citizenship; a third class are in both predicaments; and they hate and conspire against those who have got their property, and against everybody else, and are eager for revolution.
That's true.

Meanwhile the money-men, heads down, pretending not to see the people they've already ruined, stick their stinger — their money — into whoever else drops their guard. They recover the original sum multiplied many times over into a whole brood of offspring. And so they breed drones and paupers throughout the State.
Yes, he said, there are plenty of them — that's certain.
The fire blazes on, and they won't put it out — either by restricting what people do with their own property, or by another remedy.
What other remedy?

A second-best option that has the advantage of forcing citizens to look to their character: a general rule that voluntary contracts are entered at the lender's own risk. Then there'd be less of this scandalous money-grubbing, and the evils we've been describing would be greatly reduced.
Yes, greatly reduced.

As things stand, the rulers — driven by the motives I've described — treat their subjects badly. Meanwhile they and their families, especially the young men of the ruling class, live in luxury and idleness, both physical and mental. They do nothing and can resist neither pleasure nor pain.
Very true.
The rulers care only about making money and are as indifferent to virtue as the poorest paupers.
Just as indifferent.

Such is the state of affairs which prevails among them. And often rulers and their subjects may come in one another's way, whether on a journey or on some other occasion of meeting, on a pilgrimage or a march, as fellow-soldiers or fellow-sailors; aye and they may observe the behaviour of each other in the very moment of danger — for where danger is, there is no fear that the poor will be despised by the rich — and very likely the wiry sunburnt poor man may be placed in battle at the side of a wealthy one who has never spoilt his complexion and has plenty of superfluous flesh — when he sees such a one puffing and at his wits' end, how can he avoid drawing the conclusion that men like him are only rich because no one has the courage to despoil them? And when they meet in private, will not people be saying to one another, ‘Our warriors are not good for much'?
I'm well aware that's exactly how they talk, he said.

And, as in a body which is diseased the addition of a touch from without may bring on illness, and sometimes even when there is no external provocation a commotion may arise within — in the same way, wherever there is weakness in the State, there is also likely to be illness, of which the occasion may be very slight, the one party introducing from without their oligarchical, the other their democratical allies; and then the State falls sick, and is at war with herself; and may be at times distracted, even when there is no external cause.
Yes, absolutely.

Democracy comes into being when the poor defeat their opponents — killing some, banishing others — and then give everyone who's left an equal share in freedom and power. The magistrates are commonly chosen by lot.
Yes, he said, that's how democracy works, whether the revolution is accomplished by force or by the threat of it driving the other side to withdraw.
So what's their way of life, and what kind of government do they have? Because as the government goes, so goes the man.
Obviously, he said.
First and foremost, they're free, aren't they? The city overflows with freedom and frankness — a person can say and do whatever he likes.
So they say, he replied.
And where there's freedom, each individual can arrange his own life however he pleases.
Clearly.
So in this kind of state you'll find the greatest variety of human natures.
You will.

This state is likely to be the most beautiful of all — like an embroidered robe spangled with every kind of flower. Just as women and children think a riot of colors is the loveliest thing in the world, so many people will find this state, with its dazzling variety of characters and customs, the fairest of them all.
Yes.
And it's certainly a convenient place to shop for a constitution, my friend.
Why?

Because of the liberty which reigns there — they have a complete assortment of constitutions; and he who has a mind to establish a State, as we have been doing, must go to a democracy as he would to a bazaar at which they sell them, and pick out the one that suits him; then, when he has made his choice, he may found his State.
He'll certainly have plenty of patterns to choose from.

And there's no obligation for you to govern in this state, even if you're capable of it. No obligation to be governed if you don't feel like it. No need to go to war when others do, or to keep the peace when others are at peace, unless you choose to. And if some law bars you from holding office or sitting on a jury, you can perfectly well hold office and sit on a jury anyway, if you feel like it. Isn't this a delightful way to live, at least for the moment?
For the moment, yes.

And isn't there something charming about the way democracies treat the condemned? Haven't you noticed how, in a democracy, people who've been sentenced to death or exile simply stay where they are and walk around in public? Nobody sees them or cares. They parade through the streets like heroes.
Yes, he replied, I've seen plenty of that.

And think about democracy's forgiving spirit, I said — its casual disregard for all the fine principles we laid down so carefully when we founded our city. We said that no one could become a good man unless he'd been surrounded by beauty from childhood and made a study of it. How magnificently democracy tramples on all that, not caring in the least what pursuits shaped a man before he entered politics! As long as he says he's a friend of the people, that's enough to earn him honor.
Yes, she has a noble spirit indeed.
These and similar traits are what characterize democracy — a charming form of government, full of variety and disorder, distributing a kind of equality to equals and unequals alike.
We know her well.
Now consider, I said, what sort of individual corresponds to this. Or rather, as with the State, let's first consider how he comes to be.
Very good, he said.
Isn't it something like this? He's the son of the miserly, oligarchical father who trained him in his own habits.
Exactly.
Like his father, he keeps down by force the pleasures that spend money rather than earn it — the ones we call unnecessary.
Obviously.
Would you like, for the sake of clearness, to distinguish which are the necessary and which are the unnecessary pleasures?
I would.

Are not necessary pleasures those of which we cannot get rid, and of which the satisfaction is a benefit to us? And they are rightly called so, because we are framed by nature to desire both what is beneficial and what is necessary, and cannot help it.
True.
So we're not wrong to call them necessary?
We're not.

And the desires of which a man may get rid, if he takes pains from his youth upwards — of which the presence, moreover, does no good, and in some cases the reverse of good — shall we not be right in saying that all these are unnecessary?
Certainly.
Let's pick an example of each to get a clear general picture.
Very good.
Will not the desire of eating — that is, of simple food and condiments, in so far as they are required for health and strength — be of the necessary class?
I'd say so.
The pleasure of eating is necessary in two ways: it benefits us and it keeps us alive.
Yes.
But fancy seasonings and delicacies are only necessary insofar as they contribute to health?
Certainly.

And the desire that goes beyond this — for more elaborate foods and luxuries that could generally be eliminated with early training, and that are harmful both to the body and to the soul's pursuit of wisdom and virtue — that's rightly called unnecessary?
Very true.
And we can say that the unnecessary desires are the spending kind, while the necessary ones are the earning kind, because they contribute to productive work?
Certainly.
And the same applies to the pleasures of sex and all other pleasures?
True.

And the drone of whom we spoke was he who was surfeited in pleasures and desires of this sort, and was the slave of the unnecessary desires, whereas he who was subject to the necessary only was miserly and oligarchical?
Exactly.
Now let's see how the democratic man grows out of the oligarchical one. Here's how it usually happens, I suspect.
What's the process?

When a young man raised in the vulgar, penny-pinching way we described gets a taste of the drone's honey — when he falls in with bold, crafty characters who can provide him with every kind of elaborate pleasure — that's when the oligarchical principle inside him starts transforming into the democratic one.
Inevitably.

And as in the city like was helping like, and the change was effected by an alliance from without assisting one division of the citizens, so too the young man is changed by a class of desires coming from without to assist the desires within him, that which is akin and alike again helping that which is akin and alike?
Certainly.

And if the oligarchical principle inside him has any ally — whether the influence of his father or of relatives who advise and rebuke him — then a civil war breaks out within his soul, and he's at war with himself.
Naturally.
Sometimes the democratic impulse yields to the oligarchical, and some desires die while others are banished. A spirit of decency reasserts itself in the young man's soul, and order is restored.
Yes, he said, that sometimes happens.
But then the old desires, once driven out, spring up again — fresh ones, akin to them — and because the father doesn't know how to educate them properly, they grow fierce and numerous.
Yes, he said, that's how it tends to go.
These desires draw him back to his old associates. Through secret commerce, they breed and multiply within him.
Very true.

Eventually they seize the citadel of the young man's soul, which they find empty of all genuine accomplishments, fine pursuits, and truthful words — the kind of things that dwell in the minds of those who are dearest to the gods and serve as their best guardians and sentinels.
None better.
In their place, false and boastful beliefs and phrases march in and take over.
They always do.

And so the young man returns to the land of the lotus-eaters and settles in openly. If his friends send reinforcements to the oligarchical part of him, those arrogant new beliefs shut the gates of the inner fortress. They refuse to admit the embassy or listen to private advice from older, wiser counselors. There's a battle, and the new beliefs win the day. Modesty — which they call stupidity — is driven into exile in disgrace. Temperance — which they call cowardice — is trampled in the mud and thrown out. They convince the young man that restraint and orderly spending are mere vulgarity and meanness, and with the help of a mob of corrupt appetites, they drive these virtues out beyond the border.
With great enthusiasm.

And when they've emptied and swept clean the soul of their new convert — when they've initiated him into their great mysteries — the next step is to bring Insolence, Anarchy, Waste, and Shamelessness back in with full ceremony, garlands on their heads, accompanied by a great chorus singing their praises and giving them pretty names. Insolence they call 'good breeding'; Anarchy, 'freedom'; Waste, 'magnificence'; and Shamelessness, 'courage.' And so the young man passes from his original character, trained under the discipline of necessity, into the freedom and license of useless, unnecessary pleasures.
Yes, he said, the change in him is obvious enough.

After this, he lives on, spending money, effort, and time on unnecessary pleasures just as much as necessary ones. But if he's lucky and doesn't go completely off the rails — if, as the heyday of passion passes, he lets some of the banished virtues back in and doesn't surrender entirely to the newcomers — then he lives a kind of balance, putting himself in the hands of whichever pleasure wins the moment. When he's had enough of that one, he moves on to the next. He despises none of them and treats them all as equals.
Very true, he said.

Neither does he receive or let pass into the fortress any true word of advice; if any one says to him that some pleasures are the satisfactions of good and noble desires, and others of evil desires, and that he ought to use and honour some and chastise and master the others — whenever this is repeated to him he shakes his head and says that they are all alike, and that one is as good as another.
Yes, he said, that's exactly how he behaves.

Yes, I said — he lives from day to day, indulging the appetite of the hour. One day he's drinking heavily and listening to flute music. The next he's on a water diet, trying to lose weight. Then he takes up exercise. Then he's lazy and neglects everything. Then he fancies himself a philosopher. He's often drawn to politics, leaping up to say and do whatever comes into his head. If he admires a warrior, off he goes in that direction. If it's businessmen, then it's business. His life has no order or discipline, and this chaotic existence he calls joy, freedom, and happiness.
Yes, he replied — his life is all liberty and equality.

Yes, I said. His life is a patchwork of many lives, an epitome of every kind of character. He corresponds to the state we called beautiful and multi-colored. Many a man and woman will take him as their model, and many a form of government and way of life is contained in him.
Just so.
Then let him stand as the democratic man — the representative of democracy.
So be it, he said.
