Last of all comes the most magnificent of all — the tyrant and tyranny, both man and state. These we now have to examine.
Quite right, he said.
Tell me, then, my friend: how does tyranny arise? That it grows out of democracy seems obvious.
Clearly.
And does tyranny spring from democracy in much the same way democracy springs from oligarchy?
How?
The supreme good that oligarchy aimed at — and that maintained it — was excessive wealth. Am I right?
Yes.
And the insatiable desire for wealth, combined with the neglect of everything else for the sake of money — that's what destroyed oligarchy.
True.
And democracy has its own supreme good, whose insatiable pursuit leads to its destruction.
What good?
Freedom, I replied. In a democracy, they'll tell you that freedom is the state's greatest glory — and that only in a democracy will a truly free person deign to live.
Yes, you hear that everywhere.
Well, as I was about to say, the insatiable craving for freedom and the neglect of everything else is what transforms democracy — and creates the demand for tyranny.
How so?

When a democracy that's thirsting for freedom gets bad leaders presiding over the feast, and drinks too deeply of the undiluted wine of liberty, then — unless the rulers are very agreeable and provide freedom in abundance — the people accuse them of being cursed oligarchs and punish them.
Yes, he replied, that happens all the time.

And loyal citizens who obey authority are insulted as slaves and nobodies. The democracy demands subjects who act like rulers and rulers who act like subjects. Those are the kind of people it praises and honors, both in public and private life. In such a state, can liberty possibly have any limit?
Certainly not.
Bit by bit, the anarchy creeps into private homes and eventually infects even the animals.
What do you mean?

I mean the father gets used to acting like his son's equal and comes to fear him. The son treats his father as an equal, showing no respect or reverence for either parent — and that's his freedom. The resident alien is the equal of the citizen, the citizen of the alien, the foreigner as good as either.
Yes, he said, that's how it goes.

And there are other evils too, I said — smaller ones. Teachers fear and flatter their students, while students despise their teachers and tutors. Young and old are all treated alike. The young man is on a level with the old and ready to compete with him in word and deed. Old men play along, full of pleasantry and wit, terrified of seeming stern and authoritative, and so they adopt the manners of the young.
Very true, he said.
The ultimate extreme of popular liberty is when slaves — bought and paid for — are just as free as their owners. And I should mention the equality of the sexes in relation to each other.
Why not? As Aeschylus says, let's speak the word that rises to our lips.

That is what I am doing, I replied; and I must add that no one who does not know would believe how much greater is the liberty which the animals who are under the dominion of man have in a democracy than in any other State: for truly, the she-dogs, as the proverb says, are as good as their she-mistresses, and the horses and asses have a way of marching along with all the rights and dignities of freemen; and they will run at anybody who comes in their way if he does not leave the road clear for them: and all things are just ready to burst with liberty.
When I take a country walk, he said, I often experience what you describe. You and I have dreamed the same thing.

And the ultimate result of all this, I said, is that the citizens become so sensitive that they chafe at the slightest touch of authority. Eventually, as you know, they stop caring about the laws — written or unwritten — because they refuse to have any master over them at all.
Yes, I know that all too well, he said.
This, my friend, I said, is the beautiful, glorious beginning from which tyranny springs.
Glorious indeed, he said. But what comes next?

The same disease that destroyed oligarchy destroys democracy — only magnified and intensified by freedom. Excessive liberty overwhelms democracy. The truth is that any extreme tends to produce a violent reaction in the opposite direction. This happens in the weather, in plants and animals, and above all in governments.
True.
Excessive freedom, whether in states or individuals, seems to end only in excessive slavery.
Yes, that's the natural sequence.
And so tyranny naturally arises out of democracy, and the most aggravated form of tyranny and slavery out of the most extreme form of liberty?
As we'd expect.
But that wasn't quite your question, I think. You were asking about the specific disorder that arises in both oligarchy and democracy and destroys them both?
Exactly, he replied.

Well, I was referring to the class of idle spendthrifts, whose bolder members are the leaders and whose timider ones are the followers — the same people we compared to drones, some with stings and some without.
A very apt comparison.

These two classes are the plagues of every city in which they are generated, being what phlegm and bile are to the body. And the good physician and lawgiver of the State ought, like the wise bee-master, to keep them at a distance and prevent, if possible, their ever coming in; and if they have anyhow found a way in, then he should have them and their cells cut out as speedily as possible.
Absolutely, he said.

Then, in order that we may see clearly what we are doing, let us imagine democracy to be divided, as indeed it is, into three classes; for in the first place, freedom creates rather more drones in the democratic than there were in the oligarchical State.
That's true.
And in a democracy they're much more powerful.
How so?

In an oligarchy they're excluded from office and can't gain strength. But in a democracy they're practically the entire ruling class. The more aggressive ones make speeches and take action, while the rest buzz around the speaker's platform and won't let anyone else get a word in. So in democracies, the drones run almost everything.
Very true, he said.
Then there's a second class that's always separating out from the mass.
What class?
The orderly, business-minded people. In a commercial nation, they're naturally the richest.
Naturally.
They're the most squeezable — the ones who yield the most honey for the drones.
Well, he said, there's not much to squeeze from people who have nothing.
And this wealthy class is what feeds the drones.
That's about right, he said.

The third class is the people — those who work with their own hands. They're not politicians and don't have much property. But when they assemble, they're the largest and most powerful class in a democracy.
True, he said. But they rarely assemble unless they get a share of the honey.
And they do get a share, I said. The leaders strip the rich of their property and distribute it to the people — while keeping the biggest portion for themselves.
Yes, he said, that's how the people get their share.
And the people whose property is seized are forced to defend themselves before the people as best they can.
What else can they do?
And even if they have no desire for change, the others accuse them of plotting against the people and being friends of oligarchy.
True.

In the end, when these rich citizens see that the people — deceived by informers, not acting from understanding — are trying to wrong them, they're forced to become genuine oligarchs. They don't want to, but the drones' stings drive them to it, breeding revolution.
That's exactly what happens.
Then come impeachments, lawsuits, and trials on every side.
True.
The people always find some champion to set over themselves and nurse into greatness.
Yes, that's their way.
This — and nothing else — is where a tyrant comes from. When he first appears, he's a protector.
That's perfectly clear.
So how does a protector begin to turn into a tyrant? The answer is obvious once you know the tale of the temple of Zeus in Arcadia.
What tale?
The legend says that whoever tastes a single piece of human flesh — minced in with the flesh of other sacrificial victims — is destined to become a wolf. Haven't you heard it?
Oh yes.

It's the same with the people's protector. When he has a mob entirely at his command, he can't restrain himself from shedding the blood of his own people. Through the familiar method of false accusations, he hauls them into court and murders them — tasting the blood of his fellow citizens with unholy lips. Some he kills, others he banishes, while hinting at debt cancellation and land redistribution. After that, isn't his fate sealed? He must either be destroyed by his enemies or be transformed from a man into a wolf — from a protector into a tyrant.
Inevitably.
This, I said, is the man who leads the party against the rich.
The same.
He may be driven out for a while, but he comes back — despite his enemies — a fully grown tyrant.
That's clear.
And if they can't expel him or get him condemned to death through a public prosecution, they resort to assassination.
Yes, he said, that's their usual method.
Then comes the famous request for a bodyguard — the standard trick of every aspiring tyrant at this stage of his career. 'Don't let the people's friend be lost to them!'
Exactly.
The people readily agree. All their fear is for him — they have none for themselves.
Very true.
And when a wealthy man who's been accused of being an enemy of the people sees what's happening — well, my friend, as the oracle told Croesus:
'By pebbly Hermus' shore he flees and rests not, and is not ashamed to be a coward.'
Quite right too, said he. If he stayed, he'd never have the chance to be ashamed again.
If he's caught, he dies.
Of course.

And the protector — he's no longer 'larding the plain' with his bulk, as Homer says. He's the overthrower of many, standing in the chariot of state with the reins in his hand — no longer protector, but absolute tyrant.
No doubt about it, he said.
And now let us consider the happiness of the man, and also of the State in which a creature like him is generated.
Yes, let's do that, he said.

At first, in the early days of his power, he's all smiles. He greets everyone he meets. Him, a tyrant? Never! He makes promises in public and private, cancels debts, distributes land to the people and his friends — and wants to seem so very kind and good to everyone!
Of course, he said.

But once he's dealt with his external enemies — through conquest or treaty — and there's nothing left to fear from outside, then he's always stirring up some new war, so the people will need a leader.
Naturally.
And there's another purpose too: to impoverish the citizens through taxes, so they're forced to focus on daily survival and have no energy left for conspiring against him.
Obviously.

And if any of them are suspected by him of having notions of freedom, and of resistance to his authority, he will have a good pretext for destroying them by placing them at the mercy of the enemy; and for all these reasons the tyrant must be always getting up a war.
He must.
And of course, this makes him unpopular.
Inevitably.
Then some of the bolder men who helped put him in power start to speak out — both to him and to each other — criticizing what he's doing.
That's to be expected.
And the tyrant, if he intends to keep ruling, must get rid of them. He can't stop as long as he has a single friend or enemy who's worth anything.
He can't.

So he has to keep a sharp eye on who is brave, who is high-minded, who is wise, who is wealthy. Lucky man — they're all his enemies, and he must find pretexts to move against them, whether he wants to or not, until he's purged the State.
Yes, he said — quite a purge.
Yes, I said — the opposite of a medical purge. Doctors remove what's bad and leave what's good. He removes what's good and keeps what's bad.
He doesn't seem to have much choice, if he wants to rule.
What a lovely dilemma, I said: be forced to live surrounded by people who are bad and who hate you — or don't live at all!
Yes, that's the choice.
And the more detestable his actions are to the citizens, the more satellites and the greater devotion in them will he require?
Certainly.
And where will he find this devoted band?
They'll flock to him of their own accord, he said — if he pays them.
Good lord! I said. More drones — of every kind and from every land.
Yes, he said.
But won't he want to recruit locally too?
How do you mean?
He will rob the citizens of their slaves; he will then set them free and enrol them in his body-guard.
Of course, he said — and those will be the ones he trusts most.
What a blessed creature this tyrant must be — having destroyed the decent people and taken these as his trusted companions!
Yes, he said. They're exactly his type.
Yes, I said. These are his new citizens, the ones who admire him and keep him company, while the good people hate and shun him.
Naturally.
Truly, then, tragedy is a wise art, and Euripides was a great tragedian.
Why do you say that?
Because he wrote the pithy line:
'Tyrants grow wise by keeping company with the wise.'
Meaning, obviously, that the 'wise' people are the ones the tyrant keeps around him.
Yes, he said. And Euripides also praises tyranny as godlike, among many other such sentiments — shared by the other poets too.
And that's precisely why the tragic poets, wise as they are, will forgive us — and anyone who governs as we propose — if we don't welcome them into our state. They are the eulogists of tyranny.
Yes, he said, the clever ones among them will certainly forgive us.
But they will continue to go to other cities and attract mobs, and hire voices fair and loud and persuasive, and draw the cities over to tyrannies and democracies.
Very true.

And they're paid for it too, and honored — most of all by tyrants, and next most by democracies. The higher they climb up our constitutional scale, the more their influence fades, as if running out of breath.
True.
But we're getting off topic. Let's return to the question: how does the tyrant maintain that fine, large, varied, ever-changing army of his?

If, he said, there are sacred treasures in the city, he will confiscate and spend them; and in so far as the fortunes of attainted persons may suffice, he will be able to diminish the taxes which he would otherwise have to impose upon the people.
And when those run out?
Then obviously, he said, he and his drinking companions — male and female — will live off his father's estate.
You mean the people — who gave him his power — will have to support him and his friends?
Yes, he said. They won't have a choice.

But what if the people lose their temper and say that a grown son has no business being supported by his father — that it should be the other way around? They didn't create him and set him up so that, once he was powerful, they'd become the servants of their own servants, supporting him and his rabble of slaves and hangers-on. No — they created him to be their protector and liberator from the rich and the so-called aristocrats. So they order him and his companions to leave — like a father throwing out a wild son and his disreputable friends.
Then, by heaven, he said, the people will discover what kind of monster they've been nurturing. And when they try to throw him out, they'll find that they're weak and he's strong.
What! You don't mean the tyrant would actually use violence against his father — would beat him if he resisted?
Yes, he will — after disarming him first.

Then the tyrant is a parricide — a cruel guardian of a helpless old parent. And this is real tyranny, beyond any shadow of doubt. As the saying goes, the people who tried to escape the smoke of slavery to free men have fallen into the fire of slavery to slaves. In place of the generous but excessive freedom they once enjoyed, they've put on the harshest and most bitter form of slavery — slavery to slaves.
True, he said.
Well then — haven't we adequately described the nature of tyranny and how the transition from democracy to tyranny takes place?
Yes, perfectly adequately, he said.

chapters.title: Book IX
paragraphs: Last of all comes the tyrannical man. We have one more question to answer: how is he formed out of the democratic man, and how does he live — happily or miserably?
Yes, he said, he's the only one left.
There is, however, I said, a preliminary question that remains unanswered.
What question?
I don't think we've adequately identified the nature and number of the appetites. Until we do, our inquiry will stay muddled.
Well, he said, it's not too late to fix that.

Very true, I said. Here's what I want to understand: there are certain unnecessary pleasures and appetites that I'd call lawless. Everyone seems to have them, but in some people they're kept in check by the laws and by reason, and the better desires overpower them — they're either completely eliminated or reduced to a few weak ones. In others, though, they're stronger and more numerous.
Which appetites are you talking about?

The ones that wake up when the rational, human, ruling part of us is asleep. Then the wild beast within us, gorged with food or drink, shakes off sleep and goes hunting for satisfaction. In that state, there is no conceivable folly or crime — not even incest, unnatural acts, parricide, or eating forbidden food — that a person might not be ready to commit, having abandoned all shame and sense.
Very true, he said.

But when a person's constitution is healthy and temperate, and before sleep he has awakened his rational powers and fed them on noble thoughts and inquiries, settling into meditation — and after giving his appetites neither too much nor too little, just enough to put them to sleep so they don't interfere with the higher mind (which he leaves free to contemplate and reach toward knowledge, whether of past, present, or future) — and when he has also calmed the spirited element, so that he doesn't go to bed with anger against anyone burning in his chest — when he has quieted these two irrational parts and roused the third, which is reason, before he rests — then, as you know, he comes closest to grasping truth and is least likely to be disturbed by lawless visions.
I quite agree.

I've gone on a bit of a digression, I said. But the point I want to make is this: in every one of us, even the best, there is a lawless, wild-beast nature that peeks out during sleep. Think about whether you agree.
Yes, I agree.

Now remember the character we gave to the democratic man. He was supposed to have been trained from youth by a miserly father who encouraged the money-making appetites but suppressed the unnecessary ones — the ones aimed at amusement and display.
True.

And then he got into the company of a more refined, licentious sort of people, and taking to all their wanton ways, rushed into the opposite extreme from an abhorrence of his father's meanness. At last, being a better man than his corruptors, he was drawn in both directions until he halted midway and led a life not of vulgar and slavish passion, but of what he deemed moderate indulgence in various pleasures. After this manner the democrat was generated out of the oligarch?
Yes, he said, that was our view, and it still is.
And now, I said, years will have passed away, and you must conceive this man, such as he is, to have a son, who is brought up in his father's principles.
I can imagine him.

And imagine the same thing happening to the son that happened to the father: he's drawn into a completely lawless life, which his seducers call perfect freedom. His father and friends side with the moderate desires, while the opposition encourages the opposite ones. When these sinister magicians — these tyrant-makers — realize they're losing their grip on him, they implant a master passion in his soul to lord it over his idle, spendthrift appetites. This passion is a kind of monstrous, winged drone — and that's really the only image that does it justice.
Yes, he said, that's the only adequate image.

And when his other appetites, amid clouds of incense and perfume and garlands and wine and all the pleasures of a dissolute life, buzz around him and nourish the sting of desire that they've planted in his drone-like nature — then at last this lord of the soul, with Madness as the captain of his guard, breaks out into a frenzy. If he finds in himself any good opinions or worthy desires still forming, any remaining trace of shame, he destroys them and casts them out until he's purged away all temperance and filled himself with madness.
Yes, he said. That's exactly how the tyrannical man is created.
And isn't this why love has always been called a tyrant?
I wouldn't be surprised.
And doesn't a drunken man also have the spirit of a tyrant?
He does.
And you know that a deranged person, not right in his mind, fancies he can rule not only over men but over the gods themselves?
He does.

And the tyrannical man in the true sense of the word comes into being when, either under the influence of nature, or habit, or both, he becomes drunken, lustful, passionate? O my friend, is not that so?
It certainly is.
That's his nature and origin. Now, how does he live?
Why don't you tell me, as people jokingly say.
I imagine, I said, that the next stage involves feasts and parties and orgies and courtesans and all that sort of thing. Love is the lord of the household, directing all the business of his soul.
That's certain.
Yes, and every day and every night new desires sprout up, fierce and demanding.
They certainly do, he said.
Whatever income he has is quickly spent.
True.
Then come debts and the selling off of his property.
Of course.

When he has nothing left, won't those desires — packed in the nest like hungry young ravens — cry out for food? And he, goaded on by them, and especially by Eros himself who is their general, goes frantic trying to find someone to rob or defraud so he can feed them?
That's inevitable.
He must get money by any means, or suffer horrible torment.
He must.

And as in himself there was a succession of pleasures, and the new got the better of the old and took away their rights, so he, being younger, will claim to have more than his father and his mother, and if he has spent his own share of the property, he will take a slice of theirs.
No doubt.
And if his parents will not give way, then he will try first of all to cheat and deceive them.
Naturally.
And if that fails, he'll use force and plunder them.
Probably.
And if the old man and woman resist — what then, my friend? Will he feel any qualms about tyrannizing over his own parents?
I wouldn't feel very confident about his parents' safety, he said.

But for heaven's sake, Adeimantus! For the sake of some recently acquired mistress — a completely unnecessary attachment — can you believe he'd beat his own mother, his oldest friend, essential to his very existence, and put her under the authority of this new woman, once she's brought into the same house? And would he do the same to his aged, withered father — his first and most essential friend — for the sake of some newly found young beauty who is anything but essential?
Yes, indeed, he said. I believe he would.
What a blessing a tyrannical son must be to his father and mother!
A great blessing indeed, he replied.

When his parents' resources run out and the swarm of pleasures in his soul grows thick, first he breaks into houses or robs nighttime travelers of their clothes. Next he plunders temples. Meanwhile, the old convictions about right and wrong that he had as a child are overthrown by the newly liberated desires that now form the bodyguard of Eros and share his reign. These desires, which used to break free only in the dreams of sleep (back when he was still under the law and his father's authority), now govern him constantly and in waking life. What he used to be only rarely and in dreams, he now becomes always and in reality. No murder is too foul, no food forbidden, no act too horrible. Eros lives like a tyrant within him, lawless and supreme, and drives him — as a tyrant drives a state — to every reckless deed that will feed him and the mob of desires around him, whether they entered from outside through evil company or were released from within by his own corrupt nature. Isn't that a fair picture of his life?
It certainly is, he said.

And if there are only a few people like this in a State, while the rest are decent, they go abroad and become bodyguards or mercenaries for some other tyrant who needs them for a war. If there's no war, they stay home and commit petty crimes around the city.
What kind of crimes?

For example, they are the thieves, burglars, cut-purses, foot-pads, robbers of temples, man-stealers of the community; or if they are able to speak, they turn informers, and bear false witness, and take bribes.
That's a minor catalogue of evils, assuming there aren't many of them.

Minor things are minor only by comparison, I said. In terms of the misery and harm they inflict on a state, all these crimes don't come within a thousand miles of the tyrant. When this class of people and their followers grow numerous and become aware of their strength, aided by the foolishness of the people, they choose from among themselves the one whose soul is most tyrannical and make him their tyrant.
Yes, he said. He'd be the best candidate for it.

If the people submit, fine. But if they resist, just as he began by beating his own father and mother, he'll now beat his fatherland too — or motherland, as the Cretans say — keeping it in subjection to the young gang he's brought in as its rulers and masters. This is where his desires and passions lead.
Exactly.

When such men are still private citizens, before they get power, here's how they behave: they associate entirely with their own flatterers and lackeys. If they want something from someone, they'll grovel and make every show of affection. But once they've got what they want, they don't know the person anymore.
Absolutely true.
They're always either masters or slaves, never anyone's true friend. The tyrannical man never tastes genuine freedom or friendship.
Certainly not.
Can't we fairly call such men treacherous?
Without question.
And utterly unjust, if our earlier definition of justice was right?
And it was perfectly right, he said.
So let's sum up the worst man in a single phrase, I said: he is the waking reality of what we described as dream.
Exactly right.
And the person who is by nature most tyrannical, if he actually gains power, becomes more tyrannical the longer he rules.
That's certain, said Glaucon, taking his turn.

And the man who's been shown to be the most wicked — will he not also be the most miserable? The one who's ruled as tyrant longest and most completely — truly and continuously the most miserable? Even if that's not the popular opinion?
Yes, inevitably, he said.
And must not the tyrannical man be like the tyrannical State, and the democratical man like the democratical State; and the same of the others?
Certainly.
And as state is to state in virtue and happiness, so is person to person?
Of course.
Then comparing our original city, which was under a king, and the city which is under a tyrant, how do they stand as to virtue?
They're opposite extremes, he said. One is the very best, the other the very worst.

There can be no mistake, I said, as to which is which, and therefore I will at once enquire whether you would arrive at a similar decision about their relative happiness and misery. And here we must not allow ourselves to be panic-stricken at the apparition of the tyrant, who is only a unit and may perhaps have a few retainers about him; but let us go as we ought into every corner of the city and look all about, and then we will give our opinion.
A fair request, he replied. And anyone can see that a tyranny is the most wretched form of government and a kingdom the happiest.

And in estimating the men too, may I not fairly make a like request, that I should have a judge whose mind can enter into and see through human nature? He must not be like a child who looks at the outside and is dazzled at the pompous aspect which the tyrannical nature assumes to the beholder, but let him be one who has a clear insight. May I suppose that the judgment is given in the hearing of us all by one who is able to judge, and has dwelt in the same place with him, and been present at his daily life and known him in his family relations, where he may be seen stripped of his tragedy attire, and again in the hour of public danger — he shall tell us about the happiness and misery of the tyrant when compared with other men?
That too is a fair proposal, he said.
Shall we assume that we ourselves are qualified judges and have actually encountered such people? That way, we'll have someone to answer our questions.
By all means.
Let me ask you not to forget the parallel of the individual and the State; bearing this in mind, and glancing in turn from one to the other of them, will you tell me their respective conditions?
What do you mean? he asked.
Starting with the State, I replied: would you say that a city governed by a tyrant is free or enslaved?
No city could be more completely enslaved.
And yet there are some free men in such a state, as well as masters?
Yes, he said — a few. But the mass of the people, including the best of them, are miserably degraded and enslaved.

Then if the man is like the State, I said, the same picture must hold: his soul is full of servility and meanness. The best parts are enslaved, and a small ruling part — which is also the worst and maddest — is in charge.
Inevitably.
And would you say that such a soul is the soul of a free man or a slave?
A slave, in my opinion.
And a state enslaved under a tyrant is completely incapable of doing what it really wants?
Completely.
And the soul under a tyrant (taking the whole soul together) is likewise least able to do what it truly desires. It's constantly goaded by a restless sting, full of turmoil and regret.
Certainly.
And is the tyrannical city rich or poor?
Poor.
Then the tyrannical soul must also be poor — and perpetually unsatisfied?
True.
And such a state and such a person must be full of fear?
Absolutely.
Is there any state where you'll find more lamentation, sorrow, groaning, and pain?
None.
And is there any man in whom you will find more of this sort of misery than in the tyrannical man, who is in a fury of passions and desires?
Impossible.
Considering all these evils, you judged the tyrannical state to be the most miserable of all?
And I was right, he said.
Certainly, I said. And when you see the same evils in the tyrannical man, what do you say about him?
That he is by far the most miserable of all men.
There, I said, I think you're starting to go wrong.
What do you mean?
I don't think he's reached the ultimate extreme of misery yet.
Then who has?
Someone I'm about to describe.
Who?
The person who has a tyrannical nature and, instead of living a private life, has the further misfortune of being thrust into actual political tyranny.
From what you've said, I gather you're right.
Yes, I replied. But in an argument this important, we shouldn't just guess — we should be quite certain. The question of good and evil is the greatest there is.
Very true, he said.
Let me offer an illustration that may shed some light on this.
What's your illustration?
Think of the rich men in our cities who own many slaves. They're like the tyrant in that respect — the only difference is that the tyrant has more slaves.
Yes, that's the difference.
These rich men live in safety and have nothing to fear from their servants, you know.
What should they fear?
Nothing. But do you see why?
Yes — because the entire city backs up each individual owner.

Exactly, I said. But now imagine one of these men — the owner of fifty slaves, say — picked up with his whole family, property, and slaves by some god and set down in the wilderness, far from any free men who could help him. Wouldn't he be terrified that his slaves would kill him and his wife and children?
He'd be in absolute terror, he said.
He'd be forced to start flattering his own slaves, making them all sorts of promises, freeing them — much against his will. He'd have to become a servant to his own servants.
Yes, he said — that would be his only hope of survival.
And suppose the same god who carried him away to surround him with neighbours who will not suffer one man to be the master of another, and who, if they could catch the offender, would take his life?
His situation would be even worse — surrounded and watched by enemies on every side.

And is not this the sort of prison in which the tyrant will be bound — he who, being by nature such as we have described, is full of all sorts of fears and lusts? His soul is dainty and greedy, and yet alone, of all men in the city, he is never allowed to go on a journey, or to see the things which other freemen desire to see, but he lives in his hole like a woman hidden in the house, and is jealous of any other citizen who goes into foreign parts and sees anything of interest.
Very true, he said.

And amid evils such as these, will not he who is ill-governed in his own person — the tyrannical man, I mean — whom you just now decided to be the most miserable of all — will not he be yet more miserable when, instead of leading a private life, he is constrained by fortune to be a public tyrant? He has to be master of others when he is not master of himself. He is like a diseased or paralytic man who is compelled to pass his life, not in retirement, but fighting and combating with other men.
Yes, he said, the comparison is exact.
Isn't his condition utterly wretched? Doesn't the actual tyrant live a worse life than even the man you called the most miserable?
Certainly.

The real tyrant, whatever people may think, is the real slave — forced to practice the lowest flattery and servility, a toady to the vilest of men. His desires can never be satisfied. He has more wants than anyone and is truly poor, if you know how to examine his whole soul. His entire life is consumed by fear, convulsed by agony and distraction — exactly mirroring the state he rules. Isn't that right?
Very true, he said.

Moreover, as we were saying before, he grows worse from having power: he becomes and is of necessity more jealous, more faithless, more unjust, more friendless, more impious, than he was at first. He is the purveyor and cherisher of every sort of vice, and the consequence is that he is supremely miserable, and that he makes everybody else as miserable as himself.
No sensible person would disagree, he said.

Come then, I said. Like a judge at a theatrical competition delivering the final verdict, you must now decide: who ranks first in happiness, who second, and the rest in order. There are five contestants: the kingly, the timocratic, the oligarchic, the democratic, and the tyrannical.

The decision will be easily given, he replied; they shall be choruses coming on the stage, and I must judge them in the order in which they enter, by the criterion of virtue and vice, happiness and misery.

Shall we hire a herald, or shall I announce it myself? The son of Ariston has judged that the best and most just man is also the happiest — and that is the man who is most kingly, most sovereign over himself. The worst and most unjust man is also the most miserable — and that is the man who is the greatest tyrant, both of himself and of his state.
Make the announcement yourself, he said.
And shall I add: 'whether or not they are known to be such by gods and men'?
Add it.
Good, I said. That's our first proof. And here is a second that may carry some weight.
What is it?

The second proof is derived from the nature of the soul: seeing that the individual soul, like the State, has been divided by us into three principles, the division may, I think, furnish a new demonstration.
Of what kind?
It seems to me that these three parts correspond to three kinds of pleasure, three kinds of desire, and three ruling principles.
How do you mean? he said.

There's one part by which a person learns, another by which he feels anger or indignation. The third has many forms and no single name, but we call it the appetitive part, because of the extraordinary power of the desires for eating, drinking, sex, and everything else along those lines. It's also called the money-loving part, since these desires are usually satisfied through money.
True, he said.

If we were to say that the loves and pleasures of this third part were concerned with gain, we should then be able to fall back on a single notion, and might truly and intelligibly describe this part of the soul as loving gain or money.
I agree.
And isn't the spirited part entirely devoted to dominance, victory, and fame?
True.
Could we call it the competitive or honor-loving part?
That fits perfectly.
And everyone can see that the rational part is wholly directed toward truth and cares less for money or honor than either of the others.
Far less.
So 'lover of wisdom' and 'lover of learning' are fitting titles for this part of the soul?
Certainly.
And one of these three principles dominates in each person's soul?
Yes.
So we can say there are three types of people — lovers of wisdom, lovers of honor, and lovers of gain?
Exactly.
And three corresponding types of pleasure?
Very true.

Now, if you examine the three classes of men, and ask of them in turn which of their lives is pleasantest, each will be found praising his own and depreciating that of others: the money-maker will contrast the vanity of honour or of learning if they bring no money with the solid advantages of gold and silver?
True, he said.

And the lover of honour — what will be his opinion? Will he not think that the pleasure of riches is vulgar, while the pleasure of learning, if it brings no distinction, is all smoke and nonsense to him?
Very true.

And are we to suppose, I said, that the philosopher sets any value on other pleasures in comparison with the pleasure of knowing the truth, and in that pursuit abiding, ever learning, not so far indeed from the heaven of pleasure? Does he not call the other pleasures necessary, under the idea that if there were no necessity for them, he would rather not have them?
There can be no doubt of that, he replied.
So when the pleasures of each type are in dispute — and the question isn't which life is nobler or better, but simply which is more pleasant — how do we decide who's right?
I really can't say, he said.
Well, what should the criteria be? Anything better than experience, wisdom, and reason?
Nothing better, he said.

Then consider, I said. Of the three types, which has the widest experience of all the pleasures we listed? Has the money-lover experienced the pleasure of knowing truth better than the philosopher has experienced the pleasure of gain?

The philosopher, he replied, has greatly the advantage; for he has of necessity always known the taste of the other pleasures from his childhood upwards. But the lover of gain in all his experience has not of necessity tasted — or, I should rather say, even had he desired, could hardly have tasted — the sweetness of learning and knowing truth.
Then the lover of wisdom has a great advantage over the lover of gain, for he has a double experience?
A very great one.
And compared to the honor-lover — has he more experience of the pleasures of honor, or the honor-lover of the pleasures of wisdom?

Well, he said, all three types receive honor in proportion to their success — the rich man, the brave man, and the wise man all have their admirers. So they all experience the pleasures of honor. But the delight that comes from knowing true being is something only the philosopher knows.
So his experience gives him the best basis for judgment?
By far.
And he's the only one who has wisdom as well as experience?
Certainly.
Furthermore, the very instrument by which judgment is made — reason — belongs neither to the money-lover nor the honor-lover, but to the philosopher alone.
What instrument?
We said that the decision should rest with reason.
Yes.
And reasoning is distinctively the philosopher's tool?
Certainly.
If wealth and gain were the criterion, then the praise or blame of the lover of gain would surely be the most trustworthy?
Of course.
Or if honour or victory or courage, in that case the judgment of the ambitious or pugnacious would be the truest?
Clearly.
But since experience, wisdom, and reason are the criteria —
The only possible conclusion, he replied, is that the pleasures approved by the philosopher are the truest.
So we arrive at this: the pleasure of the rational part of the soul is the most genuine of the three, and the person in whom reason rules lives the most pleasant life.
Without question, he said. The wise man speaks with authority when he approves of his own life.
And which life and pleasure does our judge rank second?
Obviously the soldier's and honor-lover's — it's closer to his own than the money-maker's.
And the money-lover comes last?
Of course, he said.

So the just man has defeated the unjust twice in a row. Now comes the third and decisive round — dedicated, in wrestling fashion, to Olympian Zeus the Savior. A wise voice whispers to me that no pleasure but the philosopher's is entirely real and pure — the rest are mere shadows. And this will be the greatest fall of all.
The greatest. But can you explain?
I'll work through it and you answer my questions.
Go ahead.
Tell me — isn't pleasure the opposite of pain?
True.
And isn't there a neutral state that's neither pleasure nor pain?
There is.
A kind of midpoint — a rest of the soul between the two?
Yes.
You know what people say when they're sick?
What?
That nothing is more pleasant than being healthy. But they never realized health was the greatest pleasure until they fell ill.
Yes, I've heard that, he said.
And when persons are suffering from acute pain, you must have heard them say that there is nothing pleasanter than to get rid of their pain?
I have.
And there are many cases where mere rest and cessation of pain — not any positive enjoyment — is praised as the greatest pleasure?
Yes, he said. At those moments, they're perfectly content just to be at rest.
And conversely, when pleasure ceases, that rest will feel painful?
No doubt, he said.
So the intermediate state of rest is experienced as both pleasure and pain?
So it seems.
But can what is neither of them really be both?
I'd say not.
And both pleasure and pain are movements of the soul, aren't they?
Yes.
But we just showed that the neutral state is rest, not movement — a midpoint between them?
Yes.
Then how can it be correct to think that the absence of pain is pleasure, or the absence of pleasure is pain?
It can't.

This then is an appearance only and not a reality; that is to say, the rest is pleasure at the moment and in comparison of what is painful, and painful in comparison of what is pleasant; but all these representations, when tried by the test of true pleasure, are not real but a sort of imposition?
That follows from the argument.
Now look at pleasures that have no preceding pain, and you'll stop thinking that pleasure is always just the end of pain, or pain the end of pleasure.
What pleasures, and where do I find them?
There are many examples. Take the pleasures of smell — they can be intense, they come suddenly with no preceding pain, and they leave no pain when they depart.
Very true, he said.
So let's not be fooled into thinking that pure pleasure is merely the cessation of pain, or pain the cessation of pleasure.
No.
Still, most of the intense pleasures that reach the soul through the body are of this type — they're reliefs from pain.
That's true.
And anticipatory pleasures and pains are the same kind?
Yes.
Want me to illustrate this?
Please.
Would you grant, I said, that there's an upper region, a lower region, and a middle region in reality?
I would.

And if a person were to go from the lower to the middle region, would he not imagine that he is going up? And he who is standing in the middle and sees whence he has come would imagine that he is already in the upper region, if he has never seen the true upper world?
Naturally, he said — how could he think otherwise?
But if he were taken back down, he'd think — and correctly — that he was descending?
Of course.
All because of his ignorance of where the upper, middle, and lower regions truly are?
Yes.

Then can you wonder that persons who are inexperienced in the truth, as they have wrong ideas about many other things, should also have wrong ideas about pleasure and pain and the intermediate state — so that when they are only being drawn towards the painful they feel pain and think the pain which they experience to be real, and in like manner, when drawn away from pain to the neutral or intermediate state, they firmly believe that they have reached the goal of satiety and pleasure? They, not knowing pleasure, err in contrasting pain with the absence of pain, which is like contrasting black with grey instead of white — can you wonder, I say, at this?
Not at all — I'd be more surprised at the opposite.
Think of it this way: hunger, thirst, and similar conditions are deficiencies of the body?
Yes.
And ignorance and folly are deficiencies of the soul?
True.
And food satisfies the one, wisdom the other?
Certainly.
And which satisfaction is more genuine — the one that comes from what has less real being, or from what has more?
Obviously from what has more.

And which class of things has a greater share of pure being — the class that includes food, drink, seasonings, and every kind of physical sustenance? Or the class that contains true belief, knowledge, reason, and all the different kinds of virtue? Consider it this way: which has purer being — what is concerned with the unchanging, the immortal, and the true, and shares that nature? Or what is concerned with the changing and mortal, and is itself changing and mortal?
The being of what is concerned with the unchanging is far purer, he replied.
And does the essence of what is unchanging participate in knowledge to the same degree as in being?
Yes, to the same degree.
And in truth to the same degree?
Yes.
And conversely, what has less truth has less real being?
Necessarily.
Then, in general, those kinds of things which are in the service of the body have less of truth and essence than those which are in the service of the soul?
Far less.
And the body itself has less truth and reality than the soul?
Yes.
And what is filled with more real being, and actually has more real being, is more truly and genuinely filled than what is filled with less real being?
Of course.

So if it's pleasurable to be filled with what naturally belongs to you, then what is more really filled with more real being will enjoy a more genuine and true pleasure. What participates in less real being will be less truly satisfied and will experience a less real, more illusory pleasure.
That follows inevitably.

Those then who know not wisdom and virtue, and are always busy with gluttony and sensuality, go down and up again as far as the mean; and in this region they move at random throughout life, but they never pass into the true upper world; thither they neither look, nor do they ever find their way, neither are they truly filled with true being, nor do they taste of pure and abiding pleasure. Like cattle, with their eyes always looking down and their heads stooping to the earth, that is, to the dining-table, they fatten and feed and breed, and, in their excessive love of these delights, they kick and butt at one another with horns and hoofs which are made of iron; and they kill one another by reason of their insatiable lust. For they fill themselves with that which is not substantial, and the part of themselves which they fill is also unsubstantial and incontinent.
Socrates, said Glaucon, you describe the life of the masses like an oracle.

Their pleasures are mixed with pain — mere shadows and pictures of true pleasure, given color by the contrast between them. The contrast exaggerates both light and dark, so these counterfeit pleasures plant insane desires in the minds of fools and become objects of fierce competition — like the shadow of Helen at Troy, which Stesichorus says the Greeks fought over in ignorance of the truth.
Something like that must inevitably happen.

And must not the like happen with the spirited or passionate element of the soul? Will not the passionate man who carries his passion into action be in the like case, whether he is envious and ambitious, or violent and contentious, or angry and discontented, if he be seeking to attain honour and victory and the satisfaction of his anger without reason or sense?
Yes, he said, the same applies to the spirited element.

Then can we confidently say that when the lovers of money and honor pursue their pleasures under the guidance of reason and wisdom — when they seek and win the pleasures that wisdom recommends — they'll enjoy the truest pleasures possible for them, since they're following truth? And these will be the pleasures most naturally their own, if what's best for each person is also what's most natural?
Yes, certainly — what's best is most natural.

And when the whole soul follows the philosophical principle, and there is no division, the several parts are just, and do each of them their own business, and enjoy severally the best and truest pleasures of which they are capable?
Exactly.
But when either of the other two parts takes control, it can't find its own true pleasure and forces the other parts to pursue pleasures that are alien and false?
True.
And the further a desire is from philosophy and reason, the more alien and illusory its pleasure will be?
Yes.
And what is furthest from reason is furthest from law and order?
Clearly.
And we saw that the lustful, tyrannical desires are the furthest from reason?
And the kingly, orderly desires are the nearest?
Yes.
So the tyrant lives at the greatest distance from true, natural pleasure, and the king at the least?
Certainly.
And therefore the tyrant lives the most unpleasant life, and the king the most pleasant?
Inevitably.
Would you like to know the exact measure of the distance between them?
Tell me.

There seem to be three pleasures — one real and two counterfeit. The tyrant transgresses beyond even the counterfeit ones. He has fled from the realm of law and reason and taken up residence with certain servile pleasures. The measure of his inferiority can only be expressed mathematically.
How do you mean?
I take it that the tyrant is three places away from the oligarch, with the democrat in the middle?
Yes.
And if there is truth in what has preceded, he will be wedded to an image of pleasure which is thrice removed as to truth from the pleasure of the oligarch?
He is.
And the oligarch is third from the king, counting royal and aristocratic as one?
Yes, he's third.
So the tyrant is removed from true pleasure by the space of three times three?
Clearly.
The shadow of tyrannical pleasure, expressed as a linear number, gives us a plane figure.
Certainly.
And if you raise the power and make the plane a solid, there is no difficulty in seeing how vast is the interval by which the tyrant is parted from the king.
An arithmetician could easily work that out, he said.

Or if some person begins at the other end and measures the interval by which the king is parted from the tyrant in truth of pleasure, he will find him, when the multiplication is completed, living 729 times more pleasantly, and the tyrant more painfully by this same interval.
What an astounding calculation! The distance between the just man and the unjust in pleasure and pain is enormous!

Yet a true calculation, I said, and a number which nearly concerns human life, if human beings are concerned with days and nights and months and years. (729 nearly equals the number of days and nights in the year.)
It certainly is, he said.
So if the good and just man surpasses the evil and unjust by this much in pleasure, his superiority in grace of life, beauty, and virtue is immeasurably greater still.
Immeasurably, indeed.

Well then, I said. Now that we've reached this point in the argument, let's go back to the claim that started us off. Someone said that injustice is profitable for the perfectly unjust man who is reputed to be just. Wasn't that the claim?
Yes, it was.
Now that we've determined the power and quality of both justice and injustice, let's have a word with this person.
What shall we say to him?
Let's construct an image of the soul, so he can see what his own words really mean.
What kind of image?

An ideal image of the soul, like the composite creations of ancient mythology, such as the Chimera or Scylla or Cerberus; and there are many others in which two or more different natures are said to grow into one.
There are said to have been such creatures.
Then do you now model the form of a multitudinous, many-headed monster, having a ring of heads of all manner of beasts, tame and wild, which he is able to generate and metamorphose at will.
You suppose marvellous powers in the artist; but, as language is more pliable than wax or any similar substance, let there be such a model as you propose.
Now make a second form — a lion — and a third of a man. The lion should be smaller than the beast, and the man smaller than the lion.
That's easier. Done.
Now join the three into one.
Done.
And wrap them all in the outer shape of a single human being, so that someone who can't see inside would think it was just one creature — a man.
Done, he said.

And now, to him who maintains that it is profitable for the human creature to be unjust, and unprofitable to be just, let us reply that, if he be right, it is profitable for this creature to feast the multitudinous monster and strengthen the lion and the lion-like qualities, but to starve and weaken the man, who is consequently liable to be dragged about at the mercy of either of the other two; and he is not to attempt to familiarize or harmonize them with one another — he ought rather to suffer them to fight and bite and devour one another.
Yes, he said. That's exactly what the champion of injustice would recommend.

And the champion of justice would reply: a person should speak and act so as to give the inner man the fullest possible mastery over the whole creature. He should tend the many-headed beast like a good farmer — cultivating the gentle qualities, preventing the wild ones from growing. He should make the lion his ally. United in their care, all the parts should be in harmony with each other and with the whole.
Yes, he said. That's exactly what the defender of justice would say.
So from every angle — pleasure, honor, or advantage — the champion of justice is right and speaks the truth, and the champion of injustice is wrong, ignorant, and false?
Yes, from every angle.

Come then, let's reason gently with the unjust man, who errs not intentionally. 'My dear friend,' we'll say, 'what do you think makes things noble or ignoble? Isn't the noble what subjects the beast to the man — or rather to the god within man — while the ignoble subjects the man to the beast?' He can hardly say otherwise, can he?
Not if he has any respect for my opinion.

But, if he agree so far, we may ask him to answer another question: ‘Then how would a man profit if he received gold and silver on the condition that he was to enslave the noblest part of him to the worst? Who can imagine that a man who sold his son or daughter into slavery for money, especially if he sold them into the hands of fierce and evil men, would be the gainer, however large might be the sum which he received? And will any one say that he is not a miserable caitiff who remorselessly sells his own divine being to that which is most godless and detestable? Eriphyle took the necklace as the price of her husband's life, but he is taking a bribe in order to compass a worse ruin.'
Far worse indeed, said Glaucon — I'll answer for him.
Has not the intemperate been censured of old, because in him the huge multiform monster is allowed to be too much at large?
Clearly.
And men are blamed for pride and bad temper when the lion and serpent element in them disproportionately grows and gains strength?
Yes.
And luxury and softness are blamed because they weaken that same spirited element and make a coward of it?
Very true.

And flattery and servility — aren't they condemned because a person subordinates the spirited element to the unruly mob of desires, training it from youth to be trampled underfoot for the sake of money, turning it from a lion into a monkey?
True, he said.

And why are manual trades and menial labor considered base? Only because they indicate a weakness of the higher principle — the person can't control the beasts within, so he has to serve them, studying how to flatter them.
That seems to be the reason.

And this is why we say such a person should be governed by the best — not to his injury, as Thrasymachus supposed, but because everyone is better off being ruled by divine wisdom. Ideally this wisdom dwells within him. If not, it must be imposed from outside — so that we may all, as far as possible, live under the same government, as friends and equals.
True, he said.

And this is clearly the intention of the law, which is the ally of everyone in the city. It's also seen in the authority we exercise over children — we don't give them freedom until we've established in them a principle like a state's constitution, cultivating their higher element until we've set up a guardian and ruler in their hearts that mirrors our own. Only then do we let them go their own way.
Yes, he said, that's clearly what the law intends.
Then from what point of view can we say that injustice, intemperance, or any other vice is profitable — since it makes a person worse, even if he gains money or power?
From no point of view.

And what good does it do him if his injustice goes undetected and unpunished? He only gets worse. Whereas the person who is caught and punished has the brutal part of his nature tamed and the gentle part set free. His whole soul is perfected and ennobled through the acquisition of justice, temperance, and wisdom — and the soul is more honorable than the body, just as these improvements are more valuable than physical health and beauty.
Certainly, he said.
So the person of understanding will devote his entire life to this noble purpose. First, he'll honor the studies that shape these qualities in his soul and reject whatever doesn't.
Clearly, he said.

In the next place, he will regulate his bodily habit and training, and so far will he be from yielding to brutal and irrational pleasures, that he will regard even health as quite a secondary matter; his first object will be not that he may be fair or strong or well, unless he is likely thereby to gain temperance, but he will always desire so to attemper the body as to preserve the harmony of the soul?
He certainly will, if he has true music in him.

And in the acquisition of wealth there is a principle of order and harmony which he will also observe; he will not allow himself to be dazzled by the foolish applause of the world, and heap up riches to his own infinite harm?
Certainly not, he said.

He will look at the city which is within him, and take heed that no disorder occur in it, such as might arise either from superfluity or from want; and upon this principle he will regulate his property and gain or spend according to his means.
Very true.
And for the same reason, he'll gladly accept honors that he thinks will make him a better person, but avoid any — public or private — that might disorder his inner life.
Then he won't go into politics, if that's his concern.
By the dog of Egypt, he will! In the city that is truly his own, he absolutely will — though perhaps not in the city of his birth, unless some divine chance ordains it.
I understand; you mean that he will be a ruler in the city of which we are the founders, and which exists in idea only; for I do not believe that there is such a one anywhere on earth?

In heaven, I replied, there is perhaps a pattern of it laid up, which anyone who wishes can see. And seeing it, he can set his own inner house in order. Whether it actually exists or ever will exist on earth doesn't matter. He'll live by its principles and have nothing to do with any other city.
I think so, he said.

chapters.title: Book X
paragraphs: Of all the excellent features I see in the design of our State, none pleases me more on reflection than our rule about poetry.
What rule do you mean?
The rejection of imitative poetry. Now that we've distinguished the parts of the soul, I see even more clearly that it must not be admitted.
What do you mean?

Speaking in confidence — I wouldn't want this getting back to the tragedians and the rest of the imitative tribe — but I'll say it to you: all poetic imitation is destructive to the understanding of its listeners. Knowledge of its true nature is the only remedy.
Explain what you mean.

I'll tell you, though I've always had a deep reverence and love for Homer since childhood — a love that even now makes the words stick in my throat. He's the great captain and teacher of that whole charming tragic company. But a person must not be revered more than the truth, and so I'll speak my mind.
Very good, he said.
Then listen to me — or rather, answer me.
Ask your question.
Can you tell me what imitation is? Because I honestly don't know.
Then I'm hardly likely to know, am I?
Why not? A duller eye may sometimes spot a thing sooner than a sharper one.
That's true, he said. But with you here, even if I had some faint idea, I wouldn't dare say it. You go first.
All right. Shall we start the inquiry in our usual way? Whenever a number of individual things share a common name, we assume there's a corresponding Form or Idea. Do you follow?
I do.
Take any common example. There are beds and tables in the world — lots of them.
Yes.
But there are only two Forms — one of a bed, one of a table.
True.
And the craftsman who makes either one makes a bed or a table for our use in accordance with the Form. That's how we talk about it. But no craftsman makes the Forms themselves — how could he?
He couldn't.
Now there's another artist I'd like to ask you about.
Who?
One who makes everything that every other craftsman makes.
What an extraordinary person!

Wait a little, and there will be more reason for your saying so. For this is he who is able to make not only vessels of every kind, but plants and animals, himself and all other things — the earth and heaven, and the things which are in heaven or under the earth; he makes the gods also.
He must be a wizard!

You don't believe me? Tell me — do you think there's no such maker, or that there could be one in some sense but not another? Don't you see that there's a way you could make all these things yourself?
What way?

An easy way enough; or rather, there are many ways in which the feat might be quickly and easily accomplished, none quicker than that of turning a mirror round and round — you would soon enough make the sun and the heavens, and the earth and yourself, and other animals and plants, and all the other things of which we were just now speaking, in the mirror.
Yes, he said — but they'd only be appearances, not real things.
Good, I said — you're getting to the point. The painter is exactly the same kind of creator — a maker of appearances. Right?
Of course.
But then I suppose you will say that what he creates is untrue. And yet there is a sense in which the painter also creates a bed?
Yes, he said — but not a real one.
And what of the maker of the bed? Were you not saying that he too makes, not the idea which, according to our view, is the essence of the bed, but only a particular bed?
Yes, we did.

Then if he does not make that which exists, he cannot make true existence, but only some semblance of existence; and if any one were to say that the work of the maker of the bed, or of any other workman, has real existence, he could hardly be supposed to be speaking the truth.
Philosophers would certainly say so, at least, he replied.
No wonder, then, that the carpenter's work is only a dim reflection of truth.
No wonder.
Now, using these examples, shall we investigate who this imitator really is?
If you like.
Here are three beds: first, the one that exists in nature, which is made by God — I think we can say no one else could be the maker.
No.
Second, the one the carpenter makes.
Yes.
And third, the one the painter makes.
Yes.
Beds, then, are of three kinds, and there are three artists who superintend them: God, the maker of the bed, and the painter?
Yes, three.
God, whether by choice or necessity, made one and only one bed in nature. Two or more such ideal beds have never been and never will be made by God.
Why not?
Because if he'd made even two, a third would appear behind them — the one they both derive from — and that would be the real bed, not the other two.
Very true, he said.
God knew this. Wanting to be the real maker of a real bed, not just a particular maker of a particular bed, he created one that is essentially and by nature one only.
So we believe.
Shall we call him the natural author or maker of the bed?
Yes, he replied — since through the natural process of creation, he is the author of this and all other things.
And the carpenter — is he also a maker of the bed?
Yes.
But would you call the painter a maker?
Certainly not.
Then what is he in relation to the bed?
I think we can fairly call him the imitator of what the other two make.
Good, I said. So you call the person who is three steps removed from nature an imitator?
Certainly, he said.
And the tragic poet is an imitator, and therefore — like all imitators — three steps removed from the truth and from reality?
So it appears.
Then about the imitator we are agreed. And what about the painter? I would like to know whether he may be thought to imitate that which originally exists in nature, or only the creations of artists?
The latter.
As they really are, or as they appear? That's still to be determined.
What do you mean?
When you look at a bed from different angles — straight on, at a slant, or from any other position — the bed appears different, though there's no actual difference. The same goes for everything else.
Yes, he said — the difference is only apparent.
Now here's the key question: is the art of painting designed to imitate things as they are, or as they appear? Is it an imitation of reality or of appearance?
Of appearance.

Then the imitator is a long way from the truth. He can reproduce anything because he touches only a small part of each thing — and that part is merely an image. For example, a painter can paint a cobbler, a carpenter, or any other craftsman without knowing the first thing about their trades. If he's a good painter, he could fool children or simple people into thinking they were looking at a real carpenter, shown from a distance.
Certainly.

So whenever anyone tells us he's found a man who knows all arts, all sciences, and everything else that anyone knows — and knows each one better than any specialist — we can only conclude that the informant is a naive soul who's been taken in by some wizard or actor, and mistook the appearance of knowledge for the real thing, being unable to distinguish knowledge from ignorance and imitation.
Very true.

And so, when we hear persons saying that the tragedians, and Homer, who is at their head, know all the arts and all things human, virtue as well as vice, and divine things too, for that the good poet cannot compose well unless he knows his subject, and that he who has not this knowledge can never be a poet, we ought to consider whether here also there may not be a similar illusion. Perhaps they may have come across imitators and been deceived by them; they may not have remembered when they saw their works that these were but imitations thrice removed from the truth, and could easily be made without any knowledge of the truth, because they are appearances only and not realities. Or, after all, they may be in the right, and poets do really know the things about which they seem to the many to speak so well?
That question, he said, should definitely be examined.

Do you think that if someone could create the original as well as the copy, he'd seriously devote himself to making copies? Would he make imitation the ruling principle of his life, as if he had nothing higher in him?
I'd say not.

The real expert, who genuinely understood what he was imitating, would want to work with realities, not imitations. He'd prefer to be the subject of praise rather than its author — to leave behind real achievements rather than poems about them.
Yes, he said — that would bring far greater honor and profit.

Then, I said, we must put a question to Homer; not about medicine, or any of the arts to which his poems only incidentally refer: we are not going to ask him, or any other poet, whether he has cured patients like Asclepius, or left behind him a school of medicine such as the Asclepiads were, or whether he only talks about medicine and other arts at second-hand; but we have a right to know respecting military tactics, politics, education, which are the chiefest and noblest subjects of his poems, and we may fairly ask him about them. ‘Friend Homer,' then we say to him, ‘if you are only in the second remove from truth in what you say of virtue, and not in the third — not an image-maker or imitator — and if you are able to discern what pursuits make men better or worse in private or public life, tell us what State was ever better governed by your help? The good order of Lacedaemon is due to Lycurgus, and many other cities great and small have been similarly benefited by others; but who says that you have been a good legislator to them and have done them any good? Italy and Sicily boast of Charondas, and there is Solon who is renowned among us; but what city has anything to say about you?' Is there any city which he might name?
I don't think so, said Glaucon. Not even his biggest fans claim he was a legislator.
Well, but is there any war on record which was carried on successfully by him, or aided by his counsels, when he was alive?
None.
Or is there any invention of his, applicable to the arts or to human life, such as Thales the Milesian or Anacharsis the Scythian and other ingenious men have conceived, which is attributed to him?
Nothing at all.

But, if Homer never did any public service, was he privately a guide or teacher of any? Had he in his lifetime friends who loved to associate with him, and who handed down to posterity an Homeric way of life, such as was established by Pythagoras, who was so greatly beloved for his wisdom, and whose followers are to this day quite celebrated for the order which was named after him?

Nothing of the kind is recorded of him. For surely, Socrates, Creophylus, the companion of Homer — that child of flesh, whose name always makes us laugh — might be more justly ridiculed for his stupidity, if, as is said, Homer was greatly neglected by him and others in his own day when he was alive?

Yes, I replied, that is the tradition. But can you imagine, Glaucon, that if Homer had really been able to educate and improve mankind — if he had possessed knowledge and not been a mere imitator — can you imagine, I say, that he would not have had many followers, and been honoured and loved by them? Protagoras of Abdera, and Prodicus of Ceos, and a host of others, have only to whisper to their contemporaries: ‘You will never be able to manage either your own house or your own State until you appoint us to be your ministers of education' — and this ingenious device of theirs has such an effect in making men love them that their companions all but carry them about on their shoulders. And is it conceivable that the contemporaries of Homer, or again of Hesiod, would have allowed either of them to go about as rhapsodists, if they had really been able to make mankind virtuous? Would they not have been as unwilling to part with them as with gold, and have compelled them to stay at home with them? Or, if the master would not stay, then the disciples would have followed him about everywhere, until they had got education enough?
Yes, Socrates, I think that's exactly right.

Then must we conclude that all these poets, starting with Homer, are only imitators? They copy images of virtue and everything else but never reach the truth. The poet is like the painter who can produce a convincing picture of a cobbler without knowing anything about cobbling — good enough to fool people who judge only by colors and shapes.
Quite so.

In like manner the poet with his words and phrases may be said to lay on the colours of the several arts, himself understanding their nature only enough to imitate them; and other people, who are as ignorant as he is, and judge only from his words, imagine that if he speaks of cobbling, or of military tactics, or of anything else, in metre and harmony and rhythm, he speaks very well — such is the sweet influence which melody and rhythm by nature have. And I think that you must have observed again and again what a poor appearance the tales of poets make when stripped of the colours which music puts upon them, and recited in simple prose.
Yes, he said.
Like faces that were never really beautiful but only had the bloom of youth — once that bloom fades, you can see what they truly are.
Exactly.
Here's another point: the imitator — the image-maker — knows nothing of true reality. He knows only appearances. Right?
Yes.
Let's be thorough and not stop at half an explanation.
Go on.
A painter, we'd say, can paint reins and a bit.
Yes.
And a leather-worker and metalworker can make them.
Certainly.
But does the painter know the right form of reins and bit? For that matter, do the craftsmen who make them? Only the horseman who uses them actually knows what they should be like.
Very true.
And can we generalize this?
How?
For everything, there are three arts: the art of using, the art of making, and the art of imitating.
Yes.
And the excellence or beauty or rightness of any object — whether natural or man-made — is relative to the use for which it was designed.
True.

Then the user of them must have the greatest experience of them, and he must indicate to the maker the good or bad qualities which develop themselves in use; for example, the flute-player will tell the flute-maker which of his flutes is satisfactory to the performer; he will tell him how he ought to make them, and the other will attend to his instructions?
Of course.
The one speaks with knowledge about the quality of the instrument; the other takes his word for it and does as he's told.
True.

The instrument is the same, but about the excellence or badness of it the maker will only attain to a correct belief; and this he will gain from him who knows, by talking to him and being compelled to hear what he has to say, whereas the user will have knowledge?
True.

But will the imitator have either? Will he know from use whether or no his drawing is correct or beautiful? Or will he have right opinion from being compelled to associate with another who knows and gives him instructions about what he should draw?
Neither.
So the imitator won't have true opinion any more than he has true knowledge about what he imitates.
I suppose not.
So the imitator will be brilliantly informed about his own creations — not.
Quite the reverse.
And still he will go on imitating without knowing what makes a thing good or bad, and may be expected therefore to imitate only that which appears to be good to the ignorant multitude?
Exactly.

So we're pretty well agreed: the imitator has no knowledge worth mentioning of what he imitates. Imitation is just a form of play. And the tragic poets, whether they write in iambic verse or in epic, are imitators of the highest degree.
Very true.
And now tell me, I conjure you, has not imitation been shown by us to be concerned with that which is thrice removed from the truth?
Certainly.
Now, which part of a person does imitation appeal to?
What do you mean?
Let me explain. The same object looks large when near and small when far away.
True.

And the same object appears straight when looked at out of the water, and crooked when in the water; and the concave becomes convex, owing to the illusion about colours to which the sight is liable. Thus every sort of confusion is revealed within us; and this is that weakness of the human mind on which the art of conjuring and of deceiving by light and shadow and other ingenious devices imposes, having an effect upon us like magic.
True.

And the arts of measuring and numbering and weighing come to the rescue of the human understanding — there is the beauty of them — and the apparent greater or less, or more or heavier, no longer have the mastery over us, but give way before calculation and measure and weight?
Very true.
And this must be the work of the calculating, rational part of the soul.
It must.
And when this rational part measures and determines that certain things are equal or unequal, and yet the senses report the opposite — we have a contradiction.
True.
But we said that the same part of the soul can't hold opposite opinions about the same thing at the same time.
And we were right.
Then that part of the soul which has an opinion contrary to measure is not the same with that which has an opinion in accordance with measure?
True.
And the part that trusts measurement and calculation is the better part of the soul.
Certainly.
And what opposes it is one of the soul's inferior elements.
No doubt.

This was the conclusion at which I was seeking to arrive when I said that painting or drawing, and imitation in general, when doing their own proper work, are far removed from truth, and the companions and friends and associates of a principle within us which is equally removed from reason, and that they have no true or healthy aim.
Exactly.
Imitation is an inferior thing that consorts with an inferior part of the soul and produces inferior offspring.
Very true.
And is this confined to the sight only, or does it extend to the hearing also, relating in fact to what we term poetry?
The same probably applies to poetry.
Let's not rely on a probability from analogy with painting, I said. Let's examine directly whether the part of the mind that poetry appeals to is good or bad.
By all means.

We can put the question this way: imitation imitates people performing actions — voluntary or involuntary — which they believe have turned out well or badly, and they rejoice or grieve accordingly. Is there anything beyond this?
No, nothing else.

But in all this variety of circumstances is the man at unity with himself — or rather, as in the instance of sight there was confusion and opposition in his opinions about the same things, so here also is there not strife and inconsistency in his life? Though I need hardly raise the question again, for I remember that all this has been already admitted; and the soul has been acknowledged by us to be full of these and ten thousand similar oppositions occurring at the same moment?
And we were right, he said.
Yes, we were. But we left out something that needs to be added now.
What was that?
Didn't we say that a good man who suffers misfortune — losing a son, for instance, or something else he holds dear — will bear it more calmly than others?
Yes.
But will he feel no grief at all? Or should we say that while he can't help grieving, he'll moderate his grief?
The latter is more accurate, he said.
